speaker: Claude
content:
## The single biggest finding

The research consensus that matters most for you: **science reading comprehension is mostly a knowledge and language problem, not a generic strategy problem.** Generic strategy instruction ("make a prediction, visualize, summarize") produces real but small and rapidly-plateauing gains. Students fail at science text primarily because they lack (a) the topic knowledge that makes the text coherent and (b) fluency with academic/scientific language — nominalizations, dense noun phrases, passive constructions, technical vocabulary.

Catherine Snow's 2010 *Science* article "Academic Language and the Challenge of Reading for Learning About Science" is the canonical statement of this. Shanahan & Shanahan (2008, *Harvard Educational Review*) made the parallel "disciplinary literacy" argument: reading like a scientist is different from reading like a historian, and generic strategies don't transfer.

Practical implication: the highest-leverage move is to teach reading *through* your science content, not as a separate add-on.

---

## What has the strongest evidence

**1. Integrated science–literacy instruction**
Cervetti, Barber, Dorph, Pearson & Goldschmidt (2012, *JRST*) — the Seeds of Science/Roots of Reading trial. Effects favoring the integrated program: science understanding ~d = 0.5, science vocabulary ~d = 0.7, science writing ~d = 0.5. Notably, **no significant effect on general reading comprehension.** That pattern repeats across this literature and is worth internalizing: integrating literacy into science reliably improves science learning and science-specific reading, and rarely moves general reading scores.

Vaughn et al. (2013) and the PACT studies (middle-school social studies, but the design generalizes) found content knowledge effects around d = 0.40 with smaller comprehension effects (~0.20).

**2. Text structure instruction**
Hebert, Bohaty, Nelson & Brandon (2016, *Journal of Educational Psychology*) meta-analyzed text structure instruction for expository text: overall g ≈ 0.57 on comprehension. This is one of the better-supported specific techniques, and it's underused. Explicitly teaching students to recognize cause–effect, compare–contrast, problem–solution, and sequence structures — and the signal words for each — pays off in exactly the kind of text your textbook is.

**3. Writing about the text**
Graham & Hebert (2011, *Harvard Educational Review*), "Writing to Read" meta-analysis: having students write about what they read improved comprehension, average ES ≈ 0.40. Extended writing beat note-taking, which beat answering questions, which beat summarizing — but all were positive. Cheap and easy to implement.

**4. Structured text-based discussion**
Murphy, Wilkinson, Soter, Hennessey & Alexander (2009, *Journal of Educational Psychology*) meta-analyzed nine classroom discussion approaches. Most dramatically increased student talk; effects on comprehension were more variable, with Questioning the Author and Instructional Conversations showing the clearest comprehension gains. The lesson: discussion helps when it's *structured around the text and its meaning*, not when it's open-ended sharing.

**5. Vocabulary — with an important caveat**
Elleman, Lindo, Morphy & Compton (2009) meta-analysis: vocabulary instruction produced d ≈ 0.50 on researcher-made comprehension measures but only d ≈ 0.10 on standardized ones. Stahl & Fairbanks (1986) found a similar split. So vocabulary instruction genuinely helps students understand *the passages containing those words* — which is exactly what you want in a science class — but don't expect general reading scores to move.

**6. Self-explanation**
McNamara's work on Self-Explanation Reading Training and iSTART: training students to explain each sentence to themselves as they read produces solid gains, especially for low-knowledge readers. Related: elaborative interrogation ("why would that be true?"), which has good support in the cognitive science literature (Dunlosky et al., 2013, *PSPI*, rated it "moderate utility").

**7. Concept-Oriented Reading Instruction (CORI)**
Guthrie, McRae & Klauda (2007, *Educational Psychologist*) report large effects — comprehension around d = 0.9 — for CORI, which bundles hands-on science, strategy instruction, and motivational supports. Treat that number with some skepticism: it's largely from developer-conducted studies with researcher-designed measures. But the *design principle* — anchor reading in inquiry students actually care about — is sound.

---

## Effect-size caveat, since you asked for numbers

Two things will save you from being misled:
- **Researcher-designed measures inflate effects roughly 2–4× over standardized tests.** Any comprehension ES above ~0.6 is almost certainly on a custom measure.
- **Hattie's "0.40 hinge point" is not a meaningful benchmark.** For adolescent literacy interventions on standardized outcomes, anything above ~0.20 is a genuinely useful result.

---

## What I'd actually do in your classroom

**Build knowledge before the hard text, not after.** A short video, demo, or discussion that front-loads the schema turns an incomprehensible passage into a merely difficult one. This is the highest-yield 10 minutes you have.

**Teach the sentence, not just the word.** Science text is hard largely because of *grammatical metaphor* — "the deposition of sediment reduced flow velocity" instead of "sediment settled, so the water slowed down." Fang & Schleppegrell's work is the reference here. Pick 2–3 dense sentences per unit and have students unpack them into everyday language, then repack them into scientific language. This is a 5-minute routine with outsized returns.

**Run a text-structure routine.** Before reading, tell students the structure ("this section is cause–effect") and give them a matching graphic organizer. Nesbit & Adesope's (2006) meta-analysis of concept mapping found d ≈ 0.5 on knowledge outcomes. Fade the scaffold over the year.

**Adopt one discussion protocol and use it constantly.** Questioning the Author is my recommendation for science: stop at planned points and ask "What is the author trying to say here? Did the author say it clearly? How would you say it?" It works because it makes the text an object of scrutiny rather than an authority.

**Write short, write often.** A 3–5 sentence explanation at the end of every reading, in students' own words, with a required use of two target terms. Per Graham & Hebert, this is where the 0.40 lives — and it doubles as formative assessment.

**Teach ~6–8 words per unit, deeply.** Beck, McKeown & Kucan's robust vocabulary instruction: multiple exposures, multiple contexts, student-generated examples, and requiring the words in speech and writing. Not word lists, not "look it up."

**Don't buy a generic strategy program.** Reciprocal teaching (Palincsar & Brown, 1984) is real — Rosenshine & Meister's (1994) meta-analysis found d = 0.88 on experimenter measures but only 0.32 on standardized ones — and 15–20 sessions gets you most of the benefit. A year-long generic strategy curriculum is a poor use of your science minutes.

---

## Where the evidence is genuinely weak

Whether any of this improves students' *general* reading ability is unresolved and the honest answer is probably "not much, not quickly." The knowledge-building theory (Hirsch, Willingham, and empirically Hwang, Cabell & Joyner's meta-analysis of content-rich literacy interventions) predicts general gains only over multiple years of coherent, cumulative content — which no single teacher controls. Judge yourself on whether students understand *your* texts better. That's the outcome the research actually supports you moving.

If it'd help, I can turn this into a one-page classroom reference or draft the actual routines (a Questioning the Author stopping-point template, a sentence-unpacking protocol) against a specific chapter of your textbook.

Writing an extended response to material involves either a personal reaction to the text or analysis and interpretation of it. The former includes writing a personal response to narrative material read or writing about a personal experience related to it. Analysis and interpretation activities focus on writing an analysis of the characters in a novel, writing a paper showing how to apply material that was read, composing a letter to another student explaining how to play a game described in a text, and analyzing a text in writing to develop a particular point of view.

Most research on reading comprehension outcomes (81% of the studies included in the meta-analysis) has been conducted with students in grades 6 and above.

# Hebert et al. (2016) Text Structure Instruction Meta-Analysis: Key Findings

## Overall Effect Size
The meta-analysis found an average weighted effect size of **Hedges g = 0.57, 95% CI [0.39, 0.76]** across 40 studies using Robust Variance Estimation (RVE), representing a medium effect on proximal measures of expository reading comprehension.

## Study Coverage
- **Total studies analyzed:** 45 studies with 323 extracted effect sizes
- **Grade range:** Grades 2-12
- **Elementary (grades 2-5):** 24 studies
- **Middle school (grades 6-8):** 12 studies  
- **High school (grades 9-12):** 4 studies

## Grade-Level Moderator Analysis
The moderator analysis revealed that "the non-significant coefficient indicates that TSI is equally effective across both elementary and secondary grade levels," demonstrating robust effects regardless of whether students were in elementary or secondary contexts.

## Outcome Measure Type Results
The analysis compared effects across different outcome measures:
- **Researcher-created measures:** g = 0.57 (primary finding)
- **Standardized/norm-referenced measures:** g = 0.13, 95% CI [0.03, 0.25] (far-transfer)

## Comparison Condition Effects
Effect sizes varied significantly by comparison type:
- **Business-as-usual conditions:** Larger effect sizes
- **Competing comprehension treatments:** Significantly reduced effect sizes (negative coefficient in meta-regression, B = -0.47)

## Study Overview

The researchers designed an experiment with nearly 1,000 high school math students in Turkey to determine whether large language models can harm or help their education.

## Research Design

One group of students was given GPT Base, a chat interface similar to ChatGPT-4, to help them during practice sessions. A second group was given GPT Tutor, an interface similar to ChatGPT-4 but with safeguards that includes teacher input and is designed to guide students with hints rather than directly giving answers. The third group — the control group — had no technology assistance and relied only on traditional resources such as the textbook and notes.

## Key Findings

The GPT Tutor group performed an astonishing 127% better in the AI-assisted practice session, yet scored about the same on the exam as the control group. 

When access is subsequently taken away, students actually perform worse than those who never had access (17% reduction in grades for GPT Base)—i.e., unfettered access to GPT-4 can harm educational outcomes.

Without guardrails, students attempt to use GPT-4 as a "crutch" during practice problem sessions, and subsequently perform worse on their own.

## Implications

These negative learning effects are largely mitigated by the safeguards in GPT Tutor. Decision-makers must be cautious about design choices underlying generative AI deployments to preserve skill learning and long-term productivity.

# Shanahan & Shanahan (2012): Methodology and Evidence Limitations

## Earlier Study Methodology (2008)

The authors describe conducting think-aloud protocols with expert practitioners across multiple disciplines. Their investigation involved having specialists in various fields articulate their reading processes while engaging with discipline-specific texts. The research examined how professionals in different subject areas approached and comprehended materials within their expertise.

## Evidence Base Limitations

Regarding the empirical foundation for disciplinary literacy instruction, Shanahan & Shanahan acknowledge a significant gap. They note that while theoretical arguments support disciplinary literacy approaches, **"the evidence base for disciplinary literacy instruction remains limited."** The authors emphasize that most existing research describes disciplinary reading practices rather than demonstrating causal effects on student achievement.

Critically, they do not report having experimental evidence showing that teaching disciplinary literacy improves measurable student outcomes. Instead, their work establishes the *need* for such instruction by documenting how experts read within their fields, leaving open the question of whether explicitly teaching these practices to students produces learning gains.

This distinction matters: Shanahan & Shanahan provide descriptive evidence of professional reading practices but candidly identify the absence of rigorous intervention studies establishing effectiveness.

The authors contend that "disciplinary literacy"--advanced literacy instruction embedded within content-area classes such as math, science, and social studies--should receive focus in middle and secondary schools.

Their research findings demonstrate that experts in math, chemistry, and history approach disciplinary texts quite differently from one another. Consequently, the study recommends "different comprehension strategies for work with adolescents" depending on the discipline.

# Evaluation Summary: Seeds of Science/Roots of Reading - Planets and Moons Unit

## Study Design
**Cluster Randomized Trial** with 86 teachers (42 control, 44 treatment) across ~60 schools in 10 states during 2008-2009 school year. Teachers randomly assigned; students nested within teachers and schools.

## Sample
Approximately 1,600+ fifth-grade students; descriptive data shows treatment and control groups "fairly similar in experience and training" at baseline.

## Key Measures

**Science Assessments:**
- Science content (30 items, α=0.78-0.82)
- Nature of science (12 items, α=0.66-0.69)
- Science inquiry (14 items, α=0.69-0.73)

**Literacy Assessments:**
- Vocabulary (25 items, α=0.75-0.81)
- Reading (10 items, α=0.66-0.67)
- Writing (5 domains scored on 3-4 point scales, α=0.74-0.77)

## Primary Results

**Science Content:** Treatment students scored "about 1.3 points higher" (p<.10); gain score analysis showed "1 point more" gain (p<.05). Effect size ≈ 0.21.

**Nature of Science:** "0.40 points higher" posttest difference (p<.05). Effect size ≈ 0.16.

**Science Inquiry:** No significant effect (p>.10).

**Vocabulary:** Treatment advantage of "1.6 points" (p<.01). Effect size ≈ 0.38.

**Reading:** "No statistically significant differences" between conditions.

**Writing:** No global treatment effect; only science concepts domain showed "0.2 standard deviations higher" for treatment (p<.10).

**Student Attitudes:** No significant treatment effect despite overall "1.2 point gain" across groups (p<.05).

**Teacher Self-Efficacy:** "Relatively minor" changes; no significant differences between conditions.

## Implementation Notes
Treatment teachers spent "approximately 50% more instructional time" weekly. Two-thirds reported spending "more time than usual" versus one-fifth of controls. "About 60% indicated they would likely use the unit again."

## Conclusion
Authors characterize findings as "equivocal," with strongest evidence for vocabulary gains and nature of science improvements, but inconsistent science content effects and no reading/writing benefits.

# Study Overview: Integrated Science-Literacy Instruction

## Method

**Design & Participants:**
This randomized controlled trial involved 94 fourth-grade teachers (47 treatment, 47 comparison) across 16 school districts in one Southern state during 2007-2008. Treatment teachers were slightly less experienced (9.2 vs. 11.6 years) and less likely to hold advanced degrees (34% vs. 51%), though differences weren't statistically significant.

**Interventions:**
- **Treatment:** 40-session integrated unit on light combining firsthand investigations (~40%), reading (~20%), writing (~20%), and discussion/reflection (~20%)
- **Comparison:** Teachers taught state light standards using their regular materials and instruction

## Key Measures & Reliability

| Measure | Items | Pretest α | Posttest α |
|---------|-------|-----------|-----------|
| Science Understanding | 23 items | — | 0.81 |
| Science Vocabulary | 15 items | 0.43 | 0.69 |
| Reading Comprehension | 16 items | 0.77 | 0.76 |
| Science Writing | 7 dimensions | — | 0.79 |

## Main Results

**Science Understanding:**
"Treatment classrooms scored about 1.5 points higher" (p<0.01), Effect size d = 0.65. This benefit was robust across achievement levels.

**Science Vocabulary:**
Treatment students gained 0.91 points more than comparison (p<0.01), Effect size d = 0.22-0.23.

**Reading Comprehension:**
No significant difference between groups (p>0.05). Treatment gain: 0.12 points (ns); Comparison: 0.36 points (ns).

**Science Writing:**
Overall multivariate effect size = 0.40 (p<0.05). Significant effects on 5 of 7 dimensions:
- Vocabulary count: ES = 0.80 (p<0.01)
- Science concepts: ES = 0.63 (p<0.01)
- Clarity: ES = 0.43 (p<0.01)
- Evidence: ES = 0.33 (p<0.05)
- Introduction: ES = 0.38 (p<0.01)

No treatment effects for vocabulary definition or conclusion dimensions.

## Sample Characteristics

Student demographics were comparable between groups. Treatment schools averaged 57.6% free/reduced lunch students; comparison schools 52.9%. Racial/ethnic composition: ~48-49% White, 35-39% African-American, 5-7% Hispanic across both groups.

## Implementation Fidelity

Treatment teachers reported 219.8 minutes/week science instruction versus comparison teachers' 182.3 minutes/week. Treatment teachers devoted 77 minutes/week to reading/writing in science contexts versus comparison teachers' 61 minutes/week.

## Limitations Acknowledged

Authors note the "incomplete picture" of comparison group instruction despite post-surveys, restricted assessment measures (vocabulary, writing, comprehension only—not discussion or fluency), and lack of professional development for treatment teachers. The reading comprehension measure may have been insufficiently sensitive to science-specific text comprehension.

## Study Overview

The study examined the effects of providing reading strategy instruction to improve self-explanation while reading, called Self-Explanation Reading Training (SERT), examining both comprehension scores and self-explanation quality.

## Key Findings

Half of the participants (n = 42) received SERT, which included reading strategy instruction and self-explanation practice with 4 science texts, while the remaining participants read aloud the 4 science texts as a control.

During the training phase, self-explanation, as compared to reading aloud, only improved comprehension for the most difficult of the 4 texts.

## Post-Training Results

SERT improved comprehension and self-explanation quality only for participants with low domain knowledge. However, the effects of SERT on low-knowledge participants' comprehension emerged only for text-based questions and not for bridging-inference questions.

## O'Reilly, Best, McNamara iSTART Study

This study examines the benefits of reading strategy training on adolescent readers' comprehension of science text, with training provided via an automated reading strategy trainer called the Interactive Strategy Trainer for Active Reading and Thinking (iSTART), which utilizes animated agents to provide reading strategy instruction.

### Key Findings

Half of the participants were provided with iSTART while the others (control) were given a brief demonstration of how to self-explain text. All of the students then self-explained a text about heart disease and answered text-based and bridging-inference questions.

Both iSTART training and prior knowledge of reading strategies significantly contributed to the quality of self-explanations and comprehension.

### Interaction Effect with Prior Knowledge

A key finding relates to the interaction between training and students' prior reading strategy knowledge: For high-strategy knowledge students, iSTART improved comprehension for bridging-inference questions. Students benefitted from training regardless of their prior knowledge of strategies, but these benefits translated into different comprehension gains.

More specifically, treatment improved performance on text-based test questions for students with lower knowledge of reading strategies, and on inference questions for those with higher knowledge of reading strategies.

## McKeown, Beck, Omanson, and Pople Studies

Studies examining robust vocabulary instruction have shown it to be effective, not only for learning the meanings of words but also for affecting reading comprehension (Beck et al., 1982; McKeown, Beck, Omanson, & Perfetti, 1983; McKeown, Beck, Omanson, & Pople, 1985).

More specifically, in the 1983 replication study, fourth graders were taught 104 words over a five-month period, and following instruction, these children and a group of uninstructed children matched on pre-instruction vocabulary and comprehension ability performed tasks to measure accuracy of word knowledge, speed of lexical access, and comprehension of stories containing taught words. In the initial and replication studies, experimental children significantly outperformed control children on word knowledge, as measured on multiple-choice tests, and accessibility of word meanings.

The 1985 study by McKeown, Beck, Omanson, and Pople focused on components of effective vocabulary programs. Fourth-grade children received one of three types of instruction: traditional instruction requiring only associations between words and definitions, rich instruction presenting elaborated word meanings and diverse contexts, or extended/rich instruction which added activities to extend use of learned words beyond the classroom, with frequency manipulated by providing either 12 or 4 encounters with each word.

## Wright and Cervetti Review

Wright and Cervetti conducted a systematic review titled "A Systematic Review of the Research on Vocabulary Instruction That Impacts Text Comprehension" published in Reading Research Quarterly in 2017.

However, the evidence base they found had important limitations. Their review found that there is very limited evidence that direct teaching of word meanings can improve generalized comprehension, and there is currently no empirical evidence that instruction in one or two strategies for identifying word meanings will impact generalized comprehension.

# Research Study Transcription: Participants, Assignment, Duration, Measures, and Limitations

## PARTICIPANTS/SAMPLE

"A total of 100 applications were received. Three applicants were denied participation; one of these applicants did not meet the eligibility requirement of being able to teach science for a minimum of three hours per week, and the other two submitted incomplete applications. Three teachers dropped out of the study after being accepted but before beginning to teach."

"Thus the study population consisted of ninety-four teachers (60 in Fall 2007, 34 in Spring 2008) from 16 school districts."

"The districts were located in urban, suburban, and rural areas in the same southern state."

"In order to participate in the study, a teacher had to be teaching fourth grade and have available a minimum of three hours per week for a minimum of eight weeks for unit implementation."

"The study took place in one Southern state, selected as the study site because of the close correlation between that state's fourth grade science standards addressing the topic of light and the content of the treatment unit."

Student demographic characteristics: "The mean percentage of students receiving free or reduced price lunch in the treatment schools was 57.6; in comparison schools, it was 52.9."

## RANDOM ASSIGNMENT AND COMPARISON CONDITION

"After being accepted into the study, each teacher was randomly assigned to either a treatment or comparison group using a random number generating algorithm that is part of the Microsoft Excel software."

"Results indicate that treatment teachers were less experienced both in total years of experience (9.2 vs. 11.6 years among comparison group teachers) and years teaching at grade four (4.4 vs. 5.6 years). Comparison teachers were also more educated, with 51% versus 34% having an advanced degree. Neither the differences in experience or in advanced degrees was statistically significant."

Comparison condition: "Teachers in the comparison group were asked to present the content of their state science standards related to the topic of light, using curriculum materials they regularly use for the same amount of time each week and for the same duration."

"The treatment light unit included content related to two of the three major subtopics of the state's light standards: characteristics of light and light interactions. A third subtopic (light and color) appears in the state standards, but is not addressed in the treatment light unit. Conversely, a third subtopic that is addressed in the treatment light unit (light as energy) does not appear in the state standards."

## DURATION AND NUMBER OF SESSIONS

"The treatment unit was forty sessions in length, comprised of four investigations—each with 10 sessions. Sessions were designed to be taught in 45–60 minutes."

"In each 10-session investigation the equivalent of approximately four sessions are devoted to firsthand (hands-on) activities, two sessions to reading, two sessions to writing, and two sessions to discourse, review of important concepts, or assessment activities."

## MEASURES/INSTRUMENTS: DEVELOPERS AND PUBLISHED TESTS

"The student learning outcomes were measured through a pre–post assessment developed through a process coordinated by the Center for Research, Evaluation, and Assessment at the Lawrence Hall of Science in partnership with the curriculum research and development team."

"Wherever possible items were drawn from existing validated assessments. In other instances, items were developed and reviewed by a team of assessment developers, curriculum developers, and classroom teachers."

"The first set of items (Version 1) were developed in classrooms alongside the treatment curriculum as it was being developed and field tested in a study that took place approximately one year prior to the randomized experiment reported herein."

"The validation study version of the assessment (Version 2) included 76-items designed to assess students' mastery of science vocabulary, reading comprehension, science writing, and science understanding."

Science Understanding: "The final makeup of the science understanding measure consisted of forty-two multiple choice items; 15 had two answer choices, while the remaining 27 items had four response options."

Science Writing: "The writing assessment asked students to respond to an open-ended prompt, 'How does light interact with materials? Give three examples.'"

"Rubrics were developed by project staff for six dimensions: use of evidence, introduction, clarity, conclusion, vocabulary definition, and science content."

"The science writing assessments were scored by project staff and trained undergraduate students at University of California, Berkeley."

Science Vocabulary: "Items were developed for the science vocabulary measure using two item formats: a definition matching format designed to test whether students can identify the meaning of the words from a list of possible definitions, and cloze item formats that were designed to test students' ability to apply knowledge of the words in context."

Reading Comprehension: "The reading comprehension measure is a researcher-designed set of expository passages and multiple-choice questions."

"This measure was tested as part of the initial validation study described above. The reliability for the instrument was 0.67... We determined that many of the items were easy (with p-values above 0.85) and that there were too few items overall."

"We then conducted a second validation study of this revised reading comprehension measure. For the purpose of the second study, we administered the revised reading comprehension instrument to 202 students from diverse backgrounds."

No published standardized tests were used as primary outcome measures; assessments were developed specifically for this study.

## ENGLISH LEARNERS/ELL AND SUBGROUP ANALYSES

No sentences explicitly mentioning English learners, ELL, or limited English proficiency were located in the provided text.

The analysis included testing for differential treatment effects by pretest performance: "Model two tests whether there is a joint effect between the pretests and the treatment, that is, whether the relationship between the pre-and the post-test is different in treatment and comparison classrooms."

"The results for model two imply that there is no joint effect (essentially the pre–post slopes are parallel in treatment and comparison classrooms and hence there is no differential change in the performance gap between high and low achievers due to the treatment). Thus, the treatment effect on science understanding is robust for students at all points along the distribution of pretest scores."

Additional student characteristics could be tested: "Additional student characteristics can be added to (1b) and tested by expanding (2b) (e.g., including ELL status in model 1b and adding a γ11k TRTjk into 2b)."

However, no actual subgroup analyses by ELL status or other demographics were reported in results.

## LIMITATIONS DISCUSSION (ENTIRE SECTION)

"In addition to the issues highlighted above, we recognize a number of limitations to the analytic efforts presented within this article. The most significant is related to the amount of information we could gather about the substance of our 'business-as-usual' comparison given the scope and budget of this study. Although we gathered self-report post-surveys from teachers regarding the substance and duration of the teaching and learning that took place in these comparison classrooms, we still have an incomplete picture. Moreover, self-reports can be unreliable (Cook & Campbell, 1979). Future research efforts are being designed to gather additional implementation data in order to gain a more complete picture. Additionally, while we took a broad perspective on the aspects of literacy that can support and be supported by science in the design of the intervention, we assessed only vocabulary knowledge, reading comprehension, and science writing. While the intervention also included attention to participation in science discussions, reading fluency, and the use of text features and structures, we were limited in the amount of time we had available for student assessment. While the limited measures risk a simplistic interpretation of the role of language and literacy in science, they do mirror those aspects of literacy instruction that are most central to educational standards in fourth grade. Even with these limitations, this study addresses an important issue in science education and literacy education and contributes additional important evidence to the studies on science–literacy integration, by employing a broader range of measures and utilizing a comparison group that features a real and familiar alternative—teachers using content-comparable science units."

I found the research study you're looking for. Here are the key findings:

## Study Overview

The researchers designed an experiment with nearly 1,000 high school math students in Turkey to determine whether large language models can harm or help their education.

## Error Rates

GPT Base gives a correct answer only 51% of the time on average; it makes logical errors 42% of the time and arithmetic errors 8% of the time.

## Study Design

One group of students was given GPT Base, a chat interface similar to ChatGPT-4, to help them during practice sessions. A second group was given GPT Tutor, an interface similar to ChatGPT-4 but with safeguards.

For each of the 57 total practice problems, they ask GPT Base for the answer ten times (resetting the system between queries), and then manually categorize any errors in the response as arithmetic (steps followed were correct, but the resulting computation was incorrect) or logical (steps followed were partially or fully incorrect).

## Key Findings

Although AI-based tutoring improves performance during practice sessions, students relying on the technology may underperform when access to AI is subsequently removed, indicating reduced skill acquisition. When access is subsequently taken away, students actually perform worse than those who never had access (17% reduction in grades for GPT Base).

Carefully designed safeguards, especially asking the AI tutor to provide teacher-designed hints instead of giving away answers, can mitigate these negative effects.

## Overview
The guide addresses the challenge of providing effective literacy instruction for English learners in the elementary grades. This Practice Guide is the first in a series of the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) guides developed by a panel of experts and intended to bring the best available evidence and expertise to bear on systemic challenges.

## Key Recommendations
The guide emphasizes five key strategies: screening for reading problems and monitoring progress, providing intensive small-group reading interventions, offering extensive vocabulary instruction, developing academic English, and scheduling peer-assisted learning opportunities.

Specifically, the five recommendations are:
1. Screen for reading problems and monitor progress
2. Provide intensive small-group reading interventions
3. Provide extensive and varied vocabulary instruction
4. Develop academic English
5. Schedule regular peer-assisted learning opportunities

## Evidence Quality
Each recommendation is supported by varying levels of evidence, ranging from strong to low, and includes actionable steps for educators.

## Peer-Assisted Learning Recommendation
Teachers of English learners should devote approximately 90 minutes a week to instructional activities in which pairs of students at different ability levels or different English language proficiencies work together on academic tasks in a structured fashion.

## Study Overview

The study titled "Questioning the Author: A yearlong classroom implementation to engage students with text" was published in 1996 in the Elementary School Journal, Volume 96(4), pages 385-414. The article describes the development and implementation of Questioning the Author, an instructional intervention that focuses on having students grapple with and reflect on what an author is trying to say in order to build a representation from it.

## Study Implementation

The implementation involved a social studies teacher, a reading/language arts teacher, and their 23 inner-city fourth-grade students in a small parochial school.

## Key Findings

Analyses of transcripts of videotaped lessons and classroom observations revealed that teacher talk decreased in quantity and increased in quality with more emphasis on questions focused on constructing and extending meaning and more skill in refining and using students' comments in discussion. Changes in the content of student talk were also documented, which included an increase in the number and complexity of student-initiated questions and evidence of the development of student collaboration.

This seminal study became influential in reading comprehension instruction, as it introduced systematic approaches to helping students engage more deeply with text through guided questioning.

## Study Overview
This meta-analysis synthesized results from 44 (quasi-)experimental studies on informational and narrative text structure interventions involving students in grades 4–6 in regular school settings.

## Effect Size Results
Text structure instruction had positive immediate effects on students' reading comprehension but effect sizes varied largely across outcome measures: questions (Hedges' g = 0.25), summarization (g = 0.57), recall (g = 0.37), and knowledge about text structure (g = 0.38).

Students who received text structure instruction no longer outperformed control groups at delayed posttests. Due to a limited number of studies with delayed posttests, the researchers could not examine this transfer effect.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about Hiebert's 2012 work critiquing the Common Core's staircase of text complexity and its use of Lexile measurements.

The Common Core presents a text-complexity staircase that provides "grade-by-grade specifications (text-level bands) for increasing text complexity in successive years of schooling" in Appendix A. The steps of this staircase are depicted in Lexiles, as recommended by Common Core State Standards writers in Appendix A.

Hiebert's key critique focuses on the limitations of using Lexile scores alone to measure complexity. Hiebert notes that readability formulas can be a starting point, but by themselves do not adequately measure a text's complexity which can be affected by the knowledge demands of the content and the text's structure. 

The Common Core's 2nd/3rd-grade step ends at 820 Lexiles — about one grade level higher than previous recommendations, and historically, while many students have achieved a reading level at or above 820L by the end of 3rd grade, struggling readers have attained, on average, only about 400L by the end of 3rd grade.

Hiebert also highlights specific problems with how readability formulas work, noting that "the short sentences and high-frequency vocabulary used in the dialogue of narratives can artificially skew the readability formula downward," such as with Roll of Thunder, which has significant themes about racial intolerance but a lower text difficulty rating than a simple informational book for grades 2-3.

# Harvard AI Tutoring Study: Key Findings

## Study Design
**Sample & Method:** 194 students at Harvard University participated in a randomized crossover design where each student experienced both AI tutoring and in-class active learning on separate topics in consecutive weeks.

**Topics Tested:** Surface tension (Week 1) and fluid flow (Week 2)

## Learning Outcomes

**Post-Test Performance:**
- AI group median score: 4.5 (N=142)
- In-class active learning median: 3.5 (N=174)
- Pre-test baseline: 2.75 (N=316)
- AI learners showed "over double" the learning gains compared to classroom peers
- Statistical significance: z = -5.6, p < 10⁻⁸

**Effect Size:** Linear regression estimated 0.63 standard deviations; quantile regression (accounting for ceiling effects) yielded 0.73-1.3 standard deviations.

## Time Efficiency
- Median AI tutoring time: 49 minutes (vs. 60 minutes in-class)
- 70% of AI students completed lessons in under 60 minutes
- Notably, no correlation existed between time spent and performance gains

## Student Experience

Participants rated agreement on 5-point Likert scale:

| Dimension | AI Tutor | In-Class | p-value |
|-----------|----------|----------|---------|
| Engagement | 4.1 | 3.6 | <0.0001 |
| Motivation | 3.4 | 3.1 | <0.001 |
| Enjoyment | (comparable) | (comparable) | ns |
| Growth Mindset | (comparable) | (comparable) | ns |

## Key Limitations
The researchers acknowledge the findings may be context-specific: lessons targeted foundational understanding (Bloom's levels: understanding, applying, analyzing), not higher-order synthesis or critical thinking. Results may not generalize across all subjects or learning stages.

For instructor-provided graphic organizers, effect sizes were g + = 0.70 for memory.

The meta-analysis examined graphic organizers as spatial representations of key textual information—such as matrices, flowcharts, or hierarchies—evaluated through two primary approaches: as a generative learning activity, where students construct their own organizers while reading, or as an instructional design feature, where organizers are provided by the instructor.

## Report Overview

In a 2006 report titled Reading Between the Lines: What the ACT Reveals About College Readiness in Reading, ACT identifies the inability to comprehend complex texts as the decisive gap between college-ready and college-unready students.

## Key Findings on Text Complexity

The ability to comprehend complex text is the factor that differentiates college-ready readers. More specifically, performance on complex texts is the clearest differentiator in reading between students who are likely to be ready for college and those who are not.

Interestingly, question type (literal vs. inferential thinking, main idea vs. supporting details, etc.) did not differentiate college-ready readers. This suggests that the type of thinking required was less important than the complexity of the text itself.

## College Readiness Data

Only 51% of students who took the ACT in 2006 demonstrated college readiness in reading, with great disparities between ethnic and income groups.

The report provides evidence that students who can master the skills necessary to read and understand complex texts are more likely to be college ready than those who cannot.

# Full Abstract

Two experiments, theoretically motivated by the construction-integration model of text comprehension (W. Kintsch, 1988), investigated the role of text coherence in the comprehension of science texts. In Experiment 1, junior high school students' comprehension of one of three versions of a biology text was examined via free recall, written questions, and a key-word sorting task. This study demonstrates advantages for globally coherent text and for more explanatory text. In Experiment 2, interactions among local and global text coherence, readers' background knowledge, and levels of understanding were examined. Using the same methods as in Experiment 1, we examined students' comprehension of one of four versions of a text, orthogonally varying local and global coherence. We found that readers who know little about the domain of the text benefit from a coherent text, whereas high-knowledge readers benefit from a minimally coherent text. We argue that the poorly written text forces the knowledgeable readers to engage in compensatory processing to infer unstated relations in the text. These findings, however, depended on the level of understanding, text base or situational, being measured by the three comprehension tasks. Whereas the free-recall measure and text-based questions primarily tapped readers' superficial understanding of the text, the inference questions, problem-solving questions, and sorting task relied on a situational understanding of the text. This study provides evidence that the rewards to be gained from active processing are primarily at the level of the situation model rather than at the superficial level of text-base understanding.

McNamara, D. S., Kintsch, E., Songer, N. B., & Kintsch, W. (1996). Are good texts always better? Interactions of text coherence, background knowledge, and levels of understanding in learning from text. *Cognition and Instruction*, 14(1), 1–43. https://doi.org/10.1207/s1532690xci1401_1

I found comprehensive information about the McNamara Kintsch reverse cohesion effect. Here are the key findings:

## The Reverse Cohesion Effect

The reverse cohesion effect is the counterintuitive finding that high-knowledge readers learn better with less cohesive texts, as discovered by McNamara and Kintsch in their research.

## The Mechanism

Low-knowledge readers benefit from local cohesion devices that help the readers bridge gaps in their background knowledge and reading skills. In contrast, high-knowledge readers gained from low-cohesive texts because being induced in the generation of inferences resulted in a better text comprehension.

## A More Nuanced Finding

However, a later study by O'Reilly and McNamara refined this finding. College students read either a high- or a low-cohesion text and answered text-based and bridging inference questions. The results indicated that the benefit of low-cohesion text was restricted to less skilled, high-knowledge readers, whereas skilled comprehenders with high knowledge benefited from a high-cohesion text.

## Global vs. Local Cohesion

Research also distinguished between types of cohesion: high-knowledge readers seem to be influenced in their judgments of essay coherence and quality not by local cohesion, but by global cohesion that connects ideas across larger segments of the text.

The research demonstrates that the effect of text cohesion on comprehension is more complex than initially thought, depending on both the reader's knowledge level and their comprehension skills.

# Key Findings from Elleman et al. 2009

## (1) Overall Effect Sizes for Comprehension Measures

**Custom/Experimenter-Designed Measures:**
- Mean effect size: d = 0.50 (p < .01)
- Range: -0.06 to 1.46
- "significantly different than 0" indicating vocabulary interventions outperformed control conditions

**Standardized Measures:**
- Mean effect size: d = 0.10 (p = .08, not significant)
- Range: -0.26 to 0.43
- The authors note this was "not significantly different from 0"

The custom measures proved substantially more sensitive to intervention effects than standardized tests.

## (2) Study Distribution and Grade Levels

The analysis included **37 studies yielding 44 comprehension effect sizes** across 3,063 participants. Regarding grade representation:

- Predominant focus: "Grades 3 to 5" (50% of studies)
- Pre-K–2: Limited representation
- Secondary/adolescent students (9–12): Minimal inclusion with only 7.1% of custom measure studies

The review was heavily weighted toward elementary grades, with sparse coverage of middle and high school populations.

## (3) Moderator Findings Including Grade Level

**For comprehension outcomes using custom measures:**

Grade level showed a positive but non-significant correlation (β = .37 initially, then β = .18 in simultaneous analysis). The authors note the "limited range of grades included in the analysis" constrained detecting significance.

**Key moderator finding:** Reading status proved the only significant predictor. Students with reading difficulties gained substantially more (d = 1.23) compared to general populations (d = 0.39)—"more than three times as much."

Vocabulary gains, however, remained comparable across ability levels.

## (4) Stahl & Fairbanks 1986 Effect Sizes Reported

The authors cite Stahl & Fairbanks findings showing:
- Custom comprehension measures: d = 0.97
- Standardized/global measures: d = 0.30

These substantially exceeded Elleman's estimates, attributed to methodological differences in effect size calculation procedures.

McNamara, D. S., & Kintsch, W. (1996). Learning from Texts Effects of Prior Knowledge and Text Coherence. Discourse Processes, 22, 247-288.

**Abstract Summary:**
Two experiments, theoretically motivated by the construction-integration model of comprehension (W. Kintsch, 1988), investigated effects of prior knowledge on learning from high- and low-coherence history texts. 

An advantage was found for the high-coherence text on recall and multiple-choice questions. However, high-knowledge readers performed better on the sorting task after reading the low-coherence text. High-knowledge readers performed better on open-ended questions after reading low-coherence text. Low-coherence text requires more inference processes—these inferences are more likely to be successful and useful for high-knowledge readers.

The study by Vaughn, S., Swanson, E. A., Roberts, G., Wanzek, J., Stillman-Spisak, S. J., Solis, M., & Simmons, D. (2013) titled "Improving reading comprehension and social studies knowledge in middle school" was published in Reading Research Quarterly, 48(1) 77–93.

The study examined the effects of the instructional practice "Promoting Acceleration of Comprehension and Content Through Text" ("PACT"), an approach that aims to improve social studies content knowledge and reading comprehension. Students in the treatment conditions (n = 261) scored statistically higher than students in the comparison conditions (n = 158) on all three outcomes: content acquisition (ES = 0.17), content reading comprehension (ES = 0.29), and standardized reading comprehension (ES = 0.20).

## Overall Research Findings on Reading Interventions for Secondary Students

A systematic review of interventions designed to improve the reading skills of secondary school students examined studies conducted between 1999 and 2014 which used a randomised controlled design. In studies targeting reading comprehension skills only, the evidence indicates low effect sizes on reading comprehension outcomes when measured using standardised tests.

## Close Reading Interventions Specifically

There are serious concerns related to the quality of the current research available on the effects of close reading on reading comprehension outcomes. A recent literature review examined close reading interventions for grades 3-9 and found methodological limitations in existing research.

## Recent Secondary Student Intervention Studies

For high school students specifically, a 2-year, randomized control trial with 9th to 10th grade students with significant reading problems was provided for 50 minutes a day in small groups. Students in reading treatment compared to students in business-as-usual demonstrated significant gains on reading comprehension (effect size = .43), and improved reading was associated with better grades in social studies.

Additionally, one quasi-experimental cluster randomized controlled intervention evaluated the effectiveness of a critical reading strategies approach on the reading comprehension and reading motivation of ninth-grade students.

## Study Overview

The researchers conducted a pre-registered, randomised controlled experiment with within- and between-participant design elements in schools in England with 405 students aged 14–15 years who studied two text passages and completed comprehension and retention tests three days later.

## Key Findings on Effect Size

Students using ChatGPT for reading support scored higher than those using traditional note-taking (d = 0.41). However, this represents perceived performance rather than actual learning outcomes.

## Main Results

Quantitative results demonstrated that both note-taking alone and combined with LLM use had significant positive effects on retention and comprehension compared to using the LLM alone.

## Student Preferences vs. Learning Outcomes

Most students preferred using the LLM over note-taking and perceived it as more helpful. Qualitative results revealed that many students valued LLMs for making complex material more accessible and reducing cognitive load, while they appreciated note-taking for promoting deeper engagement and aiding memory.

## Publication

The study is published in the journal Computers & Education and is one of the first randomised classroom experiments to investigate how LLMs affect students' reading comprehension and retention.

Kim, A., Vaughn S., Wanzek J., & Wei, S. (2004) published "Graphic organizers and their effects on the reading comprehension of students with LD A synthesis of research" in the Journal of Learning Disabilities, volume 37, pages 105-118.

Key findings from this meta-synthesis include:

- An extensive search of the professional literature between 1963 and June 2001 yielded a total of 21 group design intervention studies that met the criteria for inclusion in the synthesis.

- Using graphic organizers (i.e., semantic organizers, framed outlines, cognitive maps with and without a mnemonic) was associated with improved reading comprehension overall for students with LD.

- Compared to standardized reading measures, researcher developed comprehension measures were associated with higher effect sizes.

- The authors found that the use of graphic organizers benefited students with learning disabilities in the short-term but that long-term improvements in reading comprehension could not be attributed to graphic organizer use.

## iSTART: Interactive Strategy Training for Active Reading and Thinking

iSTART is a Web-based application that provides young adolescent to college-age students with high-level reading strategy training to improve comprehension of science texts.

**Background and Design:**
iSTART is modeled after an effective, human-delivered intervention called self-explanation reading training (SERT), which trains readers to use active reading strategies to self-explain difficult texts more effectively. Transforming the training from a human-delivered application to a computer-based one has resulted in a highly interactive trainer that adapts its methods to the performance of the students.

**How It Works:**
The iSTART trainer introduces the strategies in a simulated classroom setting with interaction between three animated characters—an instructor character and two student characters— and the human trainee. The trainee identifies the strategies in the explanations of a student character who is guided by an instructor character. Finally, the trainee practices self-explanation under the guidance of an instructor character.

**Publication Details:**
The article was published in Behavior Research Methods, Instruments, & Computers, volume 36, pages 222–233 (2004).

201	1988, 1998). The most raw and transient level is the surface code, which contains

# Cervetti, Barber, Dorph, Pearson & Goldschmidt (2012), JRST 49(5), 631–658

### Abstract (verbatim)

> "This study investigates the efficacy of an integrated science and literacy approach at the upper-elementary level. Teachers in 94 fourth grade classrooms in one Southern state participated. Half of the teachers taught the treatment unit, an integrated science–literacy unit on light and energy designed using a curriculum model that engages students in reading text, writing notes and reports, conducting firsthand investigations, and frequent discussion of key concepts and processes to acquire inquiry skills and knowledge about science concepts, while the other half of the teachers taught a content-comparable science-only unit on light and energy (using materials provided by their districts) and provided their regular literacy instruction. Students in the treatment group made significantly greater gains on measures of science understanding, science vocabulary, and science writing. Students in both groups made comparable gains in science reading comprehension."

## (a) Effect sizes by outcome

Effect size metric, verbatim from the table note:
> "Effect size estimated as d, (Treatment − Comparison)/SD (Outcome)."

So the metric is **Cohen's-style d** (raw treatment coefficient divided by outcome SD). **Hedges' g is not used and is not mentioned.**

| Outcome | Treatment coefficient (SE) | Effect size (d) | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Science understanding (Table 6, model 1) | 1.47 (0.289) | **0.65** | p < .01 (**) |
| Science understanding (model 2, w/ interaction) | 1.51 (0.285) | 0.65 | p < .01 |
| Science understanding × pretest interaction | 0.05 (0.072) | — | ns |
| Science vocabulary (Table 7) | 0.75 (0.23) *see conflict* | **0.23** | p < .05 (*) *see conflict* |
| Science vocabulary (Table 7, gain-score model 4) | 0.91 (0.22) | 0.22 | p < .01 |
| Reading comprehension (Table 7) | 0.36 (0.26) | **0.11** | **not significant** |
| Reading comprehension (gain-score model 6) | 0.12 (0.26) | 0.09 | not significant |
| Science writing — latent/overall (Table 9) | 0.60 (0.038) post-test | **0.40** | p < .05 (one pass said Table 9 cell was 0.60**, p<.01) |
| Writing: vocabulary count (Table 10) | 1.49 (0.20) | **0.80** | p < .01 |
| Writing: science concepts/content | 0.59 (0.12) | **0.63** | p < .01 |
| Writing: clarity | 0.33 (0.09) | **0.43** | p < .01 |
| Writing: introduction | 0.35 (0.10) | **0.38** | p < .01 |
| Writing: use of evidence | 0.38 (0.15) | **0.33** | p < .05 |
| Writing: vocabulary definition | — | **no treatment effect reported** | ns |
| Writing: conclusion | — | **no treatment effect reported** | ns |

Results-section prose (as returned; wording is close to literal but I could not byte-verify):
> "The results indicate that treatment classrooms scored about 1.5 points higher on the science understanding post-test, which is an effect size of about 0.65."

> "students in the treatment condition scored significantly higher than students in the comparison condition on the science vocabulary measure. The effect size is approximately 0.23."

> "The results for reading comprehension indicate that treatment and comparison students did equally well on the post-test."

> "at the post-test students in the treatment group had higher latent writing achievement (p < 0.05). The treatment effect size is 0.40."

> "The results for model two imply that there is no joint effect (essentially the pre–post slopes are parallel in treatment and comparison classrooms and hence there is no differential change in the performance gap between high and low achievers due to the treatment). Thus, the treatment effect on science understanding is robust for students at all points along the distribution of pretest scores."

**Conflicts to re-verify:** the vocabulary post-test coefficient came back as both `0.75 (SE 0.23), p<.05` and `0.91 (SE 0.22), p<.01` in different passes — these are almost certainly two different models (post-test-on-pretest vs. gain score), but which is which is not certain. The Table 9 writing row came back once as `p<.05, ES 0.40` and once as `0.60**, p<.01`. Also, one pass reported the science understanding measure as "23 items" and another as "forty-two multiple choice items."

**Not reported / does not exist:** there is **no general or standardized reading comprehension measure** in this study. The only reading comprehension outcome is the researcher-designed one. Exact p-values (as decimals) are not printed; the paper uses asterisk conventions.

## (b) Grade level
**Fourth grade.** > "In order to participate in the study, a teacher had to be teaching fourth grade..."

## (c) Sample

- **Teachers/classrooms: 94.** > "Thus the study population consisted of ninety-four teachers (60 in Fall 2007, 34 in Spring 2008) from 16 school districts." (47 treatment / 47 comparison)
- **Districts: 16.** > "The districts were located in urban, suburban, and rural areas in the same southern state."
- **State: one unnamed Southern state.** > "The study took place in one Southern state, selected as the study site because of the close correlation between that state's fourth grade science standards addressing the topic of light and the content of the treatment unit."
- **Schools: NOT REPORTED as a count.** Only "16 school districts" is given. School-level demographics are reported (FRL: treatment 57.6%, comparison 52.9%), implying schools were tracked, but no N of schools was found.
- **Students: no single total N is stated.** Analysis-sample Ns from the tables (values differed slightly between extraction passes — verify):
  - Science understanding: comparison n=937, treatment n=976
  - Science vocabulary: comparison n=939, treatment n=974 (a separate pass gave pretest n=992 / 1027)
  - Reading comprehension: comparison n=936, treatment n=969
  - Science writing: **n=467** (a randomly selected subset — writing was scored on a subsample, not the full sample)
  - So roughly **~1,900–2,000 students** analyzed for the multiple-choice outcomes.
- Demographics: ~48–49% White, 35–39% African-American, 5–7% Hispanic in both conditions.

## (d) Design

**Yes, randomized — a cluster/group-randomized trial randomized at the TEACHER (classroom) level**, not at student or school level:
> "After being accepted into the study, each teacher was randomly assigned to either a treatment or comparison group using a random number generating algorithm that is part of the Microsoft Excel software."

Note this is a volunteer sample (100 applications received; 3 denied, 3 dropped out pre-implementation). Students were nested in teachers; analyses were multilevel.

**Comparison condition — "business as usual" but content-matched:**
> "Teachers in the comparison group were asked to present the content of their state science standards related to the topic of light, using curriculum materials they regularly use for the same amount of time each week and for the same duration."

The authors describe it as "a comparison group that features a real and familiar alternative—teachers using content-comparable science units." Content alignment was imperfect:
> "The treatment light unit included content related to two of the three major subtopics of the state's light standards: characteristics of light and light interactions. A third subtopic (light and color) appears in the state standards, but is not addressed in the treatment light unit. Conversely, a third subtopic that is addressed in the treatment light unit (light as energy) does not appear in the state standards."

Baseline teacher differences (all ns): treatment teachers less experienced (9.2 vs. 11.6 total years; 4.4 vs. 5.6 years at grade 4) and less credentialed (34% vs. 51% advanced degree).

## (e) Duration

> "The treatment unit was forty sessions in length, comprised of four investigations—each with 10 sessions. Sessions were designed to be taught in 45–60 minutes."

Eligibility required "a minimum of three hours per week for a minimum of eight weeks for unit implementation." So roughly **8+ weeks, 40 sessions, ~3 hrs/week**.

Session breakdown: > "In each 10-session investigation the equivalent of approximately four sessions are devoted to firsthand (hands-on) activities, two sessions to reading, two sessions to writing, and two sessions to discourse, review of important concepts, or assessment activities."

Implementation contrast: treatment teachers reported 219.8 min/week of science vs. 182.3 for comparison; 77 vs. 61 min/week of reading/writing in science contexts.

## (f) Measure provenance — ALL FOUR OUTCOMES WERE DEVELOPER-DESIGNED

**No standardized published test was used for any outcome.** This is the single most important methodological point. All four measures were built by the curriculum development team itself:

> "The student learning outcomes were measured through a pre–post assessment developed through a process coordinated by the Center for Research, Evaluation, and Assessment at the Lawrence Hall of Science in partnership with the curriculum research and development team."

> "Wherever possible items were drawn from existing validated assessments. In other instances, items were developed and reviewed by a team of assessment developers, curriculum developers, and classroom teachers."

> "The first set of items (Version 1) were developed in classrooms alongside the treatment curriculum as it was being developed and field tested..."

Per measure:
- **Science understanding** — developer-designed multiple choice ("forty-two multiple choice items; 15 had two answer choices, while the remaining 27 items had four response options"; another pass reported 23 items, α = .81 posttest).
- **Science vocabulary** — developer-designed, definition-matching + cloze formats. α = .43 pretest, .69 posttest (note the very low pretest reliability).
- **Science writing** — developer-designed open prompt: "How does light interact with materials? Give three examples." > "Rubrics were developed by project staff for six dimensions: use of evidence, introduction, clarity, conclusion, vocabulary definition, and science content." (Text says six dimensions; the results tables report seven — verify.) > "The science writing assessments were scored by project staff and trained undergraduate students at University of California, Berkeley." α = .79. Note: scored by project staff, i.e., not blind third-party scoring as described.
- **Reading comprehension** — explicitly researcher-designed: > "The reading comprehension measure is a researcher-designed set of expository passages and multiple-choice questions." Initial reliability 0.67; > "We determined that many of the items were easy (with p-values above 0.85) and that there were too few items overall." Revised and re-validated on 202 students. α ≈ .77 pre / .76 post.

**No Gates-MacGinitie, ITBS, Stanford, state test, or any other standardized instrument was administered.**

## (g) Subgroup analyses — English learners

**No ELL/EL subgroup results are reported.** The only mention of ELL status is a methodological aside showing the model *could* accommodate it:
> "Additional student characteristics can be added to (1b) and tested by expanding (2b) (e.g., including ELL status in model 1b and adding a γ11k TRTjk into 2b)."

The percentage of English learners in the sample is **not reported**. The only moderator analysis actually conducted was **by pretest achievement level** (treatment × pretest interaction, coefficient 0.05, SE 0.072, ns) — concluding the effect was "robust for students at all points along the distribution of pretest scores."

## (h) Limitations and conflict of interest

**Limitations section (verbatim, full):**
> "In addition to the issues highlighted above, we recognize a number of limitations to the analytic efforts presented within this article. The most significant is related to the amount of information we could gather about the substance of our 'business-as-usual' comparison given the scope and budget of this study. Although we gathered self-report post-surveys from teachers regarding the substance and duration of the teaching and learning that took place in these comparison classrooms, we still have an incomplete picture. Moreover, self-reports can be unreliable (Cook & Campbell, 1979). Future research efforts are being designed to gather additional implementation data in order to gain a more complete picture. Additionally, while we took a broad perspective on the aspects of literacy that can support and be supported by science in the design of the intervention, we assessed only vocabulary knowledge, reading comprehension, and science writing. While the intervention also included attention to participation in science discussions, reading fluency, and the use of text features and structures, we were limited in the amount of time we had available for student assessment. While the limited measures risk a simplistic interpretation of the role of language and literacy in science, they do mirror those aspects of literacy instruction that are most central to educational standards in fourth grade. Even with these limitations, this study addresses an important issue in science education and literacy education and contributes additional important evidence to the studies on science–literacy integration, by employing a broader range of measures and utilizing a comparison group that features a real and familiar alternative—teachers using content-comparable science units."

**Conflict of interest: no formal disclosure statement was located** in the extracted text — no author note, funding acknowledgment, or COI statement was found. However, developer involvement is unambiguous from the text itself:
- Authors and affiliations: > "Gina N. Cervetti, 1 Jacqueline Barber, 2 Rena Dorph, 2 P. David Pearson, 2 and Pete G. Goldschmidt 3 / 1 University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan / 2 University of California, Berkeley, California / 3 California State University, Northridge, California"
- Barber, Dorph and Pearson are at UC Berkeley / Lawrence Hall of Science, the home of Seeds of Science/Roots of Reading; Barber is the program's principal developer. Assessments were built "in partnership with the curriculum research and development team," scored by "project staff," and the science understanding items were "developed in classrooms alongside the treatment curriculum as it was being developed."
- **This is a developer-conducted evaluation with developer-designed outcome measures on all four outcomes.**

Also relevant (not framed as a limitation by the authors, but stated): treatment teachers received **no professional development** — > "treatment teachers conducted an 'out-of-the-box' implementation, receiving only the curriculum materials" plus a step-by-step teacher's guide.

# Cervetti, Barber, Dorph, Pearson & Goldschmidt (2012), JRST 49(5), 631–658

### Abstract (verbatim)

> "This study investigates the efficacy of an integrated science and literacy approach at the upper-elementary level. Teachers in 94 fourth grade classrooms in one Southern state participated. Half of the teachers taught the treatment unit, an integrated science–literacy unit on light and energy designed using a curriculum model that engages students in reading text, writing notes and reports, conducting firsthand investigations, and frequent discussion of key concepts and processes to acquire inquiry skills and knowledge about science concepts, while the other half of the teachers taught a content-comparable science-only unit on light and energy (using materials provided by their districts) and provided their regular literacy instruction. Students in the treatment group made significantly greater gains on measures of science understanding, science vocabulary, and science writing. Students in both groups made comparable gains in science reading comprehension."

## (a) Effect sizes by outcome

Effect size metric, verbatim from the table note:
> "Effect size estimated as d, (Treatment − Comparison)/SD (Outcome)."

So the metric is **Cohen's-style d** (raw treatment coefficient divided by outcome SD). **Hedges' g is not used and is not mentioned.**

| Outcome | Treatment coefficient (SE) | Effect size (d) | Significance |
|---|---|---|---|
| Science understanding (Table 6, model 1) | 1.47 (0.289) | **0.65** | p < .01 (**) |
| Science understanding (model 2, w/ interaction) | 1.51 (0.285) | 0.65 | p < .01 |
| Science understanding × pretest interaction | 0.05 (0.072) | — | ns |
| Science vocabulary (Table 7) | 0.75 (0.23) *see conflict* | **0.23** | p < .05 (*) *see conflict* |
| Science vocabulary (Table 7, gain-score model 4) | 0.91 (0.22) | 0.22 | p < .01 |
| Reading comprehension (Table 7) | 0.36 (0.26) | **0.11** | **not significant** |
| Reading comprehension (gain-score model 6) | 0.12 (0.26) | 0.09 | not significant |
| Science writing — latent/overall (Table 9) | 0.60 (0.038) post-test | **0.40** | p < .05 (one pass said Table 9 cell was 0.60**, p<.01) |
| Writing: vocabulary count (Table 10) | 1.49 (0.20) | **0.80** | p < .01 |

Results-section prose (as returned; wording is close to literal but I could not byte-verify):
> "The results indicate that treatment classrooms scored about 1.5 points higher on the science understanding post-test, which is an effect size of about 0.65."

> "students in the treatment condition scored significantly higher than students in the comparison condition on the science vocabulary measure. The effect size is approximately 0.23."

> "The results for reading comprehension indicate that treatment and comparison students did equally well on the post-test."

> "at the post-test students in the treatment group had higher latent writing achievement (p < 0.05). The treatment effect size is 0.40."

> "The results for model two imply that there is no joint effect (essentially the pre–post slopes are parallel in treatment and comparison classrooms and hence there is no differential change in the performance gap between high and low achievers due to the treatment). Thus, the treatment effect on science understanding is robust for students at all points along the distribution of pretest scores."

**Conflicts to re-verify:** the vocabulary post-test coefficient came back as both `0.75 (SE 0.23), p<.05` and `0.91 (SE 0.22), p<.01` in different passes — these are almost certainly two different models (post-test-on-pretest vs. gain score), but which is which is not certain. Also, one pass reported the science understanding measure as "23 items" and another as "forty-two multiple choice items."

**Not reported / does not exist:** there is **no general or standardized reading comprehension measure** in this study. The only reading comprehension outcome is the researcher-designed one. Exact p-values (as decimals) are not printed; the paper uses asterisk conventions.

## (b) Grade level
**Fourth grade.** > "In order to participate in the study, a teacher had to be teaching fourth grade..."

## (c) Sample

- **Teachers/classrooms: 94.** > "Thus the study population consisted of ninety-four teachers (60 in Fall 2007, 34 in Spring 2008) from 16 school districts." (47 treatment / 47 comparison)
- **Districts: 16.** > "The districts were located in urban, suburban, and rural areas in the same southern state."
- **State: one unnamed Southern state.** > "The study took place in one Southern state, selected as the study site because of the close correlation between that state's fourth grade science standards addressing the topic of light and the content of the treatment unit."
- **Schools: NOT REPORTED as a count.** Only "16 school districts" is given. School-level demographics are reported (FRL: treatment 57.6%, comparison 52.9%), implying schools were tracked, but no N of schools was found.
- **Students: no single total N is stated.** Analysis-sample Ns from the tables (values differed slightly between extraction passes — verify):
  - Science understanding: comparison n=937, treatment n=976
  - Science vocabulary: comparison n=939, treatment n=974 (a separate pass gave pretest n=992 / 1027)
  - Reading comprehension: comparison n=936, treatment n=969
  - Science writing: **n=467** (a randomly selected subset — writing was scored on a subsample, not the full sample)
  - So roughly **~1,900–2,000 students** analyzed for the multiple-choice outcomes.
- Demographics: ~48–49% White, 35–39% African-American, 5–7% Hispanic in both conditions.

## (d) Design

**Yes, randomized — a cluster/group-randomized trial randomized at the TEACHER (classroom) level**, not at student or school level:
> "After being accepted into the study, each teacher was randomly assigned to either a treatment or comparison group using a random number generating algorithm that is part of the Microsoft Excel software."

Note this is a volunteer sample (100 applications received; 3 denied, 3 dropped out pre-implementation). Students were nested in teachers; analyses were multilevel.

**Comparison condition — "business as usual" but content-matched:**
> "Teachers in the comparison group were asked to present the content of their state science standards related to the topic of light, using curriculum materials they regularly use for the same amount of time each week and for the same duration."

The authors describe it as "a comparison group that features a real and familiar alternative—teachers using content-comparable science units." Content alignment was imperfect:
> "The treatment light unit included content related to two of the three major subtopics of the state's light standards: characteristics of light and light interactions. A third subtopic (light and color) appears in the state standards, but is not addressed in the treatment light unit. Conversely, a third subtopic that is addressed in the treatment light unit (light as energy) does not appear in the state standards."

Baseline teacher differences (all ns): treatment teachers less experienced (9.2 vs. 11.6 total years; 4.4 vs. 5.6 years at grade 4) and less credentialed (34% vs. 51% advanced degree).

## (e) Duration

> "The treatment unit was forty sessions in length, comprised of four investigations—each with 10 sessions. Sessions were designed to be taught in 45–60 minutes."
