Session breakdown: > "In each 10-session investigation the equivalent of approximately four sessions are devoted to firsthand (hands-on) activities, two sessions to reading, two sessions to writing, and two sessions to discourse, review of important concepts, or assessment activities."

Implementation contrast: treatment teachers reported 219.8 min/week of science vs. 182.3 for comparison; 77 vs. 61 min/week of reading/writing in science contexts.

## (f) Measure provenance — ALL FOUR OUTCOMES WERE DEVELOPER-DESIGNED

**No standardized published test was used for any outcome.** This is the single most important methodological point. All four measures were built by the curriculum development team itself:

> "The student learning outcomes were measured through a pre–post assessment developed through a process coordinated by the Center for Research, Evaluation, and Assessment at the Lawrence Hall of Science in partnership with the curriculum research and development team."

> "Wherever possible items were drawn from existing validated assessments. In other instances, items were developed and reviewed by a team of assessment developers, curriculum developers, and classroom teachers."

> "The first set of items (Version 1) were developed in classrooms alongside the treatment curriculum as it was being developed and field tested..."

Per measure:
- **Science understanding** — developer-designed multiple choice ("forty-two multiple choice items; 15 had two answer choices, while the remaining 27 items had four response options"; another pass reported 23 items, α = .81 posttest).
- **Science vocabulary** — developer-designed, definition-matching + cloze formats. α = .43 pretest, .69 posttest (note the very low pretest reliability).
- **Science writing** — developer-designed open prompt: "How does light interact with materials? Give three examples." > "Rubrics were developed by project staff for six dimensions: use of evidence, introduction, clarity, conclusion, vocabulary definition, and science content." (Text says six dimensions; the results tables report seven — verify.) > "The science writing assessments were scored by project staff and trained undergraduate students at University of California, Berkeley." α = .79. Note: scored by project staff, i.e., not blind third-party scoring as described.
- **Reading comprehension** — explicitly researcher-designed: > "The reading comprehension measure is a researcher-designed set of expository passages and multiple-choice questions." Initial reliability 0.67; > "We determined that many of the items were easy (with p-values above 0.85) and that there were too few items overall." Revised and re-validated on 202 students. α ≈ .77 pre / .76 post.

**No Gates-MacGinitie, ITBS, Stanford, state test, or any other standardized instrument was administered.**

## (g) Subgroup analyses — English learners

**No ELL/EL subgroup results are reported.** The only mention of ELL status is a methodological aside showing the model *could* accommodate it:
> "Additional student characteristics can be added to (1b) and tested by expanding (2b) (e.g., including ELL status in model 1b and adding a γ11k TRTjk into 2b)."

The percentage of English learners in the sample is **not reported**. The only moderator analysis actually conducted was **by pretest achievement level** (treatment × pretest interaction, coefficient 0.05, SE 0.072, ns) — concluding the effect was "robust for students at all points along the distribution of pretest scores."

## (h) Limitations and conflict of interest

**Limitations section (verbatim, full):**
> "In addition to the issues highlighted above, we recognize a number of limitations to the analytic efforts presented within this article. The most significant is related to the amount of information we could gather about the substance of our 'business-as-usual' comparison given the scope and budget of this study. Although we gathered self-report post-surveys from teachers regarding the substance and duration of the teaching and learning that took place in these comparison classrooms, we still have an incomplete picture. Moreover, self-reports can be unreliable (Cook & Campbell, 1979). Future research efforts are being designed to gather additional implementation data in order to gain a more complete picture. Additionally, while we took a broad perspective on the aspects of literacy that can support and be supported by science in the design of the intervention, we assessed only vocabulary knowledge, reading comprehension, and science writing. While the intervention also included attention to participation in science discussions, reading fluency, and the use of text features and structures, we were limited in the amount of time we had available for student assessment. While the limited measures risk a simplistic interpretation of the role of language and literacy in science, they do mirror those aspects of literacy instruction that are most central to educational standards in fourth grade. Even with these limitations, this study addresses an important issue in science education and literacy education and contributes additional important evidence to the studies on science–literacy integration, by employing a broader range of measures and utilizing a comparison group that features a real and familiar alternative—teachers using content-comparable science units."

I found the research you're looking for. Here are the key findings from Gerlich's 2025 study published in Societies:

## Study Overview

The study investigates the relationship between AI tool usage and critical thinking skills, focusing on cognitive offloading as a mediating factor, using a mixed-method approach with surveys and in-depth interviews with 666 participants across diverse age groups and educational backgrounds.

## Main Findings

The findings revealed a significant negative correlation between frequent AI tool usage and critical thinking abilities, mediated by increased cognitive offloading.

Younger participants exhibited higher dependence on AI tools and lower critical thinking scores compared to older participants.

## Methodology

Quantitative data were analysed using ANOVA and correlation analysis, while qualitative insights were obtained through thematic analysis of interview transcripts.

## Additional Insights

Heavy AI users scored lower on critical thinking tests, especially those who used AI for tasks that require reasoning or reflection, and younger participants were both more dependent on AI and scored lower on the Halpern Critical Thinking Assessment.

Educational attainment buffered some of the negative effects, suggesting learned habits of reflection can counterbalance digital convenience.

The study was published in Societies, Volume 15, Article 6 (2025).

## Reverse Cohesion Effect - Search Results

The reverse cohesion effect is the counterintuitive finding that high-knowledge readers learn better with less cohesive texts. Students with low knowledge have been shown to better understand and learn more from more cohesive texts, whereas high-knowledge students have been shown to learn more from lower cohesion texts.

### Boundary Conditions

Research has identified important boundary conditions for this effect. The benefit of low-cohesion text was restricted to less skilled, high-knowledge readers, whereas skilled comprehenders with high knowledge benefited from a high-cohesion text. This suggests that comprehension skill is a key moderating variable that can offset or reverse the typical reverse cohesion effect.

### Theoretical Explanation

The explanation for the reverse cohesion effect is that the cohesion gaps induce inferences that enhance comprehension and that high-knowledge readers are able to generate those inferences.

# Levels of Evidence Definitions

## Strong Evidence
"Consistent and generalizable evidence that a practice causes better outcomes for students in measures of reading proficiency."

Operationalized as: systematic reviews meeting WWC standards, multiple well-designed randomized controlled trials or quasi-experiments meeting WWC standards, one large multisite RCT meeting WWC standards, or assessment evidence meeting testing standards—all with no contradictory evidence of similar quality.

## Moderate Evidence
Evidence derived from studies with "high internal validity but moderate external validity, or studies with high external validity but moderate internal validity."

Operationalized as: experiments/quasi-experiments meeting WWC standards with small samples limiting generalizability, comparison group studies without demonstrated pretest equivalence but showing consistent enhanced outcomes, correlational research with strong statistical controls, or assessment reliability meeting testing standards with validity evidence from non-representative samples.

## Low Evidence
"Expert opinion derived from strong findings or theories in related areas and/or expert opinion buttressed by direct evidence that does not rise to the moderate or strong levels."

---

# Levels of Evidence for Each Recommendation

**Recommendation 1 (Explicit Vocabulary Instruction):** "Strong" — supported by six randomized controlled experiments and three quasi-experiments demonstrating group equivalence, plus six additional weaker-design studies.

**Recommendation 2 (Comprehension Strategy Instruction):** "Strong" — supported by five randomized experimental studies and single subject design evidence examining main idea summarization effects.

**Recommendation 3 (Extended Text Discussion):** "Moderate" — supported by four small quasi-experimental studies and one large correlational study, supplemented by meta-analysis of 43 studies.

**Recommendation 4 (Motivation and Engagement):** "Moderate" — supported by two experiments and one quasi-experimental study, plus weaker-design studies and two meta-analyses.

**Recommendation 5 (Intensive Individualized Interventions):** "Strong" — supported by evidence demonstrating that assessment-based, intensive specialist-led interventions for struggling readers produce substantial literacy skill improvements.

18	Introduction 
19	National and international trends indicate that current reading comprehension 
20	instruction is not preparing citizens for full participation in 21st century societies 
21	(National Assessment of Educational Progress 2009a, b; Organization of Economic and 
22	Cultural Development, 2013). The accessibility of unprecedented amounts of 
23	information, much of it unfiltered and often contradictory, means that readers need to 
24	analyze, synthesize, and evaluate information within and across sources (e.g. print-based 
25	texts, audio and video “texts,” images). Further, adolescents are expected to build 
26	knowledge and perform discipline-specific tasks requiring specialized ways of reading, 
27	thinking, and conveying information (Alvermann & Moore, 1991; Bazerman, 1985; 
28	Bromme & Goldman, 2014; Lee & Spratley, 2010; Moje & O’Brien, 2001; Shanahan & 
29	Shanahan, 2008; Snow & Biancarosa, 2003). The need is particularly acute for science 
30	because of public participation in decision making about quality of life issues (e.g., global 
31	climate change or genetically modified foods). Yet the evidence suggests that the public 
32	is ill-equipped to deal with the science underlying such issues (National Center for 
33	Educational Statistics, 2012).  The Common Core State Standards (Council of Chief State 
34	School Officers, 2010) and the Next Generation Science Standards (NGSS) (Next 
35	Generation Science Standards Lead States, 2013) speak to these needs. For the diverse 
36	students in our nation’s middle and high schools many of whom are profoundly ill 
37	prepared for the CCSS and NGSS standards, educators must simultaneously support 
38	literacy and science learning. A critical aspect of the challenge for adolescents is that they 
39	are expected to read to understand in multiple content areas. They are presented with 
40	discipline specific tasks and texts that require specialized ways of reading, thinking, and 
41	conveying information to others (Lee & Spratley, 2010; Moje & O’Brien, 2001; 
42	Shanahan & Shanahan, 2008). Yet, the disciplinary literacies - the oral and written 
43	communication practices of disciplines (Moje, 2008) - are rarely the focus of instruction, 
44	either in content area classes or in reading or English language arts classes. 
45	Motivated in part by these gaps between the literacies citizens need in the 21st 
46	century and what they are graduating from high school with, various countries have 
47	undertaken different initiatives to redress the gap. This paper reports on the development 
48	and results of one such effort undertaken in the United States under the auspices of 
49	Project READI (Reading, Evidence, and Argumentation in Disciplinary Instruction). 
50	READI is a multi-institution collaboration of researchers, professional development 
51	designers and facilitators, and practitioners, funded in 2010 by the Institute for Education 
52	Sciences’ Reading for Understanding initiative. Project READI conceptualizes 
53	adolescent reading comprehension as evidence-based argumentation from multiple 
54	sources in the academic disciplines and subject areas. Multiple sources reflects an 
55	expanded definition beyond traditional verbal text, similar to that adopted by Kress 
56	(Kress, 1989; Kress & Van Leeuwen, 2001) and the New London Group (1996) to 
57	include multiple media and forms of information representation. In evidence-based 
58	argumentation, claims are asserted and supported by evidence that has principled 
59	connections to the claim, but the nature of claims, evidence, and principles differ 
60	depending on the discipline (Goldman, et al., 2016).

65	Project READI took on the challenge of developing adolescents’ capacity to 
66	engage in evidence-based argumentation from multiple sources in three content areas: 
67	literary reading, history, and science. To address this challenge, we pursued a set of 
68	overarching questions about forms and types of tasks, texts, instructional strategies and 
69	tools that would enable students to engage in evidence-based argumentation from 
70	multiple texts through iterative design–based research (Cobb, Confey, diSessa, Lehrer & 
71	Schauble, 2003; Reinking & Bradley, 2008) and shorter-term quasi-experiments. Design 
72	teams for each disciplinary area consisting of researchers, teacher educators, professional 
73	development and subject matter specialists, and classroom teachers collaboratively 
74	developed, implemented, and revised instructional designs for evidence-based argument 
75	instructional modules (E-B AIMs). Quasi–experimental studies tested features of tasks, 
76	texts, and supports. A third work strand focused on developing assessments that would 
77	provide evidence of student learning relative to the learning objectives.  
78	The fourth work strand focused on teachers’ opportunities to learn and followed 
79	directly from the READI theory of action. Simply put, teachers mediate students’ 
80	opportunities to learn. However, many teachers have themselves had little opportunity to 
81	engage in inquiry-based approaches to literary reading, history, or science. Meeting in 
82	Teacher Inquiry Networks over the course of the project, teachers worked within their 
83	own disciplines to explore a variety of constructs and rethink their instructional practices. 
84	Constructs explored included argumentation, close reading, and disciplinary reasoning 
85	principles. Instructional practices included tasks they were assigning, texts they were 
86	using, opportunities for students to interact and engage in collaborative as well as 
87	individual sense-making, and how they orchestrated small group but especially whole 
88	class discussions. Overall, there was a strong emphasis on teachers learning how to move 
89	the intellectual work, including reading texts, from themselves to the students.  
90	This paper reports an efficacy study of the READI science intervention design 
91	that was conducted in 9th grade biological sciences classes over the course of a semester 
92	(intended for Fall of 2014 but extended through February, 2015). Specifically, this paper 
93	examines the impact of READI instruction compared to business as usual 9

95	biology instruction. “Impact” was assessed in several areas including comprehension and 
96	use of information from multiple sources to support practices of understanding and 
97	producing models of science phenomena. In concert with the question of impact on 
98	students and consistent with the READI theory of action, a second research question 
99	addressed impact on teachers’ attitudes, beliefs, and practices of their participation in the 
100	professional development and implementation of the READI intervention. We first 
101	provide a summary of the theoretical framework of the READI approach, especially 
102	regarding the functionalities of text-based investigation in science. We then describe the 
103	design of the intervention, including its teacher professional development, and the

50	Two experiments, theoretically motivated by the construction-integration model of 
51	text comprehension (W. Kintsch, 1988), investigated the role of text coherence in 
52	the comprehension of science texts. In Experiment 1, junior high school students' 
53	comprehension of one of three versions of a biology text was examined via free 
54	recall, written questions, and a key-word sorting task. This study demonstrates 
55	advantages for globally coherent text and for more explanatory text. In Experiment 
56	2, interactions among local and global text coherence, readers' background 
57	knowledge, and levels of understanding were examined. Using the same methods 
58	as in Experiment 1, we examined students' comprehension of one of four versions 
59	of a text, orthogonally varying local and global coherence. We found that readers 
60	who know little about the domain of the text benefit from a coherent text, whereas 
61	high-knowledge readers benefit from a minimally coherent text. We argue that the 
62	poorly written text forces the knowledgeable readers to engage in compensatory 
63	processing to infer unstated relations in the text. These findings, however, depended 
64	on the level of understanding, text base or situational, being measured by the three 
65	comprehension tasks. Whereas the free-recall measure and text-based questions 
66	primarily tapped readers' superficial understanding of the text, the inference 
67	questions, problem-solving questions, and sorting task relied on a situational 
68	understanding of the text. This study provides evidence that the rewards to be 
69	gained from active processing are primarily at the level of the situation model 
70	rather than at the superficial level of text-base understanding. 
71	Requests for reprints should be sent to Danielle S. McNamara, Department of Psychology, Old 
72	Dominion University, Norfolk, VA 23529-0267. E-mail: dsm200f@oduvm.cc.odu.edu

77	2 McNAMARA, KINTSCH, SONGER, KINTSCH 
78	People learn a great deal from texts: storybooks, textbooks, newspapers, or manu- 
79	als. The process of learning from texts is complex, however, and as yet not 
80	completely understood. In order to optimize learning, should one make the 
81	comprehension process as easy as possible, or should one, as many educators 
82	insist, ensure that the learner participates actively and intentionally in the process 
83	of constructing the meaning of a text? The traditional view of learning and 
84	instructional design has long been governed by the notion that the learner's path 
85	should be made as trouble free as possible. Recent research on the acquisition 
86	of simple skills (e.g., Schmidt & Bjork, 1992), however, indicates that this 
87	approach does not always lead to optimal learning. The studies reported here are 
88	concerned with whether there are analogous effects in complex cognitive proc- 
89	essing, such as text understanding. Specifically, should we facilitate the readers' 
90	task by improving the comprehensibility of a text, or can we increase their active 
91	involvement by placing obstacles in their way? In the latter case, what sort of 
92	obstacles will have beneficial effects on learning and under what conditions? 
93	Two sets of research findings provide an empirical background for this re- 
94	search. The first set of findings refers to the impact of the coherence of a text 
95	on comprehension and the second considers the benefits of active processing for 
96	learning. 
97	The coherence of a text is a major factor in comprehension (W. Kintsch & 
98	Vipond, 1979; van Dijk & Kintsch, 1983). Recent studies have demonstrated 
99	that revisions that increased the structural and explanatory coherence of texts 
100	resulted in substantial increases in recall among fifth-grade students (Beck, 
101	McKeown, Sinatra, & Loxterrnan, 1991) and college students (Beyer, 1987,1990; 
102	Britton & Gulgoz, 1991). In Beck et al. (1991), the revisions consisted of adding 
103	clarifying and elaborative content to supply background information and explain 
104	causal relations. The revisions in Beyer (1987, 1990) and Britton and Gulgoz 
105	(1991) were based on a computer simulation of the comprehension of the original 
106	text (W. Kintsch & van Dijk, 1978; Miller & Kintsch, 1980). Whenever the 
107	simulation broke down due to coherence gaps from one proposition to the next, 
108	text was added to make the relation explicit. These text additions ranged from 
109	low-level information, such as identifying anaphoric referents, synonymous 
110	terms, or connective ties, to supplying background information left unstated in 
111	the text. Filling in this kind of information, which an author would normally 
112	expect readers to provide from their own background knowledge, proved to be 
113	very effective, particularly because the college students in their study lacked the 
114	domain knowledge to do so on their own. 
115	As described earlier, one effect of increasing the coherence of text is that the 
116	reader comprehends it better. However, another effect that this text manipulation 
117	may have is to reduce the amount of active processing during reading. That is, 
118	easing the reader's burden of figuring out the meaning of the text could result 
119	in less effective learning. According to E. Kintsch (1990), this was the case for 
120	more knowledgeable and more skilled readers who wrote better summaries of a

126	poorly organized text than of a well-organized one. In general, researchers have 
127	found that people remember information that they have actively generated better 
128	than presented information and that they are better able to put such knowledge 
129	to use in novel situations. Advantages of active processing for memory and 
130	learning are well established in the list-learning literature (e.g., Slamecka & Graf, 
131	1978) as well as for text processing and strategy use (e.g., Bereiter & Scardamalia, 
132	1989; Chi & Bassok, 1989). Active inferencing during reading, if it is successful, 
133	can benefit learning because it results in the formation of more links between 
134	the incoming information and information in the personal-knowledge base (Man- 
135	nes & Kintsch, 1987). Due to multiple ties to other concepts, well-integrated 
136	knowledge is more quickly accessed and available for use when needed. 
137	In summary, an easy to read, coherent text is generally easier to recall. On 
138	the other hand, active processing, such as that necessary for difficult text, facili- 
139	tates learning. These contradictory findings regarding easy versus difficult text 
140	may be better understood in the context of W. Kintsch's (1988, 1992) construc- 
141	tion-integration (CI) model of text comprehension. One important feature of this 
142	model is that it distinguishes several different levels in the mental representation 
143	of a text that readers construct. The two levels of understanding that are relevant 
144	here are the text base and the situation model. 
145	The text base contains the information that is directly expressed in the text, 
146	organized and structured in the way that the author had organized the material. 
147	It has a local structure (the microstructure) as well as a global structure (the 
148	macrostructure). The construction of the text base involves the extraction of 
149	semantic information from a kext. In the CI model, this takes the form of an 
150	interrelated network of propositions. The process of transformation from words 
151	to meaning units involves a certain amount of inferential activity. For example, 
152	the referents of pronouns must be identified, synonymous terms must be matched, 
153	glaring gaps in the coherence of the network must be filled by bridging inferences, 
154	and so on. In general, this is the minimum amount of processing that a cooperative 
155	and motivated reader would perform. The result is a locally and globally well- 
156	structured memory representation of the text, an episodic text memory in the 
157	form of a coherent propositional network. This representation is capable of 
158	supporting several activities. On the basis of the text base, readers can verify 
159	statements they have read, they can answer questions about the text, they can 
160	recall the text, or they can summarize it. 
161	Knowing the text at the level of the text base, however, does not necessarily 
162	ensure that the reader understands it at a deeper level. Especially in the case of 
163	a demanding scientific text, more is required for understanding than just the 
164	ability to reproduce the text itself. It is usually the case that the reader must 
165	contribute information that was not stated explicitly in the text from his or her 
166	own store of knowledge about the domain in question. Furthermore, considerable 
167	active inferencing may be required to link the text with the reader's prior 
168	knowledge (an example is discussed later). The result of such inferencing is the

174	situation model. The situation model integrates the information provided by the 
175	text with prior knowledge, often reorganizing and restructuring it in terms of the 
176	reader's understanding of the knowledge domain as a whole rather than the par- 
177	ticular text just read. The resulting mental representation allows for a deeper 
178	understanding of the text, which is no longer a separate, episodic memory unit 
179	but is linked to the reader's long-term memory and knowledge. The textual 
180	information thus becomes retrievable not only via an episodic memory trace 
181	resulting from reading the text, but also via the shared elements by which it is 
182	linked in the reader's long-term memory. The new knowledge is therefore usable 
183	in novel environments and for unanticipated problem-solving tasks. 
184	For the purpose of reproducing a text in one way or another, a good text base 
185	suffices; learning from text, however, implies more than that and requires a good 
186	situation model linked with the reader's long-term knowledge (W. Kintsch, 1994). 
187	One should not think of text base and situation model as two distinct mental 
188	structures, however. The reader constructs a single mental structure, but for the 
189	purpose of analysis it is convenient to distinguish aspects of that structure that 
190	are directly derived from the text and aspects that are more knowledge and 
191	inference based. The same elements usually will participate in both types of re- 
192	lations but in somewhat different ways. Indeed, a number of studies have suc- 
193	ceeded in demonstrating differential effects of these two levels of representation 
194	on various tasks, for example, navigating a route (Perrig & Kintsch, 1985), a 
195	computer programming task (Schmalhofer & Glavanov, 1986), and inferential 
196	reasoning (Mannes & Kintsch, 1987). More informally, consider the difficulty 
197	one may experience in following directions (e.g., through unfamiliar terrain or 
198	in order to assemble an unfamiliar device) despite an easily comprehended 
199	description. The problem does not lie at the text-base level of understanding but 
200	rather in the inability to construct from that information a representation of the 
201	situation depicted. This theoretical distinction has important implications for our 
202	understanding of the processes by which readers acquire usable information from 
203	texts. 
204	With respect to the design of instructional text, the CI theory implies that 
205	textbooks should induce students to form appropriate situation models, not just 
206	text-base representations good only for reproduction. The formation of such 
207	situation models requires two things as a basis: active inferencing and adequate 
208	prior knowledge. Without adequate prior knowledge, students are limited in their 
209	constructive processes. Nevertheless, a well-written, fully coherent, explicit text 
210	at least will allow them to form a good text base. In contrast, students who have 
211	the requisite background should be encouraged to use it. Accordingly, one way 
212	to promote deeper understanding-the construction of an adequate situation 
213	model-may be to disrupt the coherence of the text at both the local, intersen- 
214	tential level and at the level of its global organization, or macrostructure. If there 
215	is a gap in comprehension that the reader cannot bridge with an inference, this

221	forms an impasse. It is likely to be noticed, and a repair process can be initiated. 
222	This repair process necessarily forces the reader to construct a situation model 
223	because prior knowledge is necessary to do so. Hence, the repairs will be 
224	particularly beneficial because the reader may otherwise remain satisfied with a 
225	superficial text-base understanding. 
226	An example from the text used in Experiment 2 may clarify this argument. 
227	Consider the following sentence pair from a fully coherent text: "The blood 
228	cannot get rid of enough carbon dioxide through the lungs. Therefore, the blood 
229	becomes purplish." A reader can easily comprehend these sentences without ever 
230	realizing just why excess carbon dioxide would make the blood purplish. A 
231	superficial understanding may result because the reader either lacks the necessary 
232	background knowledge or just does not bother to figure it out. Readers all too 
233	frequently take the path of least resistance. To generate the low-coherence text, 
234	therefore was deleted. Without this connective, the two sentences are simply 
235	juxtaposed. It is, of course, possible to accept these two sentences as statements 
236	of facts belonging to the same topic but which are otherwise unrelated. It is more 
237	likely, however, that the reader will notice the gap and attempt to fill it This is 
238	not possible on the basis of the textual content alone: Given merely these two 
239	statements, there is a large set of potential sentence connectives, such as therefore, 
240	and, because, when, and but, and no linguistic cues that would allow a reader 
241	to choose the right one. Hence, superficial solutions to the impasse are not 
242	available. The only way to bridge the gap is by knowing certain facts, for example, 
243	that the blood that flows from the heart to the lungs is low in oxygen, high in 
244	carbon dioxide, and looks blue, whereas the blood that flows out of the lungs is 
245	high in oxygen, low in carbon dioxide, and looks bright red. Knowing these facts 
246	enables the reader to infer therefore as the right connective between these two 
247	sentences. 
248	In summary, the two sets of empirical findings regarding easy and difficult 
249	text understood in the context of the CI model suggest a possible way to improve 
250	comprehension and learning from a textbook. Although a coherent text is gen- 
251	erally easier to recall, more difficult text may induce active processing and thus 
252	facilitate learning. W. Kintsch's (1988) model of text comprehension suggests 
253	that one way to avoid a superficial understanding of a text may be to make the 
254	text more difficult by disrupting its coherence. Coherence is of crucial importance 
255	for understanding, but deeper understanding results when readers make their own 
256	bridging inferences and derive their own macrostructure. Although filling in such 
257	linguistic gaps requires a certain degree of background knowledge, doing so may 
258	force more knowledgeable readers out of a passive processing mode induced by 
259	easy text. Consequently, we hypothesize that the same text cannot be optimal 
260	for everyone: Low-knowledge readers will profit from a fully coherent text, 
261	whereas high-knowledge readers will learn better with a text that stimulates more 
262	active processing.

268	EXPERIMENT 1 
269	Experiment 2 tested our hypothesis that text coherence would differentially affect 
270	readers with low and high background knowledge. Testing this hypothesis, 
271	however, required first building a more solid empirical platform. Hence, Experi- 
272	ment 1 was designed to address several questions fundamental to investigating the 
273	complex interactions predicted by our hypothesis. First, we wanted to replicate the 
274	results of Britton and Gulgoz (1991) with a younger population of students and 
275	with a different kind of text. Britton and Gulgoz found advantages for more 
276	coherent text with college students who read a fairly difficult and unfamiliar 
277	historical text about the Vietnam War. One goal in Experiment 1 was to test whether 
278	improving the coherence of text would generalize to younger students who are just 
279	embarking on the formal study of a new domain. Thus, our target population 
280	consisted of middle school students. Moreover, because we were interested in 
281	devising ways to improve textbooks designed for instruction, it was important to 
282	determine whether previous advantages for coherent text could be replicated with 
283	instructional texts. Thus, OUT target text was an instructional biology text written 
284	for the appropriate grade level. 
285	A second goal of Experiment 1 was to compare the individual contributions 
286	of local, global, and explanatory coherence. A text is locally coherent if each 
287	sentence is explicitly related to the next, for example, via argument overlap. A 
288	text is globally coherent if the paragraphs and larger sections of text are clearly 
289	related to each other and to the overall topic. Explanatory coherence refers to 
290	content that supplies background knowledge needed to understand the text that 
291	the reader may not have. Thus, three versions of a chapter on the traits of 
292	mammals, taken from a biology text, were used to examine the effects of these 
293	three types of coherence: (a) the original school text, which was locally coherent 
294	to begin with but lacked global coherence; (b) a revised text, which added 
295	macrosignals alerting the reader to the underlying structure; and (c) an expanded 
296	text, which added explanatory coherence to the text. 
297	Our third purpose in conducting Experiment 1 was methodologically moti- 
298	vated. In previous research, the effects of text coherence have primarily been 
299	assessed by recall, which is a measure of readers' text-base knowledge: It tests 
300	how well they remember the actual content of the original text and the way it 
301	is organized. We are, however, also interested in comprehension measures that 
302	tap into the reader's understanding of the situation described by the text (i.e., 
303	the mental model that the reader constructs from the textual content). Experi- 
304	ment 1 uses a sorting task as a measure of situational understanding. This task, 
305	which involves organizing a set of key concepts into categories, poses problem- 
306	solving demands that require more than a superficial, text-base understanding of 
307	the text.

313	Method 
314	Students' preknowledge about the traits of mammals was assessed by means of 
315	the sorting task and a set of questions about the text. They then read one of three 
316	text versions, recalled it immediately afterwards, performed the sorting task again, 
317	and answered another set of questions similar to the previous one. The different 
318	measures used are intended to reflect different levels of understanding. Recall 
319	and a subset of the questions based entirely on the text content (i.e., text-based 
320	questions) were used to assess participants' ability to reproduce this content. 
321	They provide a relatively superficial index of understanding based primarily on 
322	the text base that has been constructed. In contrast, the sorting task and a subset 
323	of the questions based on both text content and prior knowledge (i.e., inference 
324	questions) were used to assess participants' deeper understanding: how their text 
325	memory (text base as well as situation model) modified their perception of the 
326	relations among the concepts to be sorted and how well the situation model could 
327	be used for inferring novel relations. 
328	Participants 
329	Thirty-six participants living in Boulder, Colorado, were each paid $10 to 
330	participate in this study. They were between the ages of 11 and 15 years old (M 
331	= 13 years, 2 months) and were entering Grades 7 through 9. Twelve participants 
332	were assigned to each of three text conditions (i.e., original, revised, expanded 
333	texts) based on the order of testing. The mean ages of the participants in the 
334	original, revised, expanded text conditions were 13.1,13 .O, and 13.5, respectively. 
335	The mean grade levels for the three conditions were 7.8,7.6, and 8.0, respectively. 
336	There were no significant differences among the three groups of participants in 
337	terms of their age or grade level. 
338	Materials 
339	Texts. Three versions of a biology text about traits of mammals were used: 
340	an original version, a revised version, and an expanded version. The original 
341	biology text (Silver Burdett & Ginn, 1987) discussed traits of mammals, a subject 
342	area reasonably familiar to students in Grades 6 through 8. The text was 1% 
343	pages long (590 words). Following the method of Britton and Gulgoz (1991), 
344	comprehension of the text was simulated by means of a computer program (W. 
345	Kintsch & van Dijk, 1978; Miller & Kintsch, 1980). A breakdown in the 
346	simulation due to lack of overlapping arguments signaled a gap in the coherence 
347	structure of the text. Because our text was instructional text written at grade 
348	level, however, there were, in fact, no such gaps at the local level. Unlike the 
349	text used by Britton and Gulgoz, not a single bridging inference was required to

354	run the simulation. On the other hand, the text had a list-like macrostructure that 
355	was less coherent. That is, the various subtopics were not always clearly marked 
356	in their relation to the overall topic and to each other. Furthermore, the paragraph 
357	structure of the text did not correspond entirely to its macrostructure. 
358	The revision consisted primarily of adding material that explicitly identified 
359	the major subtopics as traits of mammals. We use the term macrosignal to refer 
360	to these linguistic pointers to the macrostructure. This should be distinguished 
361	from the term macroproposition, which refers to the major subtopics discussed 
362	in all three text versions (i.e., the seven mammal traits in this case) whether they 
363	are signaled or not. The result of our revision was a two-page text of 821 words 
364	in which each paragraph corresponded to one of the traits discussed. The original 
365	and revised texts, therefore, have approximately the same content. The only 
366	difference is that the interconnections between the various content iunits are made 
367	explicit in the revised version, especially at the global level but to some extent 
368	locally as well. For instance, the original text merely says that "mammals are 
369	the only animals that have hair or fur," whereas the revision relates this fact to 
370	the more global topic concerning mammals' ability to live in many environments. 
371	The expanded version of the text was written because of some obvious 
372	shortcomings of both the original and the revised versions, not in their structure 
373	but in their content. Identifying various traits that mammals have does not really 
374	help a student to understand biology. It is more useful to know how these traits 
375	contribute to the success of this group of animals and their ability to survive. 
376	Hence, content to this effect was supplied in the expanded version while at the 
377	same time some irrelevant detail was omitted (e.g., the names of the four chambers 
378	of the heart). The expanded version was therefore considerably longer-4 pages 
379	or 1,167 words. In effect, a few concrete details were exchanged for some rather 
380	lengthy discussions about the functions of the traits in terms of the evolutionary 
381	success of mammals. 
382	At the local level, all three texts were coherent. At the global level, only the 
383	revised and expanded texts were coherent. In terms of content, the situation 
384	models implied by the original and the revised versions were essentially the 
385	same. That is, the additional content in the revised version was implicit in the 
386	original version for a knowledgeable reader; the equivalence would be less 
387	complete for low-knowledge readers. In contrast, the expanded version introduced 
388	a new, higher level discussion about the role that the traits of mammals play in 
389	a larger context.

404	Pretest and posttest questions. There were 32 questions consisting of 
405	multiple-choice, true-false, fill-in-the-blank, and short-answer questions concern- 
406	ing animal traits and behaviors. The questions were classified into three different 
407	types: (a) text-based questions for which the necessary information was stated 
408	in the original text (n = 19), (b) inference questions that required some type of 
409	inferencing or analytic reasoning (n = 9), and (c) nontext questions that dealt 
410	with information that did not occur in any of the three texts but was related to 
411	the general topic (n = 4). 
412	The three different types of questions were chosen for several reasons. Text- 
413	based questions were designed to assess both prior knowledge of the topic before 
414	reading as well as memory for the text information after reading. The answers 
415	to text-based questions were explicitly stated in the text and generally required 
416	only one sentence from the text to answer. An example of a text-based question 
417	pertaining to the excerpt provided in Appendix A is: "The type of teeth a mammal 
418	has is related to ?" (The answer is the kind of food the mammal eats.) 
419	Inference questions were intended to assess differential abilities to apply infor- 
420	mation in the text to a novel situation, depending on which text was read. Inference 
421	questions required linking information from separate sentences and applying the 
422	information to the stated problem. An example of an inference question is: 
423	"Mother coyotes usually give birth to a litter of pups in early spring. However, 
424	one year, soon after most of the young pups were born, a series of late storms 
425	brought snow and very cold temperatures. What would help the young coyotes 
426	survive the cold?" (Possible answers are their fur, mother's warmth, and being 
427	warm-blooded.) If a reader supplied the answer that the coyotes' fur would help 
428	them through the winter, this particular answer would require integrating and 
429	applying information from one sentence, that mammals have fur, and from 
430	another, that the fur provides insulation. Similarly, if a reader supplied the answer 
431	that being warm-blooded would help them, this requires linking and applying 
432	the separate information that mammals are warm-blooded and that being warm- 
433	blooded helps them to maintain a constant temperature. Of course, all of the 
434	correct answers to the question also required the prior knowledge that coyotes 
435	are indeed mammals. Thus, this type of question required linking together various 
436	pieces of information in the text along with an understanding of the information 
437	presented in the question itself. Nontext questions were included to ensure that 
438	there were no differences between pretest and posttest or between groups for 
439	general background knowledge. An example of a nontext question is: "Carnivores 
440	eat ?" (The answer is meat.) 
441	The 32 questions were divided pseudorandomly into two sets of 16 questions,

759	The goals of Experiment 1 were to investigate conceptual changes in readers 
760	that occur as a function of reading a text and to replicate earlier findings that

763	We were particularly interested in the sorting task as an indicator of the 
764	students' knowledge structure before and after reading a biology text. We were 
765	able to show that reading a text changes the way students organize concepts in 
766	predictable ways. Before reading, they sort on the basis of their general knowl- 
767	edge; after reading, they sort in a somewhat different way-based on their 
768	knowledge plus the episodic text memory.

770	sorting patterns or the extent to which the episodic text memory was integrated 
771	with the knowledge structure. The sorting task cannot yield a complete or direct

# Effect Sizes and Study Details: Vaughn et al. 2017

## Sample and Sites
- **Total participants:** 1,629 eighth-grade students (845 treatment, 784 comparison)
- **Schools:** 7 middle schools across 3 districts in southwestern and southeastern US
- **Teachers:** 18 eighth-grade history teachers
- **Classes:** 94 total (49 treatment, 45 comparison)
- **EL percentage:** 26.7% current or recently-exited ELs

## Effect Sizes by Outcome

### Assessment of Social Studies Knowledge (ASK)
- **Full sample:** ES = 0.40, p < .01
- **Metric:** Effect sizes calculated as "the ratio of the model-derived coefficient for Intervention and the pooled within-group standard deviation"
- **Subgroup finding:** Both ELs and non-ELs benefited equally at lower EL concentrations (<12% class ELs)

### MASK Content Reading Comprehension
- **Full sample:** ES = 0.20, p < .05
- **Pattern:** Moderating effects of classroom EL concentration were not statistically significant

### Gates-MacGinitie Reading Comprehension
- **Treatment effect:** Not statistically significant (only class % ELs main effect was significant, p < .01)

The researchers note their design controlled for "teacher effects" through within-teacher randomization, strengthening confidence in these estimates.

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about McNamara's research on text cohesion and the reverse cohesion effect. Here's what the search reveals:

The reverse cohesion effect is the counterintuitive finding that high-knowledge readers learn better with less cohesive texts (McNamara & Kintsch, 1996).

However, the research demonstrates inconsistencies in how this effect manifests. The results indicated that the benefit of low-cohesion text was restricted to less skilled, high-knowledge readers, whereas skilled comprehenders with high knowledge benefited from a high-cohesion text. This suggests that the results suggest a more complex view of when and for whom textual cohesion affects comprehension.

Regarding inconsistent findings more broadly, previous research on the relationship between cohesive devices and writing quality has yielded inconsistent results, with some studies demonstrating positive correlations between device frequency and quality, while others suggested that higher-quality writing relied on fewer explicit devices and more implicit connections for global coherence.

The search results primarily reference McNamara's 2007 work with O'Reilly rather than 2017 or 2021 reviews. If you're looking for a specific 2017 or 2021 review article by McNamara on these topics, you may need to search with more specific publication information.

70	and skills in science. In turn, few high-school students choose science majors in college. 
71	Moreover, of those who do, a good majority are either unable to complete their degree or 
72	eventually change majors to a non-science degree (National Science Board, 2003; Chen, 2013).

# Evidence Summaries for Recommendations 1-3

## Recommendation 1: Explicit Vocabulary Instruction

**Level of Evidence:** The authors identify this as "strong," grounded in "six randomized controlled experimental studies and three well designed quasi-experiments" plus six additional weaker-design studies and one single-subject design study. Research participants spanned "upper elementary, middle, and high schools from diverse geographic regions and socioeconomic backgrounds."

Key citations include Barron & Melnik (1973), Baumann et al. (2002, 2003), Bos & Anders (1990), Brett, Rothlein & Hurley (1996), and others. The authors note an important caveat: while studies show vocabulary learning effects, "only some show that explicit vocabulary instruction has effects on standardized measures of reading comprehension."

## Recommendation 2: Direct and Explicit Comprehension Strategy Instruction

**Level of Evidence:** Characterized as "strong," supported by "five randomized experimental studies" examining main idea summarization with "adolescents' comprehension of narrative and informational texts," plus a single-subject design study. This body receives support from "numerous other studies that vary in research design and quality."

Key experimental studies cited are Hansen & Pearson (1983), Katims & Harris (1997), Margosein et al. (1982), Peverly & Wood (2001), and Raphael & McKinney (1983). The panel emphasizes that "multiple-strategy training results in better comprehension than single-strategy training."

## Recommendation 3: Extended Discussion of Text Meaning

**Level of Evidence:** Rated as "moderate," based on "four small quasi-experimental studies" (Bird 1984; Heinl 1988; Reznitskaya et al. 2001; Yeazell 1982) and "one large correlational study" (Applebee et al. 2003). A limitation acknowledged is that "quality of written responses" served as outcome measures rather than standardized comprehension tests.

The authors supplement this limited direct evidence with "a recently completed meta-analysis of 43 studies" and reference Langer's (2001) large descriptive study of high-performing schools, noting these used slightly more lenient inclusion criteria than the practice guide's own search.

65	A plethora of research has demonstrated that readers' background knowledge
66	facilitates and enhances comprehension and learning (e.g., Chi, Feltovich, &
67	Glaser, 1981; Chiesi, Spilich, & Voss, 1979; McNamara, E. Kintsch, Songer, &
68	W. Kintsch, 1996; Means & Voss, 1985). Readers with greater background
69	knowledge have also been shown to employ more effective reading strategies
70	(e.g., Afflerbach, 1986; Lundeberg, 1987) and express more interest in the
71	reading material (Alexander, Kulikowich, & Schulze, 1994; Tobias, 1994); and
72	experts tend to put more effort into learning than do novices (e.g., Scardamalia &
73	Bereiter, 1991). Although some research has found little effect of background
74	knowledge on learning from text (e.g., Chi, de Leeuw, Chiu, & LaVancher,
75	1994), the bulk of the literature indicates that the more a reader knows about the
76	domain of a text, the more likely the reader will comprehend and learn from the
77	text.
78	Text comprehension can also be facilitated and enhanced by rewriting poorly
79	written texts to make them more coherent and to provide the reader with all the
80	information needed for ready comprehension (e.g., Beck, McKeown, Sinatra, &
81	Loxterman, 1991; Beyer, 1990; Britton & Gulgoz, 1991; McKeown, Beck,
82	Sinatra, & Loxterman, 1992; McNamara et al., 1996). Text coherence refers to
83	the extent to which a reader is able to understand the relations between ideas in a
84	text. This is generally dependent on whether these relations are explicit in the
85	text. Thus, the general approach to increasing text coherence is to add surface-
86	level indicators of relations between ideas in the text. Such modifications range
87	from adding low-level information, such as identifying anaphoric referents, syn-
88	onymous terms, or connective ties, to supplying background information left
89	unstated in the text.
90	The benefits found for high-coherence text may lead one to conclude that
91	facilitating the reading process by increasing text coherence should, without fail,
92	enhance text comprehension. However, making the task easier does not always
93	result in better learning. For example, it has been well established that training
94	procedures that facilitate the learning process typically result in inferior retention
95	and transfer. In many research domains it has been shown that retention and
96	transfer can be improved by making the learner's task more difficult, for exam-
97	ple, Battig (1979) for paired-associate learning, Schmidt and Bjork (1992) and
98	Healy and Sinclair (1996) for skill acquisition, and Mannes and W. Kintsch
99	(1987) and McDaniel, Blischak and Einstein (1995) for text recall. Thus, the
100	advantages found for facilitating the reading process by making text more coher-
101	ent, and the disadvantages demonstrated for facilitating the learning process in
102	other knowledge and skill paradigms present incongruous findings.
103	McNamara et al. (1996) approached these contradictory findings in terms of
104	Kintsch's model of text comprehension (W. Kintsch, 1988; van Dijk & W.
105	Kintsch, 1983). This model assumes that there are at least two levels of a text

200	THE CONSTRUCTION-INTEGRATION MODEL
201	The theoretical framework for the McNamara et al. (1996) study and the study
202	here is the construction-integration model of comprehension (W. Kintsch,
203	1988). The construction-integration model was an extension of earlier models of
204	comprehension (W. Kintsch & van Dijk, 1978; van Dijk & W. Kintsch, 1983),
205	primarily specifying computationally the role of prior knowledge during the
206	comprehension process. This framework has been applied successfully to numer-
207	ous aspects of text and discourse comprehension (e.g., W. Kintsch & Welsch,
208	1991, W. Kintsch, Welsch, Schmalhofer, & Zimny, 1990; Otero & W. Kintsch,
209	1992) as well as more complex domains such as expert-novice differences
210	in problem-solving tasks (e.g., Doan, McNamara, W. Kintsch, Poison, &
211	Clawson, 1992; W. Kintsch, 1988; Weaver & W. Kintsch, 1992). Within the
212	construction-integration framework, processing occurs in two stages. In the first
213	stage, construction, concepts from the text as well as syntax, semantic, and
214	world knowledge are activated without taking into account global constraints to
215	produce a network of activated concepts. In the second stage, integration, activa-
216	tion flows through the network of activated concepts according to connectionist
217	principles of constraint satisfaction. Concepts that are compatible with the over-
218	all context mutually enhance the activation of one another, while concepts that
219	are not compatible with the context lose activation. Thus, comprehension arises
220	from an interaction and fusion between the text information and knowledge
221	activated by the comprehender. We refer to the final product of this construction
222	and integration process as the reader's mental representation of the text.
223	Levels of Understanding
224	Within the reader's mental representation of the text, W. Kintsch's (1988) model
225	of text comprehension distinguishes between several different levels of under-
226	standing. Notice that the mental representation is a unitary structure, but it is
227	useful to distinguish between certain aspects of that structure. The levels of
228	understanding that are most relevant for our purposes are the textbase and situa-
229	tion model. The textbase consists of those elements and relations that are direct-
230	ly derived from the text itself. To construct the textbase the reader needs syntactic
231	and semantic (lexical) knowledge. The textbase is what would be obtained if a
232	patient linguist or psychologist were to translate the text into a propositional
233	network and then integrate this network cycle-by-cycle, as described earlier, but
234	without adding anything that is not directly cued by the text. In general, this
235	procedure yields an impoverished and often even incoherent network. The reader
236	must add nodes and establish links between nodes from his or her own world
237	knowledge and experience (e.g., schemas), to make the structure coherent, to
238

242	complete it, to interpret it in terms of the reader's prior knowledge, and last but
243	not least, to integrate it with prior knowledge.
244	Texts usually describe real or imaginary situations in the world. The situation
245	description that a comprehender constructs on the basis of a text as well as prior
246	knowledge and experience is called the situation model. Various sources of
247	knowledge must be used in the construction of situation models: knowledge
248	about the language, about the world in general, and about the specific communi-
249	cative situation. Furthermore, not only general knowledge enters this process,
250	but also the reader's personal experience. Such sources of knowledge may all be
251	necessary to complement the textual information, and to transform what by itself
252	is only an isolated memory structure into something that relates to, and is inte-
253	grated with, the reader's personal store of knowledge and experience. Thus, the
254	textbase comprises those nodes and links in the mental representation of the text
255	that have direct correspondences in the text itself; the situation model includes
256	the textbase, but also nodes and links that have been added on the basis of world
257	knowledge. Note that in a totally complete, explicit text, a complete and ade-
258	quate situation model would be described within the textbase. However, we have
259	yet to encounter such a text. In general, texts are incomplete and rely on the
260	comprehender to fill in gaps and make links to prior knowledge to form a
261	situation model of the text.
262	A second, orthogonal distinction is between the micro- and macro-structure of
263	the text. Micro-structure refers to local text properties, macro-structure to the
264	global organization of text. Either may be directly cued by the text or constructed
265	on the basis of the comprehender's knowledge. Micro-structure is generally cued
266	by the text via explicit indicators of relations between concepts and ideas in the
267	text (e.g., connectives, argument overlap, pronominal reference). Micro-struc-
268	ture can also be constructed on the basis of the comprehender's knowledge when
269	there are details or relations left unstated in the text. A text's macro-structure can
270	be cued directly in the text via topic headers and topic sentences, but it is often
271	left up to the reader to construct the macro-structure, for example by using some
272	type of schema to organize the text.
273	A third distinction refers to the quality of each one of these structures. One
274	may have a poor textbase (micro or macro), perhaps because the text is poorly
275	written, or perhaps because the comprehender did not encode properly what was
276	there. One may have a poor situation model (micro or macro), perhaps because
277	the comprehender lacked the required knowledge, or perhaps because he or she
278	failed to apply it. A poor textbase may be combined with a poor situation model,
279	but may also be associated with a very good situation model (e.g., Bransford &
280	Franks, 1971). Conversely, good situation models may be combined with good
281	textbases (e.g., when knowledge organization and text structure are in agree-
282	ment), or with a poor textbase (e.g., when knowledge structure and textbase are
283	in conflict, with the former being the stronger; Mannes & Kintsch, 1987).
284	Therefore, in the general case, the situation model that a reader generates
285	from a text is a mixture of text-derived (the textbase) and knowledge-derived

291	ploy it in understanding a text, the text representation will be dominated by the
292	textbase (e.g., Moravcsik & Kintsch, 1993). At the other extreme, if rich rele-
293	vant background knowledge is available and the text itself is poorly written and
294	disorganized, the reader's knowledge elaborations may come to dominate the
295	mental representation of the text and a good situation model may be obtained at
296	the expense of the textbase (e.g., Bransford & Franks, 1971). Normally, of course,
297	the two components, text-derived and knowledge-derived, are more balanced,
298	resulting in a more or less complete textbase and a more or less adequate situa-
299	tion model.
300	According to Kintsch's (1988) model, many factors contribute to learning
301	from text, but prior domain-specific knowledge and the building of a coherent
302	situation model are the driving factors. Text memory requires the formation of a
303	coherent and well-structured episodic memory representation of the text, which
304	however, may be only loosely linked to the reader's background knowledge.
305	Hence, the text information, even though it can be remembered, will not become
306	an effective part of the reader's knowledge. For learning to occur, the episodic
307	text memory must be well connected with the reader's prior knowledge. That is,
308	links between the text representation and prior knowledge must be actively
309	encoded. Therefore, the conditions for optimizing text memory versus learning
310	from text are not the same. Whereas well-structured, coherent text will facilitate
311	text memory, learning in terms of constructing a situational understanding of the
312	text requires the integration of the text representation and prior knowledge. For
313	learning to occur, a situation model must be constructed that is accessible not
314	only via the episodic memory cues, but also via its links to the reader's general
315	knowledge.
316	Knowledge Assessment
317	Corresponding to the theoretical distinction between text memory and learning
318	from text, one can distinguish between empirical measures that assess primarily
319	one or the other. Because the levels of understanding are not separate structures,
320	and moreover, because the situation model, by definition, involves both the
321	textbase and long-term memory, a comprehension measure cannot exclusively
322	tap into one level of understanding. Nevertheless, some measures are more
323	indicative of text memory (e.g., recognition, text-based questions, reproductive
324	recall) whereas other measures are more sensitive to learning (e.g., bridging
325	inference questions, recall elaborations, problem-solving tasks, keyword sorting
326	tasks). The former are referred to as textbase measures because all that is re-
327	quired for good performance is a coherent textbase understanding. The latter are
328	referred to as situation model measures because, in order to perform well on
329	them, the reader must have formed a well-integrated situation model of the text
330	during the comprehension process.
331	How can we a priori classify a measure as one type or the other? In general,
332	performance on a measure is assumed to depend primarily on the textbase when

375	notion of coherence was covered extensively by van Dijk and W. Kintsch (1983).
376	Sometimes a distinction is made between coherence and cohesion. Cohesion, as
377	used in linguistics (e.g., Halliday & Hasan, 1976), generally refers to the surface
378	indicators of relations between sentences in a text. The notion of coherence as we
379	intend is the degree to which text propositions are interconnected in the reader's

434	THE PURPOSE OF THIS STUDY
435	The purpose of this study is to replicate the findings reported by McNamara et al.
436	(1996) with adult readers and with a history text. Replicating the interactive
437	effects of knowledge and text coherence with adult readers is important because
438	it is possible that adults' superior reading skills could compensate for the lack of
439	domain knowledge. In this case we would not see an interaction of coherence and
440	prior knowledge for adult readers. However, the construction-integration model
441	would not predict that superior reading skills would eliminate the effects of prior
442	knowledge. According to this model, reading skills should primarily affect text-
443	base measures, and prior knowledge should primarily affect situation model
444	measures (e.g., Voss & Ney Silfies, 1996). Situation model measures are of the
445	greatest interest to us as an indication of learning, and the interaction of text
446	coherence and prior knowledge occurs only for these measures. Thus, according
447	to the construction-integration model, we should see for adults the same interac-
448	tive effects of prior knowledge and text coherence that we saw for younger
449	readers.
450	The domain of a text is an important factor because some domains may rely
451	more or less on situation or mental models for an adequate understanding of the
452	text information. In addition, the relevant situational knowledge may also be of a
453	completely different nature. For example, the history text to be used in this study
454	describes one phase of the Vietnam war. The situational knowledge that is most
455	relevant for an accurate understanding of the text refers to the geographical
456	layout of Vietnam, as well as knowledge of who was fighting on whose side. In
457	contrast, the situational knowledge most relevant for the McNamara et al. (1996)
458	study referred to blood flow and the structure of the heart. It is important to
459	determine that the same advantages for active processing during reading demon-
460	strated for the biology text also occur for a history text.
461	It is also important to replicate McNamara et al.'s (1996) findings with a text
462	developed by independent researchers and previously demonstrated to provide

491	EXPERIMENT 1
492	One of our concerns is related to the nature of the knowledge necessary to make
493	the inferences in low-coherence text. Is this knowledge solely the specific bits of
494	information that are added to the high-coherence text? That is, is this knowledge
495	the specific information necessary to fill in the gaps, or is it something more
496	profound than that? If we provide readers with all of the information necessary to
497	fill in the gaps in the low-coherence text beforehand, will they be able to do so?
498	We examined this question by doing just that: We provided half of our readers
499	with a brief paper-and-pencil lesson that targeted the information necessary to fill
500	in the gaps in the text, but did not cover any information covered in the text. We
501	did this by going through each modification to the high-coherence text and
502	determining what information it added to the low-coherence text. We included all
503	of this information in a brief text and worksheet covering the history and geogra-
504	phy of Vietnam (i.e., pretraining). Of course, not all participants will learn much
505	from such a brief lesson, so we pretested all participants to evaluate the actual
506	level of their knowledge about Vietnam before reading the experimental text.
507	Thus, there are three factors in Experiment 1: (a) two versions of the text, high-
508	and low-coherence; (b) pretraining and control; and (c) high- and low-knowledge
509	as determined by a pretest.

# PACT Effectiveness Trial: Key Study Parameters

## Study Design & Sample

**Geographic Scope:** 16 states plus Washington, DC (target population: 3,661 noncharter public middle schools)

**Final Sample:** 48 schools, 135 teachers, 7,183 students
- Treatment: 24 schools
- Control (BAU): 24 schools

**Randomization Unit:** Schools (stratified balanced sampling across five strata)

**Recruitment Cohorts:** 3 cohorts across 2017-2020

---

## Outcome Measures

### Researcher-Designed
- **ASK-MC** (Assessment of Student Knowledge—Multiple Choice): 42 items measuring content knowledge, administered at pretest, posttest, and 9-week follow-up
- **ASK-RC** (ASK Reading Comprehension): 21 items across 3 passages; administered only in Cohort 1

### Standardized
- **Gates-MacGinitie Reading Comprehension (4th Edition):** Commercial assessment; 35-minute duration

---

## Effect Sizes (Exact Values)

### Sample Average Treatment Effects (SATE)

**ASK-MC Posttest:**
- Hedges' g = 0.46 (unadjusted model)
- Coefficient: 3.49 (SE = 0.89, p < .001)

**ASK-MC Follow-Up (9 weeks):**
- Hedges' g = 0.40
- Coefficient: 3.26 (SE = 1.00, p = 0.001)

**ASK-RC Posttest:**
- Hedges' g = 0.15 (not statistically significant)

**Gates-MacGinitie Reading Comprehension Posttest:**
- Hedges' g = 0.14 (not statistically significant)

### Population Average Treatment Effects (PATE)

**Posttest (ASK-MC):**
- Weighted Mixed Effects (WME): g = 0.45 (SE = 0.17)
- Weighted OLS (WOLS): g = 0.37 (SE = 0.14)

**Follow-Up (ASK-MC):**
- WME: g = 0.53 (SE = 0.16)
- WOLS: g = 0.33 (SE = 0.11)

---

## Subgroup Findings

The paper reports **no differential subgroup analyses** for the effectiveness trial. Authors note this as a limitation and future research question, stating: "treatment's student-level effect did not differ for students with different reading abilities at pretest." However, differential effects by special education status and EL status were observed in earlier **efficacy trials** (class-randomized designs), not this effectiveness study.

---

## Summary Statement

This school-randomized effectiveness trial demonstrated "consistent beneficial outcomes for content knowledge" with robust treatment effects on content acquisition but non-significant effects on reading comprehension measures, though the latter effects were contextually meaningful for secondary literacy instruction.

322	their grade point average (GPA) in high school and college, and three Likert scale questions 
323	concering how much they a) enjoy learning information about science, b) enjoy learning about 
324	non-scientific information, and c) enjoy reading. The Likert scale choices were presented from 1

327	reading strategies (i.e., comprehension monitoring, paraphrasing, elaboration, logic and common 
328	sense, prediction, and bridging), a booklet with more detailed descriptions of the strategies and 
329	examples of their use in self-explanations, a video transcript and note sheet (used during the

331	The text used during practice was titled ‘Origin of the Universe.’ It contained 425 words, four 
332	paragraphs, 20 sentences, with an average of 21.25 words per sentence. The Flesch-Reading 
333	Ease Score as reported from the Coh-Metrix site (cohmetrix.memphis.edu) was 42.34, which 
334	translates to a Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level of 12. Its referential cohesion (semantic overlap

337	Semantic Sentence Overlap = 0.35; TASA-based Norm = 0.47). The word difficulty was also 
338	slightly greater than average (Minimum Content Word Frequency = 10.05; TASA Norm = 26.69;

340	challenging topic.  
341	
342	===== PAGE 15 =====
343	SERT  14 
344	SERT Training 
345	SERT training was modified from McNamara (2004) to be administered to groups of 
346	students (rather than individually), and within a 2-hour period. The modifications included using 
347	one video to demonstrate the strategies (rather than four videos), going over the video as a group, 
348	and paired practice with another participant at the end of training.  
349	Participants were told that the purpose of the study was to teach them strategies that 
350	would help them to better understand and remember what they read. The first phase of training 
351	was administered in a lecture format during which the students were provided with instruction 
352	concerning the process of self-explanation and reading strategies. Students listened to a lecture 
353	and followed a handout that described and provided examples of each strategy. Self-explanation 
354	was described as reading text aloud and explaining what the text means. The strategies focused 
355	on the benefits of using knowledge and logic to understand the text, predicting what the text 
356	would say, making bridging inferences, and monitoring comprehension.  
357	Specifically, six reading strategies were presented to the participants as a means for 
358	improving the self-explanation process. For each strategy, a description of the strategy and 
359	examples of self-explanations using the strategies were provided in lecture format. The following 
360	strategies were presented: (a) comprehension monitoring -- being aware of understanding; (b) 
361	paraphrasing -- restating the text in different words; (c) elaboration -- using prior knowledge or 
362	experiences to understand the sentence (i.e., domain-specific knowledge based inferences); (d) 
363	logic and common sense -- using general knowledge and logic to understand the text (i.e., 
364	domain-general knowledge based inferences); (e) predictions -- predicting what the text will say 
365	next; and (f) bridging – making reference to an idea presented in a previous sentence in the text 
366	to better understand relationships between sentences. Comprehension monitoring was presented 
367	
368	===== PAGE 16 =====
369	SERT 15 
370	as a strategy that should be used all of the time. Paraphrasing was presented as a basis or 
371	jumpstart for self-explanation, but not as means for self-explaining text. The remaining strategies 
372	were various forms of inferences (i.e., domain specific, domain-general, predictive, and 
373	bridging) that were expected to enhance comprehension and explanation. 
374	The students then watched one video of another student self-explaining a text about forest 
375	fires. The instructor (i.e., the experimenter) stopped at four predetermined points in the video and 
376	asked all of the students to write down the strategies the student in the video had been using to 
377	self-explain the text. After all of the students had done so, the instructor led a discussion 
378	concerning which strategies were used.

380	groups of two. Thus, in pairs, the students took turns self-explaining each paragraph of the text. 
381	After one student had self-explained each sentence of an entire paragraph, the second student 
382	summarized that paragraph. The second student then self-explained the following paragraph, and

481	Discussion 
482	This study examined the effectiveness of a reading strategy intervention called SERT, 
483	which teaches students to use reading strategies in the context of self-explanation. The effects of 
484	SERT were assessed based on the students’ performance on their three exams in an introductory 
485	biology course. The results showed that the low-knowledge students who were in the SERT 
486	condition not only showed an effect of training compared to control students on all three exams, 
487	but they also performed equivalently to their high-knowledge counterparts. Thus, the results 
488	show that SERT can help students overcome knowledge deficits when learning about science 
489	(O’Reilly & McNamara, 2007b). This further supports the notion that reading comprehension 
490	and learning are a function of a number of factors, some of which can compensate for others. In 
491	particular, these results show that a reader can better understand challenging text by engaging in 
492	inference-making activities.

495	McNamara (2004) was conducted in a controlled laboratory, with one-on-one SERT training. In 
496	contrast, the current study was conducted in large groups in a classroom setting. Further, in 
497	McNamara (2004), the targeted variable was comprehension of a text, which all of the
