501	participants had been directed to self-explain (and only the SERT participants had been provided 
502	with prior training). In contrast, in this case, the dependent variable was performance on exams, 
503	which were constructed by the professor and administered in class, and had no apparent link to 
504	the training provided to the students, other than their being told during training that the strategies 
505	should help them to understand what they read in their science course. Also, in the previous 
506	study, comprehension of only one text was assessed, immediately after reading it. In this case, 
507	the exam assessed learning from multiple sources including chapters, lectures, and notes.  
508	 Thus, an important contribution of the current study is that it provides a test of far 
509	transfer to the results reported by McNamara (2004). Many aspects of the learning environment 
510	affect the probability of transfer, but perhaps the most important one is the degree to which 
511	people learn with understanding, rather than merely memorize sets of facts or follow a fixed set 
512	of procedures (Bransford, Brown, & Cocking, 2000). Also important is the amount and quality of 
513	practice (e.g., Ericsson, Krampe, & Tesch-Romer, 1993; Singley & Anderson, 1989). There are 
514	few demonstrations of far transfer of strategy training to assessments that are independent of the 
515	training context (e.g., Rosenshine et al., 1996). As such, this study provides a rare contribution to 
516	research on reading strategy training by showing transfer of training to a context and assessment 
517	that is far removed from the experiment. 
518	The results here further indicate that the students’ performance on exams was best 
519	predicted by their knowledge of science. The importance of prior knowledge to comprehension 
520	and learning cannot be over emphasized (Shapiro, 2004). These results corroborate the findings 
521	reported by McNamara (2004) who found that comprehension of the science passages was most 
522	related to domain knowledge and was not predicted by either reading span or Nelson Denny 
523	performance (see also, O’Reilly & McNamara, 2007a, 2007b).  
524	
525	===== PAGE 22 =====
526	SERT 21 
527	One particular concern regarding the current study is that students were not randomly 
528	assigned to condition; the students in the SERT condition volunteered to participate in the 
529	training sessions. This design is partially a by-product of the interest here in classroom data in 
530	contrast to controlled laboratory data and the constraints of the particular course that agreed to 
531	participate in the study. While this is a potential concern, it is quite unlikely that the results of 
532	these two studies are due to a Hawthorne effect, or the effect of virtually any additional 
533	interaction with the students. If that were the case, and simply, additional interactions with 
534	students, regardless of their nature could improve students’ performance, we would have long 
535	ago solved the many education problems in the United States. Additionally, there were no 
536	significant differences found between the two groups of participants on a variety of measures of 
537	knowledge, reading skill, GPA, prior science courses, and how much they enjoy learning and 
538	reading. There was a marginal difference between the groups on science knowledge, indicating 
539	that the control condition knew slightly more about science than did those in the SERT 
540	condition. However, this difference was non-significant and could only have worked against the 
541	potential effects of SERT.  
542	Nonetheless, this study did not include measures of students’ motivation to succeed 
543	academically, willingness to work hard, or other goal-oriented/motivational factors. Hence, the 
544	possibility remains that these findings reflect a selection bias: those who volunteered for 
545	additional training (of any kind) might be people who would naturally work harder and attend 
546	more deeply even without the training, or who would benefit just as much or even more from a 
547	different kind of training. This is somewhat unlikely given the lack of differences in terms of 
548	GPA, knowledge, and reading skill, because motivational differences are likely to have 
549	manifested within the students’ cumulative records across time. In sum, while the data indicate 
550	
551	===== PAGE 23 =====
552	SERT  22 
553	that the SERT participants were largely equivalent to the control participants before training, 
554	additional research with randomized control trials would more clearly disentangle possible 
555	effects of learner motivation that could be involved in the effects demonstrated here.  
556	An additional concern regards the challenges of providing SERT to groups of students, 
557	particularly within the context of content area courses where the primary focus is on providing 
558	content-specific instruction. In these contexts, SERT may not always be practical. In these cases, 
559	an effective alternative to SERT is its automated counterpart called Interactive Strategy Training 
560	for Active Reading and Thinking (iSTART; McNamara, Levinstein, & Boonthum, 2004; 
561	McNamara, O'Reilly, Rowe, Boonthum, & Levinstein, 2007; Jackson & McNamara, 2013). 
562	iSTART provides automated strategy instruction via instructional videos, games, quizzes, and 
563	practice using the strategies with automated feedback (McNamara, Boonthum, Levinstein, & 
564	Millis, 2007). Like SERT, iSTART also has a positive impact on reading strategies and 
565	comprehension for middle school, high school, and college students (e.g., Jackson & McNamara, 
566	2013; Magliano et al., 2005; O’Reilly, Taylor, & McNamara, 2006), with effect sizes that have 
567	varied between 0.50 and 2.00.  
568	One advantage of iSTART over SERT is its ability to provide immediate and appropriate 
569	feedback to the student (Levinstein, Boonthum, Pillarisetti, Bell, & McNamara, 2007). By 
570	consequence, it affords greater practice on using the strategies than does SERT and allows the 
571	students to continue to practice using the strategies with a wide variety of texts across a school 
572	year. Nonetheless, while iSTART facilitates practice, this can also be achieved in classrooms 
573	using a variety of approaches. For example, the students can be placed in pairs and asked to take 
574	turns self-explaining a portion of the textbook. The teacher can also have the students self-
575	explain as a class – calling on students to begin or continue self-explanations, and asking the 
576	
577	===== PAGE 24 =====
578	SERT  23 
579	students to write out self-explanations for selected sentences in text. These simple exercises may 
580	have important benefits, particularly for the struggling students. The more that these types of 
581	strategies are embraced by the teacher, and become part of the classroom culture, the more 
582	effective they will become. As with all classroom activities, SERT is likely to be most effective 
583	if the teacher encourages the student to practice the strategies and engages in classroom activities 
584	that encourage the strategies.  
585	In conclusion, this study addressed the question of whether SERT can help students 
586	improve not only their reading comprehension under guided circumstances, but also their 
587	performance in science courses. While this study focused on science, there is little theoretical 
588	reason to believe that SERT would not also be effective within other challenging domains. 
589	Science is a complex topic, but there are many others that are knowledge demanding and 
590	challenging for students. Students are highly likely to gain from using SERT strategies in a 
591	variety of subject domains such as history and social studies, as well as science.  
592	SERT is a relatively simple training that requires only a couple of hours. However, SERT 
593	will certainly be most effective if the student practices the strategies. iSTART may provide some 
594	advantages because it affords a greater amount of practice, and feedback is automated. However, 
595	the training can be provided in the context of a classroom, without computer support. If the 
596	student practices and uses the strategies, the potential benefit to performance in difficult, 
597	knowledge demanding courses is substantial. For many students, these strategies could translate 
598	to the difference of passing or failing the course.

## Study Details

The meta-analysis is by Deng, R., Jiang, M., Yu, X., Lu, Y., & Liu, S., published in Computers & Education, 227:105224 in April 2025.

## Number of Studies

The systematic review analyzed 69 experimental studies published between 2022 and 2024 on ChatGPT's educational impact.

## Effect Size

ChatGPT interventions significantly improve academic performance with a large effect size of g+ = 0.712. (Note: This appears to be the overall effect size for academic performance specifically, rather than the g=0.87 you mentioned in your query.)

## Key Findings

Overall, ChatGPT improves academic performance, affective-motivational states, and higher-order thinking propensities; it reduces mental effort and has no significant effect on self-efficacy.

The effect size of g=0.87 you mentioned in your query may refer to a different meta-analysis or a specific outcome measure within studies examining ChatGPT's effects.

949	The Sorting Task
950	The sorting data are used to determine how strongly reading the text affected the
951	reader's conceptual structure concerning the information in the text. Of course
952	the sorting task cannot provide a complete or direct picture of the participants'
953	knowledge structure. How the keywords are sorted is only in part determined by
954	the sorter's knowledge structure. For example, the prereading sorting task may
955	have an automatic influence on the postreading sorting task. Also, to appear
956	consistent to the experimenter, the reader may intentionally use their prereading
957	sorting pattern as a model for the postreading pattern. However, because all of
958	the participants sorted the keywords before reading the text, as well as after-
959	wards, effects of prereading sorting, as well as effects of individual sorting
960	strategies, should be equally distributed across conditions. In any case, sorting a
961	set of key phrases related to the text has proven to be a sensitive method for
962	assessing the effects of reading both here and in McNamara et al. (1996).
963	In their second experiment, Britton and Gulgoz (1991) used a rating task as
964	their dependent measure of comprehension. In that task the participant rated the
965	degree of relation between each pair of their 12 keywords. Why did we choose to
966	use our sorting task in lieu of the rating task used by Britton and Gulgoz? The
967	rating task can provide a more precise measure of the participants' knowledge
968	structure. One problem with the rating task is that it is time-consuming and there
969	are fatigue effects: with 12 keywords the participant rates 66 relations between
970	concepts. The advantage of the sorting task is that it is less time-consuming.
971	Moreover, the number of keywords can be increased, without substantially in-
972	creasing the completion time of the task. We were able to use 22 keywords. In a
973	rating task, this would have resulted in 231 relations to rate: a notably time-
974	consuming and boring task for the participant.
975	One of our ulterior goals is to examine the sorting task as an alternative
976	method for assessing situation model understanding. It is a relatively new task
977	that has been used by only a few researchers. We believe that the keyword sorting
978	task has great potential as a simple task that could be used both as a method of
979	assessment and as a mode of instruction. We could not include both the sorting
980	task and the rating task without seriously compromising the results of one or the
981	other, or both. By including the keyword sorting task, we were able to replicate
982	the sorting task results of McNamara et al. (1996), while including Britton and
983	Gulgoz's (1991) multiple-choice questions allowed us to replicate their findings
984	as well. In sum, we would suggest using the rating task with adult participants

993	How does one construct a keyword sorting task, and moreover, how is it
994	scored? McNamara et al. (1996) constructed the sorting task by choosing key-
995	words that best represented the macropropositions of the text, as well as a set of
996	concepts that were related to the keywords, but were not related to the macro-
997	structure of the text. In this case, the sorting task terms were chosen first on the
998	basis of those 12 keywords originally determined by Britton and Gulgoz (1991),
999	who chose the keywords "to represent the important topics of the text" (p. 337).
1000	Our additional 10 keywords were chosen on the basis of frequency of occurrence
1001	in the text; we chose the 10 most frequent concepts (excluding the first 12
1002	keywords). These keywords were also representative of the texts' macrostruc-
1003	ture. How keywords are chosen is certainly important. Whether different individ-
1004	uals or researchers can reliably choose the same keywords from a text, or
1005	whether there is wide and unaccountable variation in keyword choices remains to
1006	be empirically tested. Our expectation is that choosing keywords is a relatively
1007	intuitive task, as long as the person choosing the keywords has a complete and
1008	knowledgeable understanding of the information in the text.
1009	How is a scoring matrix constructed? When looking at the keywords, or
1010	sorting the keywords, the first thing to notice is that there is generally no one
1011	correct way to sort them into piles. There are generally several reasonable global
1012	strategies, and within each global strategy there are several reasonable micro-
1013	strategies or pair combinations. So, how does one capture these equally reason-
1014	able sorting patterns? Our strategy has been to construct a hierarchy of the
1015	concepts based on the text's macrostructure. It is not possible to actually sort the
1016	terms into a hierarchical structure, and this structure does not include all possible
1017	relations. However, the hierarchy does tend to capture and produce high scores
1018	for most of the reasonable sorting patterns. Because our scoring matrix is based
1019	on a hierarchy, and not an actual sorting pattern, it should be noted that it is not
1020	possible for a participant's sorting pattern to obtain a score of 1.0 (which would
1021	indicate a perfect match between the participant's pattern and the scoring matrix),
1022	for example, a score of 0.5 is quite high.
1023	In this case, the scoring matrix was based on the hierarchy presented by
1024	Britton and Gulgoz (1991), with the additional terms added on to the hierarchy.
1025	This scoring matrix was constructed before we conducted the experiment. Sev-
1026	eral other scoring matrices were analyzed after conducting the experiment, but
1027	all of the sorting matrices yielded essentially equivalent results. We found the
1028	same in McNamara et al. (1996): The same patterns emerged regardless of the
1029	scoring matrix. As long as the scoring matrix is reasonably based on the texts'
1030	macrostructure, that is, on the deeper meaning of the text, the sorting task scores
1031	should yield similar results.

1036	Alternative scoring matrices do not affect the general conclusions of sorting
1037	task analyses. Why not? The principal dependent measure of interest is how
1038	much a participant changes the sorting pattern from the pretest to the posttest. We
1039	measured this change by calculating the harmony between the participant's sort-
1040	ing pattern and a standard sorting pattern (i.e., our scoring matrix). The standard
1041	pattern is intended to provide a reflection of the organization of the keywords
1042	communicated by the text. The harmony measure indicates how close the partici-
1043	pant's sorting pattern is to the standard pattern, and hence, how reasonably the
1044	participant sorted the keywords before and after reading the text. The critical
1045	factors for this measure are that the sorting standard be relatively close to the text
1046	structure and that the same standard be used for all of the participants and tests.
1047	However, regardless of what standard is used as a comparison, if a participant
1048	does not change his or her sorting pattern, the participant's score remains the
1049	same. That is, the harmony between the participant's pattern and the standard
1050	will remain the same. Also, if a participant does change the sorting pattern after
1051	reading a text, the amount of change measured in the sorting pattern relative to
1052	the other participants' patterns will remain the same regardless of what standard
1053	is used. In Experiment 1, there was a large positive change between the pretest
1054	and posttest for high-knowledge participants who read the low-coherence text
1055	and little change for other participants. This indicates that (a) the latter partici-
1056	pants changed their sorting pattern, and (b) they changed it in the direction of the
1057	text. As long as the standard pattern somehow reflects the organization of the
1058	text, these patterns remain the same. If a more naive or unreasonable sorting
1059	pattern were used as a standard, there still would have been more change for the
1060	high-knowledge/low-coherence participants relative to the other participants, but
1061	that change would be negative rather than positive. In sum, alternative scoring
1062	matrices do not affect the general conclusions of sorting task analyses because we
1063	are measuring changes in the sorting patterns and these changes are calculated by
1064	comparing the participant's pattern to some standard pattern.

1100	Recall
1101	Because recall is a textbase measure, we would predict that both text coherence
1102	and prior knowledge should enhance recall. We found a marginal advantage for
1103	the high-coherence text. We also found an advantage for prior knowledge, but
1104	only for the participants in the pretraining condition. That is, we found there was
1105	no difference in recall between low- and high-knowledge control participants, but
1106	that there was a large difference in recall between the low- and high-knowledge
1107	participants who were given the pretraining. Indeed, high-knowledge participants
1108	in the pretraining condition recalled reliably more propositions compared to
1109	participants in all other conditions. One possible explanation for this finding is
1110	that the pretraining helped to prime information that was later presented in the
1111	text. This priming may have helped the high-knowledge participants to under-
1112	stand and organize the text better while reading it, and thus recall it better later on.
1113	We included the pretraining condition to address our question regarding the
1114	nature of the knowledge necessary to make the inferences in low-coherence text.
1115	Finding that the low-knowledge participants who were given the pretraining
1116	performed so poorly on recall, in conjunction with finding that it had very little
1117	effect on the sorting task and question answering, clearly answers this question.
1118	The knowledge necessary to make the inferences in the low-coherence text is not
1119	solely the specific information necessary to fill in the gaps, but rather, it must be
1120	a knowledge base that has been well integrated over time. Finding little advan-
1121	tage for the pretraining condition (apart from a recall advantage for participants
1122	who already possessed this knowledge) cannot come as a surprise. Students
1123	simply do not learn a great deal in a brief instructional session like the one used

1131	One purpose of Experiment 2 was to examine whether open-ended questions
1132	were more sensitive to effects of text coherence and background knowledge. The
1133	second purpose of Experiment 2 was to examine long-term effects by including a
1134	delayed retention test. So far, we have only used immediate memory and knowl-
1135	edge tests in our studies. However, if one wants to investigate learning from text,
1136	it is certainly necessary to explore delayed retention tests. In spite of the less than
1137	promising results concerning the pretraining condition in Experiment 1, we

1141	Participants and Design
1142	The participants were 40 college undergraduates who participated for credit in an
1143	introductory psychology course. The experimental design included two between-
1144	subjects variables: text (low coherence, high coherence) and pretraining (control,
1145	pretraining). Half of the participants read a low-coherence text and the other half
1146	read a high-coherence text. Within each of the text conditions, half were pro-

1149	test was a within-subjects variable (immediate, delayed). One participant in

An extensive search of the professional literature between 1963 and June 2001 yielded a total of 21 group design intervention studies that met the criteria for inclusion in the synthesis.

Key findings from the study include:

- Using graphic organizers (i.e., semantic organizers, framed outlines, cognitive maps with and without a mnemonic) was associated with improved reading comprehension overall for students with LD.

- Compared to standardized reading measures, researcher developed comprehension measures were associated with higher effect sizes.

A total of 91 university students were randomly assigned to either use ChatGPT3.5 or Google to research the socio-scientific issue of nanoparticles in sunscreen to derive valid recommendations and justifications.

The study aimed to investigate potential differences in cognitive load, as well as the quality and homogeneity of the students' recommendations and justifications.

181	when they read the low-cohesion text (reverse cohesion effect) because gaps in the
182	texts force the high-knowledge reader to actively process the text (McNamara,
183	2001). In sum, we predicted that only less skilled, high-knowledge readers would
184	comprehend more from the low-cohesion text, whereas skilled, high-knowledge
185	readers would not display a reverse cohesion effect. In fact when the text is diffi-
186	cult, high-cohesion text should help (Linderholm et al., 2000) the skilled (V oss &
187	Silfies, 1996), high-knowledge reader understand more from the text.
188	Our predictions were less precise for low-knowledge comprehenders. We ex-
189	pected first that their comprehension would be relatively poor, as found by
190	McNamara (2001), given that we were using McNamara’s difficult texts on the
191	topic of mitosis. In that study, participants consecutively read two versions of the
192	same text that varied in terms of cohesion. Participants read either the same text
193	twice (high cohesion twice or low cohesion twice) or different cohesion texts (high
194	cohesion then low cohesion, or low cohesion then high cohesion). Comprehension
195	was assessed at both the textbase and situation-model level of understanding. The
196	textbase representation was measured by short-answer, text-based questions that
197	required the reader to provide an answer that could be found within a single sen-
198	tence of the text. The situation model was assessed by short-answer, bridging-in-
199	ference questions that required the reader to integrate information from multiple
200	sentences to form a correct answer. The results indicated that low-knowledge read-
201	ers benefited from cohesion when the high-cohesion text was read first, whereas
202	high-knowledge readers scored higher on text-based questions when they read the
203	low-cohesion text first. However, overall comprehension was relatively low (less
204	than 35% overall correct).
205	The text used here and in the McNamara (2001) study concerned cell mitosis,
206	and the low-cohesion version is quite difficult for students to understand. One rea-
207	son for this difficulty is because students often have little knowledge about cells

210	=== PAGE 6 ===
211	and biological processes related to cells. Cell mitosis is a complex process in that it
212	contains numerous, unfamiliar scientific terms (e.g., “telophase”) and intercon-
213	nected subcomponents and processes. Hence, we expected low-knowledge read-
214	ers’ understanding of the text to be aided by both comprehension skill and cohe-
215	sion. We expected comprehension skill to contribute because McNamara (2004)
216	found that low-knowledge readers’ comprehension of the low-cohesion version of
217	this cell mitosis text was greatly enhanced by reading-strategy training. Similarly,
218	we expected comprehension skill to help the low-knowledge reader because
219	skilled comprehenders are more likely to monitor their comprehension and use
220	whatever knowledge they possess to understand the text. We expected cohesion to
221	benefit the low-knowledge readers’ understanding because the added cohesion
222	makes the relations among the concepts more explicit and reduces the number of
223	inferences.
224	As mentioned previously, because we used the same texts as those in
225	McNamara (2001, 2004), we predicted that, overall, readers would have difficulty
226	understanding the material. McNamara (2001) argued that the difficulty of the text
227	impeded readers’ ability to develop a situation model of the material, and because
228	so few readers were able to develop a coherent situation model of the text, the de-
229	fault representation for the reader was the textbase. This notion was supported by a
230	difference of over 50% correct comparing participants’ scores on text-based ques-
231	tions and bridging-inference questions. This result contrasts with previous studies
232	in which the overall performance for text-based and bridging-inference questions
233	was, on average, only 3% higher for text-based questions as compared to bridg-
234	ing-inference questions (McNamara & Kintsch, 1996, Experiments 1 and 2;
235	McNamara et al., 1996, Experiment 2).
236	In this study, comprehension skill was measured by a standardized reading
237	comprehension test, the Nelson–Denny Reading Test (Brown, Fishco, & Hanna,
238	1993) and a measure of metacognitive reading strategy knowledge, the
239	Metacomprehension Strategy Index (MSI; Schmitt, 1990). Domain knowledge
240	was measured by a combination of multiple-choice questions on general biology
241	and open-ended questions on cell knowledge. Participants read either a high- or a
242	low-cohesion version of a text about cell mitosis (from McNamara, 2001) and an-
243	swered open-ended comprehension questions.
244	In summary, we predicted that the reverse cohesion effect would only appear for
245	less skilled, high-knowledge comprehenders. For skilled, high-knowledge
246	comprehenders, cohesion should facilitate comprehension because the readers
247	would actively process the difficult mitosis text and the more coherent textbase in
248	the high-cohesion version should lead to a more complete text representation.
249	Finally, we predicted that both comprehension skill and cohesion would help
250	low-knowledge readers because skilled comprehenders are more likely to use
251	strategies and make inferences, and the increased cohesion should allow readers to
252	form a partial model of the text.

This study examines interventions involving "weekly sessions and/or a residential campus experience" for high school and college students with disabilities interested in STEM fields. To locate the Dexter, Park & Hughes meta-analysis you're seeking, you would need to search ERIC or other databases with those specific author names and the graphic organizers focus.

## Study Overview

The study reports the results of a randomized control trial of a semester-long intervention designed to promote ninth-grade science students' use of text-based investigation to create explanatory models of biological phenomena.

## Research Questions and Outcomes

The main research question was whether the student participants in the intervention outperformed the students in the control classes, as assessed by several measures of comprehension and application of information to modeling biological phenomena not covered in the instruction. A second research question examined the impact on the instructional practices of the teachers who implemented the intervention.

## Outcome Measures

The study used multiple assessment approaches. Goldman et al. (2019) used GISA as a distal measure in a randomized controlled trial evaluating the efficacy of the READI Science intervention when compared to a business-as-usual control in grade 9. Additionally, the READI team developed the Evidence-Based Argument (EBA) assessment to evaluate evidence-based argumentation.

## Results

The results showed that GISA was sensitive to the READI intervention effects with the treatment condition scoring significantly higher. A large-scale randomized control efficacy study of the READI approach in 9th grade biological sciences indicated significant effects of the intervention over traditional instruction on the same content.

The full study was published in the American Educational Research Journal, 56(4), 1148–1216 in 2019.

811	tions, indicating that few participants (low or high knowledge) formed a coherent
812	situation model.
813	Active Processing Helps Low-Knowledge Readers
814	We also confirmed previous results showing that comprehension skill improves
815	learning for the low-knowledge readers (Adams et al., 1995; O’Reilly &
816	McNamara, 2002, in press). The skilled, low-knowledge reader can still make
817	sense of a text by actively using their general knowledge and strategies. One exam-
818	ple of how skilled comprehenders make strategic use of their knowledge is through
819	elaboration. The production of elaborations can improve comprehension by mak-
820	ing the text more memorable (e.g., Pressley et al., 1992). Recent work has shown
821	that skilled comprehenders were more likely than less skilled comprehenders to
822	produce a higher number and quality of elaborations than less skilled
823	comprehenders (Best, Ozuru, & McNamara, 2004). Furthermore, McNamara
824	140
825	O’REILLY AND MCNAMARA
826	
827	=== PAGE 21 ===
828	(2004) found that reading-strategy training helped low-knowledge participants
829	perform as well on the same low-cohesion mitosis text used in this study as did
830	high-knowledge participants who were not provided with such reading-skill train-
831	ing. Both the results of McNamara and the results of this study underscore the im-
832	portance of comprehension skill for understanding difficult texts.
833	There are several other reasons why comprehension skill may help
834	low-knowledge readers, such as increased working memory capacity (e.g.,
835	Daneman & Carpenter, 1980), better text-based inferencing ability (e.g., Long et
836	al., 1994), better lexical knowledge and lexical identification (Perfetti, 1985;
837	Perfetti & Hart, 2002), and motivation (e.g., Alexander, 1997; Guthrie & Alao,
838	1997). Although the design of this study makes it difficult to discern the precise
839	nature of how comprehension skill helps low-knowledge readers, we forward the
840	view that comprehension skill is primarily a function of readers’ effective use of
841	knowledge and strategies (e.g., McNamara, de Vega, & O’Reilly, in press;
842	McNamara & O’Reilly, in press).
843	Reinterpreting Earlier Findings
844	by McNamara and Colleagues
845	In the early research by McNamara and colleagues, it was predicted and found
846	that the reverse cohesion effect arises primarily at the situation-model level of
847	processing (McNamara & Kintsch, 1996; McNamara et al., 1996). The theoreti-
848	cal basis for this result was that inference processing would most benefit deeper
849	levels of comprehension. According to Kintsch’s (1988, 1998) construction-inte-
850	gration model, comprehension includes surface, textbase, and situation-model
851	levels, which differ in degree of depth. The surface level comprises the words
852	and syntax; the textbase is the deeper meaning of those words; and the situation
853	model is the integration of the textbase and prior knowledge. Because the re-
854	verse cohesion effect arises from the integration of the textual information with
855	related knowledge, it was expected that the effects would be most apparent on
856	measures that tapped into that integration. Indeed, McNamara et al. found the re-
857	verse cohesion effect on accuracy for problem-solving and bridging-inference
858	questions and according to a keyword sorting task. McNamara and Kintsch
859	found the reverse cohesion effect on bridging-inference questions and according
860	to a keyword sorting task. These tasks require a deep understanding and thus a
861	coherent situation model to perform well on them (e.g., Chi, 2000; Kintsch,
862	1994).
863	In contrast to the two previous studies by McNamara and colleagues
864	(McNamara & Kintsch, 1996; McNamara et al., 1996), the results reported in
865	McNamara (2001) and in this study showed a reverse cohesion effect only on
866	text-based questions, which were assumed or designed to tap into the readers’
867	textbase level of understanding. These findings are congruent with other findings
868	STRATEGIC READERS 141
869	
870	=== PAGE 22 ===
871	(Britton & Gülgöz, 1991; Magliano et al., 2005) that high-cohesion text benefits
872	comprehension on text-based questions. A highly cohesive text has more connec-
873	tions among concepts and thus facilitates the development of the textbase. In turn,
874	this improves performance on text-based questions.
875	Why did high-knowledge readers, here and in McNamara (2001), not benefit
876	from low-cohesion text as measured by the bridging-inference questions? The an-
877	swer is likely to lie in the difference between the texts used in these studies and the
878	two previous studies (i.e., McNamara & Kintsch, 1996; McNamara et al., 1996).
879	The texts in these more recent studies are more difficult; students often have little
880	knowledge about cells and biological processes related to cells. In addition, cell
881	mitosis is a complex process in that it contains numerous, interconnected
882	subcomponents and processes. The idea that the mitosis text used here (and in
883	McNamara, 2001) is more difficult than the texts used in the previous studies is
884	supported by the data. In this study and in McNamara, there was a large difference
885	(approximately 50%) for the students’ performance on text-based questions as
886	compared to bridging-inference questions. In contrast, in the previous studies, the
887	overall proportion correct for text-based and bridging-inference questions was
888	similar, and approximately only 3% higher for text-based questions over bridging
889	inference (McNamara & Kintsch, 1996, Experiments 1 and 2; McNamara et al.,
890	1996, Experiment 2). Thus, in the previous studies that found the reverse cohesion
891	effect for situational model questions (McNamara & Kintsch, 1996, Experiments 1
892	and 2; McNamara et al., 1996, Experiment 2), participants were assumed to have
893	formed an effective situation model. In contrast, for this study and McNamara,
894	which used the more difficult cell mitosis text, participants’ relative ability to form
895	a coherent situation model was lacking in relation to their ability to form an ade-
896	quate textbase.
897	As such, one explanation proposed by McNamara (2001) to account for the
898	three studies was that the high-knowledge readers were not affected by cohesion
899	according to text-based questions in the McNamara et al. (1996) and McNamara
900	and Kintsch (1996) studies because few gains were possible at the textbase level of
901	understanding. In those studies, the text topics were easier, and the high-knowl-
902	edge participants potentially answered the text-based questions from their own
903	knowledge as opposed to the text itself. McNamara proposed that high-knowledge
904	readers benefit from low-cohesion texts at the level of processing that is in most
905	need of improvement. In the case of the McNamara et al. and McNamara and
906	Kintsch studies, in which the texts were easier, high-knowledge readers were able
907	to easily construct the textbase. However, the deep-level processing induced by the
908	low-cohesion text enhanced the situation-model level of understanding. In the case
909	of McNamara. in which the text was more difficult, high-knowledge readers were
910	unable to construct the textbase without scaffolding, and thus the low-cohesion
911	text enhanced comprehension at that level.

# Close Reading as an Intervention for Struggling Middle School Readers

**Full Citation:**
Fisher, Douglas, and Frey, Nancy. "Close Reading as an Intervention for Struggling Middle School Readers." *Journal of Adolescent & Adult Literacy*, vol. 57, no. 5, Feb. 2014, pp. 367-376.

**Abstract:**
This study examined whether an after-school close reading program could enhance outcomes for struggling readers. The researchers involved 75 seventh and eighth-grade students in a close reading intervention alongside a comparison group of 247 students receiving traditional instruction. 

**Intervention Components:**
The close reading approach incorporated "annotations, repeated reading, text-dependent questions, and discussions" applied to complex texts.

**Key Findings:**
The study demonstrated that "close reading can be an effective intervention, with significant increases in student attendance, self-perception, and achievement." Results favored the close reading group over those receiving conventional interventions.

**Publication Details:**
- **ERIC Number:** EJ1028018
- **ISSN:** 1081-3004

- **Education Level:** Grades 7-8
- **Study Quality Note:** This study does not meet What Works Clearinghouse evidence standards.

# Murphy et al. (2009) Meta-Analysis Summary

**Full Citation:**
Murphy, P. Karen; Wilkinson, Ian A. G.; Soter, Anna O.; Hennessey, Maeghan N.; Alexander, John F. "Examining the Effects of Classroom Discussion on Students' Comprehension of Text: A Meta-Analysis." *Journal of Educational Psychology*, vol. 101, no. 3, pp. 740-764, August 2009.

**Key Findings:**
The study examined how classroom discussions affect student learning outcomes. According to the abstract, "several discussion approaches produced strong increases in the amount of student talk and concomitant reductions in teacher talk, as well as substantial improvements in text comprehension."

However, the results were more modest for higher-order thinking: "Few approaches to discussion were effective at increasing students' literal or inferential comprehension and critical thinking and reasoning."

**Important Limitations:**
The provided record does not specify the exact number of studies included in this meta-analysis or report numerical effect sizes. The abstract notes that findings were moderated by research design, outcome measures, and student academic ability, with most studies focusing on elementary students in grades 4-6.

36	Comprehension of expository materials is a complex process that depends on a number of factors. For example, past research

43	discern the speciﬁc nature of the contributions of two types of individual difference factors and text features to science text
44	comprehension. The two individual difference factors examined are topic-relevant prior knowledge and reading comprehension

50	often insufﬁcient for the construction of a coherent mental representation of the situation depicted by the text, requiring the
51	contribution of reader knowledge (Kintsch, 1988, 1998). In support of this argument, empirical evidence has shown that a reader’s

64	Varner, & Faust, 1990; Hannon & Daneman, 2001; Walker, 1987 ), and may include a variety of abilities such as word decoding
65	(Perfetti, 1985 ), syntactic knowledge, and high-level inferential skills ( Oakhill & Yuill, 1996 ). Of all these abilities related to
66	reading skill, one of the most important elements is the ability and propensity to connect various concepts or ideas contained in
67	the text in a coherent manner ( Hannon & Daneman, 2001; Oakhill & Yuill, 1996 ; for a review also see Zwaan & Singer, 2003 ).
68	Currently, research remains inconclusive concerning precisely what kind of cognitive factors underlie readers’ ability and
69	propensity to integrate textual information to maintain a high level of coherence. Ability to suppress irrelevant information
70	(Gernsbacher 1997; cf. McNamara & McDaniel, 2004 ), working memory capacity ( Daneman & Hannon, 2001 ), metacognition
71	(Hacker, 1998), reading strategies (McNamara, 2007), and motivation (Guthrie & Wigﬁeld, 1999) are some of the major candidate
72	factors underlying reading comprehension skill.
73	Although reading comprehension skill and prior knowledge may not be completely separable, they are assumed to contribute to
74	reading comprehension processes in somewhat different ways ( Hannon & Daneman, 2001; Walker, 1987). Prior knowledge helps
75	readers compensate for gaps in text-based information by affording quick and relatively effortless access to relevant information
76	in long-term memory based on incomplete text-based information as cues. In contrast, reading comprehension skill helps readers
77	relate multiple ideas and concepts appearing in different parts of a text through effortful inferential processes ( Daneman &
78	Hannon, 2001). This process, of relating multiple ideas, helps readers build more integrated understanding of text content even
79	when readers do not have high levels of prior knowledge to facilitate knowledge-driven recognition of the text content. Given the
80	different roles of prior knowledge and reading skill in reading comprehension, the relative contribution of prior knowledge and
81	reading skill should change depending on the type of text and the level of comprehension involved (i.e., the types of questions
82	used to assess comprehension).
83	1.1. Prior knowledge and reading skill in relation to text cohesion
84	Even within a speciﬁc genre and topic (i.e., an expository biology text), texts can vary in a number of different ways.
85	Cohesiveness of a text is one of the important dimensions along which text varies. Cohesiveness of a text, an objective feature of
86	texts, is an important factor to determine text coherence, which is a subjective psychological state of a reader ( Graesser,
87	McNamara, & Louwerse, 2003; Halliday & Hasan, 1976 ). When comprehending a text, readers must establish and maintain
88	coherence between sentences ( Oakhill, Cain, & Bryant, 2003; van den Broek, 1994 ). When reading a highly cohesive text, the
89	majority of information necessary to maintain text coherence is provided by the text itself. On the other hand, when reading a less
90	cohesive text, readers need to rely more heavily on relevant knowledge to maintain coherence.
91	Text cohesion changes by the way in which adjacent sentences are connected, such as the degree of conceptual overlap (e.g.,
92	argument overlap) between sentences and by presence of speciﬁc cues (e.g., connectives) that help readers connect ideas across
93	sentences. Text cohesion also varies as a function of the overall organization which can be expressed by the temporal and causal
94	sequence of the events in the text ( Linderholm et al., 2001 ) and the presence of headers and topic sentences ( McNamara et al.,
95	1996). These features contribute to the maintenance of text coherence by reducing the need for the reader to rely on knowledge.
96	The cohesiveness of text differs from text readability or difﬁculty which usually refers to sentence length and individual word
97	difﬁculty, e.g., Flesch Reading Ease ( Flesch, 1948).
98	Given that text cohesion inﬂuences readers’ maintenance of text coherence, readers’ prior knowledge and reading skill should
99	interact with text cohesion in different ways in inﬂuencing comprehension. With respect to readers’ prior knowledge level, the
100	beneﬁt of text cohesion should be more pronounced for readers with less knowledge. That is, whereas maintenance of text
101	coherence in a less cohesive text demands contribution of speciﬁc knowledge, a highly cohesive text is more self-contained,
102	hence, requires less contribution of topic-speciﬁc knowledge for maintenance of text coherence. This notion is supported by the
103	ﬁnding that low-knowledge readers beneﬁt from reading high-cohesion texts, whereas high-knowledge readers’ comprehension
104	often suffers when reading high-cohesion texts ( McNamara et al., 1996; McNamara & Kintsch, 1996 ).
105	On the other hand, reading skill is expected to interact with text cohesion differently. Readers with poor reading comprehension
106	skill may not beneﬁt as much as skilled readers from reading a high-cohesion text because increasing text cohesion often involves
107	adding more information ( Beck, McKeown, Sinatra, & Loxterman, 1991 ), resulting in increased text length, density, and
108	complexity. As a consequence, comprehension of a highly cohesive text may require higher level of reading skill because reading
109	a highly cohesive text involves processing larger amounts of text-based information.
110	This proposal is not entirely new. For example, the Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) postulates that many types of cognitive tasks,
111	including reading comprehension, can be understood as a process by which task performers negotiate with the task demands using

Based on the search results, I found a highly relevant study that matches your query exactly. Here are the key findings:

## Study Overview

A large-scale crowdsourced evaluation of LLM-generated plain language summaries (PLSs) was conducted using Amazon Mechanical Turk with 150 participants, assessing PLS quality through subjective Likert-scale ratings focusing on simplicity, informativeness, coherence, and faithfulness; and objective multiple-choice comprehension and recall measures of reader understanding.

## Key Findings on Readability vs. Comprehension

The results reveal an important discrepancy between perceived and actual comprehension: Participants often rated LLM-generated PLSs as similarly clear and coherent as human-authored summaries, but participants performed significantly better on the comprehension questions after reading human-written PLSs.

## Evaluation Approach

The study developed a comprehensive evaluation framework that integrates both subjective and objective measures—the former capture rater preferences, while the latter measure rater comprehension of the PLSs—with subjective evaluation conducted through perceived ratings assessing simplicity, informativeness, coherence, and faithfulness, while objective evaluation includes multiple-choice comprehension assessments and recall-based free-text responses.

This research demonstrates that subjective ratings alone are not sufficient to evaluate whether LLM-generated summaries truly improve comprehension—objective measures of actual reader understanding are essential.

182	local- and global-bridging questions based on science materials, their answer is likely to be largely based on retrieval of
183	pre-existing knowledge as opposed to the product of resource consuming reasoning processes that involve linking multiple ideas
184	in the text while reading the text.
185	With respect to the second research question, we expected both prior knowledge and reading skill to interact with text
186	cohesion. Speciﬁcally, we expected a beneﬁt of increased cohesion on comprehension especially for low-knowledge participants
187	because cohesive text ﬁlls in conceptual gaps for low-knowledge readers that cannot be resolved with prior knowledge
188	(Hypothesis 3). We also expected the beneﬁt of reading high-cohesion text to be generally larger for more-skilled readers because
189	reading skill is necessary for taking advantage of added cohesion. In particular, this interaction between reading skill and text
190	cohesion was expected to be pronounced for high-knowledge readers; that is, we expected high-knowledge participants’
191	comprehension to remain the same across low- and high-cohesion texts or even decline when reading high-cohesion texts
192	(McNamara et al., 1996 ) unless the participant has a high level of reading comprehension skill ( O’Reilly & McNamara, 2007)
193	(Hypothesis 4).
194	The formulation of Hypothesis 4 was based on the notion that a high-cohesion text may contain information that is more
195	familiar to high-knowledge readers. As a consequence, they may more shallowly process the high-cohesion text because of a false
196	sense of understanding (McNamara et al., 1996). This will occur unless they have a higher level of reading skill, which is typically
197	associated with tendency to carefully and systematically process textual information and to generate inferences that relate
198	multiple concepts in the text ( O’Reilly & McNamara, 2007 ). Thus, reading skill induces a high-knowledge reader to actively
199	process the text regardless of its cohesion.
200	The above explanation is on the surface somewhat similar to the ‘‘expertise reversal effect’’ identiﬁed in the context of CLT
201	(Kalyuga, Ayres, Chandler, & Sweller, 2003 ). According to the expertise reversal effect, providing high-knowledge participants
202	with highly cohesive texts with ‘‘unnecessary details’’ can produce adverse effects due to interference because these high-
203	knowledge readers can efﬁciently maintain coherence based on their own knowledge alone. The expertise reversal effect also
204	implies that interference from added cohesion is likely to be more pronounced among less-skilled readers because less-skilled
205	readers are typically less efﬁcient in using limited cognitive resources when processing a large amount of information ( Daneman
206	& Hannon, 2001). These two explanations, one based on less-skilled high-knowledge readers’ tendency to shallowly process
207	a high-cohesion text and the other based on the expertise reversal effect, are not the same ( Kalyuga et al., 2003 ). But within the
208	design of the current study, both explanations generate similar predictions.
209	Further, related to the second question, we also explored the level of comprehension at which the beneﬁt of text cohesion is
210	observed. We expected that the beneﬁt of reading a high-cohesion text, in particular for low-knowledge readers, will be limited to
211	relatively lower levels of comprehension de.g., answering performance on text-based questions (Hypothesis 5). This proposal is
212	based on the notion that readers are unlikely to draw inferences (i.e., local- and global-bridging inferences to attain higher level
213	comprehension) unless they are already familiar with information related to the text content ( Noordman et al., 1992 ).
214	2. Method
215	2.1. Participants
216	Participants were recruited from two distinct sources in order to manipulate the level of biology knowledge relevant to the
217	reading comprehension materials. One group of participants was 108 undergraduate students enrolled in an introductory
218	Psychology course at the University of Memphis of which 93 were female and 15 were male. Mean age of this group was 21.1
219	years (SD ¼ 3.6) with range of 18 to 37 years. The other group of participants was 62 undergraduate students enrolled in an
220	introductory Biology course at Old Dominion University of which 53 were female and 9 were male. Mean age of this group of
221	participants was 23.3 years (SD ¼ 2.3) with range of 21 to 37 years. The participants from Old Dominion University were
222	recruited because it was possible to speciﬁcally recruit students enrolled in Biology courses, and this was not possible at the
223	University of Memphis. The two universities are considered comparable according to the college rankings reported in the
224	U.S. News, 2007. Testing of the two groups of participants took place within the same year.
225	2.2. Designdmaterials
226	The 2 /C2 2 /C2 3 experimental design included text cohesion (low and high) and type of question (text-based, local-bridging, and
227	global-bridging) as within-subjects variables. Knowledge level of participants (2 levels) was included as a between-subjects

233	participants based on prior knowledge measures. In addition, participants’ reading skill was assessed and included in the analysis
234	as control variable using a median split technique. Effects of the two individual differences factors were also analyzed with
235	regression analyses.
236	2.2.1. Texts and cohesion manipulation
237	The two texts used for the reading comprehension task were taken from high-school biology textbooks and were modiﬁed to
238	produce low- and high-cohesion texts. One text described a plant’s response to an external stimulus (Plant text), and the other
239	described internal distributions of heat in animals (Heat text).
240	Manipulations to increase cohesion included: (1) replacing ambiguous pronouns with nouns; (2) adding descriptive elabora-
241	tions that link unfamiliar concepts with familiar concepts; (3) adding connectives to specify the relationships between sentences or
242	ideas; (4) replacing or inserting words to increase the conceptual overlap between adjacent sentences; (5) adding topic headers;
243	(6) adding thematic sentences that serve to link each paragraph to the rest of the text and overall topic; and (7) changing sentence
244	structures to incorporate the additions and modiﬁcations. Appendix A contains an example of the low- and high-cohesion versions
245	of one of the texts (i.e., Heat text) in which the speciﬁc changes are marked.
246	Table 1 provides key text features related to text cohesion and text difﬁculty. As indicated in Table 1, the text revisions
247	increased the text length by approximately 50%. However, this level of increase in the text length is common to past text revision
248	studies (Beck et al., 1991; V oss & Silﬁes, 1996). The levels of cohesion and text difﬁculty of the two texts were monitored based
249	on text features that are known to be indicative of text cohesion and text difﬁculty. The features that are indicative of text cohesion
250	included argument overlap and Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA) cosine between sentences. The features, which were indicative of
251	more conventional text difﬁculty and readability, included word frequency and Flesch-Kincaid grade level ( Flesch, 1948).
252	Argument overlap between sentences represents the proportion of sentence pairs (adjacent or all) in the text that share an
253	argument. Hence, adjacent and all sentence-argument overlap measures represent local and global aspects of cohesion, respec-
254	tively. The LSA cosine is a proxy measure of conceptual similarity between linguistic units (Landauer & Dumais, 1997). The LSA
255	approximates conceptual similarity using a mathematical technique similar to a factor analysis. Thus, LSA cosine represents text
256	cohesion based on conceptual similarity, not solely by overlap of a particular word (i.e., argument overlap).
257	Text difﬁculty varies due to sentence complexity and vocabulary difﬁculty. Text difﬁculty is controlled by monitoring word
258	frequency and Flesch-Kincaid grade level. Word frequency is represented by the average word frequency of the lowest word
259	frequency word in each sentence. Hence, texts with lower word frequency tend to have rare, less common, content. Flesch-
260	Kincaid grade level is computed based on word length and sentence length and thus represents difﬁculty in terms of both sentence
261	length and word difﬁculty.
262	Monitoring of these text features was achieved using the Coh-Metrix tool ( Graesser et al., 2004 ), a computer-based tool that
263	calculates over 200 measures of text features. As indicated in Table 1, in both the Heat and Plant text, there were relatively large
264	increases in Argument Overlap Adjacent, and Argument Overlap All Sentences, as well as in the LSA Adjacent, and All
265	Sentences, from the low- to high-cohesion version of the texts. These increases indicate that the cohesion manipulation increased
266	text cohesion both locally and globally. On the other hand, the word frequency measure was relatively similar across the low- and
267	high-cohesion versions of the texts, which suggests similarity of overall content before and after the manipulation. Finally,
268	Flesch-Kincaid grade level increased as the result of cohesion manipulation. This was expected given that cohesion manipulation
269	tends to increase sentence length as the result of adding connectives and other cohesive elements.
270	2.2.2. Reading comprehension questions

273	when the question could be answered based on information explicitly stated within a sentence. A question was classiﬁed as a near-

300	movement to generate heat; (b) An endotherm would decrease the blood ﬂow to extremity to reduce the heat loss to cold
301	surroundings. Participants were awarded 0.5 point for each of these ideas. Participants’ responses to the open-ended questions
302	were scored independently by two raters, and then compared. Interrater reliability was greater than 95%. Discrepancies were
303	resolved by discussion.
304	2.2.3. Individual difference measures
305	Three types of individual difference measures were collected: reading skill, biology knowledge, and topic-speciﬁc knowledge
306	on the topic of the text. Reading skill was measured using the Nelson-Denny ( Brown, Fishco, & Hanna, 1993 ) reading
307	comprehension ability test. The Nelson-Denny reading comprehension ability test is a standardized reading comprehension test
308	for college level students. Cronbach’s alpha of the 38 questions based on 170 participants in this study was 0.90.
309	Biology knowledge was assessed with 21 multiple choice questions on anatomy, reproduction, and genetics, Cronbach’s alpha
310	of these 21 questions was 0.61. Topic-speciﬁc knowledge questions on plants and the distribution of heat was measured with
311	a total of 16 open-ended questions on the knowledge of plant biology (eight questions) and animal circulatory systems (eight
312	questions). Cronbach’s alpha of these 16 questions was 0.73. The questions in the topic-speciﬁc knowledge measure involved
313	information relevant to understanding the texts, but not provided in the texts.
314	2.3. Procedure
315	Participants were ﬁrst administered the biology knowledge test, followed by the Nelson-Denny reading skills assessment. Each
316	test (i.e., prior knowledge and Nelson-Denny) was restricted to 15 min. The participants then read the texts and answered the
317	questions, which were presented in a booklet. Participants read two texts, one low-cohesion text and one high-cohesion text, on
318	two different topics (i.e., plant or heat) and then answered comprehension questions for both texts, in the order of text presen-
319	tation. Pairing of the topic and cohesion was counter-balanced such that half of the participants read the Heat text in high-cohesion
320	condition (and the Plant text in low cohesion) and the other half read the Plant text in high-cohesion condition (and the Heat text
321	in low cohesion). Order of the presentation was also counter-balanced such that half of the participants read the high-cohesion text
322	ﬁrst and the other half read the low-cohesion text ﬁrst. Hence, participants were randomly assigned to four counter-balancing
323	conditions.
324	After the participants ﬁnished reading, the experimenter took the text away from the participants so that they could not refer to
325	the text to answer the questions. The decision to use memory-based comprehension questions was based on two factors. First,
326	several studies upon which the present study builds used this technique (Linderholm et al., 2001; O’Reilly & McNamara, 2007;
327	V oss & Silﬁes, 1996). Hence, use of this technique facilitated a more direct comparison with these studies. Second, in classrooms,
328	students read science texts to prepare for exams and access to the textbook was generally restricted. Therefore, answering
329	questions based on memory for what they had read better simulates a classroom situation.
330	The participants were not allowed to return to the previous section of questions after they had moved to the next set of
331	questions. Topic-speciﬁc prior knowledge questions were then presented. We presented the topic-speciﬁc knowledge questions
332	after the reading comprehension task because being exposed to questions closely related to the text topic might inﬂuence the
333	participants’ reading behavior. Care was taken to ensure that the texts did not contain answers to the topic-speciﬁc knowledge
334	questions.

339	test) for the two groups of participants.

# McNamara (2004) SERT Study Notes

## Main Finding
Training in self-explanation strategies helped readers with lower prior domain knowledge on text-based comprehension questions, but showed no benefit for higher-knowledge readers or on bridging inference questions.

## Key Details

**Sample & Design:**
- RCT with control group receiving self-explanation introduction but no strategy instruction
- N=42 (noted as potentially underpowered for some analyses)
- Target text: ~600-word passage on cellular mitosis, deliberately low-cohesion

**Six Self-Explanation Strategies Taught:**
Comprehension monitoring, paraphrase, bridging inference, elaboration, using logic, prediction

**"Self-Explanation Score" Components:**
Elaboration, logic, prediction, and comprehension monitoring (strategies going beyond text)

**Mechanism for Low-Knowledge Readers:**
Training encouraged use of "domain-general techniques ('logic') to make more inferences. These techniques are less relevant to higher-knowledge readers."

**Why Training Didn't Help High-Knowledge Readers:**
"The low-cohesion text naturally causes them to make inferences, and they're able to do it because of their prior knowledge."

**Strategy-Performance Associations:**
Elaboration, using logic, and distant bridging inferences showed stronger correlations with comprehension. Near bridging inferences showed no performance link.

**Other Findings:**
- Reading span/skill correlations with performance: null
- No effect of training on transfer-adjacent questions

# Overall Assessments for Elaborative Interrogation and Self-Explanation

## Elaborative Interrogation

The authors conclude: "We rate elaborative interrogation as having moderate utility." They explain that effects "have been shown across a relatively broad range of factual topics," though concerns remain about lengthier or more complex materials.

Regarding learners, the technique "has been consistently documented for learners at least as young as upper elementary age," with some evidence suggesting "benefits may be limited for learners with low levels of domain knowledge."

On assessment measures, "elaborative-interrogation effects have been firmly established on measures of associative memory administered after short delays," but "firm conclusions about the extent to which elaborative interrogation benefits comprehension or...persist across longer delays await further research."

The authors note that "further research demonstrating the efficacy of elaborative interrogation in representative educational contexts would also be useful," emphasizing that the need for additional research on generalizability is "primarily why this technique did not receive a high-utility rating."

## Self-Explanation

The assessment states: "We rate self-explanation as having moderate utility." A major strength is that "its effects have been shown across different content materials within task domains as well as across several different task domains."

Regarding age, effects "have been shown across an impressive age range," though "further work is needed to explore the extent to which these effects depend on learners' knowledge or ability level."

Importantly, "self-explanation effects have been shown across an impressive range of learning outcomes, including various measures of memory, comprehension, and transfer." However, "further research is needed to establish the durability of these effects across educationally relevant delays and to establish the efficacy of self-explanation in representative educational contexts."

A final concern involves "nontrivial time demands associated with self-explanation, at least at the dosages examined in most of the research."

# Baye et al. (2019) Secondary Reading Meta-Analysis

**Study Overview:**
The analysis examined 69 studies (62 randomized controlled trials, 7 quasi-experiments) evaluating 51 secondary reading programs using rigorous experimental designs.

**Program Categories with Positive Outcomes:**

The review identified several effective approaches:
- One-to-one and small-group tutoring
- Cooperative learning methods
- Whole-school reforms including teacher teams
- Writing-focused programs
- Programs emphasizing social studies/science content
- Structured strategy instruction
- Personalized and rotation-based approaches for struggling readers

**Key Finding on Technology and Extended Instruction:**

Notably, "programs that provide a daily extra period of reading and those utilizing technology were no more effective, on average, than programs that did not provide these resources."

**Overall Conclusion:**

The research suggests that "secondary readers benefit more from socially and cognitively engaging instruction than from additional reading periods or technology," indicating that instructional quality and engagement matter more than increased time or technological resources alone.

**Citation:**
Baye, A., Lake, C., Inns, A. & Slavin, R. E. (2019). *Reading Research Quarterly*, 54(2), 133-166.

# Meta-Analysis: Integrated Literacy and Content-Area Instruction

## Study Characteristics
The meta-analysis included **35 studies** (32 peer-reviewed articles, 3 dissertations) involving **13,289 students** in kindergarten through Grade 5. Studies spanned **primary grades (K-2)** with 13 studies and **upper elementary (3-5)** with 20 studies, plus 2 spanning both ranges.

## Effect Sizes Summary

**Vocabulary outcomes (n=36 effect sizes):**
- Overall: g = 0.91, 95% CI [0.34, 1.45], p < .01 (large effect)
- Researcher-developed: g = 0.86, CI [0.33, 1.38], p < .01
- Standardized measures: g = 0.64, CI [−1.59, 2.88], p = .42 (not significant)

**Reading comprehension (n=149 effect sizes):**
- Overall: g = 0.40, 95% CI [0.19, 0.62], p < .001 (large effect)
- Researcher-developed: g = 0.54, CI [0.17, 0.92], p < .01
- Standardized measures: g = 0.25, CI [0.04, 0.46], p < .05

**Content knowledge (supplementary analysis, n=55):**
- Overall: g = 0.89, 95% CI [0.54, 1.23], p < .001 (large effect)
- Researcher-developed: g = 0.94, CI [0.53, 1.34], p < .001
- Standardized measures: g = 0.68, CI [−0.38, 1.74], p = .13 (not significant)

## Key Findings

**Proximal vs. Distal Measures:**
Research-developed measures "highly aligned to the intervention displayed a significant overall effect" for vocabulary, while less-aligned measures did not show significant effects. Standardized measures consistently showed smaller or non-significant effects.

**What Works Clearinghouse Standards:**
Among moderator analyses with adequate statistical power (≥80%), "no statistically significant moderators were identified" for research design features or intervention characteristics predicting vocabulary or comprehension outcomes.

**Publication Bias:**
Sensitivity analysis indicated effect sizes were robust. For vocabulary, "no possible level of publication bias could attenuate the effect size to zero." Similar robustness appeared for comprehension outcomes.

**Science vs. Social Studies:**
The analysis did not find significant differences between science-focused and social studies-focused integrated instruction, though social studies showed a larger vocabulary effect (g = 2.18) in one comparison.

**Developer-Conducted Research:**
The analysis did not explicitly separate developer-conducted from independent studies as a moderator, though quality of research design was examined without significant moderation effects.

**Title:** How College Students Use AI to Navigate Course Readings: Evidence from an Eight-Week Study

**Authors:** Yue Fu, Joel Wester, Niels van Berkel, Alexis Hiniker

**N:** 15 undergraduates (from 21 enrolled, 18 consented, 3 excluded for minimal engagement)

Students employed AI primarily for comprehension support (59.6% of prompts), requesting summaries and explanations rather than engaging in reasoning. Notably, "72% of sessions contained exactly three prompts, which was the required minimum." Students showed limited investment in prompt quality, with only 4.3% incorporating taught engineering strategies.

Within individual sessions, students demonstrated natural cognitive progression from comprehension toward reasoning, yet this "progression was truncated" as most stopped at the assignment minimum. Across eight weeks, engagement patterns remained stable despite course instruction on effective AI use, suggesting established habits resisted change.

## Self-Report vs. Measured Behavior

A striking disconnect emerged: students articulated clear awareness that "effective prompting required effort and yielded better results," yet rarely applied this knowledge. This intention-behavior gap reveals that intellectual understanding did not translate into sustained practice, with efficiency consistently prioritized over deeper engagement.

# Shanahan's Argument: Instructional Level vs. Grade Level Text

## Evidence Against Instructional Level Theory

Shanahan cites several studies demonstrating that instructional-level placement provides no learning advantage:

- **Morgan, Wilcox, & Eldredge (2000)**: First experimental study showing "kids made greater progress when taught reading with more challenging books"
- **O'Connor, Swanson, & Geraghty (2010)**: Found improvement in reading rate occurred with difficult texts
- **Brown (2018)**: Reached similar conclusions about challenging text benefits
- **TNTP (2024)**: Research showing "schools with the greatest achievement gains teach with grade level texts"

## Evidence For Grade Level Text

**ACT Report (2006)** - Most significant: Analyzed 563,000 students and concluded: "performance on complex texts is the clearest differentiator in reading between students who are likely to be ready for college and those who are not"

## Origin of Instructional Level Concept

Shanahan traces the theory to **Emmett Betts (1946)**, who based it on an unpublished doctoral study by P.A. Kilgallon. Crucially, Shanahan obtained Kilgallon's study and found it "included no evidence showing that teaching at an instructional level gave students any learning advantage."

## Overall Conclusion

Students should read grade-level texts with appropriate teacher scaffolding, not texts matched to perceived reading levels. This approach maximizes learning rather than minimizing teaching demands.

# Study Design Overview

## Study Structure
This two-year experimental study compared three comprehension instruction approaches with fifth graders in a low-performing urban district. The research involved **standardized lessons on common texts** to enable precise comparison of effects.

## Participants

**Year 1:** 119 students across 6 intact classrooms (44 content, 37 strategies, 38 basal)

**Year 2:** 116 students across same 6 classrooms with random assignment balanced by race and special education status (41 content, 38 strategies, 37 basal)

All students were fifth graders; 58% African American; 49% qualified for free/reduced lunch.

## The Three Conditions

1. **Content Approach:** Focused student attention on text meaning through open-ended questions like "What's going on here?" based on Questioning the Author (QtA)

2. **Strategies Approach:** Taught explicit procedures—summarizing, predicting, inferring, question generation, comprehension monitoring—with teacher reminders about strategy application

3. **Basal Comprehension Control:** Used scripted questions from the basal reader's teacher edition, limited to during-reading comprehension items

## Duration & Design

- **Year 1:** Five narrative lessons over five weeks (45-75 minutes weekly within 90-minute reading blocks)
- **Year 2:** Five narrative lessons plus three expository lessons; added transfer tasks

All lessons were scripted, teacher-delivered, whole-class instruction with interspersed questions during reading.

## Outcome Measures

### Lesson-Text Comprehension
- **Sentence Verification Technique (SVT):** Recognition-based; items tested paraphrases, local inferences, global inferences across five narratives and three expository texts
- **Oral Recall:** Scored for length (content units) and quality (major/supporting/detail units); collected for two narratives and two expository texts

### Lesson Discourse Analysis
- Proportion of text-based talk (students and teachers)
- Words per student response

### Beyond-Lesson Assessments
- **Comprehension Monitoring Task:** Pre/posttest identifying inconsistencies in nonlesson texts
- **Strategies Knowledge Task:** Multiple-choice questions on four strategies (question generation, prediction, inference, summarization)
- **Transfer Task (Year 2 only):** Five-lesson sequence with graduated responsibility, assessed via individual oral recall on final silently-read text

## Statistical Results

### Year 1

**SVT (Lesson Texts):** No significant differences across approaches on total scores or item types (all p > .62; means 76.94%-81.20% correct)

**Narrative Recall:**
- Length: Content (M=16.20) > Strategies (M=10.33), p=.001; Basal (M=14.13) > Strategies, p=.05
- Quality: Content (M=33.40) > Strategies (M=22.97), p=.001; Basal (M=29.20) not significantly different from others

**Lesson Discourse:**
- Student text-based talk: Content 94% > Strategies 75% (p=.005); Basal 86% > Strategies (p=.002)
- Teacher text-based talk: Content 50% > Strategies 27% (p<.001); Basal 47% > Strategies (p<.001)
- Words per response: Content (M=24.38) > Strategies (M=11.74) and Basal (M=13.29), p<.001

**Comprehension Monitoring:** All groups improved pre to post (p=.003), no significant approach differences (p=.638)

**Strategies Knowledge:** No significant differences (p=.16)

### Year 2

**SVT Narratives:** No significant differences (all p > .67)

**SVT Expository:** No significant differences (all p > .31)

**Narrative Recall:**
- Length: Content (M=17.32) > Strategies (M=11.77), p=.005
- Quality: Content (M=33.76) > Strategies (M=24.79), p=.01

**Expository Recall:** No length/quality differences; Knowledge probes showed Content (M=4.27) and Basal (M=4.30) > Strategies (M=3.15), p=.02

**Lesson Discourse (4 lessons combined):**
- Student text-based talk: Content 97% > Strategies 66% (p<.0005); Content > Basal 84% (p=.002); Basal > Strategies (p<.0005)
- Teacher text-based talk: Content 42% > Strategies 30% (p=.04) and Basal 27% (p=.01)
- Words per response: Content (M=26.55) > Strategies (M=9.50) and Basal (M=13.84), p<.0005

The Content approach explicitly derived from QtA methodology. The researchers noted that "content instruction focused student attention on the content of the text through general, meaning-based questions" and based their approach on QtA, which connects to Kintsch's construction-integration model of text processing emphasizing coherence development.

# Word Generation: Evidence Summary

## Study Designs

The research employed a **quasi-experimental design** comparing five schools implementing Word Generation with three comparison schools in Boston Public Schools (2007-2008). A subsequent **longitudinal follow-up study** tracked vocabulary retention and consolidation across multiple assessment points.

## Sample Characteristics

The quasi-experiment included 1,016 students across grades 6-8:
- 697 students in treatment schools (349 girls, 348 boys)
- 319 students in comparison schools (162 girls, 157 boys)
- 438 language minority students total (287 treatment, 151 comparison)
- Predominantly low-income populations

Treatment schools had lower baseline performance than comparison schools (56% failing vs. 45%).

## Vocabulary Effect Sizes

The average effect size for program participation was **0.49** on researcher-developed vocabulary assessments. Notably, "participation in 20–22 weeks of the curriculum was equivalent to two years of incidental learning."

Language minority students showed faster improvement rates than English-only peers in treatment schools.

## Reading Comprehension Findings

A significant interaction emerged between treatment and vocabulary improvement when predicting MCAS scores. Students gaining most from Word Generation achieved higher MCAS performance than peers with similar vocabulary gains from other sources. The treatment school model explained 49% of variance in comprehension outcomes compared to 41% for comparison schools.

The longitudinal follow-up confirmed vocabulary gains persisted through summer and subsequent school year.

**Citation:** Timothy Shanahan, Douglas Fisher, and Nancy Frey. "The Challenge of Challenging Text." *Educational Leadership*, Vol. 69, No. 6 (March 1, 2012).

**Arguments on Text Difficulty:**
The authors argue that text complexity results from multiple factors beyond traditional readability formulas. Rather than viewing challenging texts as obstacles, they advocate treating difficulty as "akin to weight or resistance in an exercise program" to build robust reading skills.

**Key Complexity Factors:**
- Vocabulary (domain-specific and general academic terms)
- Sentence structure and embedding
- Coherence and cohesive links
- Organizational patterns (narrative, compare-contrast, problem-solution)
- Reader's background knowledge

Teachers should guide students through increasingly complex texts through three components: skill-building (fluency, vocabulary instruction), establishing clear reading purpose, and fostering motivation.

The authors reference only one empirical study: "Stahl, S. A., & Fairbanks, M. M. (1986). The effects of vocabulary instruction: A model-based meta-analysis. *Review of Educational Research, 56*, 72–110."
