## PACT Research — Findings

**Bottom line on the premise you gave me: the "~0.40 content knowledge / ~0.21 content reading comprehension" numbers are NOT from Vaughn et al. (2013).** The 2013 study reported 0.17 / 0.29 / 0.20. The 0.40 comes from a different, later trial (Vaughn et al., 2017 JEP, the EL study), and 0.21 is most likely the What Works Clearinghouse's recomputed effect size for the *standardized* Gates-MacGinitie in the 2013 study. Details below.

---

### 1. Vaughn et al. (2013) — the original 8th-grade efficacy study

**Exact citation:** Vaughn, S., Swanson, E. A., Roberts, G., Wanzek, J., Stillman-Spisak, S. J., Solis, M., & Simmons, D. (2013). Improving reading comprehension and social studies knowledge in middle school. *Reading Research Quarterly, 48*(1), 77–93. doi:10.1002/rrq.039 (ERIC EJ996121)

**Design:** Two-stage randomization within teacher. Eighth graders were randomly assigned to 27 social studies classes taught by 5 teachers; then each teacher's class sections were randomly assigned to PACT or business-as-usual, so every teacher taught both conditions. Two Texas middle schools. Three 10-day U.S. history units.

**Sample:** Article abstract: n = 261 treatment, n = 158 comparison (419 total). WWC's analytic samples were smaller and varied by outcome: 203–218 intervention students in 16 classrooms vs. 119–126 comparison students in 11 classrooms.

**Effect sizes as reported by the authors:**
- Content acquisition (ASK Knowledge Acquisition, researcher-designed): **ES = 0.17**
- Content reading comprehension (ASK/MASK Reading Comprehension, researcher-designed): **ES = 0.29**
- Standardized reading comprehension (Gates-MacGinitie): **ES = 0.20**

All three were statistically significant in the original paper. **Metric:** the authors computed effect sizes as the model-derived intervention coefficient divided by the pooled within-group SD (a Cohen's-d-type estimate, not a bias-corrected Hedges g). The paper does not label them "Hedges g."

**Distinguishing the 2013/2015 papers** (there are at least four easily confused):
- Vaughn et al. (2013), *RRQ* 48(1), 77–93 — grade 8, Study 1, the original efficacy trial (above).
- Vaughn, S., Roberts, G., Swanson, E. A., Wanzek, J., Fall, A.-M., & Stillman-Spisak, S. J. (2015). Improving middle-school students' knowledge and comprehension in social studies: A replication. *Educational Psychology Review, 27*(1), 31–50. (ERIC EJ1051051) — grade 8, **85 classes, 19 teachers**. Knowledge/vocabulary favored treatment at post and both follow-ups (4 and 8 weeks); **no significant differences on reading comprehension.** I could not verify the exact per-outcome effect sizes in this paper from open sources.
- Wanzek, J., Swanson, E. A., Roberts, G., Vaughn, S., & Kent, S. C. (2015). Promoting acceleration of comprehension and content through text in high school social studies classes. *JREE, 8*(2), 169–188. (EJ1057099) — grade 11 (see §2).
- Swanson, E., Wanzek, J., Vaughn, S., Roberts, G., & Fall, A.-M. (2015). Improving reading comprehension and social studies knowledge among middle school students with disabilities. *Exceptional Children, 81*(4), 426–442. (EJ1065065) — SWD subsample (see §6).

Note: some search engines cross-contaminate these — I saw the 0.17/0.29/0.20 triple falsely attributed to the Wanzek 2015 high school paper. Do not trust that.

---

### 2. Replications and the scale-up

| Study | Grade / Subject | Sample | Content knowledge ES | Content reading comp ES | Standardized reading ES |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Vaughn et al. 2013, *RRQ* 48(1) 77–93 (Study 1) | 8 / U.S. history | 419 students, 27 classes, 5 teachers | 0.17 | 0.29 | 0.20 |
| Vaughn et al. 2015, *Educ Psych Rev* 27(1) 31–50 (Study 2, replication) | 8 / social studies | 85 classes, 19 teachers | favored tx at post + 4wk + 8wk (exact ES not verified) | n.s. | n.s. |
| Wanzek et al. 2015, *JREE* 8(2) 169–188 | **11** / U.S. history | 41 classes (23 tx), 14 teachers | **0.36 post; 0.22 at 4 wk; 0.24 at 12 wk** | n.s. | n.s. |
| Vaughn et al. 2017, *JEP* 109(1) 22–34 (Study 3) | 8 / U.S. history | **1,629** students (845 tx / 784 comp), 94 classes, 18 teachers, 7 schools | **0.40** (p<.01) | **0.20** (p<.05) | n.s. |
| Roberts et al. 2023, *JEP* 115(5) 665–682 — **the IES scale-up/effectiveness trial** | 8 / U.S. history | **48 schools, 135 teachers, 7,183 students, 16 states + DC** | **g = 0.46** post; **g = 0.40** at 9-wk follow-up (SATE) | **g = 0.15, n.s.** | **g = 0.14, n.s.** |
| Vaughn et al. 2025/2026, *RASE* (doi 10.1177/07419325241310499) | 8 / social studies | 893 students, 28 teachers, 20 schools | **0.07 n.s.** post; 0.08 n.s. follow-up | **−0.10 n.s.** | not reported |

**IES scale-up specifics:** "The Scale Up of Promoting Adolescents' Comprehension of Text," IES grant R305A160026 (the older IES record ID=1799 is the same line of work). **Randomization was at the SCHOOL level** (24 treatment / 24 control), using stratified balanced sampling to build a nationally representative-ish sample of middle schools teaching U.S. history. Population-average estimates: posttest g = 0.45 (weighted mixed effects) / 0.37 (weighted OLS); follow-up g = 0.53 (WME) / 0.33 (robust variance estimation). Metric explicitly **Hedges' g**.

**Did the larger effectiveness trial find SMALLER effects? No — on content knowledge it found LARGER effects.** 0.46 (effectiveness, 48 schools) vs. 0.17 (original efficacy trial) and 0.40 (Study 3). This is the explicit thesis of Vaughn, S., & Wanzek, J. (2024). Promoting adolescents' comprehension of text: Efficacy and effectiveness. *Remedial and Special Education, 45*(1), 58–67 — they set out to explain why "the typically expected differential effect sizes between efficacy and effectiveness studies were not evident," attributing it partly to unit of randomization (within-teacher class randomization in the efficacy trials likely produced treatment diffusion, deflating efficacy estimates; school randomization in the scale-up removed it). I could not access the full text of the 2024 RASE paper (SAGE 403), so I cannot confirm whether it contains a consolidated effect-size table.

**The genuine attenuation is on comprehension, not knowledge.** Content reading comprehension went 0.29 (2013) → n.s. (2015 replication) → n.s. (grade 11) → 0.20 (2017) → **0.15 n.s.** (scale-up). Standardized reading went 0.20 significant (2013) → n.s. everywhere after → **0.14 n.s.** (scale-up). The one significant standardized-reading finding in the entire program is the original 2013 trial and it has never replicated.

Also relevant, and a real caution about generality: the most recent trial (RASE 2025/2026, 893 students, 20 schools, 2021–22) found **essentially null effects for the full sample** (0.07, 0.08, −0.10).

---

### 3. Science-specific PACT

**I found no published RCT of PACT in science.** Every efficacy/effectiveness trial I could locate is social studies / U.S. history (grades 8 and 11).

The one science-adjacent item is **PACT Plus** (Meadows Center + University of Maryland, funded by OSED/OSEP 2015–2019, DC Public Schools), a tiered model in which **science, social studies, and ELA teachers** in grades 6–8 received PD to implement PACT, alongside RISD for special educators; >1,500 students with disabilities. This is an implementation/scale-up demonstration project, **not a randomized science efficacy trial, and I found no published effect sizes for it.** Searches of Elizabeth Swanson's CV surfaced no PACT-in-science empirical paper (her science publications are national survey studies of elementary science instruction, unrelated to PACT).

Conclusion: **treat PACT as a social studies/history intervention.** Any claim of science efficacy is unverified.

---

### 4. What Works Clearinghouse

**Citation:** What Works Clearinghouse (2013, August). *WWC review of the report "Improving reading comprehension and social studies knowledge in middle school."* WWC Single Study Review. ERIC ED544200.

**Rating:** "The research described in this report **meets WWC evidence standards without reservations**" — a well-implemented randomized controlled trial. (This is the strongest possible WWC rating.)

**WWC-recomputed effect sizes (these differ from the authors' published numbers):**

*Reading comprehension domain:*
- Gates-MacGinitie Reading Comprehension subtest: n = 322, mean difference 0.23, **ES = 0.21**, improvement index **+8**, p = 0.01
- ASK Reading Comprehension in Social Studies: n = 339, mean difference 0.43, **ES = 0.35**, improvement index **+14**, p < 0.01
- Domain average: **ES = 0.28, improvement index +11**, statistically significant

*Social studies domain:*
- ASK Knowledge Acquisition subtest: n = 339, mean difference 0.57, **ES = 0.31**, improvement index **+12**, p = 0.02
- Domain average: **ES = 0.31, improvement index +12**, statistically significant

WWC uses **Hedges' g** by convention. Note the discrepancy: WWC's 0.31 vs. the authors' 0.17 on content knowledge — WWC computes from unadjusted posttest means/SDs while the authors used multilevel-model-derived coefficients. **If someone cites "0.21" for PACT reading comprehension, it is almost certainly the WWC's Gates-MacGinitie figure from this review, not a content-comprehension effect.**

**A second, separate WWC record exists** (WWC Study 85559) for Vaughn et al. (2017, the EL study, n = 1,629): rated **"Meets WWC standards with reservations"** — a *compromised* cluster RCT that nonetheless satisfied baseline equivalence. WWC's June 2021 single study review found **indeterminate effects for reading comprehension** (no significant differences for ELs or non-ELs on any instrument) but **statistically significant positive effects for social studies achievement** (improvement index +13 for 359 ELs; +14 for 877 non-ELs). Evidence Tier 2 (moderate). An earlier February 2018 IES performance-measure review had scored reading comprehension as significantly positive for the full sample (improvement index +13) — WWC subsequently reversed that reading conclusion. That reversal is worth flagging to anyone citing PACT for reading gains.

---

### 5. Standardized/norm-referenced vs. researcher-designed measures — the critical distinction

**Researcher-designed (developed by the PACT team, aligned to the exact units taught):**
- **ASK** (Assessment of Social Studies Knowledge) Knowledge Acquisition — 42-item multiple choice
- **ASK-RC / MASK** (Modified ASK) Reading Comprehension — 21 items over 3 passages, content-embedded

**Standardized/norm-referenced:**
- **Gates-MacGinitie Reading Tests, 4th ed.**, Reading Comprehension subtest
- State test (STAAR social studies) in one study

**Pattern, stated plainly: virtually every positive PACT effect is on the researcher-designed content measures.**

- Content knowledge (ASK, researcher-designed): significant in almost every trial, 0.17–0.51.
- Content reading comprehension (MASK/ASK-RC, researcher-designed and content-bound): significant in 2013 (0.29) and 2017 (0.20); **null in the 2015 replication, the grade-11 study, the 2023 scale-up (g = 0.15), the 2016 SWD study (0.04), and the 2025 study (−0.10).**
- **Standardized Gates-MacGinitie: significant only once, in the original 2013 trial (0.20 / WWC 0.21). Null in every subsequent study, including the 7,183-student scale-up (g = 0.14, n.s.).**

So: PACT is well-supported as a **content-knowledge** intervention and is **not** supported as an intervention that raises general, norm-referenced reading comprehension. The MASK/ASK-RC "reading comprehension" outcome should not be read as generalized comprehension — it uses passages on the taught content, so it is partly a knowledge measure.

---

### 6. English learners, students with disabilities, struggling readers

**English learners**
- Vaughn, S., Martinez, L. R., Wanzek, J., Roberts, G., Swanson, E., & Fall, A.-M. (2017). Improving content knowledge and comprehension for English language learners: Findings from a randomized control trial. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 109*(1), 22–34. n = 1,629 grade 8 (845 tx / 784 comp), 94 classes, 18 teachers, 7 schools, 3 districts; 26.7% current/recently exited ELs. **ASK content knowledge ES = 0.40 (p < .01); MASK content reading comprehension ES = 0.20 (p < .05); Gates-MacGinitie n.s.** ELs and non-ELs both benefited; **the proportion of ELs in the class moderated gains** (benefits clearest where class EL concentration was below roughly 12%). WWC's later review (Study 85559) rated the reading comprehension finding **indeterminate** for both ELs and non-ELs, while confirming social studies gains (+13 EL, +14 non-EL improvement index).
- Wanzek, J., Swanson, E., Vaughn, S., Roberts, G., & Fall, A.-M. (2016). English learner and non-English learner students with disabilities: Content acquisition and comprehension. *Exceptional Children, 82*(4), 428–442. n = 160 SWD (59 tx / 89 comp — note these don't sum to 160; 148 SWD in 94 classes appears in some descriptions, so the exact analytic n varies by outcome and I could not fully reconcile it). 52 ELs with disabilities (32.5%), 108 non-EL (67.5%). **ASK knowledge acquisition ES = 0.51; MASK reading comprehension ES = 0.04; Gates-MacGinitie ES = 0.02.** "The effect of treatment did not differ between EL and non-EL students."

**Students with disabilities**

(2015), *Exceptional Children* 81(4), 426–442: treatment n = 72, comparison n = 58. **Knowledge acquisition ES = 0.26; content reading comprehension ES = 0.34; standardized reading comprehension not significant.** (Two years of data pooled; described in some places as quasi-experimental.)

# Recommendation 3: Evidence Base Limitations and Key Findings

## Limitations of Evidence Base

The panel identifies several constraints in the research supporting extended discussion approaches:

1. **Small sample sizes**: The four quasi-experimental studies had "small" sample sizes, limiting generalizability.

2. **Outcome measurement issues**: A potential limitation noted is that "the quality of written responses to writing prompts was the outcome assessment, rather than a more direct standardized test of reading comprehension."

3. **Design quality variations**: Among the four quasi-experimental studies, only one "demonstrated pretest group equivalence" while the other three had "less rigorous designs with low internal validity."

4. **Text type focus**: "Most experimental studies of discussion-based approaches thus far have used narrative texts, a limitation in the research base at present," meaning findings may not generalize to expository content.

## Study Findings

The document does not report specific effect sizes or quantitative findings from Bird (1984), Heinl (1988), Reznitskaya et al. (2001), Yeazell (1982), or Applebee et al. (2003). These studies are cited as supporting evidence but without disclosed numerical results or effect size metrics in the provided text.

## 2. Archived / outdated / superseded labels
- **No practice guide on the WWC list carries any "archived," "outdated," "superseded," "withdrawn," or "reviewed under older standards" label.** The listing page shows only titles, dates, topics, and grade ranges. Guides that have been updated show a "(Revised …)" date instead — that is the only currency signal WWC applies.
- **Kamil et al. 2008, "Improving Adolescent Literacy" (https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/practiceguide/8): carries NO status label of any kind.** It is presented on equal footing with every other guide, is still listed on the active practice guides index, and its ERIC record (https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED502398) likewise shows no superseded/withdrawn note. Its report number is **NCEE 2008-4027**; PDF still live at https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/docs/practiceguide/adlit_pg_082608.pdf
- Caveat worth passing on: the guide's *evidence* was assessed under WWC standards from the 2007–2008 era (pre-Handbook 4.0/5.0). WWC documents that pre-2021 reviews used topic-specific protocols plus the then-current Handbook version (https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/handbooks), but it does not retroactively flag old guides. So "reviewed under older standards" is an accurate methodological description, not an official WWC label on that page.

## 3. Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4–9
- **Report number CONFIRMED: WWC 2022007.** (Verified via ERIC ED617876: https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED617876 — "Educator's Practice Guide. WWC 2022007". The IES page itself does not display the publication number in its HTML.)
- **Full citation:** Vaughn, S., Kieffer, M. J., McKeown, M., Reed, D. K., Sanchez, M., St. Martin, K., Wexler, J., Jayanthi, M., Gersten, R., Newman-Gonchar, R., Dimino, J., Taylor, M. J., Krowka, S., Haymond, K., Wavell, S., Lyskawa, J., Morgan, S., Keating, B., & Yañez, A. (2022, March). *Providing reading interventions for students in grades 4–9* (WWC 2022007). National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (Panel authors first; the Mathematica/Instructional Research Group research staff follow. WWC's own short form on the guide page is: "What Works Clearinghouse. (2022, March). *Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4–9*. Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education.")
- Full text PDF: https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Docs/PracticeGuide/WWC-practice-guide-reading-intervention-full-text.pdf ; summary: https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Docs/practiceguide/WWC-SummaryReadingInterven4-9.pdf ; ERIC mirror: https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED617876.pdf
- **Four recommendations and ratings:**
  1. Build students' decoding skills so they can read complex multisyllabic words — **Strong evidence**
  2. Provide purposeful fluency-building activities to help students read effortlessly — **Strong evidence**
  3. Routinely use a set of comprehension-building practices to help students make sense of the text (word/world knowledge, questioning, determining gist, comprehension monitoring) — **Strong evidence**
  4. Provide students with opportunities to practice making sense of stretch (challenging) text — **Moderate evidence**
- **Relationship to Kamil 2008:** Nothing on the WWC/IES guide page, in the ERIC metadata, or in the WWC listing states that the 2022 guide supersedes, replaces, or updates the 2008 guide. **No supersession is asserted anywhere by IES/WWC.** Both guides remain listed as current. The "builds on and updates" framing comes from third parties, not IES — e.g., Keys to Literacy (Joan Sedita): "It builds on and updates the findings from several older reports including the 2008 IES report *Improving Adolescent Literacy: Effective Classroom and Intervention Practices* (Kamil et al.)…" (https://keystoliteracy.com/blog/providing-reading-interventions-grades-4-9/). The Meadows Center announcement (https://meadowscenter.org/new-wwc-practice-guide-on-reading-interventions-for-grades-4-9-is-released/) makes no reference to the 2008 guide at all. I could not machine-extract the 2022 PDF's reference list (server returns the PDF as binary and no PDF-to-text tooling is available in this environment; the archive.org djvu text URL 404s), so **whether Kamil et al. 2008 appears in the 2022 guide's reference list is unverified** — treat any claim that it does as unconfirmed. The two guides also differ in scope: Kamil 2008 covers general classroom adolescent literacy instruction grades 4–12 including motivation/engagement and extended discussion; WWC 2022007 covers *intervention* for struggling readers grades 4–9 specifically.

## 4. 2020+ guides on secondary/disciplinary/content-area literacy, science literacy, secondary writing, or ELs in content areas
**There are none.** No IES/WWC practice guide released 2020 or later addresses disciplinary/content-area literacy, science literacy, secondary writing, or English learners in content areas. The 2020+ set is entirely: K–5 behavior (2024), early childhood school readiness (2022), grades 4–9 reading intervention (2022), postsecondary advising (2021), community college career pathways (2021), elementary math intervention (2021). Friedrich, Katie Greene, James S. Kim, Carol Booth Olson; prepared by Mathematica under contract ED-IES-13-C-0010. Recommendations:
  1. Explicitly teach appropriate writing strategies using a Model-Practice-Reflect instructional cycle — **Strong evidence**
  2. Integrate writing and reading to emphasize key writing features — **Moderate evidence**
  3. Use assessments of student writing to inform instruction and feedback — **Minimal evidence**

- Adolescent/content literacy: still Kamil 2008 (#8).
- No WWC practice guide on science literacy exists at all.

## 5. IES/WWC status changes in 2025 affecting availability
- **February 2025:** DOGE terminated a large tranche of IES contracts, including the contract implementing IES's digital modernization plan, and the What Works Clearinghouse Supporting and Analyzing Grantee Evaluations (WWC-SAGE) contract was terminated before support to grantees began (https://ies.ed.gov/use-work/evaluations/what-works-clearinghouse-supporting-and-analyzing-grantee-evaluations-wwc-sage ; NCTQ statement: https://www.nctq.org/press/nctq-statement-on-institute-of-education-sciences-ies-contracts/).
- **March 11, 2025:** ED reduction in force cut roughly half of the Department's ~4,133 staff; IES was hit hardest, with reporting that ~90% of the research arm's staff were eliminated (roughly 100 of ~120 IES employees), and close to $900M in research contracts/grants terminated (https://www.faegredrinker.com/en/insights/publications/2025/3/mass-layoffs-at-the-us-department-of-education-impacts-on-higher-education ; https://www.bu.edu/articles/2025/department-of-education-cuts-high-risk-low-reward/).
- **Practical effect on the guides: they remain online and accessible.** Every ies.ed.gov practice guide URL I fetched in this session resolved normally, including the index, guide #8, guide #22, and guide #29, plus the hosted PDFs. I found no announcement of removal, archiving, or migration of practice guides.
- **The forward-looking effect is production, not availability:** the most recent practice guide is December 2024 (#31), and with the WWC contract structure disrupted there is no evidence of new or revised guides since. This is the operative risk for anything relying on an updated adolescent-literacy guide — a refresh of Kamil 2008 is not in visible progress. Also worth noting for link durability: IES has been reorganizing URLs (content now also appears under `ies.ed.gov/use-work/...`), so `ncee/wwc/...` paths should be verified before being cited in durable documents.

## 3. Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4–9
- **Report number CONFIRMED: WWC 2022007.** (Verified via ERIC ED617876: https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED617876 — "Educator's Practice Guide. WWC 2022007". The IES page itself does not display the publication number in its HTML.)

- **Four recommendations and ratings:**
  1. Build students' decoding skills so they can read complex multisyllabic words — **Strong evidence**
  2. Provide purposeful fluency-building activities to help students read effortlessly — **Strong evidence**
  3. Routinely use a set of comprehension-building practices to help students make sense of the text (word/world knowledge, questioning, determining gist, comprehension monitoring) — **Strong evidence**

## 5. IES/WWC status changes in 2025 affecting availability
- **February 2025:** DOGE terminated a large tranche of IES contracts, including the contract implementing IES's digital modernization plan, and the What Works Clearinghouse Supporting and Analyzing Grantee Evaluations (WWC-SAGE) contract was terminated before support to grantees began (https://ies.ed.gov/use-work/evaluations/what-works-clearinghouse-supporting-and-analyzing-grantee-evaluations-wwc-sage ; NCTQ statement: https://www.nctq.org/press/nctq-statement-on-institute-of-education-sciences-ies-contracts/).

- **The forward-looking effect is production, not availability:** the most recent practice guide is December 2024 (#31), and with the WWC contract structure disrupted there is no evidence of new or revised guides since. This is the operative risk for anything relying on an updated adolescent-literacy guide — a refresh of Kamil 2008 is not in visible progress. # Citation Details

**Authors:** Lisa van der Sande, Roel van Steensel, S. Fikrat-Wevers, Lidia R. Arends

**Year:** 2023

**Journal:** Educational Psychology Review

**Volume:** 35

**Issue:** Not specified in provided data

**Pages:** 1-38

**Abstract:**

"Many students have low reading motivation. Based on (reading) motivation theories, several mechanisms are distinguished that can foster reading motivation. Our goal in this meta-analysis was to examine the effects of theory-driven reading motivation interventions in school on students' reading motivation and reading comprehension as well as to test which mechanisms are particularly effective in fostering motivation and comprehension. We conducted a literature search in ten online databases and identified 39 relevant effect studies. Positive effects on affirming motivations (d = 0.38), extrinsic motivations (d = 0.42), combined motivations (d = 0.17), and reading comprehension (d = 0.27) were found. The effect on undermining motivations (d = −0.01) was not significant. In particular, interventions that aimed to trigger interest had positive effects on affirming motivations and reading comprehension. Furthermore, effects on affirming motivations were larger if the total duration of the intervention was longer and if the share of boys in the sample was higher. Interventions delivered by researchers had larger effects on reading comprehension than interventions delivered by teachers. Finally, effects on reading comprehension were larger for primary schoolers than for secondary schoolers and larger for typical readers than for struggling readers. Implications for practitioners, policymakers, and researchers are discussed."

# Snow & O'Connor's Critique of Close Reading

## Core Argument Against Close Reading

Snow and O'Connor contend that close reading, as promoted by the Common Core State Standards, is based on a flawed premise and risks creating unintended negative consequences despite well-intentioned origins.

## Four Main Objections

**1. The "Level Playing Field" Claim Is False**

The authors argue the central justification—that close reading eliminates background knowledge differences—is fundamentally wrong. They state: "It's an appealing fantasy, but that's all it can ever be." Reading comprehension research demonstrates that "lack of background knowledge and lack of familiarity with key vocabulary" are the primary reasons readers struggle, not addressable through text-alone analysis.

**2. Tedium and Demotivation**

Close reading's painstaking nature threatens struggling middle and high school readers already experiencing plummeting motivation. The authors worry that heavy reliance on close reading may "actually worsen the conditions we seek to change."

**3. Privileging Text-Based Evidence**

Restricting legitimate evidence sources to the text itself is inappropriate. "Prior knowledge, moral judgment, social norms, and other sources of information and analysis constitute legitimate bases from which to argue."

**4. Crowding Out Classroom Discussion**

The most serious concern: narrow close reading emphasis may eliminate productive classroom discussion, which research identifies as a "predictor of good student outcomes."

## Claims About Evidence Base

The authors cite Kintsch (1988), defining comprehension as "the process of integrating newly acquired information with pre-existing schemas." They reference the RAND Reading Study Group (2002) definition emphasizing "simultaneous extraction and construction of meaning through interaction with text," noting close reading foregrounds extraction while ignoring reader differences and sociocultural context.

## Background Knowledge and Text Limitations

A central argument: background knowledge is indispensable and cannot be suppressed. The Gettysburg Address example illustrates how "layers of meaning" from knowledge of the Declaration of Independence remain "completely inaccessible to students who don't know" relevant historical context.

The authors emphasize: "Texts with too many unfamiliar words are simply not comprehended, and if not comprehended cannot be a source of new word learning."

## Pre-Reading and Frontloading

Snow and O'Connor acknowledge that some close reading advocates recommend preceding close reading with relevant content access. However, they identify a practical problem: teachers must "predict what required background knowledge each of 20 to 25 different readers lacks" without "previewing the content of the text in any way"—an unrealistic demand.

They argue that restricting discussions of academic vocabulary to only "tier three" or technical terms is problematic, as disagreement exists about word classifications and insufficient vocabulary knowledge prevents comprehension and new learning.

## Recommendations

**Productive Close Reading Should Be:**

- Limited in duration: Wong Fillmore and Fillmore (2012) demonstrated value in "carefully focusing on and deconstructing a sentence...limited to one sentence and 10-15 minutes per day"
- Collaborative: conducted "in groups, with teacher support, and considerable peer discussion" rather than isolated work
- Embedded contextually: deployed "as a tool within the context of broader academically productive classroom discussion"
- Purposeful: used "in achieving purposes other than simply learning to do close reading"

**Broader Instructional Approach:**

Students need "lots of opportunities to access relevant background knowledge through videos, below-grade level texts, PowerPoint presentations, lectures, and other sources" to build the conceptual structures that motivate engagement.

The authors advocate combining close reading with "far-reaching discussions" that leverage "personal knowledge to readings of other texts, or from religious or cultural traditions to moral stances."

## Specific Programs and Studies Cited

- **Wong Fillmore & Fillmore (2012)**: Demonstrated effective collaborative close reading focused on single sentences with ELL and former ELL students
- **Bransford & Johnson (1972)**: Showed that providing informative titles greatly eases comprehension
- **Hart & Risley (1995)**: Documented vocabulary gaps between children of educated versus less educationally advantaged parents, rooted in conceptual differences
- **Guthrie, Alao & Rinehart (1997)**: Found motivation for reading plummets in middle grades, especially for struggling readers

The authors also reference Applebee, Langer, Nystrand & Gamoran (2003) and Murphy, Wilkinson, Soter, Hennessey & Alexander (2009) regarding discussion as a predictor of positive outcomes.

# Research Synthesis on Text Complexity in Elementary Grades

## Citation
Amendum, S. J., Conradi, K., & Hiebert, E. H. (2017). Does text complexity matter in the elementary grades? A research synthesis of text difficulty and elementary students' reading fluency and comprehension. *Educational Research Review*, 59 pages.

## Studies Reviewed
**26 empirical studies** published between 1970-2015, representing four design types:
- 18 correlational (69%)
- 4 quasi-experimental (15%)
- 3 experimental (12%)
- 1 single-subject (4%)

## Key Findings

### Text Difficulty vs. Fluency
**Accuracy:** "with only one exception...there was a negative relationship between text difficulty level and students' reading accuracy." Increased difficulty particularly affected struggling and beginning readers.

**Rate:** 73% of studies (11 of 15) showed decreased reading rates with increased text difficulty, though the effect diminished for skilled readers in later grades.

**Prosody:** Lower-skilled readers' prosody declined with difficulty; higher-skilled readers sometimes improved, marshaling "prosodic resources" for complex texts.

### Text Difficulty vs. Comprehension
- **53.85%** (7 studies) found negative relationships
- **38.46%** (5 studies) found no significant relationship
- **7.69%** (1 study) found optimal moderate difficulty

"No study indicated that increased text difficulty was related to an increase in students' comprehension."

## Notable Studies Mentioned

**O'Connor et al. (2010):** Students reading aloud to supportive adults improved rates regardless of difficulty; found no comprehension differences between difficulty levels.

**Morgan et al. (2000):** Intervention study with peer dyad reading found no relationship between text difficulty and comprehension despite improved overall performance.

**Stahl & Heubach (2005):** Referenced for demonstrating "benefits of reading difficult texts with others within supportive instructional contexts."

**Kuhn & Stahl (2003):** Cited regarding fluency as a three-pronged construct (accuracy, rate, prosody).

## Conclusions & Policy Implications

The authors conclude that "text complexity matters in important ways," but implementation of CCSS text complexity increases "precedes a clear understanding of effects on classroom achievement."

**Key recommendations:**
- Increased complexity without scaffolding support produces negative outcomes
- Evidence-based instructional supports must accompany complex texts
- Teachers need professional development on text complexity metrics
- New, accessible text complexity tools should be developed for practitioners

The review emphasizes that difficulty is best understood through "interaction of the reader's characteristics and the complexity of the text," moderated by task context—not as an absolute text property.

Authors not explicitly listed in header; Published in *Reading Research Quarterly*, 2026, DOI: 10.1080/02702711.2026.2644958

- Total: 19 studies

- Case studies: 6 studies

- Primary school (grades 3-6): 11 studies
- Middle school (grades 7-9): 8 studies

Core features implemented:
- Rereading: 94% of studies
- Annotation: 89%
- Text-dependent questions: 78%
- Post-reading discussion: 50%
- Post-reading writing: 61%
- Complex texts: Only 75% explicitly mentioned

Rereading typically featured "meaning-focused goals" and averaged 3.1 passes through texts. Text-dependent questions were predominantly teacher-generated (78%) and emphasized "citing textual evidence."

## Reported Effects and Effect Sizes

**Quasi-experimental studies (most rigorous):** Mixed results. One study showed "larger increases in reading comprehension" with close reading versus guided reading programs. However, two other quasi-experimental studies found no positive effects on reading comprehension outcomes.

**Pretest-posttest studies:** Generally reported improvements, though lacking causal validity.

**Case studies:** Mixed feasibility; some students found annotation "too difficult."

**No effect sizes** were systematically reported across studies.

"The quality, quantity, and generalizability of available research is still limited for this age group, and findings are mixed." The authors emphasize that "we cannot make causal claims on the effects" due to insufficient high-quality evidence and recommend schools not adopt close reading as a single comprehension approach.

# Study Design and Methods Summary

## Study Design
The researchers employed a **randomized experimental design with a control group**. From 438 eligible students scoring in the bottom 40% on state assessments across three middle schools, they "randomly assigned 100 students to one of five intervention classrooms." The experimental group included 75 students (20 at School 1; 40 each at Schools 2 and 3), while 247 students served as controls. Attrition was 25% for the experimental group and 27% for controls.

## Setting and Duration
This was an **after-school intervention**. Classes met "three times per week for 90 minutes," running "from the first week of October" through May.

## Intervention Components
Close reading was operationalized through five key features:
- Short, complex passages (3 paragraphs to 3 pages; Lexile 925-1185 for grades 6-8)
- Repeated readings for different purposes
- Annotation of texts
- Text-dependent questions requiring textual evidence
- Small-group discussion with academic language and argumentation

## Measures
Students completed the **Gates-MacGinitie Reading Test (GMRT-4)** in fall and spring. The primary outcome was performance on California's "state-administered annual assessment (California Standards Test of English Language Arts)," which is "criterion based and leveled by grade."

## Key Results
- **Attendance**: Experimental group averaged 94% versus 81% for controls (p < .01)
- **Achievement**: 64% of experimental students improved one or more levels versus 12% of controls (p < .001)
- **Self-perception**: Experimental group scored 186 versus 99 on the Reader Self-Perception Scale (p < .001)

## Limitations
The study employed a **convenience sample** of schools where "principals were receptive." Students with individualized education programs were excluded. The design lacked random school selection, potentially limiting generalizability.

# Baseball Study (Recht & Leslie, 1988) - Summary

## Sample
64 seventh and eighth grade students from Marquette University, Milwaukee.

## Design
Participants were divided into four groups based on reading ability and prior baseball knowledge. Each student read a half-page text describing a baseball inning, then recreated the action on a model baseball field to demonstrate comprehension.

## Results
Students with high baseball knowledge outperformed those without it, regardless of reading ability. Notably, "Students with high reading ability but low knowledge of baseball were no more capable of recall or summarization than were students with low reading ability and low knowledge of baseball." Conversely, lower-proficiency readers with baseball knowledge demonstrated superior performance in identifying important ideas and summarizing text.

## Measures
- Recall and summarization ability
- Accuracy of recreating described baseball action on a model field
- Identification of important textual ideas

The research demonstrated that background knowledge was as important as reading proficiency for comprehension, leading Recht and Leslie to conclude that educators must consider students' background knowledge when planning instruction.

Kim, H., Kuo, L.-J., & Eslami, Z. R. (2025). Effects of literacy-integrated content area instruction on English learners' literacy skills and content knowledge development: A meta-analysis. *Language Teaching Research*.

# Verbatim Abstract

"As the significance of academic language in fostering success across content areas garners growing attention, the incorporation of literacy instruction within content area teaching has shown promise in bolstering the academic achievements of English learners. Nevertheless, a comprehensive assessment of empirical studies exploring the impact of literacy-integrated content area instruction on English learners' literacy skills and content knowledge remains absent in the literature. The goal of the current meta-analysis is to quantitatively synthesize the studies that investigated the effects of literacy-integrated content area instruction on kindergarten to 12th grade English learners' literacy skills (e.g., reading comprehension, vocabulary, writing) and content knowledge development. Across various academic subjects, 26 studies were identified, yielding 99 effect sizes. Random-effects models revealed that the magnitude of overall effects of literacy instruction in content learning was medium in writing but large in reading, vocabulary, and content knowledge, based on the benchmark of Kraft. No publication bias was found in any of the analyses. Moderator analyses indicated that longer instructional durations (e.g., one year or longer) and small group configurations prove more effective for English learners in reading and writing, but additional research is warranted to explore the effect of literacy-integrated content instruction on English learners' writing. This study offers both theoretical and pedagogical implications."

## Summary of findings

The evidence base is real but thin, young, and heavily skewed toward short-duration studies with assisted-performance outcomes. The single most robust pattern: **AI helps while you're using it, and often hurts (or does nothing for) what you can do without it.** Very little of it is specifically about *reading science text*.

---

## 1. The two flagship RCTs

### Bastani et al. — "Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning"
**Citation:** Bastani, H., Bastani, O., Sungu, A., Ge, H., Kabakcı, Ö., & Mariman, R. (2025). *PNAS*, 122(26), e2422633122. (SSRN preprint #4895486, July 2024, titled "Generative AI Can Harm Learning." A Sept 2025 correction, PMC12403119, was purely an author-affiliation fix — no substantive change.)

- **Design:** Field RCT, one large high school in Turkey, grades 9–11, ~1,000 students across ~50 classrooms, **randomized at classroom level**. Four 90-minute after-school practice sessions, Fall 2023–24. Content: combinatorics and other previously-covered topics, ~15% of semester curriculum. Three arms: control (textbook/notes), **GPT Base** (GPT-4 chat, unrestricted), **GPT Tutor** (GPT-4 with teacher-designed hints, answers withheld).

"Effects of LLM use and note-taking on reading comprehension and memory: A randomised experiment in secondary schools." *Computers & Education*, 243, 105514. (doi:10.1016/j.compedu.2025.105514; online Nov 2025; SSRN #5095149. Cambridge University Press & Assessment + Microsoft Research.)

- **Design:** Pre-registered RCT, mixed within/between, **405 students aged 14–15 across 7 schools in England**. Each student studied two passages under different support conditions: **LLM only** (ChatGPT-3.5-turbo) vs **note-taking only** vs **LLM + note-taking**. **Unannounced comprehension and retention test 3 days later.**
- **Result:** note-taking alone **and** note-taking + LLM both significantly beat **LLM alone** on comprehension and retention. LLM-only was the worst condition.
- **Perception/performance dissociation:** most students preferred the LLM and rated it more helpful. Qualitatively they praised it for making complex material accessible and reducing cognitive load — exactly the fluency-illusion signature.

### Etkin et al. — GPT tools on standardized reading passages
**Citation:** Etkin, H. K., Etkin, K. J., Carter, R. J., & Rolle, C. E. (2025). "Differential effects of GPT-based tools on comprehension of standardized passages." *Frontiers in Education*, 10, 1506752.

Also single online session, no delay, no transfer test. Suggestive, not decisive. But note the ordering: **Socratic (least answer-giving) best for weak readers, summary (most answer-giving) worst for strong readers** — consistent with the Bastani guardrails story.

- **Fan, Y. et al. (2025).** "Beware of metacognitive laziness: Effects of generative artificial intelligence on learning motivation, processes, and performance." *British Journal of Educational Technology*, 56(2). arXiv:2412.09315. **N = 117** university students, 4 arms (ChatGPT / human expert / writing-analytics checklist / control), essay task. **ChatGPT group won on essay score improvement but showed no advantage in knowledge gain or knowledge transfer.** ChatGPT users showed fewer metacognitive processes (evaluation, orientation). Exactly the assisted-vs-independent dissociation. No motivation differences.
- **Stadler, M., Bannert, M., & Sailer, M. (2024).** "Cognitive ease at a cost: LLMs reduce mental effort but compromise depth in student scientific inquiry." *Computers in Human Behavior*, 160, 108386. **N = 91** university students randomized to ChatGPT-3.5 vs Google to research a socio-scientific issue (nanoparticles in sunscreen). LLM group had **significantly lower cognitive load but lower-quality reasoning and argumentation**. This is the best-matched study for "using AI to process difficult science content."
- **Gerlich, M. (2025).** "AI Tools in Society: Impacts on Cognitive Offloading and the Future of Critical Thinking." *Societies*, 15(1), 6. **N = 666**, mixed-methods, Halpern Critical Thinking Assessment. Significant negative correlation between AI use and critical thinking, mediated by cognitive offloading; strongest in younger participants; buffered by education level. **This is cross-sectional and correlational — it cannot support causal claims, and it has since had a published correction.** It is heavily over-cited as if causal.
- **Fluency illusion review:** *Information* (MDPI), 2026, 17(3), 299 — narrative conceptual review of 41 publications (2022–early 2026; 28 empirical). Core claim: ease of processing gets misread as understanding, reducing critical evaluation and causing premature "I've got it" judgments. Review, not new data; I couldn't retrieve the full text (403).

## 4. Meta-analyses — and a major integrity problem

**The one most people cite has been retracted.**
- **Wang, J., & Fan, W. (2025).** "The effect of ChatGPT on students' learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis." *Humanities and Social Sciences Communications*, 12, 621. Reported **g = 0.867** (performance), **g = 0.456** (perception), **g = 0.457** (higher-order thinking) from 51 studies / 72 effect sizes. **RETRACTED 22 April 2026** (retraction notice doi:10.1057/s41599-026-07310-z), for "concerns relating to discrepancies in the meta-analysis" that undermined editorial confidence in the analysis and conclusions. Concerns raised by Magnus Ingebrigtsen and Marko Lukic; **the authors did not respond to correspondence.** If anyone cites "g = 0.87 for ChatGPT," that number is retracted.

Still-standing meta-analyses:
- **Deng, R., Jiang, M., Yu, X., Lu, Y., & Liu, S. (2025).** "Does ChatGPT enhance student learning? A systematic review and meta-analysis of experimental studies." *Computers & Education*, 227, 105224. **69 experimental studies (2022–2024)**; **g+ = 0.712** on academic performance; positive on affective-motivational states and higher-order thinking; **reduces mental effort**; no significant effect on self-efficacy. (Note the pairing: better performance *plus* less mental effort is precisely what a desirable-difficulties account would predict to be a red flag for durable learning.)
- **Wu, X., Zhu, P., Zhang, J., Yin, M., & Wang, Y. (2026).** "ChatGPT's impact on student learning outcomes: a meta-analysis of 35 experimental studies." *Humanities and Social Sciences Communications* (26 Mar 2026), s41599-026-07019-z. **35 studies, 4,193 participants, 134 effect sizes. Overall g = 0.670, 95% CI [0.495, 0.844].** Cognitive g = 0.872; non-cognitive g = 0.539. Moderators: **physics g = 1.951, chemistry g = 1.276, English g = 0.994 — but "science" (general) g = 0.169, n.s.** Duration >3 months g = 1.033. No publication bias detected (fail-safe N = 3,522).

**The methodological indictment:** Weidlich, J., Gašević, D., Drachsler, H., & Kirschner, P. A. (2025). "ChatGPT in Education: An Effect in Search of a Cause." *Journal of Computer Assisted Learning*, 41(5), e70105. Argues this whole literature is **media-comparison research** that confounds instructional method with technology affordance, frequently fails to specify what the control group actually did, and uses outcome measures that are not valid indicators of learning. Conclusion: observed gains **cannot currently be attributed to ChatGPT**, and meta-analytic effect sizes may over- or under-state benefits. See also Springer's *Educational Psychology Review* (2025) "Looking Beyond the Hype: Understanding the Effects of AI on Learning," doi:10.1007/s10648-025-10020-8 (I couldn't get past the paywall for details).

## 5. LLM-adapted / simplified science text specifically

This is the **thinnest** area, and what exists mostly studies adults reading science abstracts, not students reading textbooks.

- **"Are LLM-generated plain language summaries truly understandable? A large-scale crowdsourced evaluation"** — arXiv:2505.10409, published in *Journal of Biomedical Informatics* (S1532046426000626). ~150 MTurk participants; subjective Likert ratings + objective MCQ comprehension and free-recall. **Key result: readers rated LLM-generated summaries as equally clear and coherent as human-written ones, but scored significantly worse on comprehension questions after reading the LLM versions.** This is the cleanest direct demonstration that LLM simplification can buy perceived clarity without comprehension — a text-level analogue of the fluency illusion.
- **ReLay** (Chan, Han, Chen, Fang, Gryboski, Lee, Tanna, Zhu, Lu, Wang, & Guo, 2026; arXiv:2605.00468). 50 lay participants (from 397 recruits), 6 abstracts each, static expert-written vs interactive LLM-personalized. Personalization **did** improve comprehension (9.83 vs 9.03) and all 9 quality dimensions after FDR correction — but **only 27/50 improved while 13 declined**, and the authors report a **fundamental personalization/safety trade-off: personalized summaries increased hallucination and bias-reinforcement risk.**
- General finding in this literature: **naive prompting ("make this easier") often fails to produce genuinely more readable text**, and simplification of scientific/biomedical content carries elevated hallucination and over-simplification risk.
- I found **no published RCT of LLM-simplified science text with school-age students measuring comprehension and transfer.** That appears to be a genuine gap.

Also relevant to how students actually behave: **Fu, Y., Wester, J., van Berkel, N., & Hiniker, A. (2026),** "How College Students Use AI to Navigate Course Readings" (arXiv:2602.09907). 8-week study, 15 undergraduates, 838 prompts / 239 sessions. **59.6% of prompts were comprehension support (summarize/explain) rather than reasoning; 72% of sessions contained exactly the required minimum of three prompts; only 4.3% used taught prompting strategies.** Within sessions students did progress from comprehension toward reasoning — but the progression was truncated by satisficing. Students *knew* better prompting worked and did it anyway. Tiny N, but the behavioral picture matters: the default use of AI on hard readings is answer-extraction, not scaffolded inquiry.

## 6. Direct answers to your framing questions

**(a) Answer-giver vs (b) scaffolded tutor.** The distinction is supported but weaker than usually claimed. Bastani: raw GPT-4 → −0.19 SD on unassisted exam; hint-only tutor → ~0.00, i.e., **harm removed, benefit not created**. Etkin: Socratic chatbot was the least harmful to strong readers and most helpful to weak ones; summarizer was the most harmful. Kreijkes: LLM *plus* note-taking ≈ note-taking alone, and both beat LLM alone — again, scaffolding restores baseline rather than exceeding it. Only Kestin shows a large positive, and it's on an immediate assisted-adjacent post-test. **A defensible summary: guardrails convert a harm into a wash; claims of large net gains rest on a single crossover study with no delayed or unassisted outcome.**

**(c) Assisted vs independent performance.** This is the strongest and most replicated finding in the whole literature, and it appears across math (Bastani: +48% assisted, −17% unassisted), writing (Fan: better essays, no knowledge gain or transfer), scientific inquiry (Stadler: lower cognitive load, worse reasoning), reading (Kreijkes: preferred most, learned least; Etkin: differential), and text simplification (PLS study: rated equally clear, comprehended worse). Any study reporting only an assisted or immediate outcome should be treated as measuring performance, not learning.

**Hallucination in science explanation.** Only Bastani measured it inside a learning experiment — **51% correct, 42% logical errors, 8% arithmetic errors** on high-school math. Kestin's tutor had anti-hallucination guardrails but the paper doesn't quantify residual error. The PLS/ReLay work shows simplification and personalization *increase* hallucination risk on scientific content. Abdelghani et al. found 14–15-year-olds **cannot detect vague or inadequate AI science explanations** — which is the accuracy risk that actually matters: error rate × student detection rate.

- **Small and young.** Perhaps a half-dozen credible RCTs total; most run 1–4 sessions; most use immediate post-tests; most use GPT-3.5/GPT-4 from 2023.
- **Almost nothing on adolescents reading *science* text with AI.** Kreijkes is adolescents but history text; Abdelghani is adolescents + science but n=63 and a preprint; Stadler is science inquiry but university students. The intersection you asked about is essentially unstudied.

- **The meta-analytic layer is unreliable.** The most-cited meta-analysis is retracted; the 2026 replacement reports subgroup effect sizes (physics g = 1.95) that are not credible; and Weidlich et al. argue the primary studies feeding these meta-analyses are largely uninterpretable media comparisons.

## Design and Sample

**Student Sample:** Approximately 1.2 million high school students who took the ACT and indicated they would graduate in 2005. The geographic distribution was 27% East, 40% Midwest, 14% Southwest, and 19% West.

**Data Sources:** The analysis drew from multiple cohorts across ACT's EPAS system (EXPLORE for grade 8, PLAN for grade 10, and ACT for grade 12), with approximately 352,000 students participating in all three assessments.

## Definition of "Complex Text"

Complex texts exhibit six characteristics abbreviated as "RSVP":

- **Relationships:** "Subtle, involved, deeply embedded" interactions among ideas or characters
- **Richness:** "Sizable/highly detailed" and sophisticated information through data or literary devices
- **Structure:** "Elaborate, sometimes unconventional" organization
- **Style:** "Often intricate" tone and language use
- **Vocabulary:** "Demanding, highly context dependent" word choices
- **Purpose:** "Implicit, sometimes ambiguous" authorial intent

## Key Findings

1. Only 51% of 2005 ACT-tested graduates met the College Readiness Benchmark for Reading (score of 21)
2. Performance on complex texts showed "substantially different pattern" from simpler texts, with steep improvement above the benchmark
3. Correctly answering complex text questions associated with "6 and 7 points higher" average scores than more challenging texts
4. Students were "losing momentum" during high school—62% met benchmarks in 8th grade, but only 51% by 12th grade
5. Nearly 60% of states lacked grade-specific high school reading standards

## Causal vs. Correlational Language

The report acknowledges correlational findings: "Students who meet the Reading Benchmark are more likely than students who do not meet the Benchmark to" enroll in college and earn higher grades. However, the document does not explicitly distinguish between correlation and causation throughout, presenting associations as predictive relationships rather than definitively causal ones.

# Hiebert's Argument on Text Complexity and Achievement Gap

**Core Argument:**
Hiebert contends that the Common Core State Standards' misguided push for dramatically increased text complexity has inadvertently harmed struggling readers, contributing to historic achievement gaps revealed in 2024 NAEP results.

**Key Evidence Cited:**
Hiebert presents research showing that text complexity had *already* increased substantially in the early 1990s—first-grade texts reached "their highest complexity levels in 60 years" by that decade. The CCSS developers, however, based their conclusions on outdated pre-1990s classroom analyses, leading them to wrongly assume reading materials had become easier.

**Problems with CCSS Implementation:**
When schools implemented steeper complexity escalation (with fifth graders assigned materials previously for ninth-tenth graders), teachers responded by reading texts *to* students rather than having them read independently. This reduced actual reading practice—a critical factor for building fluency and comprehension.

**Impact on Vulnerable Readers:**
Hiebert emphasizes that "struggling readers face texts beyond their instructional level and receive less reading practice, they miss crucial opportunities" to develop essential skills. This creates a harmful cycle where reading becomes increasingly difficult and discouraging.

**Her Call to Action:**
Hiebert advocates revising complexity guidelines to align with research-based development while ensuring struggling readers access appropriately-leveled texts with systematic support for progression.

# Meta-Analysis Summary: Integrated Literacy and Content-Area Instruction

## Study Overview
**Number of Studies:** 35 (32 peer-reviewed articles, 3 dissertations)
**Grade Range:** Kindergarten through 5th grade
**Total Participants:** 13,289 students (9,530 treatment, 7,934 control)

## Primary Effect Sizes

**Vocabulary (researcher-developed):** g = 0.86, significant, large effect
**Vocabulary (standardized):** g = 0.64, not significant
**Comprehension (researcher-developed):** g = 0.54, significant, large effect
**Comprehension (standardized):** g = 0.25, significant, large effect
**Content Knowledge (supplementary):** g = 0.89, significant, large effect

The authors note that "approximately 84% of treatment group students scored better than the average score of control group students for researcher-developed vocabulary measures."

## Key Distinction: Proximal vs. Distal Measures

Highly aligned researcher-developed measures showed stronger effects than less aligned measures for both vocabulary and comprehension, suggesting interventions improved students' knowledge of taught content but not necessarily generalized skills.

## Publication Bias
No substantial publication bias detected. Sensitivity analysis indicated effect sizes were robust across both vocabulary and comprehension outcomes.

## Moderator Analysis
No significant moderators emerged regarding research design features or intervention characteristics, though analyses lacked statistical power for most comparisons.

## Science vs. Social Studies
The analysis combined both content areas, finding comparable patterns between integrated science and social studies instruction approaches.

Educational Testing Service (ETS) scenario-based literacy assessment (biology form), designed to measure strategic reading processes aligned with Common Core standards and Next Generation Science Standards.

**Statistically significant finding favoring lower-performing students**: Students with lower incoming achievement showed differential positive impacts, though specific effect sizes and p-values for this subgroup analysis are not explicitly reported in the executive summary or results sections provided.

Teachers showed significant improvements across multiple dimensions (effect sizes ranged 0.236-0.619):

- Teacher confidence in literacy instruction: ES = 0.619, p = .004

- Students practicing metacognitive inquiry: ES = 0.457, p = .003
- Variety of text types: ES = 0.393, p = .033
- Fostering student independence: ES = 0.382, p = .034

No relationship between teacher instructional practice improvements and student achievement gains was observed in correlational analyses.

Based on the abstract, this systematic literature review identifies a significant gap in the research landscape. While "Literacy research has investigated disciplinary literacy for over a decade," the authors note that "research exploring the professional development in-service teachers receive specific to delivering disciplinary literacy instruction remains limited."

The review synthesized 58 articles and identified four key themes connecting professional development to disciplinary literacy:

1. **Strategy instruction approaches** to disciplinary literacy
2. **Differentiation practices** within disciplinary contexts
3. **Measurement methods** for assessing disciplinary literacy
4. **Professional development models** themselves

Regarding implementation difficulties, the authors' conclusion emphasizes "both successes and challenges for PD in disciplinary literacy," suggesting that while some positive outcomes exist, considerable obstacles remain for educators attempting to implement this approach in content-area classrooms.

The key takeaway is that despite disciplinary literacy being "integrated into national standards and classroom implementation," the professional development supporting teachers in this work remains underdeveloped and underexamined in the research literature.

# Abstract (Verbatim)

Students with low knowledge have been shown to better understand and learn more from more cohesive texts, whereas high-knowledge students have been shown to learn more from lower cohesion texts; this has been called the reverse cohesion effect. This study examines whether students' comprehension skill affects the interaction between text cohesion and their domain knowledge. College students (n = 143) read either a high- or a low-cohesion text and answered text-based and bridging inference questions. The results indicated that the benefit of low-cohesion text was restricted to less skilled, high-knowledge readers, whereas skilled comprehenders with high knowledge benefited from a high-cohesion text. Consistent with McNamara (2001), the interaction of text cohesion and knowledge was restricted to text-based questions. In addition, for low-knowledge readers, the benefits of high-cohesion texts emerged in their responses to bridging inference questions but not text-based questions. The results suggest a more complex view of when and for whom textual cohesion affects comprehension.

# Full Citation (APA Format)

O'Reilly, T., & McNamara, D. S. (2007). Reversing the reverse cohesion effect: Good texts can be better for strategic, high-knowledge readers. *Discourse Processes*, *43*(2), 121-152. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15326950dp4302_2

Institute of Cognitive Science, University of Colorado, Boulder. DOI 10.1207/s1532690xci1401_1

**Experiments:** 2

### Experiment 1
- **N = 36**, paid $10 each, living in Boulder, Colorado, tested individually in homes or university lab. Ages 11–15 (M = 13 yr 2 mo), **entering Grades 7–9**. 12 per text condition. Mean grade levels 7.8 / 7.6 / 8.0.
- **Text/topic:** Biology — **traits of mammals**, from Silver Burdett & Ginn (1987) school text. Original = 1.5 pages/590 words; revised = 821 words; expanded = 4 pages/1,167 words.
- **Coherence manipulation:** Three versions. "(a) the original school text, which was locally coherent to begin with but lacked global coherence; (b) a revised text, which added macrosignals alerting the reader to the underlying structure; and (c) an expanded text, which added explanatory coherence." Kintsch–van Dijk simulation found **no local gaps** in the original ("not a single bridging inference was required to run the simulation"). Propositions: 55 / 57 / 73 complex; micropropositions 48 / 50 / 66 plus 7 macropropositions common to all.
- **Prior knowledge:** Not a classifying variable in Exp 1; preknowledge assessed via pretest sorting + 32 pretest questions (all researcher-designed).
- **Measures (all researcher-designed):** free recall (oral, propositional, lenient scoring); 32 pre/post questions — text-based (n=19), inference (n=9), nontext (n=4); key-word sorting (16 animal-characteristic cards: 7 mammalian, 4 shared, 5 nonmammalian) scored by a Smolensky (1986) harmony statistic (range ±1.0).

**Statistics (Exp 1):**
- Recall main effect of text: **F(2, 33) = 3.7, MSE = .038**; revised M = .53 > expanded M = .43 and original M = .38, **F(1, 33) = 6.8**; expanded vs original **F(1, 33) < 1**.

Abstract: **"We found that readers who know little about the domain of the text benefit from a coherent text, whereas high-knowledge readers benefit from a minimally coherent text… These findings, however, depended on the level of understanding, text base or situational, being measured by the three comprehension tasks… This study provides evidence that the rewards to be gained from active processing are primarily at the level of the situation model rather than at the superficial level of text-base understanding."**

Prediction: **"For low-knowledge participants, the fully coherent text CM should be best; in contrast, for high-knowledge participants, the text with coherence gaps, cm, should be best. On the other hand, for measures that primarily reflect the readers' text base, CM should always be better than cm."**

### VERBATIM — replication status and boundary conditions

**"In summary, low-knowledge readers benefited from text cohesion but only according to their performance on the bridging-inference questions. However, irrespective of cohesion, low-knowledge readers benefited from comprehension skill. On the other hand, less skilled, high-knowledge readers showed better textbase comprehension of the low-cohesion texts (i.e., they exhibited the reverse cohesion effect), whereas skilled, high-knowledge readers benefited from reading the high-cohesion text."**

**"Our findings indicate that the reverse cohesion effect occurs only for less skilled, high-knowledge readers."**

**"There was no impairment from increasing cohesion for skilled, high-knowledge comprehenders. In fact, skilled, high-knowledge readers performed better on the high-cohesion text."**

**Partial replication with a level shift:** the reverse cohesion effect appeared **only on text-based (textbase) questions**, not on situation-model/bridging questions — the opposite level from 1996: **"In contrast to the two previous studies by McNamara and colleagues (McNamara & Kintsch, 1996; McNamara et al., 1996), the results reported in McNamara (2001) and in this study showed a reverse cohesion effect only on text-based questions, which were assumed or designed to tap into the readers' textbase level of understanding."**

Boundary condition = text difficulty: **"In this study and in McNamara, there was a large difference (approximately 50%) for the students' performance on text-based questions as compared to bridging-inference questions. In contrast, in the previous studies, the overall proportion correct for text-based and bridging-inference questions was similar, and approximately only 3% higher for text-based questions over bridging inference."** And: **"McNamara proposed that high-knowledge readers benefit from low-cohesion texts at the level of processing that is in most need of improvement."**

Boundary condition = reading skill/strategy: **"By active processing we mean two things: Learners use prior knowledge and reading strategies to build a coherent mental representation of the text, and readers closely monitor whether their mental representation of a text corresponds to the situation described in the text… We do not mean that the less skilled comprehenders are not capable of active processing but that they are less likely to do so on their own. Cohesion gaps scaffold less skilled readers to generate knowledge-based inferences."**

# Five Recommendations from the WWC Adolescent Literacy Practice Guide

**Full Citation:**
Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., & Torgesen, J. (2008). *Improving adolescent literacy: Effective classroom and intervention practices: A Practice Guide* (NCEE #2008-4027). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education.

## Five Recommendations with Evidence Levels

1. **Provide explicit vocabulary instruction** — Strong
2. **Provide direct and explicit comprehension strategy instruction** — Strong
3. **Provide opportunities for extended discussion of text meaning and interpretation** — Moderate
4. **Increase student motivation and engagement in literacy learning** — Moderate
5. **Make available intensive and individualized interventions for struggling readers** — Strong

## Recommendation 3: Supporting Evidence Summary

The moderate evidence base includes:

- **Four quasi-experimental studies**: Three studies (Bird 1984; Heinl 1988; Yeazell 1982) used less rigorous designs with low internal validity. One study (Reznitskaya et al. 2001) demonstrated rigorous pretest group equivalence.

- **One large correlational study** (Applebee et al. 2003): Examined sustained discussion duration in middle/high school language arts classes, finding classrooms averaging only 1.7 discussion minutes per 60-minute period.

- **Supplementary evidence**: A meta-analysis of 43 studies and a descriptive study of high-performing schools supported findings.

**Note:** The guide does not explicitly report individual effect sizes for these studies within the provided sections.

**N / population / setting:** 42 undergraduates. "The participants were 42 undergraduate psychology and biology students who participated for course credit. Half of the participants were randomly assigned to the SERT condition and the other half to the control condition." **Lab study**, one-on-one: "The experiment required a total of five experimental one-on-one sessions."

**Design:** 2 (condition: SERT vs. read-aloud control) × 2 (knowledge: high/low, median split) between, × question type (text-based vs. bridging-inference) within. Training = 4 science texts (acid rain, carbon cycle, forest fires, petroleum); posttraining target text = 650-word low-cohesion **cell mitosis** text (the low-cohesion version from McNamara, 2001). Both conditions self-explained the target text; only SERT had prior strategy training.

**How the aptitudes were measured:**
- **Reading skill: Nelson-Denny.** "Reading comprehension was assessed using Forms G and H of the Nelson Denny Adult Reading Comprehension Test (J. I. Brown, Fishco, & Hanna, 1993). This measure included a total of seven passages and 38 questions... the standard time of 20 min."

- **Prior knowledge: researcher-made, topic-specific.** "The participants also answered questions designed to assess their prior knowledge related to the cell mitosis text. - **Comprehension outcomes: researcher-designed, open-ended**, not standardized. "All of the questions were open-ended questions requiring the integration of separate ideas from the text."

**Correlations among aptitudes:** "Reading span was not correlated to reading skill or prior knowledge. Prior knowledge and reading skill were moderately correlated (r = 0.325, p = .035)." > "Reading span did not; it failed to correlate with comprehension performance during training, and did not interact with any of the variables. However, reading skill, as measured by Nelson Denny (J. I. Brown et al., 1993) performance, reliably correlated with overall comprehension during training (r = .35, p = 0.05). There was better comprehension by skilled readers (i.e., according to a median-split, n = 20, M = 0.58) than less-skilled readers (n = 22, M = 0.49), F(1, 40)= 4.70. Interestingly, prior knowledge of cell biology also correlated with overall comprehension performance during training (r = .44, p < .01)... high-knowledge readers (according to a median split) better understood the training texts (n = 21, M = 0.58) than did low-knowledge readers (n = 21, M = 0.48), F(1, 40)= 4.82. > "Neither reading span nor reading skill showed strong correlations with comprehension performance, and training effectiveness did not depend on those abilities."

> "There was a significant effect of question type, F(1, 38) = 54.36, and prior knowledge, F(1, 38) = 23.47, and a marginal effect of condition, F(1, 38)= 3.67, p = .063. > "For bridging inference questions, only prior knowledge affected performance, F(1, 38) = 20.79. For text-based questions, there were reliable effects of training condition, F(1, 39) = 4.20, and prior knowledge, F(1,38) = 15.16. In addition, there was a marginal interaction between condition and prior knowledge, F(1,38) = 3.99, p = .053. 1. **Prior knowledge is the moderator; reading skill is not.** In both McNamara (2004) and McNamara (2017), Nelson-Denny reading skill neither predicted the outcome strongly nor interacted with training. Reading span (Engle) was irrelevant in 2004.

3. **In the lab, the benefit is confined to text-based (textbase) questions; bridging-inference comprehension shows a null training effect for everyone.** "For bridging inference questions, only prior knowledge affected performance, F(1, 38) = 20.79."
4. **The compensation mechanism is domain-general logic, not domain-specific elaboration.** Low-K SERT participants used correct logic far more than low-K controls (15.3 vs. 2.0; F(1,10)=10.15) and made fewer incorrect paraphrases (11.0 vs. 18.3; F(1,10)=5.90), but the elaboration increase was **not** reliable (F(1,10)=2.47).
5. **Training equalizes: it removes the knowledge gap rather than lifting everyone.** 2017: knowledge effect F(1,203)=27.98, p<.001 in controls but F<1 in the SERT group.

## Abstract (Verbatim)

"Interactive Strategy Training for Active Reading and Thinking (iSTART) is a Web-based application that provides young adolescent to college-age students with high-level reading strategy training to improve comprehension of science texts. iSTART is modeled after an effective, human-delivered intervention called self-explanation reading training (SERT), which trains readers to use active reading strategies to self-explain difficult texts more effectively. ## The Six Steps

1. Provide a description, explanation, or example of the new term
2. Ask students to restate the description, explanation, or example in their own words

# Summary of Shanahan's Close Reading Framework

## Definition
Shanahan defines close reading as "an intensive analysis of a text in order to come to terms with what it says, how it says it, and what it means." The approach requires three distinct phases: first understanding literal content, then analyzing authorial craft and structure, and finally evaluating meaning and significance.

## Research Evidence
While Shanahan mentions that research supports both strategy-based and practice-based comprehension approaches, he does not provide extensive citations of empirical studies in this article. He notes that his definition of close reading may overlap with comprehensive definitions of reading comprehension itself.

## Rereading Requirement
Shanahan emphasizes that close reading genuinely requires rereading texts, though not every text warrants such treatment. However, rereading need not mean reading entire texts multiple times—teachers can conduct targeted, partial rereads focusing on key passages or sections.

## Pre-Reading and Frontloading
Shanahan advises against extensive pre-reading activities like picture walks or guided previews. He permits brief, student-directed previews and allows necessary background instruction only when information cannot be gleaned from the text itself.

## Text-Dependent Questions
Text-dependent questions should require textual knowledge to answer, though they need not be literal. These questions should avoid revealing information students can discover independently through reading.

(2016). *Effectiveness of Internet-Based Reading Apprenticeship Improving Science Education (iRAISE): A report of a randomized experiment in Michigan and Pennsylvania.* Empirical Education Inc. (ERIC ED570998; https://www.empiricaleducation.com/pdfs/iRAISEfr.pdf)

**3. RAISE scale-up (the follow-on to Greenleaf 2011) — effect sizes not retrieved.**

(ERIC ED583147); with Year 1 (ED583146) and Year 2 (ED583145) interim reports. Tested Reading Apprenticeship in **U.S. history, biology, and ELA**. **Pooled/main effect sizes: could not verify.**

An ERIC-surfaced summary indicated a 2023 WWC review with **3 studies meeting standards without reservations, 6 meeting standards with or without reservations, 3 not meeting standards.** A second, larger set of counts (26/43/22) also appeared. **These counts conflict and I could not reconcile them against the WWC intervention report directly** — the WWC intervention-report URLs I tried resolved to unrelated interventions (STeLLA, TCAD). **Treat the Reading Apprenticeship WWC ratings as unverified.**

| Guide | Year | Grades |

| **Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4–9** | 2022 | 4–9 |
| Teaching Academic Content and Literacy to English Learners in Elementary and Middle School | 2014 | K–8 |
| Effective Literacy and English Language Instruction for English Learners in the Elementary Grades | 2007 | elementary |

**Grades 4–9 guide (2022) recommendations and evidence levels:**
1. Build students' decoding skills so they can read complex multisyllabic words — **Strong**
2. Provide purposeful fluency-building activities — **Strong**
3. Routinely use a set of comprehension-building practices — **Strong**
4. Provide opportunities to practice making sense of stretch (challenging) text — **Moderate**

**Critically: there is no WWC practice guide on disciplinary literacy, and no recommendation in the 4–9 guide is framed as discipline-specific literacy instruction in science.** The closest is Recommendation 4 (stretch text), rated only **Moderate**. This absence is itself evidence that the WWC has not found a disciplinary-literacy evidence base sufficient to support a guide.

## The proximal/distal pattern — what the numbers actually show

**Supporting the pattern (strongly):**
- Hwang et al. (2022) vocabulary: fully-aligned researcher-designed **g = 1.05** → less-aligned researcher-designed **g = 0.11 (null)** → standardized **g = 0.64, ns**
- Hwang et al. (2022) content knowledge: researcher-developed **g = 0.94** (significant) → standardized **g = 0.68, p = .13 (null)**
- Hwang et al. (2022) comprehension: researcher-developed **g = 0.54** → standardized **g = 0.25** (roughly halved)
- Hwang et al. (2023) review: vocabulary **g = .29** on researcher-developed, **non-significant on standardized vocabulary**
- Design quality: weak designs **g = 2.32** (vocab) vs. strong designs **g = 0.54**
- iRAISE: large significant effects on **teacher practice** measures (ES 0.38–0.62), **null on student achievement**

**Refuting / complicating the pattern:**
- Hwang et al. (2022) standardized comprehension **g = 0.25, CI [.04, .46], p < .05** — small but genuinely significant on distal measures
- Greenleaf et al. (2011) reported gains on **state standardized** ELA, reading comprehension, and biology assessments (effect sizes unverified)

**Design & Sample:**
A two-year experimental study with fifth-grade participants from a low-performing urban district in Pennsylvania, comparing three instructional conditions.

**Conditions:**
1. **Content Instruction:** "student attention on the content of the text through open, meaning-based questions"
2. **Strategies Instruction:** Teaching "specific procedures to guide their access to text during reading"
3. **Control:** Standard basal reading program questions

The research demonstrated that emphasizing text meaning and engaged discussion outperformed explicit strategy instruction for this population, challenging conventional comprehension pedagogy.
