Note: three key iSTART primaries are closed-access with no OA copy anywhere (verified via OpenAlex `is_oa=False`, Semantic Scholar, ERIC API, and the SOLET lab's own now-dead file host). Those are flagged as secondary-source-only below.

---

# A) SERT / iSTART

### A1. McNamara (2004) — VERIFIED, with an important restriction

**McNamara, D. S. (2004). SERT: Self-Explanation Reading Training. *Discourse Processes*, 38(1), 1–30.**

- **N = 42 undergraduates** (21 SERT / 21 control), one-on-one **lab** study, five sessions. Not a classroom trial.
- Training texts: 4 science texts. Target text: 650-word **low-cohesion cell mitosis** passage (the low-cohesion version from McNamara 2001).
- **Prior knowledge: researcher-made**, topic-specific open-ended cell-biology questions. **Reading skill: Nelson-Denny (standardized)**. Working memory: Engle reading span. **Outcomes: researcher-designed open-ended questions** — no standardized comprehension outcome anywhere in this study.
- Training phase: main effect of condition **F(1,40) = 5.46** (SERT M = .56 vs control M = .47), but the abstract concedes self-explanation "only improved comprehension for the most difficult of the 4 texts."
- **The ATI, verbatim:** "there was a reliable three-way interaction of question type, condition, and knowledge, **F(1,38) = 4.17**." Decomposed: "For bridging inference questions, only prior knowledge affected performance, **F(1,38) = 20.79**." For text-based questions: condition **F(1,39) = 4.20**, knowledge **F(1,38) = 15.16**, Condition × Knowledge **F(1,38) = 3.99, p = .053** — "Training had little effect for high-knowledge participants (**F < 1**), but had a substantial effect for low-knowledge participants, **F(1,19) = 11.07**."
- **The only effect size in the paper** (Figure 1 caption): "reliable effects of training only for low-knowledge participants' performance on text-based questions (**Cohen's D = 1.92**)." That is one cell of a three-way interaction, n ≈ 21, researcher-designed measure.
- **Reading skill did NOT moderate training**: "Neither reading span nor reading skill showed strong correlations with comprehension performance, and training effectiveness did not depend on those abilities."

### A2. McNamara (2017) — VERIFIED, but quasi-experimental

- Prior knowledge: **researcher-assembled 54-item MC test** (items from GMAT-style banks). Reading skill: **Nelson-Denny**.

- Equalization result: knowledge effect **F(1,203) = 27.98, p < .001** among controls but **F < 1** among SERT students.
- **Reading skill again did not moderate** (footnote 1).
- **Key limitation, author's own words:** "students were not randomly assigned to condition; the students in the SERT condition volunteered" — plus no motivation measures, so "the possibility remains that these findings reflect a selection bias."

**McNamara, D. S., Levinstein, I. B., & Boonthum, C. Verified from the open-access ODU DigitalCommons copy and PubMed (PMID 15354687). If a summary cites it for effect sizes, that is a **misattribution**.

**McNamara, D. S., O'Reilly, T. P., Best, R. M., & Ozuru, Y. (2006). 1. **The moderator is prior knowledge of reading strategies (a Schmitt-type metacomprehension questionnaire), not prior domain knowledge.** Conflating this with the SERT domain-knowledge ATI is the single most common error in secondary summaries.
2. **The direction is split, not "helps low-knowledge."** Low-strategy-knowledge students gained on text-based questions; **high**-strategy-knowledge students gained on bridging-inference questions.
3. McNamara's own 2022 review describes the same study as showing that "**students who had greater prior knowledge of reading strategies produced better quality self-explanations** after this short intervention" — i.e., a high-knowledge advantage.

- No large randomized classroom trial with a standardized comprehension outcome was located. iSTART-Early RCT pilots using the Gates-MacGinitie are listed as IES-funded work, not published effect sizes.

# B) The reverse cohesion effect

### B1. McNamara, E. Kintsch, Songer & W. Kintsch (1996) — VERIFIED, and the precise form matters

**McNamara, D. S., Kintsch, E., Songer, N. B., & Kintsch, W. (1996). Are good texts always better? Interactions of text coherence, background knowledge, and levels of understanding in learning from text. *Cognition and Instruction*, 14(1), 1–43.**

- **Domain: science (biology), and the two experiments used different topics.** Exp 1: **traits of mammals** (N = 36, ages 11–15, entering **grades 7–9**, tested in Boulder CO homes/lab). Exp 2 — the famous one: **heart disease** (N = 56, ages 10–15, entering **grades 7–10**, 14 per cell).
- Exp 2 manipulated **local and global coherence orthogonally (2×2)**: CM, Cm, cM, cm. Prior knowledge = a **researcher-made** test on heart structure/function (41 pts), **median split** (high M = .48 vs low M = .20, F(1,48) = 152.9).
- All outcomes **researcher-designed**: free recall; 41 short-answer questions (9 text-based, 13 elaborative-inference, 9 bridging-inference, 10 problem-solving); 18-card keyword sorting scored by harmony.

**The interaction, verbatim:** "As predicted, the interaction between text and knowledge was reliable for both the **problem-solving questions, F(1,24) = 5.5, MSE = .025**, and the **bridging-inference questions, F(1,24) = 4.8, MSE = .030**. High-knowledge readers performed better on these questions with the low-coherence text, whereas the opposite was the case for low-knowledge readers. This interaction was not, however, reliable for the **elaborative-inference questions, F(1,24) < 2**. Also as predicted, the pattern of results for the **text-based questions** mirrors that of the recall data: **Both high- and low-knowledge participants did somewhat better with the coherent text, F(1,24) = 2.8, p = .11**."

Overall triple interaction on questions: **F(1,48) = 6.4, MSE = .086** (by items F(1,37) = 42.7). Sorting: four-way Test × Local × Global × Knowledge **F(1,48) = 8.1**; CM-vs-cm subanalysis **F(1,24) = 8.7, MSE = .004**.

Cell means (proportion correct), high-knowledge: bridging CM .48 vs **cm .68**; problem-solving CM .46 vs **cm .61**; text-based CM **.64** vs cm .51. Low-knowledge: every measure favors CM (text-based .47 vs .26; bridging .40 vs .31; problem-solving .30 vs .17).

**Precise statement of the effect:**
- **Low-knowledge readers benefit from HIGH cohesion on *every* measure** — textbase and situation model alike.
- **High-knowledge readers benefit from LOW cohesion only on situation-model measures** (bridging inference, problem solving, keyword sorting). On **text-based questions and free recall, high cohesion was better or neutral for them too**.
- Authors: "the rewards to be gained from active processing are primarily at the level of the **situation model** rather than at the superficial level of text-base understanding."

**Effect sizes: none are reported.** The paper gives F and MSE only. Any d attributed to this study is a reconstruction.

**Authors' own boundary condition, verbatim:** "The better performance of the high-knowledge participants with the low-coherence text may be limited to materials of just the right degree of difficulty. If the text is too hard, the construction of coherence may fail; on the other hand, if the text is too easy, the gains through more active processing may be too small."

### B2. McNamara & Kintsch (1996, *Discourse Processes*) — VERIFIED, but note the domain is HISTORY and one measure failed to replicate within the paper

**McNamara, D. S., & Kintsch, W. (1996). Learning from texts: Effects of prior knowledge and text coherence. *Discourse Processes*, 22(3), 247–288.**

- **Not science — history: the Vietnam War**, texts taken from Britton & Gülgöz (1991). **Local coherence only** was manipulated ("The coherence of the texts that we used here was manipulated only at the local level").
- **College students, N = 40 (Exp 1) and N = 39 analyzed (Exp 2)**, Old Dominion University. Prior knowledge = **researcher-made** map-drawing + 16-term identification; **mean split**. Additional between factor: a pretraining booklet.
- **Exp 1:** high-coherence advantage on recall (**F(1,32) = 3.14, p = .086**, marginal) and on multiple-choice questions (**F(1,32) = 14.85, p < .001**). The knowledge × coherence interaction appeared **only on keyword sorting**: Text × Knowledge × Test **F(1,32) = 4.64, p = .038**. Critically, **the MC questions showed no interaction at all** — "An interaction between knowledge and text coherence was not found with either form of question (i.e., text-based or bridging)."
- **Exp 2 (open-ended versions of the same questions):** three-way Text × Knowledge × Question type **F(1,31) = 7.83, p = .009**; high-knowledge/low-coherence readers were the only group with **no gap** between text-based and bridging questions (**F(1,6) < 1**).
- **Internal replication failure, verbatim:** "we did not find in Experiment 2 the predicted advantage of low-coherence texts for the high-knowledge readers on this measure [sorting] as demonstrated by two previous experiments." The authors explicitly rejected low power ("there is not even a trace of such effects") and attributed it to procedure.
- Also: the pretraining manipulation **abolished** the interaction — "the rich became much richer, and the poor became poorer."

### B3. Replications — CORRECTED: the effect has migrated levels and is now bounded by reading skill

**McNamara, D. S. (2001). Reading both high-coherence and low-coherence texts: Effects of text sequence and prior knowledge. *Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology*, 55(1), 51–62.** N = 80 college, **cell mitosis**. First text × Knowledge **F(1,72) = 4.92**; three-way with question type **F(1,72) = 8.10**. But: "these effects emerged on the **text-based questions**, rather than the situation model questions. Indeed, there was little effect of text for the situation model questions for either high- or low-knowledge participants." **This is the opposite level from 1996.** Also: high-knowledge benefit required reading the low-coherence text **first**; low-knowledge readers benefited from high coherence regardless of sequence.

**O'Reilly, T., & McNamara, D. S. (2007). Reversing the reverse cohesion effect: Good texts can be better for strategic, high-knowledge readers. *Discourse Processes*, 43(2), 121–152.** N = **143** college (Old Dominion), cell mitosis texts. Knowledge = researcher-made biology MC + cell questions, median split; **reading skill = Nelson-Denny (standardized)**, median split. Four-way interaction **F(1,135) = 3.96, MSE = .03, p < .05**.
- **Less-skilled, high-knowledge: low-cohesion .66 > high-cohesion .44, t(28) = 2.12, d = .79 — "This result is a reverse cohesion effect."**
- **Skilled, high-knowledge: high-cohesion .77 > low-cohesion .61, t(40) = 2.16, d = .65 — the effect reverses back.**
- **Low-knowledge readers: high-cohesion helped only on bridging-inference questions**, F(1,69) = 11.61, **d = .83**; text-based F < 1.
- Verbatim conclusion: "**the reverse cohesion effect occurs only for less skilled, high-knowledge readers**." And the level shift is acknowledged: "In contrast to the two previous studies... the results reported in McNamara (2001) and in this study showed a reverse cohesion effect only on **text-based questions**."

**Ozuru, Y., Dempsey, K., & McNamara, D. S. (2009). Prior knowledge, reading skill, and text cohesion in the comprehension of science texts. *Learning and Instruction*, 19(3), 228–242.** N = **170** college (108 psychology students = low-knowledge; 62 biology students = high-knowledge), two biology texts (plant tropism; heat distribution in animals), cohesion **within-subject**. Reading skill = Nelson-Denny; groups equated on it.
- **The simple knowledge × cohesion interaction FAILED to replicate**: "we did not observe a two-way interaction between level of knowledge and text cohesion... Instead, the effect of text cohesion mainly depended on reading skill." (Their Hypothesis 3, explicitly not confirmed.)
- What replicated instead: **Reading skill × Cohesion F(1,162) = 4.17, p < .05, partial η² = 0.03**; three-way with question type **F(2,324) = 3.35, p < .05, partial η² = 0.02**.
- Less-skilled + high-knowledge: low-coh .50 vs high-coh .41, **t(38) = −2.44, p < .05, d = 0.33** (reverse cohesion). More-skilled + high-knowledge: low-coh .55 vs high-coh .68, **t(22) = 2.461, p < .05, d = 0.59** (normal cohesion benefit). Low-knowledge readers: **no significant cohesion effect either way**.
- **Everything was confined to text-based questions**: "both beneficial and detrimental effects of text cohesion were limited to performance on text-based questions." Cohesion effects on local-bridging (**F < 1, p = .9**) and global-bridging (**F < 1, p = .5**) were flat null.
- Authors' own alternative explanation for the text-based benefit: target information appears ~1.4 times in low-cohesion vs ~2 times in high-cohesion texts — a repetition confound, not necessarily inference.

**McNamara, D. S., Ozuru, Y., & Floyd, R. G. (2011). Comprehension challenges in the fourth grade. *International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education*, 4(1), 229–257.** Fourth graders; a reverse cohesion effect appeared for high-knowledge readers on **low-cohesion narrative** texts — i.e., a genre boundary condition. (Abstract-level only; I did not read the full text.)

## Verdict table

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| SERT (McNamara 2004) especially helps low **domain**-knowledge readers | **VERIFIED**, but only on **text-based** questions; null on bridging inference; d = 1.92 from a single interaction cell, N = 42, lab, researcher-designed measures |
| SERT effects generalize to real coursework for low-knowledge students | **VERIFIED** (McNamara 2017, N = 265, instructor-written exams, d = .74/.50/.43) — but **non-randomized, self-selected**, and the overall effect is non-significant by Exams 2–3 |
| Reading skill moderates SERT benefits | **CORRECTED — no.** Nelson-Denny and reading span did not moderate in either 2004 or 2017 |
| iSTART especially helps low-knowledge readers | **CORRECTED.** The 2006 flagship moderator is **reading-strategy knowledge**, not domain knowledge, and its direction is split (low-strategy → text-based gains; **high**-strategy → bridging-inference gains). Later iSTART work makes **reading skill**, not knowledge, the compensated aptitude |
| McNamara, Levinstein & Boonthum (2004) is an efficacy study | **CORRECTED — it is a system description with no experiment** |
| iSTART effect sizes of 0.50–2.00 / 0.68–1.12 | **UNVERIFIABLE from primaries.** Author-narrative ranges only; underlying primaries are closed-access; no meta-analysis and no WWC report exist |
| 1996 reverse cohesion: high-knowledge readers do better with **low**-cohesion text | **VERIFIED, but only on situation-model measures** (bridging inference, problem solving, sorting). On text-based questions and recall, high cohesion was better or neutral for everyone. No effect sizes reported in the paper |
| Low-knowledge readers benefit from high cohesion | **VERIFIED and the most robust part** — true on every measure in 1996 CI Exp 2, and never reversed in any later study |
| The 1996 CI study was on science text | **VERIFIED** — biology (mammal traits in Exp 1; **heart disease** in Exp 2), grades 7–10, N = 36 and N = 56 |
| McNamara & Kintsch (1996, DP) is the same science finding | **CORRECTED — it is a HISTORY text (Vietnam War)**, college students (N = 40/39), local cohesion only; the sorting-task interaction **failed to replicate within the paper** (Exp 2) |
| The reverse cohesion effect replicates | **CORRECTED — partially, with the level shifted and a hard boundary condition.** In McNamara (2001), O'Reilly & McNamara (2007) and Ozuru et al. (2009) it appears **only on text-based questions**, and in the latter two **only for less-skilled, high-knowledge readers**; skilled high-knowledge readers show the ordinary cohesion *benefit* (d = .65, .59). Ozuru et al. (2009) explicitly failed to find any knowledge × cohesion interaction |

**One stable generalization across all five cohesion papers:** low-knowledge readers never benefit from low cohesion, and high-knowledge readers are the only group that ever does — but *which measure* shows it and *whether it survives controlling for reading skill* are both unstable.

Minor housekeeping note: one research agent flagged unexpected files appearing in its scratchpad mid-task. That was the second agent working in the same shared scratchpad directory — benign, and no findings depend on those files.

- Equalization result: knowledge effect **F(1,203) = 27.98, p < .001** among controls but **F < 1** among SERT students.
- **Reading skill again did not moderate** (footnote 1).
- **Key limitation, author's own words:** "students were not randomly assigned to condition; the students in the SERT condition volunteered" — plus no motivation measures, so "the possibility remains that these findings reflect a selection bias."

### A3. iSTART — the claim needs CORRECTION

**McNamara, D. S., Levinstein, I. B., & Boonthum, C. (2004). iSTART: Interactive strategy training for active reading and thinking. *Behavior Research Methods, Instruments, & Computers*, 36(2), 222–233.** — **This is a system-description paper, not an efficacy trial.** It reports no experiment, no N, no effect size. Verified from the open-access ODU DigitalCommons copy and PubMed (PMID 15354687). If a summary cites it for effect sizes, that is a **misattribution**.

**McNamara, D. S., O'Reilly, T. P., Best, R. M., & Ozuru, Y. (2006). Improving adolescent students' reading comprehension with iSTART. *Journal of Educational Computing Research*, 34(2), 147–171.** — full text **not obtainable** (closed; no OA copy exists). From the publisher/ASU abstract, verbatim: *"Adolescents with less prior knowledge about **reading strategies** performed significantly better on text-based questions if they received iSTART training. Conversely, for high-strategy knowledge students, iSTART improved comprehension for bridging-inference questions."*

Three corrections follow:
1. **The moderator is prior knowledge of reading strategies (a Schmitt-type metacomprehension questionnaire), not prior domain knowledge.** Conflating this with the SERT domain-knowledge ATI is the single most common error in secondary summaries.
2. **The direction is split, not "helps low-knowledge."** Low-strategy-knowledge students gained on text-based questions; **high**-strategy-knowledge students gained on bridging-inference questions.
3. McNamara's own 2022 review describes the same study as showing that "**students who had greater prior knowledge of reading strategies produced better quality self-explanations** after this short intervention" — i.e., a high-knowledge advantage.

**Sample size:** secondary notes give **n = 17 trained vs n = 21 control (N ≈ 38)** — very small. Flag as secondary; I could not confirm against the article.

**Reading skill, not knowledge, is the moderator in later iSTART work.** From McNamara et al. (2022, *IJHCI*, ERIC ED628155), verbatim: with eight 1-hour sessions "less-skilled students showed a greater increase in the quality of their self-explanations compared to more-skilled students"; and over a 6-month deployment "less-skilled students improved more than the more-skilled students, and the abilities of skilled and less-skilled students converged." So the aptitude that iSTART compensates for shifts to **decoding/comprehension skill** as dosage increases.

### A4. Effect-size claims for iSTART — UNVERIFIABLE from primaries

Two ranges circulate, both from the authors' own narrative summaries, neither traceable to a computed pooled estimate:
- "**effect sizes that have varied between 0.50 and 2.00**" — McNamara (2017), citing Jackson & McNamara (2013), Magliano et al. (2005), O'Reilly, Taylor & McNamara (2006).
- "**average effect sizes ranging from .68 to 1.12 depending on prior knowledge of the learner**" — Jackson, Snow, Varner & McNamara (2013), citing McNamara, O'Reilly et al. (2007), a book chapter.

Treat both as **secondary/self-reported**. All underlying outcomes I could inspect were **researcher-designed, passage-specific** open-ended questions on the trained text.

**Papers I could not obtain in full** (closed, no OA copy, ERIC has stub records only): McNamara et al. (2006, *JECR* 34(2)); **Magliano, Todaro, Millis, Wiemer-Hastings, Kim & McNamara (2005), *JECR* 32(2), 185–208**; **Jackson & McNamara (2013), *Journal of Educational Psychology*, 105(4), 1036–1049**. From an open companion paper (Jackson, Snow, Varner & McNamara, 2013, ERIC ED588487), the JEP study was **N = 126 high school students, three conditions, 11 sessions, lab-based**, with **researcher-designed passage-specific** outcomes — i.e., not a classroom efficacy trial with standardized outcomes.

### A5. Missing evidence — worth stating explicitly
- **No meta-analysis of iSTART or SERT exists.** OpenAlex and ERIC title/keyword searches return zero. The 2019 Xu et al. *BJET* meta-analysis of ITS for K-12 reading (overall random effect **d = 0.60, 95% CI [0.36, 0.85]**) is about ITSs generally, not iSTART.
- **No What Works Clearinghouse intervention report** for SERT or iSTART.
- No large randomized classroom trial with a standardized comprehension outcome was located. iSTART-Early RCT pilots using the Gates-MacGinitie are listed as IES-funded work, not published effect sizes.

---

# B) The reverse cohesion effect

### B1. McNamara, E. Kintsch, Songer & W. Kintsch (1996) — VERIFIED, and the precise form matters

**McNamara, D. S., Kintsch, E., Songer, N. B., & Kintsch, W. (1996). Are good texts always better? Interactions of text coherence, background knowledge, and levels of understanding in learning from text. *Cognition and Instruction*, 14(1), 1–43.**

- **Domain: science (biology), and the two experiments used different topics.** Exp 1: **traits of mammals** (N = 36, ages 11–15, entering **grades 7–9**, tested in Boulder CO homes/lab). Exp 2 — the famous one: **heart disease** (N = 56, ages 10–15, entering **grades 7–10**, 14 per cell).
- Exp 2 manipulated **local and global coherence orthogonally (2×2)**: CM, Cm, cM, cm. Prior knowledge = a **researcher-made** test on heart structure/function (41 pts), **median split** (high M = .48 vs low M = .20, F(1,48) = 152.9).
- All outcomes **researcher-designed**: free recall; 41 short-answer questions (9 text-based, 13 elaborative-inference, 9 bridging-inference, 10 problem-solving); 18-card keyword sorting scored by harmony.

**The interaction, verbatim:** "As predicted, the interaction between text and knowledge was reliable for both the **problem-solving questions, F(1,24) = 5.5, MSE = .025**, and the **bridging-inference questions, F(1,24) = 4.8, MSE = .030**. High-knowledge readers performed better on these questions with the low-coherence text, whereas the opposite was the case for low-knowledge readers. This interaction was not, however, reliable for the **elaborative-inference questions, F(1,24) < 2**. Also as predicted, the pattern of results for the **text-based questions** mirrors that of the recall data: **Both high- and low-knowledge participants did somewhat better with the coherent text, F(1,24) = 2.8, p = .11**."

Overall triple interaction on questions: **F(1,48) = 6.4, MSE = .086** (by items F(1,37) = 42.7). Sorting: four-way Test × Local × Global × Knowledge **F(1,48) = 8.1**; CM-vs-cm subanalysis **F(1,24) = 8.7, MSE = .004**.

Cell means (proportion correct), high-knowledge: bridging CM .48 vs **cm .68**; problem-solving CM .46 vs **cm .61**; text-based CM **.64** vs cm .51. Low-knowledge: every measure favors CM (text-based .47 vs .26; bridging .40 vs .31; problem-solving .30 vs .17).

**Precise statement of the effect:**
- **Low-knowledge readers benefit from HIGH cohesion on *every* measure** — textbase and situation model alike.
- **High-knowledge readers benefit from LOW cohesion only on situation-model measures** (bridging inference, problem solving, keyword sorting). On **text-based questions and free recall, high cohesion was better or neutral for them too**.
- Authors: "the rewards to be gained from active processing are primarily at the level of the **situation model** rather than at the superficial level of text-base understanding."

**Effect sizes: none are reported.** The paper gives F and MSE only. Any d attributed to this study is a reconstruction.

**Authors' own boundary condition, verbatim:** "The better performance of the high-knowledge participants with the low-coherence text may be limited to materials of just the right degree of difficulty. If the text is too hard, the construction of coherence may fail; on the other hand, if the text is too easy, the gains through more active processing may be too small."

### B2. McNamara & Kintsch (1996, *Discourse Processes*) — VERIFIED, but note the domain is HISTORY and one measure failed to replicate within the paper

**McNamara, D. S., & Kintsch, W. (1996). Learning from texts: Effects of prior knowledge and text coherence. *Discourse Processes*, 22(3), 247–288.**

- **Not science — history: the Vietnam War**, texts taken from Britton & Gülgöz (1991). **Local coherence only** was manipulated ("The coherence of the texts that we used here was manipulated only at the local level").
- **College students, N = 40 (Exp 1) and N = 39 analyzed (Exp 2)**, Old Dominion University. Prior knowledge = **researcher-made** map-drawing + 16-term identification; **mean split**. Additional between factor: a pretraining booklet.
- **Exp 1:** high-coherence advantage on recall (**F(1,32) = 3.14, p = .086**, marginal) and on multiple-choice questions (**F(1,32) = 14.85, p < .001**). The knowledge × coherence interaction appeared **only on keyword sorting**: Text × Knowledge × Test **F(1,32) = 4.64, p = .038**. Critically, **the MC questions showed no interaction at all** — "An interaction between knowledge and text coherence was not found with either form of question (i.e., text-based or bridging)."
- **Exp 2 (open-ended versions of the same questions):** three-way Text × Knowledge × Question type **F(1,31) = 7.83, p = .009**; high-knowledge/low-coherence readers were the only group with **no gap** between text-based and bridging questions (**F(1,6) < 1**).
- **Internal replication failure, verbatim:** "we did not find in Experiment 2 the predicted advantage of low-coherence texts for the high-knowledge readers on this measure [sorting] as demonstrated by two previous experiments." The authors explicitly rejected low power ("there is not even a trace of such effects") and attributed it to procedure.
- Also: the pretraining manipulation **abolished** the interaction — "the rich became much richer, and the poor became poorer."

### B3. Replications — CORRECTED: the effect has migrated levels and is now bounded by reading skill

**McNamara, D. S. (2001). Reading both high-coherence and low-coherence texts: Effects of text sequence and prior knowledge. *Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology*, 55(1), 51–62.** N = 80 college, **cell mitosis**. First text × Knowledge **F(1,72) = 4.92**; three-way with question type **F(1,72) = 8.10**. But: "these effects emerged on the **text-based questions**, rather than the situation model questions. Indeed, there was little effect of text for the situation model questions for either high- or low-knowledge participants." **This is the opposite level from 1996.** Also: high-knowledge benefit required reading the low-coherence text **first**; low-knowledge readers benefited from high coherence regardless of sequence.

**O'Reilly, T., & McNamara, D. S. (2007). Reversing the reverse cohesion effect: Good texts can be better for strategic, high-knowledge readers. *Discourse Processes*, 43(2), 121–152.** N = **143** college (Old Dominion), cell mitosis texts. Knowledge = researcher-made biology MC + cell questions, median split; **reading skill = Nelson-Denny (standardized)**, median split. Four-way interaction **F(1,135) = 3.96, MSE = .03, p < .05**.
- **Less-skilled, high-knowledge: low-cohesion .66 > high-cohesion .44, t(28) = 2.12, d = .79 — "This result is a reverse cohesion effect."**
- **Skilled, high-knowledge: high-cohesion .77 > low-cohesion .61, t(40) = 2.16, d = .65 — the effect reverses back.**
- **Low-knowledge readers: high-cohesion helped only on bridging-inference questions**, F(1,69) = 11.61, **d = .83**; text-based F < 1.
- Verbatim conclusion: "**the reverse cohesion effect occurs only for less skilled, high-knowledge readers**." And the level shift is acknowledged: "In contrast to the two previous studies... the results reported in McNamara (2001) and in this study showed a reverse cohesion effect only on **text-based questions**."

**Ozuru, Y., Dempsey, K., & McNamara, D. S. (2009). Prior knowledge, reading skill, and text cohesion in the comprehension of science texts. *Learning and Instruction*, 19(3), 228–242.** N = **170** college (108 psychology students = low-knowledge; 62 biology students = high-knowledge), two biology texts (plant tropism; heat distribution in animals), cohesion **within-subject**. Reading skill = Nelson-Denny; groups equated on it.
- **The simple knowledge × cohesion interaction FAILED to replicate**: "we did not observe a two-way interaction between level of knowledge and text cohesion... Instead, the effect of text cohesion mainly depended on reading skill." (Their Hypothesis 3, explicitly not confirmed.)
- What replicated instead: **Reading skill × Cohesion F(1,162) = 4.17, p < .05, partial η² = 0.03**; three-way with question type **F(2,324) = 3.35, p < .05, partial η² = 0.02**.
- Less-skilled + high-knowledge: low-coh .50 vs high-coh .41, **t(38) = −2.44, p < .05, d = 0.33** (reverse cohesion). More-skilled + high-knowledge: low-coh .55 vs high-coh .68, **t(22) = 2.461, p < .05, d = 0.59** (normal cohesion benefit). Low-knowledge readers: **no significant cohesion effect either way**.
- **Everything was confined to text-based questions**: "both beneficial and detrimental effects of text cohesion were limited to performance on text-based questions." Cohesion effects on local-bridging (**F < 1, p = .9**) and global-bridging (**F < 1, p = .5**) were flat null.
- Authors' own alternative explanation for the text-based benefit: target information appears ~1.4 times in low-cohesion vs ~2 times in high-cohesion texts — a repetition confound, not necessarily inference.

**McNamara, D. S., Ozuru, Y., & Floyd, R. G. (2011). Comprehension challenges in the fourth grade. *International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education*, 4(1), 229–257.** Fourth graders; a reverse cohesion effect appeared for high-knowledge readers on **low-cohesion narrative** texts — i.e., a genre boundary condition. (Abstract-level only; I did not read the full text.)

---

## Verdict table

| Claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| SERT (McNamara 2004) especially helps low **domain**-knowledge readers | **VERIFIED**, but only on **text-based** questions; null on bridging inference; d = 1.92 from a single interaction cell, N = 42, lab, researcher-designed measures |
| SERT effects generalize to real coursework for low-knowledge students | **VERIFIED** (McNamara 2017, N = 265, instructor-written exams, d = .74/.50/.43) — but **non-randomized, self-selected**, and the overall effect is non-significant by Exams 2–3 |
| Reading skill moderates SERT benefits | **CORRECTED — no.** Nelson-Denny and reading span did not moderate in either 2004 or 2017 |
| iSTART especially helps low-knowledge readers | **CORRECTED.** The 2006 flagship moderator is **reading-strategy knowledge**, not domain knowledge, and its direction is split (low-strategy → text-based gains; **high**-strategy → bridging-inference gains). Later iSTART work makes **reading skill**, not knowledge, the compensated aptitude |
| McNamara, Levinstein & Boonthum (2004) is an efficacy study | **CORRECTED — it is a system description with no experiment** |
| iSTART effect sizes of 0.50–2.00 / 0.68–1.12 | **UNVERIFIABLE from primaries.** Author-narrative ranges only; underlying primaries are closed-access; no meta-analysis and no WWC report exist |
| 1996 reverse cohesion: high-knowledge readers do better with **low**-cohesion text | **VERIFIED, but only on situation-model measures** (bridging inference, problem solving, sorting). On text-based questions and recall, high cohesion was better or neutral for everyone. No effect sizes reported in the paper |
| Low-knowledge readers benefit from high cohesion | **VERIFIED and the most robust part** — true on every measure in 1996 CI Exp 2, and never reversed in any later study |
| The 1996 CI study was on science text | **VERIFIED** — biology (mammal traits in Exp 1; **heart disease** in Exp 2), grades 7–10, N = 36 and N = 56 |
| McNamara & Kintsch (1996, DP) is the same science finding | **CORRECTED — it is a HISTORY text (Vietnam War)**, college students (N = 40/39), local cohesion only; the sorting-task interaction **failed to replicate within the paper** (Exp 2) |
| The reverse cohesion effect replicates | **CORRECTED — partially, with the level shifted and a hard boundary condition.** In McNamara (2001), O'Reilly & McNamara (2007) and Ozuru et al. (2009) it appears **only on text-based questions**, and in the latter two **only for less-skilled, high-knowledge readers**; skilled high-knowledge readers show the ordinary cohesion *benefit* (d = .65, .59). Ozuru et al. (2009) explicitly failed to find any knowledge × cohesion interaction |

**One stable generalization across all five cohesion papers:** low-knowledge readers never benefit from low cohesion, and high-knowledge readers are the only group that ever does — but *which measure* shows it and *whether it survives controlling for reading skill* are both unstable.

## 1. What "close reading" operationally means in the CCSS/Fisher & Frey tradition

**Core citations**

- Fisher, D., & Frey, N. (2012). Close reading in elementary schools. *The Reading Teacher*, 66(3), 179–188. DOI 10.1002/trtr.01117. Defines close reading as a routine in which students deeply analyze a *short, challenging* passage. Components: multiple readings of a brief complex text, annotation, text-dependent questions, discussion, and an oral/written response. Framed as importing a high-school/college practice downward.
- Fisher, D., & Frey, N. (2014). Closely reading informational texts in the primary grades. *The Reading Teacher* (DOI 10.1002/trtr.1317). Same architecture: text selection, initial reading, repeated reading, annotation, text-based discussion, responding.
- Fisher, D., & Frey, N. (2014). Close reading as an intervention for struggling middle school readers. *Journal of Adolescent & Adult Literacy*, 57(5), 367–376.
- Fisher, D., & Frey, N. (2015). *Text-Dependent Questions, Grades K–5* and *Grades 6–12: Pathways to Close and Critical Reading*. Corwin. (Question ladder: what the text says → how it works → what it means → what it inspires you to do.)
- Shanahan, T. (2011). Common Core Standards: Are we going to lower the fences or teach kids to climb? *Reading Today*, 29(1), 20–21. The "climb the fence" metaphor is the policy warrant for keeping text hard and scaffolding rather than leveling.
- Shanahan, T., Fisher, D., & Frey, N. (2012). The challenge of challenging text. *Educational Leadership*, 69(6), 58–62. Difficulty is analogized to "weight or resistance in an exercise program." **Notably, this article's only empirical citation is Stahl & Fairbanks (1986), a vocabulary-instruction meta-analysis** — nothing supporting the harder-text-plus-scaffolding claim itself.
- Shanahan's own operational stance (shanahanonliteracy.com): close reading = intensive analysis in three passes (what it says / how it works / what it means); rereading is required but may be partial; extensive frontloading (picture walks, guided previews) is discouraged; text-dependent questions must not give away what reading would reveal.

**Empirically documented operationalization.** The 2026 review below coded 19 close-reading intervention studies: rereading 94% (mean 3.1 passes, meaning-focused goals), annotation 89%, text-dependent questions 78% (teacher-generated, evidence-citing), post-reading writing 61%, post-reading discussion 50%, and **only 75% explicitly used complex text** — i.e., the "complex text" leg of the definition is inconsistently implemented even in studies claiming to test close reading.

## 2. Experimental evidence for close reading as a routine at secondary level: essentially absent

The definitive source is a brand-new review:

**"Still Too Close to Call: A Literature Review on Close Reading Interventions and Their Effects on Reading Outcomes in Grades 3–9," *Reading Psychology* (published online 2 April 2026), DOI 10.1080/02702711.2026.2644958.** (Radboud/Erasmus authors; I could not retrieve the author list — both repository copies 403'd.)

- 19 studies total. Designs: **4 quasi-experimental with a control group; 9 pretest–posttest without control; 6 case studies. Zero RCTs.**
- Publication status: **only 3 peer-reviewed journal articles; 11 master's theses; 5 doctoral dissertations.**
- **Median sample size = 11 participants** (mean 18.6, SD 18.4). 84% were teacher-researcher studies.
- Grades: 11 studies grades 3–6; 8 studies grades 7–9.
- **No effect sizes were systematically reported anywhere in the literature.**
- Among the controlled studies, results are mixed-to-null: one showed larger comprehension gains vs. guided reading; **Cowden (2019) and Higdon (2019), both quasi-experiments vs. business-as-usual, found no positive effect.**
- Authors' conclusion: quality, quantity, and generalizability are limited; **"we cannot make causal claims on the effects"**; schools should not adopt close reading as their single comprehension approach.

**The flagship Fisher & Frey secondary study, examined closely** (Fisher & Frey, 2014, *JAAL* 57(5), 367–376):
- 438 eligible students (bottom 40% on state ELA) across 3 middle schools; 100 randomly assigned to 5 after-school intervention classrooms → 75 analyzed; 247 non-participants served as comparison. Attrition 25% treatment / 27% comparison.
- After-school, 3×/week × 90 min, October–May. Passages 3 paragraphs–3 pages, Lexile 925–1185.
- Measures: GMRT-4 fall/spring; primary outcome California Standards Test ELA.
- Results: attendance 94% vs 81% (p<.01); 64% vs 12% improved ≥1 performance level (p<.001); Reader Self-Perception Scale 186 vs 99 (p<.001).
- **Fatal confounds:** the contrast is "attended a well-run after-school program" vs. "did not," not close reading vs. another literacy routine; the comparison group was not randomly formed; volunteering/attendance differences are themselves an outcome; no reported effect sizes on a standardized comprehension measure. **ERIC/WWC flags this study as not meeting What Works Clearinghouse evidence standards.**

**Bottom line for Q2:** There is no randomized trial, and no well-controlled quasi-experiment, showing that close reading *as a routine* improves secondary reading comprehension. The evidence base is descriptive, practitioner-generated, small-n, and dominated by unpublished theses. Close reading was scaled nationally on the strength of professional consensus and a policy argument, not efficacy trials.

## 3. The text-complexity premise: does harder text help?

**ACT (2006). *Reading Between the Lines: What the ACT Reveals About College Readiness in Reading*. Iowa City: ACT.**
- ~1.2 million 2005 ACT-tested graduates; ~352,000 with EXPLORE (gr. 8) → PLAN (gr. 10) → ACT (gr. 12) longitudinal data.
- "Complex text" defined by the RSVP heuristic (Relationships, Richness, Structure, Style, Vocabulary, Purpose).
- Findings: 51% met the Reading Benchmark (score 21); performance on *complex* passages, not question type (literal vs. inferential, main idea vs. detail), was the sharpest discriminator between benchmark-meeters and non-meeters.
- **Design status: purely correlational/predictive.** It shows that students who *can* read complex text are more college-ready. It contains no manipulation of instructional text difficulty and therefore cannot support the inference that *assigning* harder text *causes* better comprehension. This is the single load-bearing citation in CCSS Appendix A for the text-complexity staircase, and it does not bear the weight.

**Amendum, S. J., Conradi, K., & Hiebert, E. H. (2018). Does text complexity matter in the elementary grades? A research synthesis of text difficulty and elementary students' reading fluency and comprehension. *Educational Psychology Review*, 30, 121–151. DOI 10.1007/s10648-017-9398-2.**
- 26 studies, 1970–2015: **18 correlational (69%), 4 quasi-experimental (15%), 3 experimental (12%), 1 single-subject (4%).**
- Accuracy: negative relationship with text difficulty in all but one study; effect strongest for struggling/beginning readers.
- Rate: 11 of 15 studies (73%) showed slower rates with harder text.
- Prosody: declined with difficulty for lower-skilled readers.
- Comprehension: **7 studies (53.8%) negative, 5 (38.5%) null, 1 (7.7%) optimal at moderate difficulty. "No study indicated that increased text difficulty was related to an increase in students' comprehension."**
- Conclusion: CCSS-driven complexity increases "precede a clear understanding of effects on classroom achievement"; increased complexity *without* scaffolding produces negative outcomes.

**O'Connor, R. E., Swanson, H. L., & Geraghty, C. (2010). Improvement in reading rate under independent and difficult text levels: Influences on word and comprehension skills. *Journal of Educational Psychology*, 102(1), 1–19.**
- **True RCT. N = 123 poor readers, grades 2 and 4**, randomly assigned to three conditions: guided oral reading to an adult with text at **independent level (92–100% word accuracy)**, at **difficult level (80–90% accuracy)**, or **untreated control**. 20 weeks; pre/mid/post assessment.
- Findings: both treatment groups > control on rate, word recognition, and comprehension; no treatment effects on decoding or vocabulary. **Critically, there were no significant differences in growth between the independent-level and difficult-level conditions.**
- Interpretation: this is the strongest experimental test available and it **does not support** the claim that harder text produces better outcomes. What produced gains was *supported reading practice volume*, not text difficulty. Shanahan cites it as evidence *against* instructional-level theory (harder text was not worse); Hiebert cites the same result as evidence that harder text confers no benefit. Both readings are consistent with the data — which is precisely the point: the study is null on the difficulty contrast.

**Hiebert, E. H. (2012). The Common Core's staircase of text complexity: Getting the size of the first step right. *Reading Today*, 29(3), 26–27** (see also Hiebert's TextProject papers on readability and the staircase).
- Argues the staircase is expressed in Lexiles, which index sentence length and word frequency only, and are blind to knowledge demands and structure. Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry rates lower than a simple grade 2–3 informational book because narrative dialogue depresses the formula.

- Hiebert's later work (TextProject, post-2024 NAEP) argues CCSS developers misread the historical record: first-grade text complexity had already peaked in the early 1990s; the perceived "dumbing down" was based on pre-1990s analyses. Her documented downstream effect: teachers read hard texts *aloud to* students instead of having them read, reducing independent reading volume — the mechanism that actually drove gains in O'Connor et al.

**Fluency/challenging-text line (Stahl & Heubach; Kuhn & Stahl).** Stahl & Heubach (2005, *Journal of Literacy Research*, Fluency-Oriented Reading Instruction) is the most-cited support for challenging text, and Amendum et al. characterize it correctly: it shows benefits of reading difficult texts *with others in supportive instructional contexts* — i.e., the effective ingredient is scaffolding, repeated reading, and volume, not difficulty per se. Kuhn & Stahl (2003) is a fluency-construct review (accuracy/rate/prosody), not a difficulty manipulation.

**The counter-case (Shanahan).** Shanahan's "Rejecting Instructional Level Theory" argument: Betts's (1946) 95–98% accuracy criterion traces to an unpublished dissertation by Kilgallon that contained **no evidence that instructional-level placement conferred any learning advantage** — a genuinely strong historiographic point. His positive evidence is thin: Morgan, Wilcox & Eldredge (2000) with first graders in peer dyads (Amendum et al. note this study found *no* relationship between text difficulty and comprehension), O'Connor et al. (2010) (null on difficulty), Brown (2018), and TNTP's non-experimental Opportunity Myth-style analyses. **Net: the strongest defensible claim is that instructional-level placement lacks an evidentiary basis — not that harder text is better.** Both sides of this debate are arguing from an evidentiary vacuum, and the vacuum is asymmetrically damaging to the CCSS position because CCSS made the affirmative policy claim.

## 4. Snow's critique

**Snow, C. E., & O'Connor, C. (2016). Close reading and far-reaching classroom discussion: Fostering a vital connection. *Journal of Education*, 196(1), 1–8** (expanded from the 2013 International Reading Association / Literacy Research Association policy brief of the same title).

Their four objections:

1. **The "level playing field" rationale is false.** The central justification for close reading — that restricting students to the text equalizes background-knowledge differences — is, in their words, an appealing fantasy. Comprehension research (they invoke Kintsch, 1988, comprehension as integration of new information with existing schemata; and RAND Reading Study Group, 2002, simultaneous *extraction and construction* of meaning) establishes that missing background knowledge and vocabulary are the *primary* causes of comprehension failure, and text-only analysis cannot remedy them. Close reading foregrounds extraction and ignores construction, reader variation, and sociocultural context.
2. **Background knowledge cannot be suppressed and shouldn't be.** Their Gettysburg Address example: layers of meaning dependent on the Declaration of Independence are simply inaccessible to students lacking the historical frame. They cite Bransford & Johnson (1972) on titles/context enabling comprehension and Hart & Risley (1995) on conceptually rooted vocabulary gaps. Also: "texts with too many unfamiliar words are simply not comprehended, and if not comprehended cannot be a source of new word learning" — which undercuts the harder-text-builds-vocabulary argument directly.
3. **The frontloading prohibition is operationally incoherent.** Even where advocates permit some pre-teaching, teachers are asked to anticipate which background knowledge each of 20–25 different readers lacks *without previewing the text's content* — an impossible demand. They likewise reject confining vocabulary work to "tier three" technical terms.
4. **Restricting legitimate evidence to the text is wrong on the merits**: prior knowledge, moral judgment, social norms, and cultural traditions are legitimate warrants in argument.
5. **Motivation/tedium**: painstaking repeated close reading targets exactly the middle- and high-school struggling readers whose motivation is already collapsing (Guthrie, Alao & Rinehart, 1997) and may worsen the problem.
6. **Crowding out** — their gravest concern: close reading displaces academically productive classroom discussion, which *does* predict good outcomes (they cite Applebee et al., 2003, and Murphy et al., 2009).

Their prescription: close reading should be *brief* (Wong Fillmore & Fillmore, 2012: one sentence, 10–15 min/day), *collaborative* (small groups with teacher support and peer talk, not solitary annotation), *embedded* inside broader dialogic discussion, and *instrumental* to some purpose beyond doing close reading. **Hinchman, K. A., & Moore, D. W. (2013). Close reading: A cultural response. *Journal of Adolescent & Adult Literacy*, 56(6), 441–450.** — Caveat: I was unable to retrieve or verify this record (ERIC returned no match for the title and for "Hinchman Moore close reading"; the only Hinchman item surfacing was *Best Practices in Adolescent Literacy Instruction*, Hinchman & Sheridan-Thomas, Guilford, 2008). **Murphy, P. K., Wilkinson, I. A. G., Soter, A. O., Hennessey, M. N., & Alexander, J. F. (2009). Examining the effects of classroom discussion on students' comprehension of text: A meta-analysis. *Journal of Educational Psychology*, 101(3), 740–764. DOI 10.1037/a0015576.**

**Applebee, A. N., Langer, J. A., Nystrand, M., & Gamoran, A. (2003). Discussion-based approaches to developing understanding: Classroom instruction and student performance in middle and high school English. *American Educational Research Journal*, 40(3), 685–730.**

## Synthesis

The CCSS/Fisher & Frey close-reading package rests on a three-link chain, and every link is weak in a different way. Link 1 (ACT 2006) is a correlation between *being able to* read complex text and college readiness, converted without warrant into a prescription to *assign* harder text. Link 2 (harder text improves comprehension) is contradicted by the only relevant RCT (O'Connor et al., 2010: null on difficulty) and by a 26-study synthesis in which **not a single study** found increased difficulty associated with improved comprehension. Link 3 (the close-reading routine itself) has no RCT at any grade level, and its controlled quasi-experiments are unpublished dissertations with null results and median samples of eleven students.

content:
## 1. The original 1969 document: what it actually was

**Citation (correct form):** Frayer, D. A., Fredrick, W. C., & Klausmeier, H. J. (1969). *A schema for testing the level of concept mastery: Report from the Project on Situational Variables and Efficiency of Concept Learning.* Working Paper No. 16. Madison, WI: Wisconsin Research and Development Center for Cognitive Learning. **32 pages.** (Note: "Fredrick," not "Frederick"; it is **Working Paper** No. 16 — many secondary sources miscite it as "Technical Report No. 16.")

**What it is:** A non-peer-reviewed institutional working paper — a **conceptual/technical assessment framework**, not an instructional method and not a controlled empirical study. It was funded under a federally sponsored R&D center project on concept learning, and its purpose was to specify how one would *test* whether a learner had mastered a concept.

**What it actually contained** — confirmed from a downstream Wisconsin R&D Center report that operationalized the schema (Voelker & Sorenson, ED049036), which lists the schema as **twelve multiple-choice test-item task types**:

1. Given name of attribute, select example
2. Given example of attribute, select name
3. Given name of concept, select example
4. Given name of concept, select non-example
5. Given example of concept, select name
6. Given name of concept, select relevant attribute
7. Given name of concept, select irrelevant attribute
8. Given meaning of concept, select name
9. Given name of concept, select meaning
10. Given name of concept, select supraordinate concept
11. Given name of concept, select subordinate concept
12. Given two concepts, select principle relating them

That report states plainly: these "tasks were part of a schema for testing the level of concept mastery (Frayer, Fredrick, & Klausmeier, 1969)."

**Does the four-quadrant template appear in it?** There is no evidence that it does, and the content above is inconsistent with it. The 1969 paper is an **item-specification taxonomy for assessment**, tied to Klausmeier's Conceptual Learning and Development (CLD) theory. The familiar 2×2 box (Definition / Characteristics / Examples / Non-examples) is a **later practitioner adaptation**, most commonly traced to Buehl, D. (2001), *Classroom Strategies for Interactive Learning* (International Reading Association), and to content-literacy PD materials of the same era. Frayer's own 12-task schema contains categories (supraordinate/subordinate/coordinate concepts, relevant vs. irrelevant attributes) that the popular four-box template **drops**.

**Notable archival fact:** the 1969 working paper is **not indexed in ERIC**. An ERIC author search on "Frayer, Dorothy A." returns eight records (1970–1973); Working Paper No. 16 is absent. It survives mainly in library catalogs (WorldCat OCLC 5085175; Google Books). So the single most-cited source for a ubiquitous classroom tool is a grey-literature document most citers have never read.

## 2. Rigorous experimental evidence for the Frayer template specifically

**Short answer: essentially none at the standard of a well-powered, peer-reviewed RCT with a business-as-usual control and a Frayer-vs-something contrast.** No WWC intervention report or study review exists for the Frayer Model.

The full ERIC corpus for "Frayer model" is **23 records total**, of which ~12 are journal articles — and most of those are descriptive/practitioner pieces (*Teaching Children Mathematics*, *Science and Children*, *Journal of Physical Education*, *Clearing House*, *Communication Teacher*), not intervention studies.

**The closest things to real evidence:**

- **Peters, C. W. (1974/1975).** "A comparison between the Frayer model of concept attainment and the textbook approach to concept attainment." Wisconsin R&D Center Technical Report No. 290 (ERIC **ED163452**); journal version in *Reading Research Quarterly* (ERIC EJ114119). **N = 360 ninth graders**, stratified by reading proficiency, social studies concepts, also crossing example-sequence (chronological/topical/reverse). Result: Frayer-model materials produced significantly higher comprehension than textbook-organized materials at **both** reading levels; example sequence had no effect. This is the strongest single study — but it is (a) 50+ years old, (b) authored inside the same R&D center that produced the model, (c) tests the *Frayer definitional procedure* (genus/differentia, relevant vs. irrelevant attributes, examples/non-examples, supraordinate/subordinate/coordinate relations), **not** the modern four-box worksheet, and (d) reports no effect size by modern conventions.

- **Reed, D. K., Jemison, E., Sidler-Folsom, J., & Weber, A. (2019).** "Electronic graphic organizers for learning science vocabulary." *Journal of Experimental Education, 87*(4), 552–574 (ERIC EJ1222717). **N = 92 fourth graders**, randomly assigned to complete electronic Frayer Models **alone vs. with a synchronous online partner**, 7 weeks, life science. Result: all students improved on science content, **d ≈ 0.60**, but the two conditions **did not differ** after controlling for pretest. Critically, **there was no non-Frayer control group** — the d ≈ 0.60 is pre-post growth across seven weeks of science instruction, not an estimate of the Frayer template's causal effect. This is the best-designed US study and it does **not** test whether Frayer beats an alternative.

- **Palmer, Boon & Spencer (2014),** *Reading & Writing Quarterly* — concept mapping for vocabulary, small-N special education, adjacent rather than Frayer-specific.

**The rest of the literature — characterized honestly.** The bulk of "Frayer works" citations are small, non-peer-reviewed or predatory-adjacent EFL studies from Indonesia and the Philippines, typically two intact classes, no randomization, teacher-made outcome measures, no effect sizes, implausibly large gains:

| Study | Venue / country | Design | n | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Panjaitan & Sihotang (2020), ERIC EJ1297676 | *Acuity* (Indonesia) | Non-randomized 2-group pre/post, intact classes | 80 (40/40), Grade 11 | Post: FM 87.0 vs CMS 84.4; normalized gain .816 vs .763; p = .000. **No effect size.** Authors concede treatments ran at different times of day; pilot found 13 items with "very low" validity |
| SMPN 10 Kota Serang (UNTIRTA thesis, eprints 63400) | Undergraduate thesis | Nonequivalent control-group | Grade 8 | 83.15 vs 77.71, p = .027 |
| SMPN 1 Tompobulu | ResearchGate preprint | Quasi-experimental | Grade 8 | Experimental 36.80 → 76.80 vs control 50.88 → 55.52; t = 5.951. A **40-point** gain against a 4.6-point control gain is not a credible instructional effect |
| Modified Frayer, QC Polytechnic University (Philippines) | Conference/academia.edu | "Randomized" pre/post control | 60 (30/30), senior HS | 14.80 vs 13.10 — a **1.7-point** raw difference reported as meaningful |
| Bagbag NHS (Philippines) | *Journal of Development Research* (SF Publishing) | Quasi-experimental | Grade 9 | "Significant difference" |
| Hulderman & Wageman (2025), *TESL-EJ*, ERIC EJ1477809 | TESL-EJ (US, Upper Midwest) | **Case study, no control group**, convenience sample | **n = 5** ELs, grades 9–12 | 57% mean score gain over 6 weeks |

Common failure modes across this set: intact-class assignment, no blinding, outcome tests written by the person delivering the treatment and aligned only to the taught words, no fidelity data, no maintenance or transfer measures, no effect sizes, and pre-test non-equivalence that swamps the treatment contrast. Several also confound "Frayer" with "extra instructional time on vocabulary." **None would meet WWC standards even with reservations.**

## 3. The well-established evidence is for rich vocabulary instruction generally, not for the template

**Stahl, S. A., & Fairbanks, M. M. (1986).** "The effects of vocabulary instruction: A model-based meta-analysis." *Review of Educational Research, 56*(1), 72–110. ERIC EJ335314. Model-based meta-analysis (~52 studies).
- **ES = .97** for comprehension of **passages containing the taught words**
- **ES = .30** for **global/standardized comprehension** measures
- Both significantly different from zero
- **Method effects (the key finding):** methods providing **both definitional and contextual** information ("mixed method") substantially outperformed definition-only instruction. The extraction I obtained gives mixed-method ≈ **1.05** vs. definitional-only ≈ **.37** (non-significant). *Caveat: I could not open the full tables behind a paywall; treat the method-level split as approximate and verify against the printed article before quoting.* The .97 / .30 figures are directly from the published abstract and are solid.
- Also: effective methods gave **more than one or two exposures** and required **deeper processing**. Correlation between instructional time allocated and passage-comprehension ES was **r = .65 (N = 26, p < .001)**.

**Elleman, A. M., Lindo, E. J., Morphy, P., & Compton, D. L. (2009).** "The impact of vocabulary instruction on passage-level comprehension of school-age children: A meta-analysis." *Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 2*(1), 1–44. ERIC EJ866970. **37 studies**, pre-K–12.
- Comprehension, **researcher/custom-designed measures: d = 0.50**
- Comprehension, **standardized measures: d = 0.10**
- Students with **reading difficulties d = 1.23** vs. **without d = 0.39** on custom measures (>3× benefit)
- Correlation between vocabulary and comprehension effects within studies: **r = 0.43**

The 5:1 gap between custom and standardized measures in Elleman, mirroring the .97/.30 gap in Stahl & Fairbanks, is the single most important number for calibrating any Frayer claim: **near-transfer gains on taught words are easy; general comprehension gains are not.**

**Beck & McKeown "robust vocabulary instruction" (the real experimental base):**
- **Beck, I. L., Perfetti, C. A., & McKeown, M. G. (1982).** "Effects of long-term vocabulary instruction on lexical access and reading comprehension." *Journal of Educational Psychology, 74*(4), 506–521. Fourth graders taught **104 words over a five-month program**; instructed students compared with matched controls equated on pre-instruction vocabulary. Instructed students outperformed controls on semantic decision tasks ranging from single-word judgments to sentence verification, plus word knowledge and comprehension of passages containing instructed words. Design: quasi-experimental with matched controls, not randomized.
- **McKeown, M. G., Beck, I. L., Omanson, R. C., & Pople, M. T. (1985).** "Some effects of the nature and frequency of vocabulary instruction on the knowledge and use of words." *Reading Research Quarterly, 20*(5), 522–535. ERIC EJ323481. Fourth graders; factorial crossing of **instruction type (traditional definitional vs. rich vs. rich + extended/out-of-class encounters)** × **frequency (4 vs. 12 encounters)**. Findings: definitional association alone is sufficient for basic word knowledge; **12 encounters > 4**; but **rich** and especially **rich + extended** instruction was required for fluency of access, context interpretation, and **story comprehension**. This is the study that actually establishes *why* deep processing plus many encounters matters — and note that a one-off Frayer worksheet is a single encounter, the condition that did *not* move comprehension.

**Marzano's six-step process (2004, *Building Background Knowledge for Academic Achievement*; 2009, "Six Steps to Better Vocabulary Instruction," *Educational Leadership, 67*(1), 84–85).** Steps: (1) teacher description/explanation/example, (2) student restatement in own words, (3) student nonlinguistic representation, (4) periodic activities extending knowledge, (5) periodic student discussion, (6) periodic vocabulary games. **Evidence base is Marzano's own in-house action research**, not peer-reviewed RCTs: he reports 50+ teacher-conducted studies over five years, with an **average 24-percentile-point gain across 24 elementary teachers** — but also that **nine studies showed negative effects** while six showed gains >40 percentile points. That dispersion, and the unblinded teacher-as-researcher design, means the six-step process should be described as *research-informed*, not *research-proven*. It is worth noting Marzano's steps are almost entirely **generative and repeated over time**, which is exactly what Frayer worksheets usually are not.

**National Reading Panel (2000), Chapter 4 Part I.** The Panel reviewed roughly 50 studies meeting criteria but **could not conduct a formal meta-analysis on vocabulary** because of heterogeneity in methods and outcome measures; it produced a narrative synthesis of ~21 instructional methods. Conclusions: vocabulary should be taught both directly and indirectly; **repetition and multiple exposures** matter; tasks should be **restructured** when necessary; **active engagement** beyond definitional copying is required; and dependence on a single method is inadvisable. The NRP endorses no specific graphic organizer.

## 4. Graphic organizer meta-analyses

**Kim, A.-H., Vaughn, S., Wanzek, J., & Wei, S. (2004).** "Graphic organizers and their effects on the reading comprehension of students with LD: A synthesis of research." *Journal of Learning Disabilities, 37*(2), 105–118. ERIC EJ694460. **21 group-design intervention studies** (15 articles), 1963–June 2001, **848 students with LD**, elementary through high school.
- **Posttest d = 1.04; follow-up d = 0.60**
- Semantic organizers (9 studies): **d = 0.81–1.69**
- Cognitive maps *with* mnemonic (3): **d = 0.81–0.91**
- Cognitive maps *without* mnemonic (7): **d = 0.96–5.07** (single-group designs); **d = 1.34–1.79** (treatment-comparison)
- Framed outlines (2): **d = 0.80–1.78**
- **Measure type: "Intervention effects based on researcher-developed reading tests were significantly larger than those based on standardized tests."** Neither of the two studies using standardized measures found significant differences.
- **Transfer: no statistically significant differences** — students did not generalize to novel passages.
- **No mention of Frayer; no vocabulary-specific outcomes.**

**Dexter, D. D., & Hughes, C. A. (2011).** "Graphic organizers and students with learning disabilities: A meta-analysis." *Learning Disability Quarterly, 34*(1), 51–72. ERIC EJ931412. **16 articles, 21 samples, 808 participants, grades 4–12; 55 posttest ES, 29 maintenance ES.**
- **Overall posttest ES = .91 (SE .062); maintenance ES = .56 (SE .074)**
- Near-transfer posttest **ES = 1.07** (n = 45); near-transfer maintenance **.78** (n = 27); far-transfer posttest **ES = .61** (n = 10); far-transfer maintenance **.69** (n = 2)
- By organizer type: **semantic mapping 1.25**, semantic feature analysis **1.19**, SM/SFA combination **1.06**, syntactic/semantic feature analysis **.91**, cognitive mapping **.89**, visual display **.75**
- By subject: **science 1.05** (n = 23), **social studies 1.04** (n = 19), **English/reading/writing .96** (n = 11), **mathematics .59** (n = 4)
- **Critical caveat: "All but one study used measures that were researcher-created"** (only Boyle, 1996 used standardized measures). The near/far transfer gap (1.07 vs .61) is the internal signature of measure-alignment inflation.
- **Frayer is not mentioned anywhere in this meta-analysis.**

**Dexter, D. D., Park, Y. J., & Hughes, C. A. (2011).** "A meta-analytic review of graphic organizers and science instruction for adolescents with learning disabilities." *Learning Disabilities Research & Practice, 26*(4), 204–213. **23 ES from 6 articles, 271 participants, grades 6–12.** GOs associated with increased vocabulary knowledge and factual comprehension **as measured by researcher-generated multiple-choice tests**; **maintenance ES = 0.80**. Again, entirely near-transfer, researcher-made outcomes.

**Nesbit, J. C., & Adesope, O. O. (2006).** "Learning with concept and knowledge maps: A meta-analysis." *Review of Educational Research, 76*(3), 413–448. **67 standardized mean-difference ES from 55 studies, 5,818 participants**, grade 4 through postsecondary, across science, psychology, statistics, nursing. Concept map use was associated with increased knowledge retention, with effects "varying from small to large" depending on implementation and comparison condition, and **significant heterogeneity in most subsets**. *I could not retrieve the moderator table (map-construction vs. map-study; vs. reading text / lectures / discussion) — the commonly quoted sub-effect sizes should be verified against the article before use.*

## Abstract

"The role of classroom discussions in comprehension and learning has been the focus of investigations since the early 1960s." This meta-analysis examined empirical studies to determine how classroom discussion affects student comprehension and critical thinking. Key findings indicate that "several discussion approaches produced strong increases in the amount of student talk and concomitant reductions in teacher talk, as well as substantial improvements in text comprehension." However, few approaches effectively enhanced literal or inferential comprehension and reasoning skills. Effects varied based on study design, outcome measures, and student academic ability, with most research conducted among elementary students (grades 4-6).

- Outcomes: **teacher and student talk only** — teacher talk decreased in quantity and shifted toward meaning-construction questions; student-initiated questions increased in number and complexity.
- **No student comprehension outcome measure. No control group. No effect sizes.** This foundational paper is not an efficacy study and never claimed to be.

**Sandora, C., Beck, I. L., & McKeown, M. G. (1999). "A comparison of two discussion strategies on students' comprehension and interpretation of complex literature." *Reading Psychology*, 20(3), 177–212.**
- QtA (during-reading discussion) vs. Great Books Shared Inquiry (after-reading discussion), predominantly African American, lower-SES middle school.
- **Fatal design flaw: condition is fully confounded with grade level** — the sixth graders got QtA, the seventh graders got Great Books. Any QtA "advantage" is inseparable from cohort, teacher, and grade effects.
- Findings: QtA students had greater recall and higher scores on interpretive questions. **No usable effect sizes; not a WWC-eligible design.**

**Beck, McKeown & Worthy (1995), *RRQ* 30(2), 220–238, "Giving a text voice can improve students' understanding"** — often cited in QtA lineages but is a *text-revision* experiment (rewriting textbook passages), not a test of the discussion routine.

### The important one: McKeown, Beck & Blake (2009)

**McKeown, M. G., Beck, I. L., & Blake, R. G. K. (2009). "Rethinking reading comprehension instruction: A comparison of instruction for strategies and content approaches." *Reading Research Quarterly*, 44(3), 218–253.** Full text retrieved and read.

- **Design:** two-year experiment, fifth grade, low-performing urban district, 6 intact classrooms. Year 1: n = 119 (44 Content / 37 Strategies / 38 Basal). Year 2: n = 116, **with random assignment of students balanced on race and special-education status** (41/38/37). 58% African American; 49% FRL.
- **Conditions:** (a) **Content** — explicitly derived from QtA; open meaning-based queries ("What's going on here?"); (b) **Strategies** — summarizing, predicting, inferring, question generation, comprehension monitoring; (c) **Basal control** — scripted basal teacher-edition questions. All lessons scripted, whole-class, teacher-delivered.
- **Dose:** Year 1, five narrative lessons over five weeks (45–75 min/week). Year 2, five narrative plus three expository lessons, plus a transfer task.
- **Results (reported as p-values and means; the article does not report standardized effect sizes):**
  - **Sentence Verification Technique: null in both years, all text types** (Y1 all p > .62; Y2 narrative p > .67, expository p > .31).
  - **Narrative recall:** Y1 length Content M = 16.20 vs Strategies 10.33 (p = .001), Basal 14.13 > Strategies (p = .05); quality Content 33.40 vs Strategies 22.97 (p = .001). Y2 length 17.32 vs 11.77 (p = .005); quality 33.76 vs 24.79 (p = .01).
  - **Y2 expository knowledge probes:** Content 4.27 and **Basal 4.30** both > Strategies 3.15 (p = .02). No recall differences.
  - **Comprehension monitoring: null** (p = .638). **Strategies knowledge: null** (p = .16).
  - **Discourse:** Y2 student text-based talk Content 97% vs Strategies 66% vs Basal 84%; words per student response Content 26.55 vs Basal 13.84 vs Strategies 9.50 (p < .0005).
  - Transfer (Y2 only): "a modest effect in favor of the Content students."

**How to read this honestly.** It is a genuine experiment and the best QtA-relevant study in existence. But the headline is *not* "QtA works." It is: **QtA-style content questioning beat explicit strategy instruction, while the ordinary basal control frequently also beat strategy instruction and was statistically indistinguishable from Content on several measures.** On the most objective comprehension measure (SVT) everything was null. The robust finding is about the *quality and volume of text-focused student talk*, where Content was dramatically superior.

### Later / secondary and science evidence

- **Sencibaugh, J. M., & Sencibaugh, A. M. (2015). "The effects of Questioning the Author on the reading comprehension of middle school students." *Reading Improvement*, 52(3), 85–92.** **n = 6 eighth graders, one-group pretest–posttest, no control** (Woodcock Reading Mastery). This is the study most often cited as "QtA works at secondary level."
- **Crosson, McKeown, Matsumura & Correnti, IES award 2015–2018 ("For Argument's Sake," $1.5M, Penn State)** — a **development** grant (intervention "Triple Q" applying QtA queries to argument writing), not an efficacy trial. Reported positive effect on argument writing, but this is developer-run pilot work.
- **No QtA study in a secondary science context was located.**

### WWC status

- **There is no WWC intervention report for Questioning the Author.** It appears in **no** WWC intervention report, evidence snapshot, or practice-guide recommendation.
- In the IES/WWC practice guide **Kamil et al. (2008), *Improving Adolescent Literacy* (NCEE 2008-4027)**, Recommendation 3 ("Provide opportunities for extended discussion of text meaning and interpretation") is rated **Moderate** (vs. Strong for vocabulary, strategy instruction, and intensive intervention). Its evidence base is four small quasi-experiments (Bird 1984; Heinl 1988; Yeazell 1982 — three of which the panel says had "less rigorous designs with low internal validity"; Reznitskaya et al. 2001 was the only one demonstrating pretest equivalence) plus Applebee et al. (2003), correlational. The panel explicitly notes small samples, writing-prompt rather than standardized outcomes, and that "most experimental studies of discussion-based approaches thus far have used narrative texts." **QtA is mentioned only once — in "Potential roadblocks and solutions," as a recommended teacher resource** (Beck & McKeown, 2006), not as an evidence-supported intervention.
- **Vaughn et al. (2022), *Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4–9* (WWC 2022007)** does not mention QtA at all.
- **Murphy, Wilkinson, Soter, Hennessey & Alexander (2009), *JEP* 101(3), 740–764** includes QtA among nine discussion approaches. The published finding: several approaches produced strong increases in student talk and reductions in teacher talk and "substantial improvements in text comprehension," but **few raised literal or inferential comprehension or critical thinking**, with effects moderated by design and outcome measure; most studies were grades 4–6. *I could not open the per-approach weighted effect sizes — do not quote a QtA-specific ES from this meta-analysis without opening the tables.* Note also that QtA's contribution to that meta-analysis rests largely on Sandora et al. (1999), with its grade confound.

### Verdict: **WEAKLY-SUPPORTED**

Justification: one real experiment (McKeown, Beck & Blake 2009) with partial randomization, standardized dosing, and mostly null results on objective comprehension but consistent advantages over strategy instruction on recall and large advantages on text-focused talk. Everything else is descriptive (1996), confounded (1999), or n = 6 (2015). It clears the bar of "not made up" — which is more than many PD staples — but it is not established as an efficacious intervention, has no WWC standing, and has essentially no evidence base at secondary level or in science. The defensible claim is narrow: *asking open, meaning-focused questions during reading produces more and better text-based student talk than teaching comprehension strategies does, and does no worse on comprehension.*
