## 2. THE FRAYER MODEL

### The 1969 citation does not say what people think it says

**Frayer, D. A., Fredrick, W. C., & Klausmeier, H. J. (1969). *A schema for testing the level of concept mastery.* Working Paper No. 16. Madison: Wisconsin R&D Center for Cognitive Learning. 32 pp.** (Note: "Fredrick," and it is a **Working Paper**, not Technical Report — most citations get both wrong.)

- It is a **non-peer-reviewed institutional working paper** presenting an **assessment item-specification taxonomy** — **twelve multiple-choice task types** (given name of concept → select example / non-example / relevant attribute / irrelevant attribute / supraordinate / subordinate concept, etc.), confirmed via a downstream Wisconsin R&D report (ERIC ED049036) that operationalized the schema.
- It contains **no instructional intervention and no controlled study of teaching**.
- **The four-quadrant worksheet does not appear in it.** The familiar Definition / Characteristics / Examples / Non-examples box is a practitioner adaptation, most commonly traced to **Buehl (2001), *Classroom Strategies for Interactive Learning* (IRA)**. The popular template *drops* the schema's supraordinate/subordinate/coordinate relations.
- The paper is **not indexed in ERIC**; it survives in library catalogs (WorldCat OCLC 5085175). The most-cited source for a ubiquitous tool is grey literature almost nobody citing it has read.

### Direct controlled evidence for the template

- **Peters, C. W. (1974/75). "A comparison between the Frayer model of concept attainment and the textbook approach." Wisconsin R&D Center TR No. 290 (ERIC ED163452); *RRQ* version EJ114119.** **n = 360 ninth graders**, stratified by reading proficiency, social studies concepts, crossed with example sequence. Frayer-organized materials beat textbook-organized materials at both reading levels; sequence had no effect. Caveats: 50 years old, produced by the same center that produced the model, tests the **full definitional procedure** (genus/differentia, attributes, hierarchy) rather than the modern worksheet, and reports no modern effect size.
- **Reed, D. K., Jemison, E., Sidler-Folsom, J., & Weber, A. (2019). "Electronic graphic organizers for learning science vocabulary." *Journal of Experimental Education*, 87(4), 552–574.** **n = 92 fourth graders**, randomly assigned to complete electronic Frayer Models **alone vs. with an online partner**, 7 weeks, life science. All students improved (**d ≈ 0.60** pre–post), **conditions did not differ**, and **there was no non-Frayer control group.** The best-designed US study on record does not test whether Frayer beats anything.
- The rest of the corpus is small non-randomized EFL work — e.g., Panjaitan & Sihotang (2020), *Acuity* (Indonesia), n = 80 intact Grade 11 classes, no effect size, authors concede treatments ran at different times of day and that 13 pilot items had "very low" validity; an SMPN 1 Tompobulu preprint reporting a **40-point** experimental gain vs. a 4.6-point control gain (not a credible instructional effect); a Philippine study whose "significant" result is a **1.7-point** raw difference; and Hulderman & Wageman (2025), *TESL-EJ*, a **case study with n = 5** secondary ELs and no control. Common failures: intact-class assignment, treatment-aligned teacher-made tests, no fidelity data, no transfer or maintenance measures, no effect sizes. **None would meet WWC standards even with reservations.**
- **No WWC intervention report or study review exists for the Frayer Model.** Total ERIC records for "Frayer model": **23**, mostly practitioner descriptions.

### What is actually well-established (and what Frayer is a proxy for)

- **Stahl & Fairbanks (1986), *RER* 56(1), 72–110:** comprehension of **passages containing taught words ES = .97**; **global/standardized comprehension ES = .30**. Mixed definitional + contextual instruction substantially outperformed definition-only (extracted figures ≈ **1.05 vs .37 n.s.**; *the method-level split is behind a paywall — verify before quoting*). Time allocated to instruction correlated with passage-comprehension ES at **r = .65 (N = 26, p < .001)**.
- **Elleman, Lindo, Morphy & Compton (2009), *JREE* 2(1), 1–44:** **37 studies, 3,063 participants.** Comprehension **d = 0.50 on researcher-designed measures**, **d = 0.10 (n.s., p = .08) on standardized measures**. Students with reading difficulties **d = 1.23** vs. **d = 0.39** without. Incidentally, **four of the five reading-difficulty studies used semantic mapping or semantic feature analysis** — the closest cousins of Frayer.
- **McKeown, Beck, Omanson & Pople (1985), *RRQ* 20(5), 522–535:** factorial instruction-type × frequency. Definitional association alone suffices for basic word knowledge; **12 encounters > 4**; but **rich, and especially rich + extended out-of-class encounters, were required for fluency of access and story comprehension.** This is the crucial one: **a one-off Frayer worksheet is a single encounter — the condition that did not move comprehension.**
- **Beck, Perfetti & McKeown (1982), *JEP* 74(4), 506–521:** 104 words over five months, matched controls; gains on semantic decision, word knowledge, and comprehension of passages containing instructed words. Quasi-experimental.
- **Marzano's six-step process (2004/2009):** evidence is **in-house teacher action research** — an average 24-percentile-point gain across 24 elementary teachers, but **nine studies showed negative effects** and six showed gains >40 points. Research-informed, not research-proven.
- **NRP (2000), Ch. 4:** could not meta-analyze vocabulary due to heterogeneity; narrative conclusions endorse repetition/multiple exposures, restructuring tasks, active engagement, and no single method. **Endorses no specific graphic organizer.**

### Graphic organizer meta-analyses

- **Kim, Vaughn, Wanzek & Wei (2004), *JLD* 37(2), 105–118:** 21 group-design studies, **848 students with LD**, elementary–HS. **Posttest d = 1.04; follow-up d = 0.60.** Semantic organizers d = 0.81–1.69. **Researcher-developed tests produced significantly larger effects than standardized tests**; neither study using standardized measures found a significant difference; **transfer was null.** Frayer not mentioned; no vocabulary-specific outcomes.
- **Dexter & Hughes (2011), *LDQ* 34(1), 51–72:** 16 articles, 21 samples, 808 participants, grades 4–12. **Posttest ES = .91; maintenance .56.** Near-transfer 1.07 vs far-transfer .61. Semantic mapping 1.25; semantic feature analysis 1.19; science 1.05, social studies 1.04. **"All but one study used measures that were researcher-created."** Frayer not mentioned.
- **Dexter, Park & Hughes (2011), *LDRP* 26(4), 204–213:** 23 ES, 6 articles, 271 participants, grades 6–12, science. Gains in vocabulary and factual comprehension **on researcher-generated multiple-choice tests**; maintenance ES = 0.80.
- **Nesbit & Adesope (2006), *RER* 76(3), 413–448:** 67 ES from 55 studies, 5,818 participants. Concept maps associated with increased retention, effects small to large depending on comparison, with significant heterogeneity. *Moderator table not retrieved.*

### Practice guides

- **Kamil et al. (2008):** Rec. 1, explicit vocabulary instruction = **Strong** (six RCTs, three strong quasi-experiments). **Frayer, word maps, and "concept of definition" are not named.** Generic endorsement of "graphic displays of the relationships among words and concepts such as semantic maps."
- **Vaughn et al. (2022):** Rec. 3 comprehension-building = **Strong** (34 studies). Vocabulary sits in Rec. 3A. **Frayer not named**; the guide's "word map" example (3A.6) is a *morphological family* map (bio-), a different tool.

### Verdict: **POPULAR-BUT-UNEVIDENCED** (as a specific template) / the underlying practice is WELL-ESTABLISHED

Justification: the canonical citation is a 1969 assessment taxonomy that contains neither the template nor an instructional study. The only well-designed modern US study (Reed et al., 2019) had no non-Frayer control. Everything else is small, non-randomized, and outcome-inflated. Meanwhile the *class* of instruction the template gestures at — definitional plus contextual information, many encounters, deep processing — is genuinely well-established, and every one of those literatures shows the same signature: **large effects on taught words on aligned measures, small-to-null effects on standardized comprehension and transfer** (.97/.30 in Stahl & Fairbanks; 0.50/0.10 in Elleman; 1.04 posttest but null transfer in Kim et al.). The defensible claim is *"the Frayer Model is a reasonable delivery vehicle for practices that are evidence-based,"* not *"the Frayer Model is evidence-based"* — and only if it is used repeatedly with generative work over time, not as a single worksheet.

## 3. CLOSE READING AT SECONDARY LEVEL

### What it is

Fisher & Frey (2012, *The Reading Teacher* 66(3), 179–188; 2014, *TRT*, primary grades; 2015 *Text-Dependent Questions* K–5 and 6–12, Corwin) define it as: short complex passage, multiple readings, annotation, teacher-generated text-dependent questions, discussion, written response, minimal frontloading. Shanahan (2011, "Lower the fences or teach kids to climb?", *Reading Today* 29(1)) supplies the policy warrant; Shanahan, Fisher & Frey (2012, "The challenge of challenging text," *Educational Leadership* 69(6), 58–62) analogize difficulty to "weight or resistance in an exercise program" — and **cite exactly one empirical study, Stahl & Fairbanks (1986), a vocabulary meta-analysis that has nothing to do with the claim.**

### Direct evidence: essentially none

**"Still Too Close to Call: A Literature Review on Close Reading Interventions and Their Effects on Reading Outcomes in Grades 3–9," *Reading Psychology* (online 2 Apr 2026), DOI 10.1080/02702711.2026.2644958.** (Author list not retrievable — both repository copies 403'd; treat the citation as provisional.)
- **19 studies. Zero RCTs.** Four quasi-experiments with a control group; nine pretest–posttest without control; six case studies.
- **Only 3 peer-reviewed articles; 11 master's theses; 5 doctoral dissertations.** 84% teacher-researcher studies.
- **Median n = 11** participants (mean 18.6). 11 studies grades 3–6; 8 grades 7–9.
- **No effect sizes systematically reported anywhere in the literature.**
- Controlled results are mixed-to-null; **Cowden (2019) and Higdon (2019)**, both quasi-experiments vs. business-as-usual, found **no positive effect**.
- Component coding: rereading 94% (mean 3.1 passes), annotation 89%, text-dependent questions 78%, post-reading writing 61%, discussion 50% — and **only 75% actually used complex text.**
- Authors' conclusion: "we cannot make causal claims on the effects."

**The flagship secondary study — Fisher & Frey (2014), "Close reading as an intervention for struggling middle school readers," *JAAL* 57(5), 367–376.** 438 eligible students (bottom 40% on state ELA) across 3 middle schools; 100 assigned to 5 after-school classrooms → 75 analyzed; 247 non-participants as comparison; attrition 25%/27%. After-school, 3×/week × 90 min, Oct–May. Results: attendance 94% vs 81%; 64% vs 12% improved ≥1 CST performance level; self-perception 186 vs 99. **Confounds are fatal:** the contrast is "attended a well-run after-school program" vs. "did not"; the comparison group was not randomly formed; attendance is itself an outcome; no effect sizes on a standardized comprehension measure. **ERIC/WWC flags it as not meeting WWC evidence standards.**

### The text-complexity premise underneath it

- **ACT (2006), *Reading Between the Lines*.** ~1.2M 2005 ACT graduates (≈40% of US seniors); ~352k with EXPLORE→PLAN→ACT longitudinal data; college-outcome analyses on 98 institutions and 90,000+ students. Finding: performance on **complex passages** — not question type — was the sharpest discriminator of readiness; below-benchmark students answered complex-text items at near-chance (~25%). **Purely correlational/predictive; no manipulation of instructional text difficulty.** Its own appendix concedes: "While this may not constitute a nationally representative sample, we believe that we cannot ignore what the data are telling us." This is the load-bearing citation in CCSS Appendix A, and it cannot support the inference that *assigning* harder text *causes* better comprehension.
- **Amendum, Conradi & Hiebert (2018), "Does text complexity matter in the elementary grades?" *Educational Psychology Review* 30, 121–151.** 26 studies, 1970–2015: 18 correlational, 4 quasi-experimental, 3 experimental, 1 single-subject. Accuracy declined with difficulty in all but one study; rate slower in 11/15 (73%); comprehension **7 studies (53.8%) negative, 5 (38.5%) null, 1 (7.7%) optimal at moderate difficulty**. Their flat statement: **"No study indicated that increased text difficulty was related to an increase in students' comprehension."**
- **O'Connor, Swanson & Geraghty (2010), *JEP* 102(1), 1–19.** The strongest experimental test: **true RCT, n = 123 poor readers, grades 2 and 4**, randomly assigned to guided oral reading at **independent level (92–100% accuracy)**, at **difficult level (80–90%)**, or untreated control; 20 weeks. Both treatment groups beat control on rate, word recognition, and comprehension — but **no significant growth difference between independent-level and difficult-level conditions.** What produced gains was *supported reading volume*, not difficulty. Shanahan cites this as evidence against instructional-level theory; Hiebert cites it as evidence that harder text confers no benefit. Both readings are consistent, which is the point: **it is null on the difficulty contrast.**
- **Hiebert (2012), "The Common Core's staircase of text complexity," *Reading Today* 29(3), 26–27.** The staircase is expressed in Lexiles, which index only sentence length and word frequency and are blind to knowledge demands and structure (*Roll of Thunder* rates below a simple grade 2–3 informational text because dialogue depresses the formula). The grade 2–3 band topping out at 820L is roughly a grade above prior norms while struggling readers end grade 3 near 400L. Her documented downstream effect: teachers read hard texts *aloud to* students rather than having them read — reducing the very reading volume that drove gains in O'Connor et al.
- **Stahl & Heubach (2005) FORI**, the most-cited support for challenging text, shows benefits of reading difficult text **with others in supportive contexts** — the active ingredient is scaffolding, repetition, and volume, not difficulty.
- **Shanahan's counter-case** is historiographically strong but evidentially thin: Betts's (1946) 95–98% instructional-level criterion traces to an unpublished Kilgallon dissertation containing **no evidence that instructional-level placement conferred any learning advantage**. But his positive citations are Morgan, Wilcox & Eldredge (2000) (which Amendum et al. note found *no* relationship between difficulty and comprehension), O'Connor et al. (null), and non-experimental TNTP-style analyses. **The strongest defensible claim is that instructional-level placement lacks an evidentiary basis — not that harder text is better.**

**Where the WWC actually lands:** Vaughn et al. (2022), Rec. 4, "Provide students with opportunities to practice making sense of **stretch text** (i.e., challenging text)," is rated **Moderate**, 15 studies. Note the how-to steps: select challenging grade-level text, **then provide pre-reading support including world-knowledge development and essential-word instruction** ("a brief 3–5-minute introduction on the topic before reading"; "select one or two of the essential words to teach before reading"), assist during reading, follow up. **The federally endorsed version of hard-text instruction explicitly includes the frontloading that close-reading orthodoxy discourages.**

### Snow's critique

**Snow, C. E., & O'Connor, C. (2016). "Close reading and far-reaching classroom discussion: Fostering a vital connection." *Journal of Education*, 196(1), 1–8** (expanded from the 2013 IRA/LRA policy brief). Their argument:
1. **The "level playing field" rationale is false.** Restricting students to the text does not neutralize background-knowledge differences; comprehension is extraction *and* construction (Kintsch 1988; RAND 2002), and missing knowledge and vocabulary are the primary causes of comprehension failure.
2. **Background knowledge cannot be suppressed** — their Gettysburg Address example; Bransford & Johnson (1972); Hart & Risley (1995). Also: texts with too many unfamiliar words are not comprehended, and therefore cannot teach vocabulary — which directly undercuts the harder-text-builds-vocabulary claim.
3. **The frontloading prohibition is operationally incoherent**: teachers are asked to anticipate which knowledge each of 25 readers lacks *without previewing content*.
4. **Confining legitimate evidence to the text is wrong on the merits** (prior knowledge, moral judgment, cultural traditions are legitimate warrants).
5. **Motivation**: laborious repeated reading targets precisely the adolescents whose engagement is already collapsing.
6. **Crowding out** — their gravest worry: close reading displaces productive dialogic discussion, which *does* predict good outcomes (Applebee et al. 2003; Murphy et al. 2009).

Their prescription: close reading should be brief (one sentence, 10–15 min/day à la Wong Fillmore & Fillmore 2012), collaborative, embedded in broader discussion, and instrumental to a purpose.

*Caveat:* **Hinchman & Moore (2013), "Close reading: A cultural response," *JAAL* 56(6), 441–450** could not be verified in ERIC — treat as unconfirmed pending a database check.

### What does have evidence at secondary level

- **Applebee, Langer, Nystrand & Gamoran (2003), *AERJ* 40(3), 685–730:** **64 middle/high school English classrooms**, grades 7–12, four states; **observational/longitudinal HLM**, not experimental. Discussion-based approaches predicted spring performance controlling for fall, across achievement levels; authors caution about track confounding. Striking datum: classrooms averaged **1.7 minutes of sustained discussion per 60-minute period**.
- **Baye, Inns, Lake & Slavin (2019), *RRQ* 54(2), 133–166:** **69 studies (62 randomized, 7 strong quasi-experiments), 51 programs**, standardized outcomes. **Overall weighted mean ES = +0.09.** One-to-one tutoring +0.28; writing-focused +0.13; personalization +0.13; cooperative learning +0.10; content-focused +0.08; strategy-focused +0.09; **whole-school without organizational reform 0.00; intensive decoding/fluency 0.00; vocabulary-focused +0.06 n.s.** An extra daily reading period (+0.09) conferred no advantage over programs without it (+0.10); technology (+0.08) none over non-technology (+0.10). Conclusion: adolescents benefit from socially and cognitively engaging instruction, not more minutes or devices.

### Verdict: **POPULAR-BUT-UNEVIDENCED**

Justification: the routine rests on a three-link chain and every link is weak in a different way. **Link 1** (ACT 2006) is a correlation between *being able to* read complex text and college readiness, converted without warrant into a prescription to *assign* harder text. **Link 2** (harder text improves comprehension) is contradicted by the only relevant RCT (O'Connor et al., null on difficulty) and by a 26-study synthesis in which **not one study** found increased difficulty associated with improved comprehension. **Link 3** (the close-reading routine itself) has **no RCT at any grade level**, and its controlled quasi-experiments are unpublished dissertations with null results and a **median sample of eleven students**. It appears in no WWC practice-guide recommendation. The WWC's nearest analogue — "stretch text," Moderate evidence — explicitly prescribes the pre-reading knowledge-building that close-reading orthodoxy discourages.

The honest framing is not "discussion beats close reading." Baye et al.'s +0.09 ceiling means the best-evidenced adolescent literacy practices produce small effects, and **close reading has not yet earned entry into that comparison.** The sharpest single artifact: the *Educational Leadership* case for challenging text cites one 1986 vocabulary meta-analysis; Snow & O'Connor's rebuttal is grounded in Kintsch, RAND, Bransford & Johnson, Hart & Risley, Applebee, and Murphy. The asymmetry in evidentiary density between the promotion and the critique is itself the finding.

# Science reading comprehension: what the evidence actually supports

**Standing caveat on effect sizes:** Kraft (2020, *Educational Researcher*, 49[4], 241–253) argues Cohen's benchmarks badly mislead in education; for causal studies with standardized achievement outcomes he proposes <0.05 small, 0.05–0.20 medium, ≥0.20 large. Effects on researcher-made tests routinely run 3–5× larger than on standardized tests. I could not machine-extract Kraft's PDF, so treat those cutoffs as reported from my own knowledge, not verified this session.

---

## 1. Is science reading difficulty a LANGUAGE problem?

### Snow (2010) — an argument, not a study
**Snow, C. E. (2010). Academic language and the challenge of reading for learning about science. *Science*, 328(5977), 450–452.** PMID 20413488.

This is a **3-page Education Forum/Perspective essay, not an empirical paper.** No study, no data, no effect sizes. Her argument: academic language is engineered for concision, precision, and authority, and the devices that achieve this — nominalization, passive voice/agent deletion, heavy subjects, center-embedding, dense information-bearing words, precision of reference, epistemic verbs, evidence-based rather than opinion-based claims — are exactly what disrupts comprehension. Her worked example is a physics definition: *"Torque is the product of the magnitude of the force and the lever arm of the force,"* where everyday senses of "product" and "arm" actively mislead. Her recommendation is that academic-language instruction be embedded in the science curriculum, and she points to her own **Word Generation** program.

**Verdict: the framing claim is REASONABLE AND WIDELY ACCEPTED, but Snow 2010 itself is WEAK EVIDENCE for it — it is advocacy in a high-prestige venue.** The support has to come from elsewhere. It does exist:

- **Word Generation quasi-experiment** (Boston Public Schools 2007–08; 1,016 students grades 6–8, 5 treatment vs 3 comparison schools; treatment schools *lower* at baseline, 56% vs 45% failing): **d = 0.49** on researcher-designed academic vocabulary. 20–22 weeks ≈ two years of incidental word learning. Comprehension evidence was indirect (a treatment × vocabulary-gain interaction on MCAS).
- **Word Generation RCT** — Jones, LaRusso, Kim, Kim, Selman, Uccelli, Barnes, Donovan & Snow (2019), *Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness*, 12(3). **7,752 students, grades 4–7, 25 schools, school-level randomization.** Effects on curriculum-targeted vocabulary: **0.22 (yr 1) and 0.28 (yr 2) for grades 4–5; 0.13 and 0.16 for grades 6–7.** Year 2 also showed effects on academic language and "deep" reading comprehension in both cohorts. Note the pattern: **large on taught words, modest on comprehension, and comprehension effects only emerged in year 2.**
- **Lawrence et al. (2015), *AERJ*, 52(4), 750–786** found classroom **discussion mediated** the vocabulary effect — the mechanism is talk, not word lists.
- The genuinely causal test of the language claim is **text-revision experiments**: McKeown, Beck, Sinatra & Loxterman (1992), *RRQ*. Grade 5, American Revolution social-studies text. Students reading the **coherence-revised** text recalled significantly more and answered more questions correctly than those reading the original. This is direct causal evidence that the *language* of the text — independent of content — limits comprehension.

### Shanahan & Shanahan (2008) — how thin it really is
**Shanahan, T., & Shanahan, C. (2008). Teaching disciplinary literacy to adolescents: Rethinking content-area literacy. *Harvard Educational Review*, 78(1), 40–59.**

The actual design: three teams (history, chemistry, math), each with **2 disciplinary experts + 2 teacher educators + 2 high school teachers**. That is **six disciplinary experts total, two per field**, roughly 18 people. Methods were **think-aloud protocols, focus-group transcripts, member checking, and cross-disciplinary comparison** — a qualitative/design-research study reporting the **"first two years"** of a project. The authors' own word is **"preliminary."** Follow-up: Shanahan, Shanahan & Misischia (2011), *Journal of Literacy Research*, 43(4), 393–429.

**Verdict: DESCRIPTIVE, PRELIMINARY, AND MASSIVELY OVER-CITED AS SETTLED.** It is a study of how *six experts* read, not a study of whether teaching students to read that way helps them. It has ~thousands of citations and is embedded in state standards and PD decks as if it were an efficacy trial. It is not. Howell, Barlow & Dyches (2021), *Journal of Language and Literacy Education*, 17(1) — a systematic review of 58 articles — found the PD research base for disciplinary literacy "remains limited." My own ERIC sweeps for experimental disciplinary-literacy studies at secondary level with achievement outcomes returned almost nothing; what exists is mostly history/writing (e.g. De La Paz et al. 2017).

**One caution:** a WebFetch summarizer returned a direct-looking quote from Shanahan & Shanahan (2012) that "the evidence base for disciplinary literacy instruction remains limited." I could not independently verify that wording (the PDF would not parse) and would **not** put it in quotation marks in the teacher summary.

### The causal evidence that does exist for science reading
- **Greenleaf, Litman, Hanson, Rosen, Boscardin, Herman, Schneider, Madden & Jones (2011), *AERJ*, 48(3), 647–717.** Group-randomized trial of **10 days of Reading Apprenticeship PD** for high school biology teachers. Treatment students outperformed controls on state standardized **biology, reading comprehension, and ELA**. I could not extract the effect sizes (all hosts paywalled/403).
- **Goldman, Greenleaf, Yukhymenko-Lescroart, Brown, Ko, Emig, George, Wallace, Blaum & Britt (2019), *AERJ*, 56(4)** — Project READI. Stratified RCT, schools randomized within six strata, semester-long, grade 9 science, text-based investigation to build explanatory models. Significant effects on students and teachers. Effect sizes not retrievable.
- **Fang & Wei (2010), *Journal of Educational Research*, 103(4), 262–273.** 10 sixth-grade science classes, one school, inquiry science vs inquiry science + explicit reading strategy instruction + science trade books. ISR beat IS on all science-literacy measures via ANCOVA. Small, single-site; effect sizes not in the abstract.
- **Counter-evidence worth knowing:** the WWC's own review of Reading Apprenticeship (Intervention Report #414, July 2010, Tier 3) rates it only **"potentially positive" for comprehension at grade 9, on 1 of 3 eligible studies.** The study that *met standards without reservations* — Kemple et al. (2008), Enhanced Reading Opportunities, **2,329 ninth-graders, 17 schools, 10 districts, RCT** — found **no statistically significant positive effects** on GRADE comprehension or vocabulary. So: the *embedded-in-biology PD* version worked; the *standalone supplemental literacy course* version did not.

---

## 2. Fang & Schleppegrell — is there experimental evidence?

**Key works:** Fang (2005), *Science Education*, 89, 335–347; Fang (2006), *International Journal of Science Education*, 28(5), 491–520; Fang, Schleppegrell & Cox (2006), *Journal of Literacy Research*, 38(3); Fang & Schleppegrell (2008), *Reading in Secondary Content Areas: A Language-Based Pedagogy* (Michigan); Fang & Schleppegrell (2010), *JAAL*, 53(7).

They identify four features of scientific language — **technical vocabulary, abstraction, high lexical density, tightly knit structure** — and propose **Functional Language Analysis (FLA)**: teaching students to interrogate clauses (who/what is doing what to whom, what is packed into this noun phrase) and to unpack nominalizations back into processes.

**Direct answer to your question: NO. I found no experimental or quasi-experimental study testing whether teaching students to unpack nominalizations or dense noun phrases improves comprehension.** Three independent ERIC sweeps — "functional language analysis," "nominalization instruction + comprehension + experiment," "grammatical metaphor + science text + comprehension" — returned **zero controlled intervention studies with student comprehension outcomes.** The FLA literature is descriptive linguistic analysis, worked textbook examples, teacher-education case studies, and design proposals.

Two honest qualifications:
- Where SFL *has* been reviewed for outcomes, the finding is agnostic, not negative: a systematic review of genre/SFL pedagogy concluded there was **insufficient evidence to determine whether it worked or did not work**, because almost nothing met experimental inclusion criteria. (Reported in a 2024 methodological piece in Springer's *Journal of Literacy Research/*related venue that I could not fully fetch — treat the exact citation as unverified.) SFL researchers have pushed back that experimental criteria are the wrong yardstick. That is a live methodological dispute, not a settled refutation.
- The *general* claim underneath FLA — that linguistic form causally constrains comprehension — **is** supported, by McKeown et al. (1992) text revision, and by cohesion research: McNamara & Kintsch's **reverse cohesion effect** (low-knowledge readers benefit from high-cohesion text; high-knowledge readers can benefit from low-cohesion text because gaps force inference), refined by O'Reilly & McNamara (2007), *Discourse Processes*, 43(2) — the low-cohesion benefit is restricted to **less-skilled but high-knowledge** readers; skilled high-knowledge readers do better with high-cohesion text. Also Reed & Kershaw-Herrera (2016), *Journal of Experimental Education*: 103 high school seniors randomly assigned to 4 versions of the same passage varying in readability and cohesion.

**Verdict: FANG & SCHLEPPEGRELL'S FRAMEWORK IS DESCRIPTIVE/THEORETICAL, NOT CAUSALLY EVIDENCED.** It is a good analysis of *why* science text is hard. It has never been shown to work as a teaching method. Present it to the teacher as a lens, explicitly not as an evidence-based intervention.

---

## 3. The knowledge–comprehension link

### Recht & Leslie (1988) — real, small, over-extended
**Recht, D. R., & Leslie, L. (1988). Effect of prior knowledge on good and poor readers' memory of text. *Journal of Educational Psychology*, 80(1), 16–20.**

**64 junior high students** (Marquette University, Milwaukee), 2×2: reading ability (high/low) × baseball knowledge (high/low). Each read a **half-page account of one half-inning**, then recalled it nonverbally (moving figures on a model field) and verbally. **Significant main effect for prior knowledge on all measures; no knowledge × ability interaction.** High-knowledge/poor readers matched or beat low-knowledge/good readers on recall and summarization.

**Verdict: WELL-ESTABLISHED AS A FINDING, ROUTINELY OVER-CLAIMED AS A MANDATE.** n = 64, one passage, one topic, one age band, memory-for-text outcomes — not comprehension of unfamiliar science, not a curriculum test. The best critique (Thomas White, Human Restoration Project) is explicitly *not* methodological: it accepts the result and objects that Core Knowledge advocates extract prescriptive teaching demands from a descriptive laboratory finding. It cannot tell you *how* to build knowledge, or which knowledge is worth building.

### O'Reilly, Wang & Sabatini (2019) — the strongest modern evidence
**O'Reilly, T., Wang, Z., & Sabatini, J. (2019). How much knowledge is too little? When a lack of knowledge becomes a barrier to comprehension. *Psychological Science*, 30(9).**

**3,534 high school students, 37 U.S. schools.** Domain: **ecosystems**. Knowledge measured by (a) selecting which of 44 words related to ecosystems and (b) multiple-choice factual items; comprehension by 34 items (summarizing, identifying opinion, applying content).

**The threshold: ~33.5 points, about 59% correct. Below it, β = 0.18 (weak). Above it, β = 0.81 (strong and positive).**

Also: recognizing *core* terms (ecosystem, habitat, species) predicted crossing the threshold better than recognizing exotic ones (bioremediation, fauna). Effects were **topic-specific**, not general knowledge.

**Verdict: WELL-ESTABLISHED and the single most useful finding for a science teacher.** It reframes the problem: below a topic-knowledge floor, comprehension doesn't degrade gracefully — the knowledge–comprehension relationship essentially disconnects. Reading strategies cannot rescue a student who is below the floor. Caveat: cross-sectional, single domain, one assessment battery; the threshold value is specific to this instrument and topic and should **not** be reported to teachers as "59% is the magic number."

### Smith, Snow, Serry & Hammond (2021)
***Reading Psychology*, 42(3), 214–240.** Critical review, **23 studies**, mid-to-late primary years. Conclusions: background-knowledge effects are **conditional**, moderated by text type, the depth of situation model required, and — importantly — **reader misconceptions**, which can make knowledge actively harmful. Low-knowledge readers benefit more from high-cohesion text; weak readers partially compensate via knowledge. **Limitation for your purposes: it is a primary-school review, not adolescent, and I could not verify how strongly they qualify causality (Taylor & Francis 403'd).**

### Causal knowledge-building evidence
The best is **James Kim's Model of Reading Engagement (MORE)**: a first-grade RCT, **38 classrooms, 674 students, 10 schools**, produced **ES 0.30 vocabulary depth, 0.40 listening comprehension, 0.24 argumentative writing, but only 0.11 on distal reading comprehension** — with no aptitude × treatment interaction. Note the shape: **big on the knowledge you taught, small on general comprehension.** Two MORE studies meet WWC standards without reservations. This is grade 1, so transfer to secondary science is an assumption, not a finding.

---

## 4. What Works Clearinghouse

### Kamil et al. (2008) is NOT superseded and NOT archived
**Kamil, M. L., Borman, G. D., Dole, J., Kral, C. C., Salinger, T., & Torgesen, J. (2008). *Improving Adolescent Literacy: Effective Classroom and Intervention Practices* (NCEE 2008-4027).** Guide #8, grades 4/5–12. Still listed as an active guide, no "Revised" date, no archived/withdrawn label.

| # | Recommendation | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Explicit vocabulary instruction | **Strong** |
| 2 | Direct and explicit comprehension strategy instruction | **Strong** |
| 3 | Extended discussion of text meaning and interpretation | **Moderate** |
| 4 | Increase student motivation and engagement | **Moderate** |
| 5 | Intensive, individualized intervention by trained specialists | **Strong** |

**Correction to your brief: nothing here was rated low or minimal.** 3 strong / 2 moderate / 0 low. But "strong" is doing less work than it sounds:

- WWC's **moderate** tier explicitly admits comparison-group studies *without demonstrated pretest equivalence* and *correlational research with statistical controls*.
- The guide concedes its authors "seldom conduct the types of systematic literature searches that are the backbone of a meta-analysis" and instead "use their expertise to identify the most important research." These are panel judgments over a hand-assembled corpus.
- **Rec 1's own caveat:** "only some show that explicit vocabulary instruction has effects on standardized measures of reading comprehension" — most effects are on the taught words. This matches **Elleman, Lindo, Morphy & Compton (2009)**, 37 studies: **d = 0.50 on researcher-designed comprehension measures, substantially smaller on standardized ones.**
- **Rec 3 is the weakest**: 4 small QEDs + 1 large correlational study (Applebee et al. 2003, ELA classrooms), and the guide itself concedes "most experimental studies of discussion-based approaches thus far have used narrative texts, a limitation in the research base at present." **This matters — discussion is the recommendation with the least transfer to science text.**
- **Rec 4 is thinnest**: 2 experiments + 1 QED without baseline equivalence, plus meta-analyses the guide flags as low external validity.
- **Rec 2's evidence is 5 RCTs concentrated on main-idea summarization in reading/ELA settings, not science classrooms.**
- **Almost none of the causal evidence comes from science classrooms.** The guide's line that the first four recommendations apply "regardless of the content areas they teach" is a **panel assertion, not a finding.**

### Newer guides — supplement, don't supersede
**Providing Reading Interventions for Students in Grades 4–9 (WWC 2022007, March 2022, guide #29):**
1. Build decoding of multisyllabic words — **Strong**
2. Purposeful fluency-building — **Strong**
3. Routine comprehension-building practices (word/world knowledge, questioning, gist, monitoring) — **Strong**
4. Practice making sense of **stretch text** — **Moderate**

It is an *intervention* guide for struggling readers, not general classroom instruction, so it supplements Kamil rather than replacing it.

**Teaching Academic Content and Literacy to English Learners (Baker et al., 2014, guide #19):** intensive multi-day academic vocabulary — **Strong**; integrate oral/written English into content teaching — **Strong**; structured written-language opportunities — **Minimal**; small-group intervention — **Moderate**.

**There has never been a WWC practice guide on science literacy, and none on disciplinary/content-area literacy at any date.** Only six practice guides exist from 2020 onward and only one is literacy-related. Following the February–March 2025 IES contract terminations and ~90% research-staff reduction, **no guide has been issued or revised since December 2024, and a Kamil refresh is not visibly in progress.** Note IES is migrating URLs (`ies.ed.gov/use-work/…`), so verify links before putting them in a durable handout.

**Relevant critique:** Reynolds, D. (2021), *JAAL*, doi:10.1002/jaal.1176, argues the 2008 guide is outdated; Moje (2010), *Journal of Literacy Research*, makes precisely the disciplinary-literacy objection that generic strategy recommendations don't map onto science reading.

---

## 5. Classroom routines: what survives scrutiny

*(The dedicated agent for this item hadn't reported by the time I finished; the following is from my own primary-source verification, so treat the coverage as solid but not exhaustive on meta-analytic detail.)*

### Questioning the Author — WEAKLY-SUPPORTED as a branded routine, but the underlying principle is well-supported
- **Beck, McKeown, Worthy, Sandora & Kucan (1996), *Elementary School Journal*** — a **yearlong single-classroom implementation study**. Primary reported outcome: **"teacher talk decreased in quantity and increased in quality."** That is a *teacher* outcome. No control group, no student comprehension effect.
- **Sandora, Beck & McKeown (1999), *Reading Psychology*** — QtA vs Great Books shared inquiry, QtA students "provided longer recalls." **Serious confound: the QtA group were sixth graders and the Great Books group were seventh graders.** Different grades in different conditions. This does not support a causal claim.
- **The strong one: McKeown, Beck & Blake (2009), *Reading Research Quarterly*, 44(3).** Two-year study, **fifth graders in a low-performing urban Pennsylvania district**, three conditions: **content instruction** (open, meaning-based questions — the QtA principle), **strategies instruction**, and a **basal control**. Content instruction beat strategies instruction on narrative recall and expository learning probes across both years; no differences on sentence-verification; content students produced longer responses and more substantive discussion; modest transfer advantages for content.

**Verdict: the specific finding worth telling a science teacher is McKeown, Beck & Blake (2009) — asking open questions about what the text means outperformed teaching named comprehension strategies.** That is a real, well-designed, replicated-across-two-years result, and it directly undercuts the strategy-instruction orthodoxy in Kamil Rec 2. But it is **fifth grade, not secondary**, and QtA's own foundational papers are descriptive. QtA is not in the WWC intervention database as far as I could find.

### Frayer model — WEAKLY-SUPPORTED, and the modern version isn't what was tested
- **Frayer, Frederick & Klausmeier (1969)** is the origin.
- **Peters (1974), Technical Report No. 290 (ERIC ED163452): 360 ninth graders**, good and poor readers, social studies concepts. Students using **material organized according to the Frayer model scored significantly higher on comprehension** than students using textbook-style definitions — for **both** good and poor readers. Example sequencing made no difference.
- **Monroe & Pendergrass (1997)**, grade 4 math vocabulary: an integrated graphic-organizer + Frayer-discussion model beat definition-only.

**Critical distinction nobody makes in PD: Peters tested Frayer-*organized instructional materials*, not the student-completed four-square worksheet that "the Frayer model" now means.** The 1974 study is 50 years old, in social studies, and I could not find modern replication with the graphic-organizer template at secondary level in science.

**Verdict: WEAKLY-SUPPORTED. There is *some* old experimental evidence, more than I expected — but it does not test the artifact teachers are actually handed in PD.** What *is* well-supported is the general principle it instantiates: rich, multi-exposure, discussion-embedded vocabulary instruction (Kamil Rec 1, Strong; Elleman et al. 2009 d = 0.50 on custom measures; Word Generation d = 0.49). Recommend the *principle*, and the four-square as one convenient vehicle for it — not as an evidence-based intervention in its own right.

### Close reading at secondary level — POPULAR-BUT-UNEVIDENCED
My ERIC sweep for close reading + secondary + experimental + comprehension returned **no experimental or quasi-experimental studies of close reading as a routine.** Everything returned was a different intervention that happened to match on the word "close" (Read 180, Readable English, Switch-On Reading). The Common Core / Fisher & Frey close-reading push has essentially **no controlled evidence base at secondary level.**

The adjacent, harder question — *does making students read harder text help?* — has a real but mixed literature: Amendum et al. (2018) integrative review of 26 studies on text difficulty; Reed & Kershaw-Herrera (2016) experimental manipulation with 103 high school seniors; and the cohesion work above showing **the answer depends on the reader's knowledge**. WWC 2022007 Rec 4 ("stretch text") is rated only **Moderate**. And O'Reilly et al. (2019) implies a hard limit: below the knowledge threshold, harder text is not productive struggle, it is noise.

**Verdict: POPULAR-BUT-UNEVIDENCED as a named routine.** Flag this clearly — close reading is the most PD-saturated and least evidenced item in this whole review.

---

## 6. AI chatbots and reading difficult science text (2022–2026)

**Headline: AI helps while you're using it and often hurts what you can do without it.** That dissociation is the most replicated finding in this literature. Almost nothing studies adolescents reading *science* text with AI.

### The two flagship RCTs
**Bastani, Bastani, Sungu, Ge, Kabakcı & Mariman (2025), *PNAS*, 122(26), e2422633122** (SSRN preprint 2024, "Generative AI Can Harm Learning"). Field RCT, one Turkish high school, grades 9–11, **~1,000 students, ~50 classrooms, classroom-level randomization**, four 90-min sessions, math. Arms: control, **GPT Base** (unrestricted GPT-4), **GPT Tutor** (teacher-designed hints, answers withheld).
- **Assisted practice:** GPT Base **+48%**, GPT Tutor **+127%** over control.
- **Unassisted exam, AI removed:** GPT Base **−17%, p < .05 (≈ d −0.19)**; GPT Tutor **−0.4%, n.s.**
- **Read the guardrails result carefully: the tutor did not improve independent learning. It neutralized the harm.** "Guardrails help" means "guardrails get you back to baseline," not "beats teaching as usual."
- **Hallucination measured inside the same experiment:** across 57 problems queried 10× each, **GPT Base was correct only 51% of the time — 42% logical errors, 8% arithmetic errors.**

**Kestin, Miller, Klales, Milbourne & Ponti (2025), *Scientific Reports*, 15.** Randomized crossover, Harvard Physical Sciences 2, **N = 194**, custom GPT-4 tutor with Socratic scaffolds. **≈0.63 SD by linear regression, 0.73–1.3 SD by quantile regression**; ~half the time (49 vs 60 min). **But the outcome was an immediate post-test taken right after the AI session, with no delayed and no unassisted-transfer measure** — i.e. roughly the same measure on which Bastani's GPT Base also looked great before collapsing. Elite institution, novelty effects, bespoke engineered tutor, not ChatGPT. The two studies are far less contradictory than headlines suggest.

### Closest to reading comprehension
**Kreijkes, Kewenig, Kuvalja, Lee, Hofman, Vitello, Sellen, Rintel, Goldstein, Rothschild, Tankelevitch & Oates (2026), *Computers & Education*, 243, 105514.** Pre-registered RCT, **405 students aged 14–15, 7 schools in England**, three conditions: LLM only / note-taking only / LLM + note-taking, **unannounced test 3 days later.** **Note-taking alone and note-taking + LLM both beat LLM alone on comprehension and retention. LLM-only was worst.** Yet most students *preferred* the LLM and rated it most helpful. Passages were **history, not science.** (A "d = 0.41" figure circulating for this study refers to students' *perceived* advantage, not a learning gain.)

**Etkin, Etkin, Carter & Rolle (2025), *Frontiers in Education*, 10.** N = 195, ACT passages, five conditions. **Lower performers improved** (Socratic d = 0.86, outline 0.74, tutor 0.50, summary 0.45); **higher performers got worse** (summary d = 0.83, outline 0.51, tutor 0.37, Socratic 0.33). Vulnerable to regression to the mean, single session. Note the ordering though: least answer-giving best, most answer-giving worst.

**Abdelghani, Murayama, Kidd, Sauzéon & Oudeyer (arXiv:2505.01106, preprint, not peer-reviewed).** **N = 63, ages 14–15, science investigation task.** Students **could not discriminate efficient from inefficient prompts, failed to detect vague AI explanations, and stopped inquiry prematurely.** This is the closest study to your exact population and material, and it is tiny and preliminary.

### Offloading and shallow processing
- **Stadler, Bannert & Sailer (2024), *Computers in Human Behavior*, 160, 108386.** N = 91, ChatGPT vs Google researching a socio-scientific issue (nanoparticles in sunscreen): **lower cognitive load but lower-quality reasoning and argumentation.** Best-matched study for "using AI to process difficult science content."
- **Fan et al. (2025), *BJET*, 56(2).** N = 117: ChatGPT group produced better essays but **no advantage in knowledge gain or transfer**, with fewer metacognitive processes ("metacognitive laziness").
- **Gerlich (2025), *Societies*, 15(1), 6.** N = 666, negative association between AI use and critical thinking. **Cross-sectional and correlational — cannot support causal claims, has a published correction, and is being systematically over-read.**
- **LLM-simplified text specifically:** a large crowdsourced evaluation (arXiv:2505.10409, *Journal of Biomedical Informatics*) found readers rated **LLM-generated plain-language summaries as equally clear and coherent as human-written ones, but scored significantly worse on comprehension questions after reading them.** This is the cleanest demonstration that AI simplification buys perceived clarity without understanding.

### Meta-analyses — with an integrity problem
- **Wang & Fan (2025), *Humanities and Social Sciences Communications*, 12, 621 — RETRACTED 22 April 2026** (notice doi:10.1057/s41599-026-07310-z), for discrepancies in the meta-analysis; authors did not respond. **If anyone cites "g = 0.87 for ChatGPT," that number is retracted.**
- Still standing: **Deng, Jiang, Yu, Lu & Liu (2025), *Computers & Education*, 227, 105224** — 69 experimental studies, **g+ = 0.712** on performance, *plus reduced mental effort* (a red flag on a desirable-difficulties account). **Wu et al. (2026), *HSSC*** — 35 studies, 4,193 participants, **g = 0.670 [0.495, 0.844]**; but subgroup values are not credible (**physics g = 1.951** while general "science" g = 0.169, n.s.), signalling unstable coding.
- **Weidlich, Gašević, Drachsler & Kirschner (2025), *Journal of Computer Assisted Learning*, 41(5), e70105 — "ChatGPT in Education: An Effect in Search of a Cause."** Argues this literature is media-comparison research confounding method with technology, frequently failing to specify what controls did, with outcome measures that are not valid indicators of learning. **Observed gains cannot currently be attributed to ChatGPT.**

**Verdict: THIN, YOUNG, ESSENTIALLY UNREPLICATED.** ~6 credible RCTs, mostly 1–4 sessions, mostly immediate post-tests, mostly 2023-vintage models. Neither Bastani nor Kestin has been independently replicated. **The intersection you actually asked about — adolescents reading science text with AI — is essentially unstudied.** The one defensible classroom rule: **any AI use whose benefit is only measured while the AI is present is measuring performance, not learning.**

---

## Summary table

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| Academic language is a real barrier to science reading | **WELL-ESTABLISHED** (but Snow 2010 is an essay; support comes from text-revision and Word Generation trials) |
| Snow 2010 as evidence | **WEAK** — Perspective piece, no data |
| Shanahan & Shanahan 2008 as settled science | **WEAKLY-SUPPORTED** — 6 experts, think-alouds, self-described "preliminary," cited as if definitive |
| Disciplinary literacy instruction improves student outcomes | **WEAKLY-SUPPORTED** — near-zero secondary experimental evidence |
| Fang/Schleppegrell FLA, unpacking nominalizations | **DESCRIPTIVE ONLY — no causal evidence found** |
| Prior knowledge drives comprehension | **WELL-ESTABLISHED** (Recht & Leslie 1988; O'Reilly et al. 2019 β 0.18→0.81) |
| Knowledge threshold below which comprehension collapses | **WELL-ESTABLISHED in one large study**, single domain, needs replication |
| Explicit vocabulary instruction | **WELL-ESTABLISHED for taught words (d ≈ 0.50); weak for standardized comprehension** |
| Comprehension strategy instruction | **STRONG per WWC, but evidence is ELA/summarization; McKeown et al. 2009 found content questions beat it** |
| Extended discussion of text | **MODERATE, and the guide concedes the studies used narrative text** |
| Reading Apprenticeship PD embedded in biology | **MODERATE-TO-GOOD** (Greenleaf 2011 RCT) — but the standalone course version (Kemple 2008 RCT, n=2,329) was null |
| Questioning the Author | **WEAK as a brand; the underlying "content questions" principle is well-tested (McKeown, Beck & Blake 2009)** |
| Frayer model | **WEAKLY-SUPPORTED — one 1974 study of Frayer-organized *materials*, not the modern worksheet** |
| Close reading at secondary | **POPULAR-BUT-UNEVIDENCED** |
| AI helps students read hard science text | **UNRESOLVED / LEANING NEGATIVE for unscaffolded use; essentially unstudied for adolescents + science text** |

## Three things I'd flag hardest for a teacher-facing summary

1. **The two most-cited foundations of the disciplinary-literacy movement — Snow 2010 and Shanahan & Shanahan 2008 — are an essay and a six-expert think-aloud study.** Neither is efficacy evidence. This is the single biggest gap between how often something is cited and what it actually shows.
2. **O'Reilly et al. (2019) is the most actionable finding here** and points somewhere other than where most science-literacy PD points: pre-teach topic knowledge to a floor *before* assigning the text, rather than teaching strategies to apply to it.
3. **Close reading and the Frayer worksheet are the two things most likely to be in the teacher's PD folder and least likely to have earned their place** — Frayer at least has a 1974 experiment behind a different version of itself; close reading has essentially nothing.

**Method caveats:** the session's web-search budget was exhausted, and ies.ed.gov / ERIC / SAGE / T&F PDFs would not machine-parse (no PDF tooling locally), so several effect sizes — Greenleaf 2011, Project READI 2019, Fang & Wei 2010, Elleman's standardized-measure figure, Kraft's exact cutoffs — are named but not numerically verified. The Kamil recommendation ratings were confirmed on two independent fetches.

# Summary of Murphy et al. (2009) Meta-Analysis on Classroom Discussion and Text Comprehension

## Study Overview

This comprehensive meta-analysis examined how classroom discussions affect students' text comprehension and critical thinking. The researchers analyzed 42 empirical studies published between 1964 and 2002, investigating nine discussion approaches categorized by their primary stance toward text.

## Nine Discussion Approaches Analyzed

The approaches were grouped into three stances:

**Critical-Analytic Stance** (emphasizing interrogation of text):
- Collaborative Reasoning
- Paideia Seminar
- Philosophy for Children

**Efferent Stance** (focusing on information retrieval):
- Instructional Conversations
- Junior Great Books Shared Inquiry
- Questioning the Author

**Expressive Stance** (emphasizing affective responses):
- Book Club
- Grand Conversations
- Literature Circles

## Key Findings

### Effects on Student/Teacher Talk
Several approaches substantially increased student participation while reducing teacher dominance. "Collaborative Reasoning was associated with an increase in student talk of 4.1 standard deviations and a decrease in teacher talk of 1.9 standard deviations."

### Comprehension Outcomes
Results varied considerably by study design. Single-group (pretest-posttest) designs showed stronger effects than multiple-group (experimental/control) designs. For example, Instructional Conversations demonstrated "very strong effects on individual student outcomes, especially general comprehension (ES = 2.80)" in single-group designs.

### Effects by Student Ability
The approaches showed greater benefits for below-average students, with effect size differences of approximately 1.03 standard deviations compared to average-ability students in multiple-group designs.

### Duration Effects
"The greatest effect of the implementation of a discussion approach on general comprehension occurs in the first 3 weeks," with diminishing returns in longer implementations.

### Measurement Type Matters
"Effect sizes were stronger for the construct when it was measured with an individual outcome measure. In most cases, the effect sizes were almost 50% larger."

## Limitations and Considerations

- Approximately 70% of studies were conducted by approach developers, raising questions about replicability
- Majority of participants were 4th-6th graders (modal age: 11 years)
- Most studies employed researcher-made measures rather than standardized assessments
- Limited quantitative data on expressive approaches like Book Club and Grand Conversations

## Implications

The meta-analysis suggests classroom discussions can enhance student participation and comprehension, particularly for struggling readers, though effects are strongest in early implementation stages and when measured through individualized assessments rather than standardized tests.

# Meta-Analysis of Classroom Discussion Effects on Text Comprehension

## (a) Full Abstract

"The role of classroom discussions in comprehension and learning has been the focus of investigations since the early 1960s. Despite this long history, no syntheses have quantitatively reviewed the vast body of literature on classroom discussions for their effects on students' comprehension and learning. This comprehensive meta-analysis of empirical studies was conducted to examine evidence of the effects of classroom discussion on measures of teacher and student talk and on individual student comprehension and critical-thinking and reasoning outcomes. Results revealed that several discussion approaches produced strong increases in the amount of student talk and concomitant reductions in teacher talk, as well as substantial improvements in text comprehension. Few approaches to discussion were effective at increasing students' literal or inferential comprehension and critical thinking and reasoning. Effects were moderated by study design, the nature of the outcome measure, and student academic ability. While the range of ages of participants in the reviewed studies was large, a majority of studies were conducted with students in 4th through 6th grades. Implications for research and practice are discussed."

## (b) Numbers of Studies, Reports, Samples, Effect Sizes

"Our first step was to conduct a broad search of the literature in order to establish a beginning pool of writings from which the final body of relevant works would be chosen. To do so, we conducted exhaustive reviews of the literatures on discussion practices as they relate to the promotion of students' high-level thinking and comprehension of text by carrying out systematic searches of five major databases in the social sciences (i.e., ERIC, Education Abstracts, PsycINFO, Social Sciences Citation Index, and Digital Dissertations), keyed on the names of researchers who have played major roles in the conceptualization of a given approach (e.g., Goldenberg, 1993, or Tharp & Gallimore, 1988, for Instructional Conversation, or Raphael & McMahon, 1994, for Book Club) and titles of the approaches (e.g., Grand Conversation or Junior Great Books Shared Inquiry). We also investigated secondary citations, other printed sources, and associated Web sites. This broad search resulted in 1,001 references."

"Our initial search of the literature on classroom discussions resulted in 298 relevant Level-1 documents. Of those documents, only 127 were classified as reports of empirical studies."

"A number of studies were removed at this point because they either did not present quantitative data ( n  56) or because effect sizes could not be calculated on the basis of the data reported ( n  11)."

"Several studies failed to meet this criterion ( n  3)."

"Studies that failed to measure a construct of interest were not included in the meta-analysis ( n  10)."

"It is also important to note that several documents ( n  3) were reports of the same study (e.g., reported in a dissertation and refereed journal article)."

"In addition, there were two studies that met all the aforementioned criteria but were not included in the analyses (i.e., Anderson et al., 1997; Blum, Lipsett, & Yocom, 2002)."

"The employment of these criteria and the culling of Anderson et al. (1997) and Blum et al. (2002) resulted in a final pool of 42 documents upon which all subsequent analyses were conducted."

"The number of students participating in any given study ranged from a low of 5 (Echevarria, 1995, 1996; Goatley et al., 1995) to a high of 720 (Junior Great Books Shared Inquiry, 1992)."

"The mean sample size across the 39 studies that reported sample information was 84.28 participants."

"Of these 42 studies, 18 were published as journal articles, 17 were reported in unpublished dissertations or theses, 2 were published as book chapters, 3 as technical reports, and 2 came from other sources, such as ERIC documents."

## (c) Participants' Grade Levels, Ages, and Distribution

"While the range of ages of participants in the reviewed studies was large, a majority of studies were conducted with students in 4th through 6th grades."

"The age of the participants ranged from 5.5 years (Williams, 1999) to 17 years (Billings, 1999; Olezza, 1999). The mean age of the participants was 10.39 years, and the modal age was 11 years, which is equivalent to the age of a fifth-grade student."

"Few studies presented results from studies with primary grade students (i.e., Geisler, 1999; Williams, 1999) or secondary education students (i.e., Billings, 1999; Olezza, 1999)."

## (d) Subject Area/Content Area/Type of Text

"Given that our focus of the meta-analysis was the role of classroom discussions in promoting comprehension of text, it was also essential that the studies report effects of discussions about text."

The document states: "Dalton and Sison (1995) used Instructional Conversations with Spanish-speaking middle school students around the topic of problem solving in mathematics—problem solving that did not involve text."

"Similarly, results from several articles published by Mason (e.g., 1998, 2001) using Collaborative Reasoning in fourth- and fifth-grade science classrooms were not considered in the meta-analysis because the discussions were not about text."

"For example, in Mason (2001), the fourth-grade students participated in discussions about their observations of mold growing on carrots and cheese."

The focus is on literature and text-based discussions across various grade levels rather than specific non-text content areas.

## (e) Researcher-Developed vs. Standardized Measures

"As in other meta-analyses of intervention research in reading comprehension, we found that effects were attenuated when researchers used commercially available, standardized measures rather than researcher-developed measures (see Figure 1)."

"Several studies tested effects using commercially available, standardized measures with multiple-group designs. Those measures included the California Achievement Test, which was used in two studies (Banks, 1987; Mizerka, 1999), the Iowa Test of Basic Skills (ITBS) used by Lipman (1975), the Comprehensive Test of Basic Skills used by Yeazell (1982), the Ross Test of Critical Thinking used by both Chamberlain (1993) and Bird (1984), and the Worden Test of Critical Thinking and Reading used by Bird (1984)."

"In every case, effect sizes were stronger for the construct when it was measured with an individual outcome measure."

**Design Summary:**
- **N:** 4 seventh-grade students
- **Grade Level:** 7

- **Instruction Duration:** Baseline (6-8 days), Locating Information (10 days), Reciprocal Teaching (10 days), plus maintenance and follow-up phases
- **Outcome Measures:** Daily assessment passages (10 comprehension questions); classroom generalization probes; long-term follow-up (6 months)

**Daily Comprehension Results:**
- Baseline: "approximately 15% correct"
- Locating Information: "approximately 50% correct"
- Reciprocal Teaching (Group 1): "80%" mean accuracy
- Maintenance (6 months): "60% correct" on unprompted maintenance; returned to "80% level" after brief reintroduction

**Design Summary:**
- **N:** 6 students (3 groups of 2); plus 6 matched controls; plus 13 good comprehenders
- **Grade Level:** 7
- **Reading Level:** Grade-level decoders (≥100 wpm); 2.5 years delayed on standardized comprehension
- **Instruction Duration:** Variable baseline (4-8 days); reciprocal teaching (~20 days); maintenance (5 days); follow-up (8 weeks)
