JGB: TE 2.345, TI 2.135, CT/R 2.392 single-group → TE 0.005, TI 0.786, Comp 0.176 multiple-group. Teacher-talk values are *reductions* reported as positive.

**Critical gap: the paper does not report k per cell.** There is no number of studies behind any individual approach × outcome effect size, and none can be supplied. Confidence intervals and heterogeneity statistics by approach were also not found.

### THE CLAIM — **CORRECTED on both halves**

Claim: "most approaches greatly increased student talk but comprehension effects were variable, with Questioning the Author and Instructional Conversations showing the clearest comprehension gains."

- **"Most approaches greatly increased student talk" — FALSE.** Only three did: CR (4.097), IC (1.962), LC (1.637). QtA 0.330, PS 0.220, BC 0.050 are small; P4C, JGB and GC have **no student-talk data at all**. The paper says QtA "exhibited only a moderate negative effect on student talk." The published abstract (independently verified by me via ERIC and OpenAlex) says "**Several** discussion approaches produced strong increases," not most.
- **"Questioning the Author … clearest comprehension gains" — FALSE.** QtA's general comprehension ES is **0.205** — described as "weak effects." Its standout result is **critical thinking/reasoning, ES = 2.499**. The claim inverts QtA's profile.
- **"Instructional Conversations" — VERIFIED**, and IC is the strongest comprehension result in the paper (Comp = 2.798, quoted as "IC exhibited very strong effects on individual student outcomes, especially general comprehension (ES = 2.80)") — but almost entirely from single-group designs.
- **Your JGB suspicion — SUPPORTED.** Junior Great Books Shared Inquiry has the second-strongest comprehension profile (TE 2.345, TI 2.135 single-group), again design-dependent.
- **Your Collaborative Reasoning suspicion — NOT SUPPORTED.** CR's comprehension effects are among the *weakest* (Comp 0.262, TI 0.082). CR's headline is talk and reasoning, not comprehension.

**Accurate restatement:** A few approaches (Collaborative Reasoning, Instructional Conversations, Literature Circles) sharply increased student talk and reduced teacher talk; comprehension effects were highly variable and heavily design-dependent, with Instructional Conversations and Junior Great Books showing the largest comprehension effects (almost entirely in single-group pre-post designs), while Questioning the Author's strength was critical thinking/reasoning (2.50) rather than comprehension (0.21). The published abstract's own summary — which I verified directly from ERIC — is: "**Few approaches to discussion were effective at increasing students' literal or inferential comprehension and critical thinking and reasoning.**"

### Grade levels — VERIFIED (independently, from ERIC/OpenAlex)
Abstract, verbatim: "a majority of studies were conducted with students in **4th through 6th grades**." Method (mirror text): ages ranged **5.5 to 17 years**; **mean age 10.39**, **modal age 11** (≈5th grade); "Few studies presented results from studies with primary grade students … or secondary education students." **No grade-by-grade frequency distribution is published.** Note the implication: this meta-analysis is a weak basis for any secondary-level claim.

### Science subset — **NO. Explicitly excluded.**
This is important and cuts against citing this meta-analysis for science classrooms. Inclusion required that discussions be **about text**. Verbatim (mirror text): "results from several articles published by Mason … using Collaborative Reasoning in fourth- and fifth-grade science classrooms were **not considered** in the meta-analysis because the discussions were not about text… the fourth-grade students participated in discussions about their observations of mold growing on carrots and cheese." A math study (Dalton & Sison, 1995) was excluded on the same ground. The corpus is literacy/ELA. (The paper does not tabulate narrative vs. expository *text type*, so some included studies may have used informational texts — it simply doesn't report that.)

### Measure types — researcher-designed dominate overwhelmingly
Verbatim: "we found that effects were attenuated when researchers used commercially available, standardized measures rather than researcher-developed measures (see Figure 1)." Only **six of 42** studies used standardized instruments (CAT: Banks 1987, Mizerka 1999; ITBS: Lipman 1975; CTBS: Yeazell 1982; Ross Test of Critical Thinking: Chamberlain 1993, Bird 1984; Worden Test: Bird 1984). **Only three approaches (JGB, P4C, LC) have any standardized-measure comprehension data at all**; Figure 1's numeric values were not extractable. Also: "In every case, effect sizes were stronger for the construct when it was measured with an individual outcome measure. In most cases, the effect sizes were almost 50% larger."

**One extraction I explicitly distrust:** the converted text yielded a sentence saying "Philosophy for Children evidenced the strongest positive effects on student comprehension" with "ES = 0.55," which contradicts Table 2's P4C Comp = 0.333. Probably a garbled Figure 1 / single-study (Lipman 1975, ITBS) reference. **Do not use it.**

---

## TARGET 3 — Rosenshine & Meister (1994) and reciprocal teaching

### A) .88 / .32 — **VERIFIED as medians**

Rosenshine, B., & Meister, C. (1994). Reciprocal Teaching: A Review of the Research. *Review of Educational Research, 64*(4), 479–530. DOI 10.3102/00346543064004479. Article body is **closed access** (Unpaywall: closed, no OA locations). Abstract, verbatim:

> "When standardized tests were used to assess comprehension, the median effect size, favoring reciprocal teaching, was **.32**. When experimenter-developed comprehension tests were used, the median effect size was **.88**."

- Explicitly **medians**, not means — VERIFIED.
- **16 quantitative studies** — VERIFIED from the abstract.
- **Per-measure study counts in the 1994 published article: UNVERIFIABLE** (body inaccessible). Do not claim "16 studies contributed to each" — studies using both test types are double-counted.
- **No range, SD, or CI is reported** for the medians. Do not cite a range from the published article.

**Precursor (full text read by me directly via ERIC):** Rosenshine, B., & Meister, C. E. (1993). *Reciprocal Teaching: A Review of 19 Experimental Studies*. Technical Report No. 574, Center for the Study of Reading, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (ERIC **ED356456**, not ED354564 — that number is a different document on debate language).

Tech-report figures: **standardized tests used in 13 studies** (4 of 13 significant), **experimenter-developed tests used in 11 studies** (8 of 11 significant); 5 studies used both (13+11−5 = 19). Median ES **.32** standardized and **.87** experimenter-developed, each computed on **9 effect sizes**. Overall median across all 19 = **.57**. Other rows: explicit-teaching-plus-RT .60 (8); RT-only .34 (5); good–poor/all students .57 (9); below-average students .48 (4). Table note confirms studies using both test types were "included in both categories and, therefore, counted twice." The .87 → .88 shift reflects the 19 → 16 study change between report and article.

### B) "15–20 sessions gets most of the benefit" — **CORRECTED. Rosenshine & Meister found the opposite of a dose-response relationship.**

Technical Report No. 574, verbatim (OCR spacing normalized):

> "The number of instructional sessions provided in these studies ranged from **6 sessions to 100 sessions**… We found **no differences in the median number of sessions for significant, mixed, and non-significant studies** across different types of students… Overall, there were more instructional sessions in studies involving below-average students, but again, **more sessions were not associated with greater success**."

Supporting detail: for good–poor/all students, "both the significant and non-significant studies lasted for a median of **20 sessions**, and the median was 17 for the studies with mixed results"; for below-average students, "the median was **28** sessions for the two significant studies and **29** sessions for the four non-significant studies." Also, comparing explicit-teaching+RT vs RT-only: "We found no differences in the total number of sessions for the two types of studies."

So: ~20 sessions is the **typical study length**, and at that length studies split evenly between significant and non-significant. There is no dose-optimum claim in the paper and the data would not support one. **The attribution is wrong and should be dropped or rewritten.**

Caveat: this passage is from the 1993 technical report; I could not confirm identical wording survives into the 1994 RER article.

**Where "15–20 sessions" probably comes from: Palincsar & Brown's own study design.** Their training ran ~20 days, and in the 1983 technical report students were "consistently scoring about 70% by the **fifteenth day**," with days-to-criterion of 13, 13, 9 and 5 across four groups. That is a description of one study's training schedule, not a meta-analytic finding.

### C) Palincsar & Brown (1984) — VERIFIED, with corrections to the popular shorthand

Palincsar, A. S., & Brown, A. L. (1984). Reciprocal teaching of comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring activities. *Cognition and Instruction, 1*(2), 117–175. DOI 10.1207/s1532690xci0102_1. Read from a hosted copy (scholastic.co.uk and eclass.uoa.gr).

**Two studies**, not three.
- **Study 1:** "Thirty-seven seventh-grade students took part in this study. Twenty-four of the students had reading problems, 13 did not." The 24 poor comprehenders (adequate decoders, comprehension ≥2 years below grade level, baseline <40% correct on the experimental task) were assigned in groups of 6 to reciprocal teaching, "locating information," test-only, and untreated control. Instruction by an **adult investigator**, **~20 days**.
- **Study 2:** reciprocal teaching moved to "naturally occurring groups" — two classroom reading groups plus two resource-room remedial groups — with "a 'real' teacher, not an investigator." Otherwise "a replica of Study 1." (N commonly cited as 21; not cleanly confirmed in extraction.)
- **Measures:** daily **researcher-designed** expository passages (400–475 words, 7th-grade level, 10 questions classified text-explicit / text-implicit / script-implicit); classroom generalization probes in social studies and science; transfer tests; plus the **Gates-MacGinitie standardized** comprehension test.

**Gains (all headline gains are on researcher-designed daily probes):** baseline "not exceeding 40% correct"; "Four of the six reached a stable level of **80% correct**," another "reached a stable level of 70% correct in 12 days"; the RT group "improved to the level set by the average readers" (~75%). Classroom generalization probes rose "from approximately **20% to 60% correct**." Standardized Gates-MacGinitie: "The average gain, including all six students, was **15 months**" (grade-equivalent months — not an effect size). The 1983 technical report (ED225135) gives a parallel study with a 7.3-month Gates-MacGinitie gain and a smaller pilot going "From their baseline performance of 15% correct … to accuracy levels of 85%."

**On the "~30% → ~70–80%" shorthand: broadly right, but two corrections.** Baselines were ~40% in the main studies (15% in the smallest pilot), not 30%; and 70–80% was a **preset mastery criterion**, not a free-running ceiling. The standardized-test gain was modest.

### D) Newer secondary-level evidence — reciprocal teaching looks much weaker

**What Works Clearinghouse (2010).** *WWC Intervention Report: Adolescent Literacy — Reciprocal Teaching*, September 2010. 164 studies screened; **6 met standards** (5 RCTs, 1 QED with reservations). Comprehension domain: **average improvement index +6 percentile points, range −23 to +42**. Rating: "**mixed effects** in the comprehension domain for adolescent learners"; extent of evidence medium to large. No qualifying studies in alphabetics, fluency, or general literacy achievement. Under the Students with Learning Disabilities protocol, WWC found **no** qualifying studies.

**Okkinga, M., van Steensel, R., van Gelderen, A. J. S., van Schooten, E., Sleegers, P. J. C., & Arends, L. R. (2018). Effectiveness of Reading-Strategy Interventions in Whole Classrooms: a Meta-Analysis. *Educational Psychology Review, 30*(4), 1215–1239.** DOI 10.1007/s10648-018-9445-7. **Abstract-level only** — I verified the abstract verbatim from the VU Amsterdam repository record (research.vu.nl); the Springer full text and the EUR repository PDF were both blocked (cookie-wall / CAPTCHA).

- **N studies = 52, K = 125 effect sizes.**
- Reading comprehension, **standardized tests: Cohen's d = .186** ("a very small effect")
- Reading comprehension, **researcher-developed tests: Cohen's d = .431** ("a small effect")
- **Strategic ability: d = .786** ("a medium overall effect")
- Moderators named in the abstract: including "setting reading goals" in the strategy package → larger effects; "effects were larger for interventions in which the **trainer was the researcher as opposed to teachers**"; "effect sizes tended to be larger for studies conducted in **grades 6–8**"; studies not modelling the hierarchical data structure showed inflated effects.
- **Important correction on the whole-class vs small-group point:** there is **no within-meta numeric contrast**. This meta-analysis includes *only* whole-classroom, teacher-led studies. The contrast is rhetorical, set up in the abstract's opening: "Research has demonstrated that in controlled experiments in which small groups are being tutored by researchers, reading-strategy instruction is highly effective (Palincsar & Brown, 1984)… It is unclear, however, whether reading-strategy interventions are equally effective in whole-classroom situations." Do not quote a numeric whole-class-minus-small-group difference from this paper.
- **UNVERIFIABLE:** CIs, SEs, p-values, and per-outcome k.

**Okkinga, M., van Steensel, R., van Gelderen, A. J. S., & Sleegers, P. J. C. (2018). Effects of reciprocal teaching on reading comprehension of low-achieving adolescents. The importance of specific teacher skills. *Journal of Research in Reading, 41*(1), 20–41.** DOI 10.1111/1467-9817.12082. Read from the Erasmus repository author version (REPUB_94294).
- **369 seventh-grade low-achieving students** (189 treatment / 180 control; N = 338 analysed), **20 teachers / 20 classes** (10 vs 10), one school year (~7 months of weekly RT lessons), intensive teacher training and coaching, business-as-usual control.
- Outcome: **SALT reading test — a standardized comprehension measure** validated for low-achieving adolescents (8 tasks, 59 items).
- **Result: NULL.** "After 1 year of implementing reciprocal teaching, **no main effects of the treatment were established**" (ΔIGLS = 0.458, n.s.).
- Quality of strategy instruction significantly moderated the effect (**B = 3.183, SE = 1.311, df = 14, p < .05**), explaining an additional **37% of class-level variance** — benefit appeared only where teachers delivered high-quality instruction.

**Okkinga, M., van Gelderen, A. J. S., van Schooten, E., van Steensel, R., & Sleegers, P. J. C. (2021). Implementation quality of principles of reciprocal teaching in whole-classroom settings: a two-year study with low-achieving adolescents. *Reading Psychology, 42*(4), 323–363.** DOI 10.1080/02702711.2021.1887019. **SECONDARY-SOURCE FLAG:** obtained only via OpenAlex metadata and a machine-reconstructed abstract, not verbatim publisher text. Two-year study, 10 experimental vs. control teachers, **238 seventh-graders**, **no overall effect on reading comprehension**, with the *modeling* principle positively moderating. Exact statistics not retrieved.

### Synthesis for Target 3
The durable, replicated finding is the **measure-type split**, not the magnitude: Rosenshine & Meister (1994) .88 experimenter-developed vs .32 standardized; Okkinga et al. (2018) d = .431 researcher-developed vs d = .186 standardized across 52 whole-class studies. When reciprocal teaching moves from researcher-led small groups to teacher-led whole classrooms and is measured on standardized tests, effects shrink toward zero — WWC rates it "mixed effects" (+6 percentile) for adolescents, and two well-powered Dutch classroom RCTs with low-achieving adolescents found no main effect.

# Fact-Check Report

**Method note / limitation up front:** no Bash and no PDF renderer were available in this session (`pdftoppm` missing, so the Read tool could not open the local PDFs; no `pdftotext`/`pypdf`). All extraction was done via WebFetch, routing PDFs through the `r.jina.ai` text-extraction proxy. That means every "verbatim" quote below is text-layer extraction relayed through a summarizing model, not eyeball-verified against a typeset page. Where a number came from an abstract, a repository record, or an unofficial mirror rather than the primary body text, I say so.

---

## TARGET 1 — Graham & Hebert, *Writing to Read*

Primary text used: Graham, S., & Hebert, M. (2010). *Writing to Read: Evidence for How Writing Can Improve Reading. A Report from Carnegie Corporation of New York* (Time to Act report). Washington, DC: Alliance for Excellent Education. Extracted independently from **two** hosts (media.carnegie.org and nildcanada.org) with matching numbers.

**The 2011 HER version is UNOBTAINABLE.** Graham, S., & Hebert, M. (2011). "Writing to Read: A Meta-Analysis of the Impact of Writing and Writing Instruction on Reading." *Harvard Educational Review, 81*(4), 710–744. DOI 10.17763/haer.81.4.t2k0m13756113566. Unpaywall: `is_oa: false`, `oa_locations: []`, `has_repository_copy: false`; Semantic Scholar: CLOSED, `openAccessPdf` empty. The one circulating PDF (richardcolby.net) is an **image-only scan** — extraction returns only the title page and repeated "Reproduced with permission of the copyright owner" notices. ERIC EJ961480 has abstract only, with no numbers. Academia.edu copy is metadata only.

### 1. Overall effect for "writing about text" — **CORRECTED**

The claimed **~0.35 (9 studies) standardized / ~0.49 (44 studies) researcher-designed is NOT what the Carnegie report says**, and I could not verify it in any source.

Carnegie 2010, verbatim:
- "Average Weighted Effect Size = **0.40** Published Standardized or Norm-Referenced Tests (**Based on 11 Studies**)"
- "Average Weighted Effect Size = **0.51** Researcher-Designed Tests (**Based on 50 Studies**)"
- "fifty-seven out of sixty-one outcomes (93 percent) were positive"

**Verdict: CORRECTED to 0.40 / 11 and 0.51 / 50.** Whether the HER 2011 version reports 0.35/9 and 0.49/44 is **UNVERIFIABLE** — I found no source, primary or secondary, containing those figures. Targeted searches for ".35", "44 studies", and "9 studies" in connection with this meta-analysis returned nothing. Do not use those numbers without page-level access to HER 81(4).

### 2. Effect sizes by writing-activity subtype — mostly VERIFIED

All four are **researcher-designed measures**:

| Practice | ES | Studies | Positive outcomes | Grades |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Respond to a text in writing (personal reaction, analysis & interpretation) | **0.77** | 9 | 9/9 | — |
| Write summaries of a text | **0.52** | 19 | 17/19 (89%) | 3–12 |
| Write notes about a text | **0.47** | 23 | 21/23 (91%) | — |
| Answer / generate written questions about a text | **0.27** | 8 | 8/8 | 6–12 |

- (a) extended writing 0.77, n=9 — **VERIFIED**
- (b) summaries 0.52, n=19 — **VERIFIED**
- (c) note-taking 0.47, n=23 — **VERIFIED**
- (d) answering questions = **0.27, 8 studies**, described as "a small but consistently positive impact," all 8 positive. The report does not print a p-value or explicit significance statement for this estimate in the extracted text; it presents it as a positive recommended practice. **Treat "statistically significant" as not directly confirmed** — the report's own framing is "small but consistently positive."

The only explicit non-significance statement I found anywhere in the report concerns lower-achieving students: an average weighted effect size "not greater than zero when [summary writing was] not explicitly taught," with the authors cautioning that small samples make this fragile.

### 3. THE RANK-ORDER CLAIM — **CORRECTED**

Claimed: extended writing > note-taking > answering questions > summarizing.
**Actual: extended writing (0.77) > summarizing (0.52) > note-taking (0.47) > answering questions (0.27).**

Two errors: summarizing was moved from 2nd to last, and answering questions was moved from last to 3rd. Note also that summarizing (0.52) and note-taking (0.47) are close enough that ordering them is not meaningful, whereas the gap between the top (0.77) and bottom (0.27) practices is real.

### 4. Grades — partially CORRECTED

- Grade range: **grades 2–12** for the writing-about-text analyses, verbatim: "students participating in this research were in grades 2–12, with the majority in middle or high school." The **overall meta-analysis** (all three recommendations, including the writing-instruction and writing-volume studies) spans **grades 1–12**, across "ninety-three comparisons examining the effects of writing on reading," with studies "from the 1930s to the present." So "grades 1–12" is right for the report as a whole; "grades 2–12" is right for writing about text. **VERIFIED with that distinction.**
- 81% figure: **VERIFIED**, verbatim: "most of the research (**81 percent**) examining the effectiveness of writing about text activities was conducted with students in **grade six or above**."
- **Grade-band moderator analyses: only ONE was reported.** For summary writing, verbatim: "While summary writing significantly improved middle and high school students' comprehension of text (average weighted effect size = **0.33** based on **eleven studies**), it had an even stronger effect on elementary students' comprehension (average weighted effect size = **0.79** based on **four studies**)." No grade-band split is given for note-taking, for responding to text, or for writing about text overall.
- Secondary-student benefit: this is **direct, not inferred** — 81% of the writing-about-text comparisons were grade 6+, so the pooled 0.40/0.51 estimates are dominated by secondary samples, and the questions practice is reported for grades 6–12. The report's own generalization is soft: "The impact of writing about reading applied broadly across different levels of schooling." Note the one place a grade contrast *is* reported, the secondary estimate is the **weaker** one (0.33 vs 0.79 for summarization).

### 5. Other two recommendations — VERIFIED

**Teach writing skills and processes** (effect on reading):
- Reading comprehension: **0.18** on standardized/norm-referenced tests (**12 studies**); **0.27** on researcher-designed tests (**5 studies**)
- Reading fluency: **0.71** combined (**4 studies**, grades 1–7)
- Word reading: **0.68** combined (**5 studies**, grades 1–5)

**Increase how much students write**: **0.30** on published standardized norm-referenced tests (**6 studies**, grades 1–6).

### 6. Discrepancy check (2010 Carnegie vs 2011 HER) — **partly UNVERIFIABLE**

- The ".40 / 11 studies" figure is **not a discrepancy** — it is the Carnegie report's **standardized/norm-referenced** estimate. The report's own headline framing pairs it with the researcher-designed estimate of 0.51 (50 studies); a summary that presents ".40 based on 11 studies" as *the* overall effect is quoting only the standardized half of a two-part result. That is the single most important framing correction here.
- Carnegie 2010 vs HER 2011 numeric comparison: **UNVERIFIABLE.** HER full text is inaccessible by every route tried.
- **Science / content-area text: YES, the Carnegie report addresses it**, verbatim: "These positive effects were evident when students wrote about text in **science and social studies** as well as in English (**60 percent of comparisons** involved these disciplines; see Appendix B)." No separate science-only effect size is reported — this is a statement of breadth, not a subgroup estimate.

---

## TARGET 2 — Murphy, Wilkinson, Soter, Hennessey & Alexander (2009)

Full citation: *Journal of Educational Psychology, 101*(3), 740–764. DOI 10.1037/a0015576.

**PROVENANCE WARNING — read before using any number in this section.** The article is genuinely closed (OpenAlex, Unpaywall `is_oa: false` / `oa_locations: []`, Semantic Scholar CLOSED, CORE/BASE all negative; ERIC EJ861185 has abstract only). The full text below was obtained by a subagent **from a shadow-library mirror**, converted through a text proxy. I did not verify it against a legitimate copy, and I flag it as such: **these numbers are not from an authorized source and should be confirmed against the published article before publication.** What I *can* independently corroborate from legitimate sources (ERIC EJ861185 and OpenAlex, fetched by me directly) is the abstract wording and the grade-level statement — those are marked below.

### Number of studies — VERIFIED (from mirror text)
"**42 documents**" (the paper's own word — not "42 intervention studies"). Funnel: 1,001 references → 298 Level-1 → 127 empirical → exclusions (no quantitative data n=56; ES not calculable n=11; discussion not about text n=3; no construct of interest n=10; duplicate reports n=3) plus 2 culled → 42. ### The nine approaches — **CORRECTED**
Grouped by stance toward text:
- **Critical-analytic:** Collaborative Reasoning (CR), **Paideia Seminar (PS)**, Philosophy for Children (P4C)
- **Efferent:** Instructional Conversations (IC), Junior Great Books Shared Inquiry (JGB), Questioning the Author (QtA)
- **Expressive:** Book Club (BC), Grand Conversations (GC), Literature Circles (LC)

**"Point-Counterpoint" is not one of the nine** — the term does not appear in the paper. The correct ninth approach is **Paideia Seminar**. (Point/Counterpoint is a later Wilkinson-lab approach.)

### Effect sizes by approach and outcome (Table 2, pooled rows)

Single- vs multiple-group design splits matter enormously. ## 1. Graham & Hebert — mostly CORRECTED

Source: Graham & Hebert (2010), *Writing to Read*, Carnegie Corporation / Alliance for Excellent Education.

**Your rank order is wrong.** Actual, all **researcher-designed** measures:

| Practice | ES | k |
|---|---|---|
| Respond to text in writing (extended) | **0.77** | 9 |
| Write summaries | **0.52** | 19 |
| Write notes | **0.47** | 23 |
| Answer/generate written questions | **0.27** | 8 |

Claimed: extended > note-taking > questions > summarizing. **Actual: extended > summarizing > note-taking > questions.** Two errors — summarizing moved from 2nd to last, questions from last to 3rd. (Summarizing vs note-taking, .52 vs .47, isn't meaningfully orderable; the .77-vs-.27 gap is real.)

**The ES≈0.40 claim needs reframing.** 0.40 is not "the" overall effect — it is the **standardized/norm-referenced** half (11 studies). The researcher-designed half is **0.51** (50 studies). Quoting .40 alone quotes half a two-part result. Note: a search snippet attributed **0.35 (9 studies) / 0.49 (44 studies)** to the 2011 HER version — plausibly the discrepancy you were asking about, but **UNVERIFIABLE**; no source containing those figures could be found. Don't use them.

**Grades: VERIFIED.** Grades 2–12 for writing-about-text (1–12 for the report overall); **81% of writing-about-text comparisons were grade 6+**, so the pooled estimates are secondary-dominated — direct, not inferred. But the *only* grade-band moderator reported cuts against you: for summarization, middle/high **0.33** (11 studies) vs elementary **0.79** (4 studies).

Other recommendations: teaching writing skills → comprehension **0.18** standardized (12 studies) / **0.27** researcher-designed (5); increasing writing volume → **0.30** standardized (6 studies, grades 1–6). Science relevance: 60% of comparisons were science/social studies, but **no separate science effect size** is reported.

## 2. Murphy et al. (2009) — CORRECTED (both halves of your claim)

*J. Educational Psychology*, 101(3), 740–764. 42 documents, studies 1964–2002.

- **"Most approaches greatly increased student talk" — FALSE.** Only three did: Collaborative Reasoning (4.10), Instructional Conversations (1.96), Literature Circles (1.64). QtA was 0.33; three approaches have no student-talk data. The abstract says "*several*," not most.
- **"QtA … clearest comprehension gains" — FALSE.** QtA general comprehension = **0.205** (weak). Its standout is **critical thinking/reasoning = 2.499**. Your claim inverts its profile.

- **No science subset — science studies were explicitly EXCLUDED** (Mason's CR-in-science studies were dropped because discussions weren't about text). The corpus is literacy/ELA.

- **WWC (2010)** adolescent literacy: "**mixed effects**," improvement index **+6 percentiles**, range −23 to +42 (6 studies).

**Reverse cohesion (McNamara, E. Kintsch, Songer & W. | Write notes | **0.47** | 23 |

Three of the four threads are back. The verification was unkind to my first answer — **four of the numbers I gave you were wrong, and two were wrong in ways that would have misled you.** Here's the reconciliation.

## Corrections to what I told you

**Cervetti et al. (2012) — I inflated the vocabulary effect by 3×.** Actual: science understanding d = 0.65, vocabulary **d = 0.23** (not 0.70 — it's the *smallest* significant effect in the study, not the largest), writing d = 0.40, reading comprehension 0.11 ns. Worse, I said "no effect on general reading comprehension" — no standardized reading test was administered at all. All four outcomes were built by the developers at Lawrence Hall of Science; vocabulary pretest reliability was α = .43, which is poor. And it's **grade 4**. I handed a high school teacher an elementary study without saying so.

**PACT — I merged numbers from three different studies.** Vaughn et al. (2013) actually reported content knowledge 0.17, content comprehension 0.29, Gates-MacGinitie 0.20. My "0.40" is from the 2017 English learner trial; my "0.21" is the What Works Clearinghouse's recomputed Gates-MacGinitie figure. More importantly: **there are no science PACT studies.** Every trial is social studies or US history. I shouldn't have offered it to you as if it generalized. The 2023 scale-up (7,183 students) found *larger* knowledge effects (0.37–0.45) but comprehension went null and has stayed null in every study since 2013.

**CORI — the 0.9 doesn't hold up.** It's the top of a 0.65–0.93 range from a meta-analysis of the developer's own studies. The WWC reviewed 48 CORI studies and concluded that **none met evidence standards**. Independent syntheses (van der Sande et al., 2023, 39 studies) put reading comprehension at d = 0.27, with effects *smaller for secondary students than elementary*. I flagged the developer problem but still led with the inflated number.

**Stahl & Fairbanks (1986) — I had the two figures backwards.** The 0.97 is comprehension of passages *containing the taught words*; 0.30 is global comprehension. I attributed 0.97 to vocabulary measures. The correct reading actually strengthens the practical advice but I stated it wrong.

**Graham & Hebert — my rank order was wrong.** Actual: extended written response 0.77, **summarizing 0.52**, note-taking 0.47, answering questions 0.27. I put summarizing last; it's second. Also, 0.40 isn't the overall effect — it's the standardized half; researcher-designed was 0.51. One genuinely good piece of news for you: **81% of these comparisons were grade 6+**, so this is one of the few findings actually sampled from your population.

**Questioning the Author — I recommended it on a backwards reading.** In Murphy et al., QtA's comprehension effect is 0.205, which is weak; its standout is critical thinking/reasoning at 2.499. I told you it showed the clearest *comprehension* gains. Also: that meta-analysis excluded science studies entirely, is dominated by grades 4–6, and ~70% of its studies were run by the approach's own developer. Two separate threads flagged that the per-approach numbers could only be obtained from an unauthorized source and **should be treated as unverified.** I'd hold the specific figures loosely.

**"15–20 sessions of reciprocal teaching gets most of the benefit" — I made this up, effectively.** Rosenshine & Meister found the *opposite*: sessions ranged 6 to 100 with no relationship to success, and significant and non-significant studies had the same median. The 0.88/0.32 figures are correct (they're medians). But newer secondary evidence is much weaker — Okkinga et al. (2018) whole-class: d = 0.186 standardized, and a full-year RCT with 369 low-achieving 7th graders was **null**.

**Self-explanation — I got the moderator wrong.** In iSTART the compensated aptitude is *reading strategy knowledge and reading skill*, not domain knowledge, and the direction splits (low-strategy students gained on text-based questions, high-strategy on inference). The robust, well-replicated finding you can actually use is the cohesion one: **low-knowledge readers always benefit from high-cohesion text** (McNamara, Kintsch, Songer & Kintsch, 1996 — and that one *is* a science study, biology, grades 7–10).

## The pattern I under-weighted

Every headline number in my first answer was a researcher-designed measure, and each collapses to roughly 0.10–0.30 on standardized tests. This isn't a footnote — it's the finding:

| | Researcher-made | Standardized |
|---|---|---|
| Text structure (Hebert et al. 2016) | 0.57 | **0.13** (8 studies, half negative) |
| Vocabulary (Elleman et al. 2009) | 0.50 | **0.10, ns** |
| Reciprocal teaching (Rosenshine & Meister) | 0.88 | 0.32 |
| Reciprocal teaching (Okkinga 2018) | 0.43 | 0.19 |
| Integrated literacy K–5 (Hwang et al. 2022) | 0.91 vocab | 0.25 comprehension |

Sobering context: Baye, Inns, Lake & Slavin (2019, *RRQ*) reviewed secondary reading programs and found an overall effect of **+0.09**. That's the realistic baseline for what a reading intervention does to a standardized score in your grade band.

Also, one citation fix: Hebert et al.'s fourth author is **Brown**, not Brandon. And Hwang, Cabell & Joyner is *Scientific Studies of Reading* 26(3), not *Journal of Research in Reading* — and it's **K–5 only**, so I over-extended it.

## What survives and is actually defensible for your classroom

**Strongest single finding for a secondary science teacher: write about the text.** Graham & Hebert's corpus is 81% grade 6+, and extended written response is 0.77. Have students write a real explanation, not fill in a blank.

**Text structure instruction holds up** at 0.57, and the elementary/secondary moderator was non-significant — though Pyle et al. (2017) found moderators favoring elementary, so treat "works equally at high school" as *not disproven* rather than established.

**Reading Apprenticeship is the best standardized evidence in secondary science.** Greenleaf et al. (2011, *AERJ*) — group-randomized biology, effects of 0.23 ELA / 0.24 reading / 0.28 biology **on California Standards Tests**. Real tests, real science classrooms. Two caveats: the internet-delivered scale-up (iRAISE) was null on student achievement despite moving teacher practice, and WWC's 2023 review downgraded it to "uncertain effects."

**Project READI** (Goldman et al., 2019, *AERJ*) — grade 9 biology, 1,400 students: 0.32 on the externally-developed GISA assessment. Small but it's your exact population and subject.

**Concept mapping is weaker than advertised.** Overall 0.60, but versus *outlining or writing summaries* — the realistic alternative — it's **0.19**. If you were already going to have students summarize, mapping adds little.

**Drop the Frayer model and close reading as evidence claims.** Frayer has essentially no rigorous evidence; the 1969 source is an unpublished assessment taxonomy that doesn't contain the four-box template. A 2026 review of close reading found 19 studies, zero RCTs, median n = 11, mostly master's theses, with the controlled studies null. Both may be fine delivery vehicles for practices that *are* evidenced — just don't believe they're doing the work.

## Revised recommendation

Narrow to three things, all of which survive scrutiny for secondary students: **build prior knowledge before hard text; have students write extended explanations of what they read; teach the structure of the passage explicitly.** Expect gains on your unit tests and your texts — not on state reading scores. The evidence that any of this transfers to general reading ability is genuinely weak, and I stated that too confidently the first time in the other direction too.

The fourth thread — academic language, the knowledge-threshold research, and whether unpacking nominalizations has any experimental support — is still running; that one bears on my framing claim that this is fundamentally a language problem, so I'll follow up when it lands.

**1. Snow (2010), *Science*, 328(5977), 450–452.**
A three-page Education Forum piece — an argument, not a study. No data, no effect sizes. Claim: academic language is engineered for concision, precision and authority, and the devices achieving that (nominalization, agentless passives, heavy subjects, center-embedding, high density of information-bearing words, epistemic verbs, evidence-based rather than opinion-based claims) are precisely what breaks comprehension. Worked example: *"Torque is the product of the magnitude of the force and the lever arm of the force,"* where everyday senses of "product" and "arm" actively mislead. Recommends embedding academic-language instruction in the science curriculum; points to her own Word Generation program.
**WEAKLY-SUPPORTED as evidence** (position piece in a high-prestige venue). The underlying claim is separately supported: Word Generation RCT — Jones, LaRusso, Kim, Kim, Selman, Uccelli, Barnes, Donovan & Snow (2019), *JREE* 12(3), 7,752 students, grades 4–7, 25 schools, school-level randomization: taught vocabulary 0.22/0.28 (gr. 4–5) and 0.13/0.16 (gr. 6–7) across years 1/2; academic language and deep comprehension effects only in year 2. Earlier Boston quasi-experiment (1,016 students, grades 6–8): d = 0.49 on researcher-designed vocabulary. Lawrence et al. (2015), *AERJ* 52(4): discussion mediated the effect. **WELL-ESTABLISHED that language is a real barrier; the causal test is McKeown, Beck, Sinatra & Loxterman (1992), *RRQ* — grade 5, coherence-revised history text produced significantly better recall and question performance than the original, holding content constant.**

**2. Shanahan & Shanahan (2008), *Harvard Educational Review*, 78(1), 40–59.**
Three teams (history, chemistry, math), each with 2 disciplinary experts + 2 teacher educators + 2 high-school teachers — **six disciplinary experts total, ~18 people**. Methods: think-aloud protocols, focus-group transcripts, member checking, cross-disciplinary comparison. Reports the "first two years" of a project; the authors' own word is **"preliminary."** Follow-up: Shanahan, Shanahan & Misischia (2011), *JLR* 43(4), 393–429.
**WEAKLY-SUPPORTED.** It documents how six experts read. It does not test whether teaching students to read that way helps. It is cited in standards documents and PD as though it were an efficacy trial. Howell, Barlow & Dyches (2021), *JLLE* 17(1), reviewing 58 articles, found the disciplinary-literacy PD base "remains limited"; my ERIC sweeps for secondary experimental disciplinary-literacy studies with achievement outcomes returned almost nothing outside history/writing.

**3. Fang & Schleppegrell — the straight answer: NO experimental evidence.**
Key works: Fang (2005), *Science Education* 89, 335–347; Fang (2006), *IJSE* 28(5), 491–520; Fang, Schleppegrell & Cox (2006), *JLR* 38(3); Fang & Schleppegrell (2008), *Reading in Secondary Content Areas*; Fang & Schleppegrell (2010), *JAAL* 53(7). They identify four features of science language — technical vocabulary, abstraction, high lexical density, tightly knit structure — and propose Functional Language Analysis: interrogating clauses, unpacking nominalizations back into processes.

**I found no experimental or quasi-experimental study testing whether teaching students to unpack nominalizations or dense noun phrases improves comprehension.** Three independent ERIC sweeps ("functional language analysis"; "nominalization instruction + comprehension + experiment"; "grammatical metaphor + science text + comprehension") returned zero controlled intervention studies with student comprehension outcomes. Fourth thread is in. It corrects my framing claim and kills one of my classroom recommendations.

## My framing was half wrong

I told you science reading difficulty is "mostly a knowledge and language problem" and leaned on Snow (2010) and Shanahan & Shanahan (2008). Both are weaker than I implied:

- **Snow (2010)** is a three-page *Science* Education Forum piece — an argument with no data. Prestigious venue, but a position paper.
- **Shanahan & Shanahan (2008)** is a qualitative study of **six disciplinary experts** (~18 people total), which the authors themselves called "preliminary." It documents how experts read. It never tested whether teaching students to read that way helps. It gets cited in standards documents as though it were an efficacy trial. I did the same thing.

**The knowledge half, though, is much stronger than I made it sound** — and it's the single most useful finding in this whole sweep:

**O'Reilly, Wang & Sabatini (2019, *Psychological Science*)** — 3,534 high school students, 37 schools, ecosystems content. They found a **knowledge threshold at ~59% correct**. Below it, the knowledge–comprehension relationship is β = 0.18. Above it, β = 0.81. Comprehension doesn't degrade gracefully as knowledge drops — it *disconnects*. Below the floor, no amount of strategy instruction rescues a reader. Recognizing core terms (ecosystem, habitat, species) predicted crossing the threshold better than exotic ones. Don't treat 59% as a universal number — it's instrument-specific — but the shape of the finding is the thing.

This is your population, your subject, and a real sample. It's the strongest warrant for "front-load knowledge before the hard text" that exists, and I buried it under weaker citations.

## The recommendation I need to withdraw

I told you to unpack dense noun phrases and nominalizations — "a 5-minute routine with outsized returns," citing Fang & Schleppegrell. **There is no experimental evidence for that.** Three separate ERIC sweeps for controlled studies testing whether teaching students to unpack nominalizations improves comprehension returned *zero*. The framework is descriptive linguistics, worked textbook examples, and teacher-education case studies. It's a good lens for understanding *why* your textbook is hard; it is not a validated method, and "outsized returns" was an invention.

What *is* causally established nearby: **McKeown, Beck, Sinatra & Loxterman (1992, *RRQ*)** — revising a text for coherence, holding content constant, significantly improved recall and question performance. So linguistic form does causally constrain comprehension. That supports *giving students better-written text*, not a student-facing grammar routine.

## What the last thread adds that's genuinely useful

**McKeown, Beck & Blake (2009, *RRQ*)** — two years, fifth graders, three conditions: content instruction (open, meaning-based questions about what the text says), strategies instruction, and control. **Content instruction beat strategies instruction** on recall and expository learning probes across both years. **Word Generation** (Jones, LaRusso, Kim et al., 2019, *JREE*) — 7,752 students, grades 4–7, school-randomized: taught vocabulary effects 0.13–0.28, with academic language and deep comprehension effects appearing only in **year 2**. Real evidence that academic language instruction works, but slowly.

**Reading Apprenticeship has an important asymmetry.** The version embedded in biology PD (Greenleaf et al., 2011) worked on state tests. But Kemple et al. (2008) tested RA as a **standalone course** — 2,329 ninth graders, 17 schools — and found **no significant effects**. Embed it in your science teaching; don't send kids to a separate reading class.

**Author & Publication:** Pat Rubio Goldsmith, American Educational Research Journal, Vol. 48, No. 3 (June 2011), pp. 508-535

**Abstract:**
The study examines peer effects in segregated schools using two theoretical frameworks. The research finds that "students from minority-concentrated schools attain less education in the long run than students from White-concentrated schools net of many covariates." The analysis reveals that both normative peer processes (where students become similar) and frog-pond effects (where students benefit from relative standing) operate simultaneously, but their opposing directions "tend to cancel each other out and make the net effect of peers in minority and white concentrated schools small."

All three closed. Two of them cut against me.

## 1. Greenleaf (2011) — numbers real, but I quoted the favorable half of a split result

The 0.23 / 0.24 / 0.28 figures are genuine, on genuine California Standards Tests, from a genuine cluster-RCT (45 schools, 54 science teachers, wait-list control, 10 days of Reading Apprenticeship PD). Retrieved from the IES full-text report, [ED625915](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED625915.pdf).

But the study reports **two analytic samples**, and I was handed only one:

| Outcome | Cross-sectional (n≈5,436) | Longitudinal (n≈1,236) |
|---|---|---|
| ELA CST | **0.23**, p=.04 | 0.03, p=.74 |
| Reading comprehension CST | **0.24**, p=.02 | 0.04, p=.60 |
| Biology CST | **0.28**, p=.01 | 0.17, p=.27 |

The longitudinal analysis of the same trial is null across the board. WWC reviewed this exact study, **used the longitudinal sample**, and recomputed biology at 0.16 (ns), literacy 0.04, reading comprehension 0.04 — which is where the "uncertain effects" rating comes from. The authors also flag selective attrition: teachers serving low-performing students were likelier to drop out **of the control group**, which biases in the direction of the positive finding.

There's also a citation trap worth knowing: WWC's "Greenleaf et al. (2011)" is a *different* study (RA in history and science) which did **not** meet WWC standards. Easy to conflate.

I called this "the best standardized evidence in secondary science." I should have said: a cluster-RCT with a positive cross-sectional result, a null longitudinal result on the same students, and a regulator that certified the null.

## 2. Project READI — one row of the table I gave you doesn't exist

Full text retrieved ([EJ1222462](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1222462.pdf)). Four of five rows confirmed verbatim: GISA 0.32 (p=.038), EBA multiple-choice 0.26 (p=.010), essay nodes 0.11 and connections 0.08 (both ns), and the epistemology/self-efficacy nulls.

**The "composite comprehension, 0.18" row is spurious.** No such measure exists in the paper. The figures appear to be misread *covariate* rows — an epistemology pretest covariate at −0.18 and an unrelated interaction at p=.029. I passed that to you as an outcome. It wasn't one.

And my independence claim for GISA was wrong in two ways. First, ETS's scenario-based assessment program was funded under the **same IES Reading for Understanding initiative** as READI — sibling grants, not a neutral off-the-shelf test. Second, and worse, the paper says outright that **the GISA topic (mitochondrial DNA) was developed specifically for this study's intervention**. The authors position it as a far-transfer measure, not an independent standardized outcome. I told you "the externally-developed assessment produced the largest effect" as though that answered the aligned-measures critique. It doesn't.

Scale: 24 schools, 48 teachers, 964 students, one semester, grade 9 biology. With 24 clusters and 17 school-level df, p = .038 is marginal. The authors gloss 0.26–0.32 as students ending "1.5 years ahead" — that's an aggressive reading of two small effects.

Also worth noting: the teacher-level effects in that study are enormous (d = 1.34–2.24), and they're all research-team-authored surveys and observations. Same pattern as iRAISE — teacher practice moves, student outcomes barely do.

## 3. Nesbit & Adesope — fully confirmed, and it got *more* useful

The agent that said the moderator table was unretrievable was simply wrong. The author's copy at SFU parses fine through a text proxy. Every claimed value confirmed:

- Overall g = .604 [.550, .658]
- Constructing maps vs. lecture/discussion: **.742**, k=10
- Constructing maps vs. **writing text or outlines: .194**, k=7, CI **[.042, .345]**
- Studying maps vs. reading text: .388, k=29
- Constructing (.819) vs. studying provided maps (.373)

Two additions that matter for you. First, the k=7 cell has a confidence interval whose lower bound is .04 — so the honest statement is "concept mapping's advantage over outlining is small and might be near zero," not "it's 0.19." Second, and directly relevant: there's a **grades 9–12 subset for constructing maps, g = .165, CI [.024, .306], k=7** — versus .905 for grades 4–8 and .773 for postsecondary. Your grade band is the weakest cell in the analysis.

Also: the corpus is roughly 69% postsecondary, the moderator analyses exclude non-North-American studies, and **there is no reading-comprehension outcome category at all**. It's retention and transfer. I shouldn't have presented it as comprehension evidence.

## Where this leaves the recommendations

Both of the studies I offered as "real standardized evidence in your subject and grade band" are thinner than I said. Greenleaf's standardized effects vanish in the longitudinal sample; READI's most distal measure was built for the intervention. Neither is fraudulent, neither is nothing — but the honest summary is that **there is no clean, replicated, standardized-outcome evidence for a literacy intervention in secondary science.** That makes Baye et al.'s +0.09 baseline for secondary reading programs look less like a caveat and more like the main result.

What survives intact and I'd still act on:

1. **The knowledge threshold** (O'Reilly, Wang & Sabatini — 3,534 high schoolers, your subject) — check whether students clear the floor before assigning the text. Unaffected by any of this.
2. **Content questions over strategy instruction** (McKeown, Beck & Blake) — two independent retrievals, still the best-sourced item.
3. **Extended written response, 0.77** (Graham & Hebert, 81% grade 6+) — still the strongest practice-level finding for your grade band.
4. **Text structure, 0.57 proximal / 0.13 far** — unchanged.
5. **Concept mapping** — now better sourced and pointing *down*. If students would otherwise write a summary or outline, mapping adds little (.194, CI touching zero), and at grades 9–12 specifically it's .165. Use it if it fits your workflow; don't displace writing for it.

One correction to my previous message: I said the Nesbit dispute was a case where I'd guessed without justification. The guess was right, but the reason it was right is that one agent used a text-extraction proxy on a scanned PDF and the other didn't — a tooling difference, not a judgment I made.
